paragraphs.text: On Admonition
The first homily of Mar Jacob the Teacher: on admonition.

I will stir my voice to your praise, Son of God,
and let all my senses praise you with their songs.
Since my tongue was fashioned from the beginning for your praise,
whoever ceases from your praise deserves the lash.
Let me not, my Lord, cease from meditating on your songs,
lest I be scourged by justice with a just judgment.
The mouth of man is fashioned for the praise of the Godhead,
and whoever neglects praise is wicked and perverse.
The Creator, when he created it, placed in the mouth
voice and speech, so that it might be stirred to give praise.
So everyone who perceives that there is a Creator is bound
to give praise, as a debt owed, to the Lord who created him.

Vain songs and words that are unseemly—
the mouth of man has no right to make use of them.
The Creator fashioned it thus when he was creating:
a mouth for his praise, not for the use of vain things.
"Cry out with your throat and lift up your voice like a trumpet,"
says the Lord to whoever neglects his praise.
I am your creature, my Lord; grant me to be watchful over your works,
and as you have created me, grant me to be stirred to praise.
Grant the heart, with thoughts of holiness,
to serve you, for you are awesome over all creatures.
Sanctify my tongue from all worldly affairs,
and by meditation on you may it be stirred to praise.
Behold, my mouth is open to you; fill it, my Lord, with praise, as you have promised,
and let no vain word pass through it to be used.
Let my voices be stirred over your gift, so full of wonder,
Son of God, as I give thanks for your praise.
Ended.
On the Descent of the Most High onto Mount Sinai
Again, Homily 2, on the descent of the Most High onto Mount Sinai (and its symbolism of the Church), composed by Mar Jacob.

Mighty One of the worlds, who bent his strength down upon Mount Sinai,
grant me to sing with my voice the power of your might.
Holder of the ends of the earth, who humbled himself so that Sinai could hold him,
let my mind hold you, though not in a way that contains you, but as far as it can.
O you who came down without coming down to the high mountain,
come down in truth to the height of the mind that waits for you.
Through you let my mind become fiery like Mount Sinai,
and let the flame of the voices of your glory rise up from it.
Grant me to tell how the mountain bore you in a borrowed manner,
and how the arm of your power rested on it and it trembled throughout.
To the summit of Sinai, the mountain of stone, you came down in a borrowed way;
come to the spiritual mind, for see, it looks to you.
The earth cannot perceive you, so as to hold you as the mind does,
nor can the mountains receive you as thoughts do.

The mind is greater in its breadth than Mount Sinai;
rest upon it, and let it grow rich in the voice of thanksgiving.
Instead of her whom you betrothed at the place of Sinai, who did not [?] it,
come, betroth the soul that hangs on the beauty of your songs.
The congregation of the people whom you loved played the harlot with the calf;
my Lord, let not silence enter my mind and play the harlot in it.
Let your story be a husband to my speech, and its support as well,
and let it be joined to it, so that it too may yield fruits of praise.
Be zealous like Moses, and scatter silence as he did the calf,
so that the soul may cling to your theme in its songs.
Your Word is greater than all the mouths of Watchers and of men,
and spiritual minds cannot reach you in their thoughts.
Your story is beyond those who speak and those who hear,
and your being is hidden from those above and those below.
Your dwelling is hidden from bodily beings and from spiritual ones,
and your place is far from earthly beings and from heavenly ones.
The power that holds the ends of the world cannot be contained,
nor can the sign that is swifter even than lightning be outrun.
It cannot be spoken by tongues of flame,

For he is not in a place, nor in a spot, nor in a corner;
he cannot dwell and be seen except in a type.
This power for which places are too small —
did it then come down to Mount Sinai and dwell there?
Float, my mind, on the waves of the discourse of his wonder,
and with these voices sing his story, which cannot be comprehended.
Shall I take up my narrative about this: that he came down upon Mount Sinai?
Or about this: that he never came down, except in likeness?
Let us search out here, in the narrative, how he cannot be contained,
and draw near to speak of his descent with great wonder.
Look, discerning one, at the beginning of a discourse of questions,
and make your hearing ready to receive praises.
Let it be made plain by this Mighty One who holds the ends
what cause called him to come down upon Mount Sinai.
His mercies drew him toward humankind, to show it favor,
and in his love he came to betroth and take the daughter of the earth.
He desired that congregation, the daughter of the righteous, because of her lineage,
since she was related to that family of the house of Abraham.
He saw the girl while the Egyptians were abusing her,

and that Holy One did not turn in disgust from the harlot.
He sent a matchmaker after her to turn her toward him,
so that by union with him she might be sanctified, for she was a daughter of the righteous.
He made Moses a matchmaker and sent him to her,
to go down and settle the terms with her as a mediator.
He gave him strength and might as he went down,
so that he might persuade her with wonders to come up with him.
The Levite went down, tended her wounds, led her and brought her up,
and placed in her hand the signet ring he had taken from the bush.
He betrothed her to the Holy Name and brought her up out of Egypt,
for he was keeping her for the [?] of the house of God.
He set on her head the crown of salvation and went out with her;
he called on creation to escort her with their lyres.
And because Pharaoh the reckless wished to keep her from him,
the Holy One was zealous, swept him into the sea, and led her up.
He sent after her and set her free from Egypt when she was redeemed;
the waves escorted her, and she crossed the sea in great wonder.
Horeb received her and brought forth gifts beyond the usual;
the wilderness bowed down to her as she entered it with its offerings.
All creation was sensing to whom she had been betrothed,
and all natures came and gathered round her to escort her.

The luminaries and all the elements carried her and went before her,
pressing to come with her to the Holy One.
The great pillar of light ran to shine before her,
and like a torch for the bride it surrounded her and went with her.
Every day gifts from the creatures surrounded her,
as she was adorned with the choicest provisions.
The height washed her with the manna it sent her,
and the depth fattened her with the quails it brought her.
Blessed waters flowed to her from the rock,
and all natures nourished her, to adorn her.
All creatures gathered to go with her,
so that the world might see the great wedding being held for her.
She was escorted in her caravans as far as Sinai,
and came to the place where her Lord had appointed to meet her.
Moses led her to face the mountain, left her and went up,
to go and see when the bridegroom would come to meet her.
He heard the Hidden One commanding him: "Go down and say to her,
to this bride whom you redeemed and brought out of Egypt:
'Behold, I have carried you as on eagles' wings through the air,
and led you through places without harm.'

'Let the agreement between me and you be made in love and stand firm,
and then I will come and become your bridegroom in holiness.
Before the whole feast I make my will known to you:
if you consent to me, come to the wedding I desire for you.
In pure union I want you to be with me,
not throwing yourself to another to play the harlot.
Forever I settle you upon my hope; and further,
you must not be drawn after another to come in to you.
In holiness I take you, if you are mine;
but if you are disgraced with strangers, I will put you away.
Let me not see in you the hateful sign of adulteries,
nor the ways that are found in stealing away.
Show me no shameful signs of wanton women,
and do not turn about in the arts of the dissolute.
Show to no one the bowing of your face except to me,
and from now on belong to no other covenant.
Be holy, modest, chaste and without blemish,
radiant and adorned, clear and pure in every way.
Be constant, guarded and pure, calm and quiet,
serene and watchful, gentle and comely and without stain.'

'And if you come to me thus with unveiled face,
you will be mistress, answerable to no one, over all that I have.
I give you a great crown, the crown fit for kings;
I place in you holiness, the treasure of priests.
Prophets who reveal hidden things shall be yours,
and priests who atone for sins shall dwell with you.
Behold, Levites like attendants shall go with you,
and ministers like servants shall accompany you.
Heaven shall drop its dew on your land faithfully,
and earth shall multiply good things before you richly.
The air shall pour every delight upon your camp;
the sun shall ripen sweet fruits for your food.
You shall inherit the land of all the kings who strive with you,
and you shall not be defeated by the mighty who come out to meet you.
You shall set your heel upon the neck of the rulers of the earth,
to trample all crowns beneath your dominion.
I hand over to you a deed in my own hand concerning these things,
and if you are to me according to my will, all of them are yours.'
This covenant the bridegroom sent by the hands of Moses,
that he might go down and see whether the bride consented to the bridegroom.
The mediator, the son of the Hebrews, came down from the top of the mountain,

and called the heads of the house of Jacob and its rulers.
He recited before them the bridegroom's words just as they were,
to see whether they consented to the terms he had made, or not.
They answered him lovingly, rejoicing in him:
"We consent to your mediation, Moses our scribe.
How fair is the bridegroom who seeks our daughter in holiness!
Who would grant us that that family should be joined to our family?
We are too small for such a bridegroom to be named for us;
who are we, that he should marry among us? It is a great grace.
Here before you is the girl whom the house of the Egyptians raised;
learn from her about the terms your Lord has made."
Moses called her to question her before the elders,
and rejoicing she gave her word to go with him.
The Levite heard that she had given herself of her own will,
and rejoicing he turned back to his Lord to tell him:
"My Lord, the girl has consented to our mystery as you wished,
and she does not refuse to live in holiness.
See, she has made a good agreement with me, as you taught me,
and if she is true, as she says, she will not be stolen away."
He answered Moses again and told him to return to her:

"Go down and adorn her, both openly and secretly.
Outwardly let her put on white garments, to shine in them;
inwardly, thoughts of holiness, to be beautiful in them.
Let her be sanctified for me today and tomorrow, in mystery,
and on the third day I will come to her in might."
Moses went down and began to adorn the bride;
he toiled and rejoiced in preparing her for the entering in.
He taught the [?] not to be disgraced,
and charged her: "Let not the hidden bridegroom find you loathsome.
Pour out holiness for him on the road by which he will be escorted,
so that in purity you may see his face when you receive him.
Set the crown of holiness on your head when he sees you,
so that in radiance you may enter with him into the bridal chamber of light."
A great mystery has met me here and held me back toward it,
and because I neglected it, see, it quarrels with me and reproaches me:
"Why, unlearned one, have you not adorned me as you passed by?
Do not be ashamed of me, for I am the beauty of your songs."
The story of the Son has dawned in the midst of the discourse on his Father,
demanding of me: "Unless you sing of me, you shall not pass.
Do not divide us in your findings, foolish one who has gone astray;
our story is one; let it not be divided between your lips."

The truth has compelled me, and I cannot escape it;
I will cast my voices upon the Son of the Living One, and then I pass on.
Let not the likeness of Moses slip away from that of the Messiah;
let us see here in what he resembled the Son of God.
In that descent of his from the mountaintop to the Hebrews,
the way of Jesus is seen in him by one who considers.
In his mediation, in which he went down and up to the daughter of Jacob,
what Christ would do for humankind was being sketched.
Listen, wise ones, how the servant resembled his Lord,
and how in a mystery the prophet called him "like me."
Through him the daughter of Abraham was redeemed from Egypt,
and through him she was betrothed, to become that Holy One's bride.
By his hand she drew near to become the bride of the King her Lord;
he sanctified her, so that she might be seen in radiance by the Exalted.
The mediator between God's house and his camp
resembled his Lord, through whom the Father was reconciled to the world.
In this type Christ came down to humankind:
he redeemed her, sanctified her, cleansed her, washed her and betrothed her.
In place of the white garments in which Moses clothed the daughter of Jacob,
Jesus made the soul white in holiness from within the waters.

For three days Moses sanctified that daughter of the people,
but by the hands of our Lord holiness stands forever.
The shadow of the Son of God dwelt there,
and as it passed it sketched the likeness of true things.
Through these mysteries, which were fulfilled by the hands of Moses,
the prophet boldly called the Son of God "like me."
But if I open the door to the mysteries of my whole narrative,
they will not let me come near the end.
For hosts of hidden things press upon me;
I am not able to bring their revelations to completion.
I have undertaken to speak of the descent of the Exalted One to Sinai;
I will run my word swiftly toward the goal of the story.
Let my words not be confused among the mysteries of all my words;
this much is plain: they cannot be contained, nor have they ever been.
I will hasten along the road of the discourse toward the end,
leaving many things in the middle of the story.
So Moses went down to adorn the bride he had brought,
that the bridegroom to whom she was betrothed might see her in beauty.
He gave her his charge; she dressed herself and rejoiced, and adorned herself beautifully;
he increased her radiance, set her wisdom in order, and perfected her beauty.
For three days Moses labored with her, teaching her

and charging her in what manner she should see her Lord.
He carved out wise words for her and put them in her mouth,
so that if the glorious bridegroom called her, she would know how to answer him.
Moses was wise as her teacher and her nurturer,
so that through her he might have boldness before the Holy One.
When she had learned in what manner she would see the bridegroom,
and in what attire she should dress before him when he arrived,
and when she had prepared herself for three days in holiness,
then the bridegroom went out from his place to come down to her.
The Strong One rose up and put on the strength of might,
to come in power and in haste.
He moved without moving, to come down to earth without coming down,
and cast urgency upon height and depth, for he was coming.
A command stirred the hosts of heaven,
and the King made ready to be seen, without changing.
The legions of fire before him hurried, for he was coming;
they were set in motion to go mightily before his coming.
The ranks drew up in haste, one after another,
and the bands of the sons of light were joined together.
The hosts of the height were appointed to come down to the earth,
and the burning ones and the flying ones flew through the air before the Mighty One.

A commotion broke out in the assemblies of the height, and they hastened to come,
for they heard the Fiery One roaring behind them.
Thousands of ranks of flame gathered
to escort the living fire coming down to earth.
A command went down sharply to the meadows of light,
and swiftly gathered the angels within them.
The spiritual beings were stirred, for he was coming to descend to the mountain,
and the voices of the hosts that went out with him hurried them along.
A new report astonished the heavenly beings:
that the Hidden One had set his course to come down to earth.
They gathered to see what place it was from which he went out,
where he had been hidden, how he was coming, and on what he rode.
And as the swift legions were thrown into confusion, the Power looked out,
and the burning fire, the hidden Dwelling, a wondrous vision.
The Watchers did not see him who has no body in an image,
for not in reality did he look out from the height into the depth.
Under a borrowed name he came down to the mountain in might,
so that the daughter of Abraham might long for his majesty.
So he went out, though he did not come except in a type;
he stirred creation with the shout of joy of his hosts.
He sent forth a sound at which the roots of the mountains trembled,

so that the world might feel the wedding feast to which he was descending.
The horn of the chief of the angels sounded mightily;
the sound was raised, and creatures quaked in their natures.
The trumpet cried out from the top of that height of heaven
and shook the rocks with the might of its lofty sound.
He set out to come in awe, amid great wonder;
he went out of his place and passed the firmament, about to descend.
He gathered up lightning and went out into the air swiftly,
to tread upon and cross over the rays of poured-out light.
He kindled fire in steeds of fire and harnessed them,
so that like torches they might go before him brightly.
He blazed through the air in his radiance
and dazzled eyes, so that they could not look on him as he is.
Voices cried out in the height of that vault of heaven:
"How fitting is the acclamation for the bridegroom, that it come with him!"
Outstretched lightnings were bent over the creatures,
threads of fire which the living [?] had spun.
The Strong One came down, dwelt upon the mountain and shook it all;
it smoked and melted from the blaze that rested upon it.
The cloud surrounded it and cooled it with coolness,
with the gentle dew which the command sprinkled on its burning.

The flame of its burning rose up like a furnace,
as the rocks burned with a fire that was not felt.
Wondrous to tell: as the crags melted there,
the rocks too were burning like brushwood.
The flame clung even to the clefts;
smoke rose even from the stones, as from wood.
The fire was loosening the mountain, and it was about to fall,
but the Power that carries creatures held it up by a sure sign.
That Mighty One who trod upon it and shook it all,
he himself held up the mountain by his power, so that it would not give way.
The mountain of stones could not endure
the Power that carries the ends of the world in its might.
He carried the mountain that carried him as he rested upon it,
for he is the Power that suffices for all in his hiddenness.
That the Lord came down to Mount Sinai — this has been heard;
how he came down is a wonder to tell, among marvels.
Let our story blend together that he came down and did not come down;
let me fold the word that I cannot comprehend together with what has been comprehended.
To the simple let us say that he came down in power;
but to the subtle it is plain that he did not come down at all.
He whose hiddenness the heavens cannot contain —

was the small spot of Mount Sinai enough for him?
He for whom the earth is a footstool beneath his feet —
how could the corner of the footstool suffice for him to dwell upon?
He came down in a borrowed way, uncontained, on the top of the mountain,
without changing from where he is to where he came down.
He bowed, bowing the arm of his power down upon Mount Sinai,
though he did not come down from there to here in that descent of his.
While he dwelt on high, he dwelt on the mountain and was not contained;
and though he did not move, in a type a descent was felt.
He sketched a likeness full of motion from within the bush,
while he remains where he is.
Words fail; the story is fearsome and the discourse mighty,
and the tongue too flees from it in its weakness.
If a mouth could recount it as is fitting,
even the hearing would need to be hidden away.
If I were able to speak of his fearsomeness,
I would cast amazement upon the hearers out of terror.
If my mind did not rebuke me, so that I say no more,
I would not comprehend that descent in common words.
How shall I speak, how much shall I say, and when shall I fall silent?

With what shall I bound the boundless in the narrative?
If Mount Sinai, though it was a crag, melted before him,
will not a tongue of flesh shrink back from telling of him?
That Holy One made a wedding for a feast,
and came to her so that by union with him she might be sanctified.
He pitched his canopy of thick cloud on the summit of Sinai,
a great bridal chamber of flame in a high place.
And so that at the feast the acclamation might be unceasing and great gladness found,
he made voices heard at which the bride would rejoice on the day of her joy.
The cloud became a bridal chamber on the mountain for the Bridegroom King,
and he dwelt there, exalted amid fearsome things.
Voices came out of the dark clouds that bowed down to the earth,
wondrous visions on whose rays the eye floats.
Lightnings blazing, flashing swiftly;
a tumult of fire glittering, burning;
legions of Watchers whirling about in spirit;
thousands of hosts singing praise mightily.
The sound of the horn was strong and fair, and shook the mountain,
and it dismayed and terrified the hearing with wonder.
Let us too hear it with wonder and with comfort,
and attend to the wonders with discernment.

What was the horn that cried out there on Mount Sinai,
and how could it be, if it was truly a horn?
Look, wise one, through questions, at how mighty these things are,
and in that order of hidden things, how strong.
He made voices heard that were in nothing, as though in something,
and called it the sound of a horn, though it was not a horn.
He commanded the air, and all of it cried out facing Sinai,
a sound not confined in horns or in pipes.
As if through a horn, the command blew within the dark clouds,
and there came forth thunder that bowed the earth by its might.
In this order too the custom of the wedding was kept,
for at the sound of the horn the bridegroom enters his bridal chamber.
This sign he had given to Moses before he came down
to that people, while he alone knew of it:
that when the horn fell silent on the mountain, the people should go up.
In an ordered sequence it would rise and fall silent.
When it rose, so that the hearing would not be overcome by it,
it was softened, so as not to weary those who heard it.
When the hidden power cried out through it, it lowered it again,
so that it might be borne steadily upon the hearing.
By this vision, which was fearful to the earthly ones,

the people thought that the whole Lord was dwelling on the mountain.
These sounds, which a hidden mystery had fashioned,
the childish suppose a hollow horn gave birth to.
Because it was heard that the Lord came down, the simple trembled,
as though the height on high were emptied of Him because He was on the mountain.
Because it was heard that the sound of the horn was very strong,
they suppose that He too spoke in a compound, bodily way.
Through the questions that were raised for their help,
those who went astray thought the Uncompounded One compounded.
The revelation, too, is set out to suit their childishness,
(and with the mind one can weigh even visions.
In its measure: for the intellect gazes and casts its look upon the mind,
(so that each one may see Him according to his thought, as far as he is able.
A cause called Him to bend His strength down upon Mount Sinai,
that the congregation might be adorned with a vision of glory.
Had He not come down, she would have said after her adultery,
"Since I never saw what He is like, how should I wait for Him?"
And since the reason for the questions was so well composed,
and the word went out, "Behold, the Lord will come down upon the mountain,"
He displayed a wonder, as though He dwelt wholly on the mountain;

and Sinai trembled because a mighty Power had trodden on its summit.
Smoke went up like a furnace over the whole mountain,
to confirm the fire that dwelt there.
The rocky heaps melted in the fire that clung to them,
so that it might be believed that the One wrapped in burning coal was there, as it were.
Lightnings rushing, thunders massing, fearful sounds—
so that they would think the whole Shekhinah was there.
A cloud—or rather a thick one—stretched out and encircled the mountain,
as though He were within it, wholly confined.
He spread out darkness like veils on every side,
as though the glory outside them belonged, so to speak, to their chamber.
He kindled rays in the air, light like torches,
as though He had in truth kindled glories before Him.
And since He thus gave no occasion for questions,
and truly gave no excuse to the daughter of Abraham;
and when He had made her dwell near—He came to her and dwelt beside her—
after a little while she cast a calf to play the harlot with it.
It is not her adultery we must speak about now;
that is kept for another discourse, which will lay bare her falsehood.

I set out my words on the Lord's descent to Sinai;
let me not stray from a story that cannot be grasped.
The Mighty One came down and dwelt on the mountain as He came down,
and Moses came down to call the bride to come to Him.
She went out, stood, shook, was astounded, waited, fainted;
turned back, knelt, felt her guilt, trembled, arrived, shrank back;
quaked, fell, fell silent, was quenched, feared, perished;
was swallowed up, died, and her spirit went from her, taken away.
The sounds struck her, the lightnings terrified her, the thunders roared at her;
the visions frightened her, and she could not bear them.
The Bridegroom began to speak to her in holiness,
and she could not bear to hear Him gently.
She cried out to Moses: "You, humble one, speak to me;
the voice of the Lord is casting me into the place of death!"
To that adulteress the voice was not pleasant,
because she had turned from purity in her wickedness.
She asked Moses to speak the Bridegroom's word to her,
since it was easy for her to quarrel with him boldly.
Because these sounds from Mount Sinai gave her no rest,
she cried out, for if she disputed, the fire would be against her.
She said to that humble one, "You speak with me,"

for she knew that he could be slapped and would not rebuke her;
that she could strike him when he spoke to her,
and hurl back at him the [?] cries of dissent.
The voice that thundered from within Sinai was no slight thing,
that she could despise it or murmur against its might.
She called on Moses so that he might be lashed by her impudence,
for she was confident that if he resisted, his death would be easy.
The roar of the Lion, which shook Sinai, terrified her,
and she wanted the lamb Moses to turn to her tenderly.
The Eagle's cry shook her, the hateful kite,
and she asked for the chick set between her talons.
She begged off from that voice that shakes mountains,
and longed for the halting speech of Moses.
The horn crying out from the top of the air shook her,
and she longed to hear the stammerer's word, for it was sweet to her.
Yet it was not that Moses was dear to her, that he should speak with her;
she was withdrawing from God [?].
She heard the Bridegroom warning her against strange gods,
and the pure word was not sweet to the [?] woman.
She devised a pretext to keep the voice of the Holy One from her;
craftily she called on Moses: "You speak with me."

For had she not been set on lewdness there,
she would not have withdrawn from the Bridegroom who came to her.
Had her eye not been cast upon strange gods,
she would not have chosen Moses' speech over the Hidden One's.
Had she not held the Bridegroom in contempt to His face,
she would not have turned from His converse once she had received Him.
Had her heart not loved her corrupter,
she would have accepted that the Betrothed of truth should speak with her.
If she was pure, why was she ashamed before the Holy One?
It was revealed of her that she was a scorner, because she had turned away.
She saw that the hour had come when the Bridegroom seeks the truth,
and she betrayed her secret to her guardian: that she was corrupt.
She called on Moses to speak to her as she wished,
for she thought that her adultery was hidden.
"You speak with me, O humble one," she kept saying to him,
"but let God restrain His voices, which shake me."
Moses soothes and encourages her like a young girl:
"He wishes to test you; do not be terrified of the Mighty One.
He will make a covenant and go up to His high place;
enter into His covenant, for see, the thunder of His voices is silent.
Come and see Him: I am not ashamed of the One to whom I betrothed you;

Then the daughter of Abraham despised this Bridegroom,
for she took no pleasure in His converse; she was the calf's companion.
Two curtains—of speckled air outside the mountain,
and canopies of fire—and Sinai was overlaid with darkness.
The Bridegroom brought out wondrous garments of flame
from that divine cloud that came down with Him.
The tent was hot with woven hangings of burning coal,
and spread within it was a couch of fire that cannot be grasped.
Around her were the hangings of the doors that cannot be touched,
which had been prepared on that loom of the house of God.
(And stretched outside was a mantle of cloud,
its color dusky, its texture dense, its strength lessened.
The Spirit folded it back a little, as if to give an opening,
so that the congregation might see the beauties within it:
inside, darkness and fire burning on the mountain-top,
and outside it, air as dense as befitted its glory.
The glory was hidden within that wall of clouds,
which showed and did not show how He is.
The cloud within it hid the splendor of His face,
while it sifted a little brightness onto the onlookers.

From its wings blessed light was flowing,
a little less than the glory they saw with Him.
When the splendor broke forth and was about to appear to His bride from the cloud,
Mount Sinai groaned and was about to split, but a sign upheld it.
When a little glory peeped out of the darkness,
He held it back with the cloud, so that it would not flow over the onlookers.
They saw Him and did not see Him, in truth,
for the glory within kindled again in their minds.
Even that sight was hidden from their eyes;
it spurred them to learn that what was within was something great.
Something of the brightness moved within the darkness;
they feared that if it flowed out, it would burn up the world.
They saw it through the covering of the cloud,
and because it was hidden, it astonished all around Him.
For whatever is kept far off and hidden is very precious;
therefore the cloud became a covering for the mountain.
Smoke went up to confirm that the fire was there;
the darkness thickened so that the flame might be tempered.
Voices went out as though a horn were crying beside Him;
the mountain shook like a man pressed down by the weight upon him.

It became a furnace, so that the flame might be confirmed,
and Sinai thundered as though His Shekhinah dwelt in it.
There the swift voices of the heavenly ones were stirred,
for the Lord of the heights, it is said, was on the mountain with His camp.
Creation was in tumult with voices and fearful visions,
for the Lord of creation was upon Sinai and in the darkness.
Thunders were let loose to proclaim on the mountain-top,
and with their cry they signified as much as this: that the King was here.
Trumpets blew mightily on the height of Sinai,
so that the earth might gather to meet the voice of the Lord there.
The song of the Watchers rang out within the clouds,
so that those outside might think that He was within.
When the brightness of the fire moved within the darkness,
the gloom outside held it in so that it would not flow out.
When the flame poured out above the mountain,
the cloud dammed it up so that it would not burst upon those below.
When waves of coals rose on the summit of Sinai,
the quaking air received them gently.
The cloud was outside, and within it the flame,
so that the heat might be tempered by coolness.
The fearful splendor flashed on the mountain-top,

and was mightily covered so that it would not be seen.
The light was bound in the thick wing of clouds,
gathered and tied up so that it would not flood the whole earth.
From within the bush the hosts of Watchers were heard,
and like the sound of the sea they surged in their praises.
They hid in the thicket that surrounded them on every side,
and struck up sounds from the gloom outside the mountain.
Hidden and praising, near and yet far,
hidden from the eyes, revealed to the ears, in two ways.
The mountain bore Him, though it could not endure that Mighty One,
and had there been a way to flee, it would not have stayed.
Sinai trembled, and its rocks burned with live coal,
and by its smoke its burning was confirmed.
The angels marveled that the Uncontainable dwelt on the mountain,
and though His height was very great, Sinai did not let its burden fall.
The hosts who came down with Him were overjoyed
that they were counted worthy to accompany Him on His way to the creatures of dust.
The companies that remained in the heights were proud as well,
for like members of the household they stayed there in His high place.
These thought that He was with them in the height above,
and those reflected that He was with them on Mount Sinai.

These stood by the chariot to gaze on Him,
and those stood on the mountain-top to behold Him.
He was hidden from these and from those, on both sides,
and concealed in His place from those above and those below.
Those below saw the fire burning on the mountain-top,
and those above saw the brightness encircling the chariot.
In His hiddenness His Shekhinah dwells and is not seen,
nor is it shown in its depth, but only by ordered measure.
It is not possible for Him to be confined and to dwell in places,
for in Him all creatures are contained—so where would He go down?
He was on the mountain, and in the height, and everywhere,
and on the chariot, and in the bush, and in every direction.
He showed a likeness of burning on the mountain-top,
so that with wonder He might make a wedding among the earthly.
He sought a wondrous sight for the daughter of Abraham,
so that with wonder the sight might snatch the bride to Him.
Mount Sinai was upheld by Him while it bore Him,
just as the Cherubim hang on His arm and carry Him in procession.
On Him hang all creatures and their ends,
and He devised a means of help, that He might dwell on the mountain.
He showed a likeness of burning on the side of the mountain,

so that with wonders He might bind her to Himself in holiness.
But when the lover of adultery drew near to come to Him,
she drew back so as not even to hear His teaching.
Moses calmed her, that she might stay quiet for a full season,
until the covenant was confirmed with her and the Bridegroom went up.
And while the Shekhinah overspread the mountain in great wonder,
the Lord called the champion Moses to come in to Him.
A voice went out like a person after Moses,
that he should enter (to receive the covenant with Him) into the darkness.
He entered the cloud as though going up to the Holy One,
and the voice ran ahead and traced for him the path of flame.
It lifted before him the curtains of that door of clouds,
that he might enter and see the Bridegroom in His glory as He is.
A command went out and cut him a road into the darkness,
so that the lofty brightness from within Sinai would not terrify him.
Moses went into the tent of the Bridegroom King,
to learn His mysteries and bring the bride to the Holy One.
He went in and learned, and came out to bring her, as he was commanded,
that she might come near and hear the teaching of the house of God.
He did not lead her into the chamber to enter, for she was not pure;
she stood outside to hear and learn the Bridegroom's will.

Then the voice thundered to her from the darkness,
that there should be a covenant of truth both for Him and for her.
He undertook to set out the teaching for her in a loud voice,
and to speak the truth to her openly and with might.
He multiplied her warnings with commandments that were plain,
for He laid no heavy yoke upon her neck.
That she should not make herself carved images, He taught her,
and that she should not turn away from Him, He warned her.
That He was jealous and an avenger, He made known to her,
and that He repays after generations, He made clear to her.
Ten milestones He set on the road of righteousness,
that one after another they might lead her to the house of the kingdom.
At her head He set one lamp, and ten before her,
that the fair light of the law might lead the way before her.
While she was being commanded how to keep it and with what she should be adorned,
she scorned and abandoned the awesome things that were spoken.
The Lord speaks, and Sinai trembles, and the place is fearful;
great is the awe, and mighty the Power on the mountain-top.
The Lord spoke wondrous words before the people;
fearful thunders rumbled before the darkness.

With these voices, full of tremors of flame,
He taught her to hear them with dread.
With an eloquent mouth that sets coals upon the lips,
He sprinkled upon her the voice of the commandments, that she might learn them.
With that tongue which flashed with burning coal,
He held out to her the speech of truth, that she might be confirmed in it.
The flute of flame played on the mountain's summit,
and the voice that shakes from the burning coal alarmed them.
With the lyre that the voice of fire plucked, He laid down the law,
and built a fence so that she would not stray from the commandment.
And she who had heard the speech that called and urged her
begged off from even hearing the teaching.
Here the discourse of the Church lays hold of me in simplicity,
and gives me a hand to approach it, toward the conclusion.
Let today's fearful, boundless homily be brought to an end,
so that its order may turn me toward the beginning of another discourse.
The mind has been schooled in the discourse of the mountain, and it is boundless;
it wants to rest, and yet it keeps turning back to its story.
See, the tongue has set up a finger on the path of the discourse,

to deliver the hidden things in their full season.
The word that flew upon Mount Sinai seeks to make me wise;
its wing has grown weary, and the height of the homily is boundless.
The discourse is strong, and the intellect weak—how can it be?
It seeks rest, to lean upon another beginning.
For it is not fitting that the daughter of Jacob be compared with her,
as though one should speak of her in a single breath and so seal her story.
The one despised that Mighty One in His majesty,
while this pure one clung to the Son in His lowliness.
Not with angels did He come down to her, as upon Sinai,
nor with heavenly horns did He shout to her;
not with laws, nor with darkness, nor with clouds,
not with burning coals, nor with lightnings of flame;
not with the house smoking because of Him where He dwelt:
in humility the Son of the Mighty One came down to earth.
In lowly things He showed Himself to humanity:
in hunger and thirst, in sleep and toil and need;
when He was tempted by Satan in a desolate wilderness,
when the unbelievers called Him the chief of demons;

In all these the Church saw Him as the Son of God.
Blessed is He who caught her away from the idols of paganism!
Here ends the homily on the descent of the Most High upon Mount Sinai.
On the consecration of the Church, and on Moses the prophet
Again, Homily 3, on the consecration of the Church and on Moses the prophet, composed by Mar Jacob the teacher.

You who are rich, give to the needy one who asks of you,
for however much he takes, nothing stops him coming back to ask again.
Throw your gift to the beggar, though he is not worthy;
the poor man knocks at your door: my Lord, do not send him away poor.
However much you give me, I ask again that you give me more,
for I have not been filled by your gift; it has only made me hungry.
Through the drink of your story, which flows richly to me,
great thirst has been added to me by its sweetness.

With these lips, through which my tongue pants from its story,
the thirst of my mind has not been quenched, so eager has it grown.
Moses is a spring, and however much I draw from him, he grows greater;
give me a land that will receive the water and yield fruit.
Let your story yield its harvest of praise from the hearers,
that to you be glory, to them help, and to me mercy.
I have gone into the field of Moses to reap a handful of your mysteries;
prepare for me laborers of praise for your sheaves.
I have begun to pile a heap of ten on your threshing floors;
grant me to reach the blessed measure that yields a hundredfold.
Your body was too great for speakers and for hearers;
therefore I have pressed on to recount the beauty of your shadow.
In your reality the mind cannot gaze upon you,
so through it your image is seen in me in all the stories.
Moses, your likeness, is now proclaimed between my lips,
and since you called him a prophet like yourself, I have portrayed him wholly in you.
The shadow of Simon sustained the sick;
sustain my mind, which is weak in Moses, by your shadow.
I do not tire of telling how much he resembles you in his story,
and since I see you in him, how can I keep silent about his subject?
It entices me to go out after it lightly,
making me think that it is bringing me near the end.

But when I come to the end of that great story, saying, 'Now I will rest,'
its end appears to me as a beginning once more.
So I will flee and enter the harbor of silence,
so as not to explore, halfway along, the long road of his mysteries.
I shall keep silent about much and speak a little of his wonders,
taking a taste of the marvels in brief measures.
By the hand of Moses the Church was sketched in mystery,
and the tabernacle was named after the type.
It was not truly his building, for he was not her Lord;
he sketched her outline mystically, then let her be and passed on.
For the Church, chosen from eternity, was already being built,
and Moses, who saw her likeness on Mount Sinai, bears witness.
It was not my thoughts that set down this exposition hastily;
the Truth has hinted to me that this verity should be spoken through you.
Moses had seen the original of the Church on the mountain,
and he brought down her outline into the camp, that she might be confirmed in it.
When he was commanded about building the tabernacle,
it was the very likeness of the Church that he truly saw.
Hear, you who are discerning, this plain truth without dispute,
for it is the Truth itself, speaking through me although I am unable.
For when his Lord commanded Moses, He showed him how to make
the Tent of Meeting, which served for a time in the mysteries of the Church.

Whoever supposes that all my colors end here,
I will show you, I say, through the likeness seen on the summit of the mountain.
He went up, and He showed him the Church already built, within the thick darkness;
it was the free Jerusalem above that he saw there.
For the apprentice of a craft who is learning something
looks at the finished work and so approaches it.
The master does not labor to teach with words;
he shows the finished work to the one who is learning.
For no one can make a thing without having seen it,
since a craft is not learned without a demonstration.
And when a master sets about teaching without wearying himself,
he sets a finished piece before his disciple.
In just this way the Creator dealt with Moses His servant:
He showed him the perfect Church there, that he might sketch her likeness,
so that her form would not slip from him as he came down;
he saw her in truth so that he would not forget her when she was being drawn.
Through what the ear hears, the likeness of a thing is not grasped;
it is sight that can gather and hold all forms.
Had Moses not seen with his eyes the Church that was built,
he would not have been able to make her whole adornment.
For in the likeness that appeared to him on Mount Sinai

he came down and completed that structure without confusion.
He saw the edifice of the bride in flaming splendor,
and the spiritual nature of her who dwells in delight in the great height.
He saw her dwelling, perfect in its being,
and her vast abode, which was mighty, the house of the angels.
He saw that the ends of the height hold her and are too small for her,
that her edges reach to the corners and stretch beyond.
He saw her bosom, in which the hosts of the height are gathered
and dwell, not crowded though they are many.
He saw the Shekinah dwelling within her in the Holy of Holies,
and the legions of fire jubilating in her with voices of praise.
He saw the troops standing in her spiritually,
and the long ranks extended in her like fire.
He saw the orders of heavenly beings who dwell there,
and the Watchers who in praise cry out the cries of holiness.
He saw her full, yet however many enter, her bosom holds them,
and she waits for those of the body, to receive them as she does the Watchers.
Moses saw her, her adornment perfected from glowing coals,
and her great house, which is all fire on every side.
He saw the assemblies of praisers rejoicing in her,
while exalted Sanctuses poured forth in her from their mouths.
He saw that creation had been made a footstool for her feet,

while she, like freedom, was exalted in the height above.
He saw her above the furthest ends of all the heights,
and above her only her Lord is, as head.
He saw the splendor of the ministers, how fervent they are,
and the voices of those who bless, how mighty they are.
He saw in her a place that is glorious and exalted and cannot be described,
and within it one that is hidden and fair and cannot be searched out.
He saw in her light poured out, wide open, which has no bound,
a fearful radiance of flame that cannot be spoken.
He saw the shape of gates opening one before another,
where splendor is spread and the Shekinah dwells within the light.
He saw the likeness of an inner house like the one he made,
and around it an outer court like the one he prepared.
He saw rows of pillars too surrounding her,
work of light, cut and carved from glowing coals.
He saw clouds bound about her,
and in their place he made curtains for his own.
He saw her overlaid with the color of fire in every form,
and he dyed the skins he was to make in those colors.
He saw the moon in the likeness of that bow in the clouds,
and he dyed the blue and the variegated to look like it.
He saw her among the cherubim, borne on a shoulder of fire,

and he made poles so that the Levites might carry his own.
As he saw her, so he sketched her exactly;
had he not seen her, would he have completed all her adornments?
Here the mystery was revealed like the sun in its reality,
and it moves me to speak of it plainly.
Moses resembled our Lord in the things he did,
for he is His likeness, His shadow, and the image of His body.
In that structure which that Levite saw on the mountain,
he portrayed the Church after the likeness of Christ.
And that the Church was already being built in mystery from that time,
David testifies, who also saw her there, just as Moses did.
'Remember your congregation, which you acquired of old': behold, openly
David proclaimed the building of the perfected bride.
Moses saw her perfection and brought down her outline,
and he carried the mystery of the Church and of our Lord into her building.
These things I have said are not obscure, O hearers,
though they call for discernment, and so they are understood.
Now I have undertaken to show you truly
how Moses sketched the Church in every form.
In the tabernacle he portrayed the seat of the bride,
and in the Holy of Holies the resplendent altar, Lady of the mysteries.
In the seventy leaders of the people he portrayed the apostles,

and in the twelve, those heads of the tribes whom he chose.
From the Spirit that was in Moses there was poured out on these,
as Christ breathed out on His apostles from the breath of His mouth.
They became teachers for the whole people at the hands of Moses,
and he was honored like a god in the camp.
The seventy received of his spirit and went out among the tribes,
as Christ was proclaimed by the band of the seventy.
This mystery clung to the son of Jochebed,
and for this reason he received authority to be a god.
This order, which came into the world through our Lord,
was already being carried by Moses in mystery [?].
For had Moses not portrayed Him wholly in all things,
He would not truly have called him a prophet like Himself.
Mysteries clung to him until he burned and his body shone,
and his form shared in the great splendor of the Godhead.
He was fervently tempered in the type of His furnaces,
until he shone like a being of fire in the glory he had put on.
He entered into the likeness and seethed in it as in fire,
and came out of it glowing like a burning coal.
His face acquired its burning from Christ,
and the people regarded him as God, in great fear.

The mystery wove for him a nest of fire in his face,
and it brooded in him, and he struck terror into those who saw him.
His whole image was portrayed on him by that Savior,
and because of His beauty he cast dread on all who beheld him.
He blazed with colors that were mingled in him from Christ,
and he came close to making the people think he was God.
He was rising toward the height of the mysteries and ascended far,
and was on the point of sharing the adorable name of the Godhead.
The whole earth was amazed at him for the wonders he did,
and was close to believing that he was its Lord.
The name of mightiness clung to him among the nations,
and they supposed that he was ruler over all creatures.
The camp saw him giving commands to height and depth,
and lifted its eye to see him under the name of Creator.
The people even mistook him for God, who was hidden,
and Moses, who was near, filled the place of his Lord.
Thus far Moses has drawn me on with his wonders,
and I can no longer come near him to unfold him for myself.
For the story of the son of the Levites presses upon me,
since the more I say, the more it grows, and it has no end.
If my mind had not grown weak from the story,

now I would have begun to speak in earnest.
If the mind were not swimming in so much abundance,
this would be the beginning, not the end, of the homily on Moses.
Here I set down the anchor of silence as at a harbor,
and if there is time, I will sail again on the course of Moses.
Wondrous is the mystery that served there, and it cannot be spoken,
and I keep silent, lest the great type be diminished by me.
That descent from the top of the mountain to the people:
who then is able to tell how it was?
Until then he had been serving in glorious mysteries,
and then he took up the great image of the King and came down.
He dawned like the sun upon the Hebrews and dazzled them;
rays went out from his face upon the camp.
His light flashed, and the people marveled at his might;
his beams came down, and the tribes trembled in amazement at what they saw.
The sun of flesh, wrapped in rays, came down from the mountain,
and with a veil he covered his majesty from those who looked on.
O veil wrapped in mysteries, you fill me with wonder,
for your measure is portrayed in the humanity of the Son of God!
In that veil which Moses cast over his face,
the bodily nature of the Son of God was seen.
Because of these mysteries of truth that Moses put on,

his Lord [?] called him a prophet like Himself.
Within the veil the glory of Moses was gathered,
and in His humanity the Church received our Lord.
The veil fell over the face of Moses near the camp:
this very type the Church took hold of in our Lord, in His body.
These mysteries were sung in beautiful fashion,
and with [?] and a keen mind were enriched still more.
And since the story of Moses has been told by me so meagerly,
do not, my Lord, reject the small labor of a feeble man.
Receive kindly the weakness of this homily,
and let my hearer fall at your table with discernment.
That I have not told all of you, I am not to blame, my Lord, in truth;
for who can tell your story to the end?
Receive the gift of the small voices my tongue has sent,
and keep for me with you a treasure of mercies until I come.
In return for the short pieces I have sung feebly here,
may your mercies be long, your mercies, and by them may I live long.
Son of God, of whom Moses your servant wrote,
to you be praise, to your Church hope, and to me forgiveness.
On the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up in the wilderness
(By the holy Mar Jacob, Homily 4, on the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up in the wilderness

To the sea of your mysteries my words have brought me down, Son of God;
by you let me be drawn up from the floods that surround me.
The waves of your stories have multiplied their tumults upon me;
you, the Pilot, steer me to the harbour of truths.
Moses the shepherd, who led the flock through the floods,
let him lead me to the sea of mysteries, that I may enter his writings.
Lord of Moses, draw me out of the sea as you drew Moses,
as I bring up a great abundance from reading him.
All the wonders that came about by the hands of Moses
were depicting you along the whole road on which he had set out.
With the rod he took you from your Father's side on Mount Sinai,
and he followed you and came as a shadow of the great Body.
He showed Egypt the cross of your grace when he entered it,
and it trembled before it and yielded to its might.
A great image he carried in the wilderness as he passed through,
and the mountains leapt when they saw your likeness upon the Hebrews.

The heights saw your great Passover and skipped like lambs,
that the procession of your image might be honoured in the lands.
Your standard, our Lord, Moses set up in the wilderness,
and when the natures saw it they were all confounded.
He became a painter and mixed the colours of prophecy,
and in the desert he painted an image full of wonder.
With that serpent of bronze he portrayed you and lifted you up,
that your likeness might be a remedy for his people.
Your mystery he set up against the venom of the serpents,
that by you he might heal with life the bites of his people.
Here let love tell you, hearers,
and from it learn all the hidden things that Moses spoke.
With the eyes of the soul look upon these mysteries,
for the beauties of the Son are all carried in their arms.
By him the great Moses performed all that he performed,
in Egypt, and in the sea, and in the desert place.
He carried the likeness of the Son, and it went before the camp,
and by it he warded off all harm from among his people.
He showed the glory of the Son to the worlds and made them afraid;
creation saw the sign of his slaying and trembled before it.
He set up the cross at every station where he camped,

so that the people might dwell without fear beneath its shadow.
There was no place where he was not sheltered by the cross;
it became a wall for him, and within it his camp rested.
In many ways Moses depicted the Son of God,
and throngs of mysteries surrounded him all along his way.
Let us leave aside today the many that cannot be grasped,
and speak of one that is full of wonder to whoever looks upon it.
Let us speak now of the mystery of that serpent of bronze,
and for what purpose Moses set it in the camp.
Let us tell first about the bites of the serpents,
and for what reason they were sent upon the Hebrews.
The people were eating manna and murmured against the Creator,
and in their gluttony they gave no praise for their food.
They withheld the thanks that was due for their meal,
and in great plenty did not give thanks to the One who fed them.
The bread of the Watchers was sent to them to be fed with,
and that provision did not please them, wicked as they were.
Instead of the thanksgiving that was owed for the gift,
their mouths were full of murmuring, scorning the One who fed them.
Glorious bread was sent to them from the thick cloud,
and the greedy despised it, because they were fed without toil.

The winds of plenty served the ungrateful [?] people,
and while being fed they grumbled every day against the Giver.
They were filled and murmured, for they were wicked;
they were nourished and gave no thanks, for they were not upright.
Good things and fine food of many kinds were laid before them,
yet they knew nothing but blasphemy while they were enjoying it.
The greedy grew weary of the manna, and the quails were contemptible to them;
they were sick of their food, and like the hungry they wailed and wailed and blasphemed.
In the desert they drank water blessed from the flint,
and did not marvel at that wonder, marvellous as it was.
Clouds and winds brought them provisions,
and they were loath to give praise for what they ate.
They became disciples of the great Moses of the house of God,
and learned only to blaspheme against the Creator.
Their heart was dull, and they did not love instruction;
they were greedy for food and would not give praise.
Their soul was darkened by food, for they were gluttons,
and they would not consent to give praise to the One who fed them.
They murmured against Moses and blasphemed every day against their God,
and greatly wronged the goodness that had been shown them.
"Why did you bring us out of Egypt?" they would say,

"Our soul is weary of this meagre bread," and they grew bitter.
The bread of the Watchers the wicked called "meagre bread,"
and greatly despised that provision of the house of God.
The longed-for manna sent to them was small in their eyes,
and instead of praise they sent murmuring by the hands of Moses.
Sweet food came to them from on high;
they tasted it and in their insolence blasphemed the One who fed them.
Their food was sweet, but their belly was very bitter;
they ate honey and belched bitterness, for they were perverse.
And when their bitterness had grown strong in great murmuring,
Justice chastised them with serpents that belch venom.
That bitter people it punished by means of bitter creatures,
for its judgement is just, and it does not colour it with partiality.
It kindled the vipers with venom and sent them against the wicked,
that the evil people might be punished [?] by the hateful viper.
Because they had not given praise for being rescued [?] from the Egyptians,
snakes came to bite them bitterly.
He conquered Leviathan, who is Pharaoh, and crushed his heads,
and the people that gave no thanks was devoured by the heads of serpents.
That great serpent of Egypt he choked in the sea,
and without partiality [?], to the place of judgement against the wicked,

so that vengeance might be taken on them for their insolence toward the One who fed them.
And as these things were being said by Justice
to the greedy servant who blasphemed what he ate:
"Snakes eat dust and are silent, without blasphemy,
whereas you eat sweet manna and blaspheme.
By serpents that never cease against the one rejected [?],
see, you wicked, how much you have blasphemed against the One who feeds you.
Vipers eat dust and are silent, bitter though they are,
and you greedy ones eat the bread of Watchers and are not silent."
The serpent is bitter, but not as bitter as the Hebrew:
he is evil by his own will; his bitterness is not of nature.
The snake is evil, but the Jew is more evil than it,
for his food is sweet and his mouth is bitter with blasphemy.
Under his lips is the venom of the asp, as it is written,
and while sweet manna was given him to eat, he belched bitterness.
Therefore he was chastised by serpents
and struck down by the bites of vipers.
He was flogged with evil scourges,
that by blows he might be sweetened, for he was bitter.
Ranks of vipers surrounded him in the wilderness,
and with their bites they poured their venom upon the rebels.
Snakes sprang up from every side against the wicked,

and his spirit was distressed, and he began to flee to supplication.
He knew why he was being chastised,
and began to entreat Moses to deliver [?] him from the chastisement.
"We have sinned in murmuring against you and against the Lord," they said to him;
"pray that we may be rescued from the snakes that surround us."
The people were being devoured until they confessed that they were sinners;
the vipers bit them, and in their distress they were humbled to plead.
And when the supplication was brought to the Lord by the hands of Moses,
a command went forth as to what the son of the Hebrews should do.
The Lord said to him: "Make a serpent of bronze,
and set it as a sign in the midst of the camp of your people.
Whoever the serpent bites, let him look at it and live."
And Moses did as he was commanded by God.
He made a serpent and set it as a sign in the camp,
and whoever a serpent bit would look at it.
And when he looked at it, he was healed with great wonder;
but if he did not look, he was tormented with great pain.
This work shows something great within it,
and whoever looks with discernment sees it too.
Here the cross showed its power clearly,
and its mystery healed the people that the serpents were devouring.

Its image, then, was painted in that serpent that Moses made,
and when pain saw it, it fled from the limbs.
It was brought forward against the venom of the serpents,
and when the venom saw it, it quietly subsided.
Moses the physician cut the root of the crucifixion
and set it in the assembly before the Hebrews, to heal them.
He saw the daughter of Jacob delivered over to the snakes,
and set the sign of our Lord in the desert, that she might be healed by it.
A troop of serpents went out against the rebellious one,
and like a commander the cross went out and scattered them.
The vipers waged a great war against the Hebrews,
and the cross of our Lord stood in the midst as a deliverer.
A legion of hateful vipers came against the daughter of the people,
and the mystery of Jesus, like a mighty warrior, fought it off from her.
The cross gave battle to the tongues of the serpents,
quenched their venom and drove it from the Hebrews.
The Sweet One rose to fight against the bitter ones,
and his taste conquered them in a sight full of wonder.
When they poured out this venom upon the Hebrews,
he poured his shade over them and sweetened them.
When venom flew from the snakes into bodies,

they were sweetened by the sweetness of the Crucified Light.
The mystery of our Lord became a stag against the serpents,
and in the desert it cried out and put them to flight.
The cross was lifted up, and the people who had been bitten saw it,
and the venom fled from their crushed limbs.
Moses made a parable in the wilderness before the eyes of the Hebrews,
and our Lord explained it, teaching with a loud voice:
"Just as Moses lifted up the serpent for the people in the wilderness,
so I too am lifted up, for the whole world to look on me."
The great image that Moses painted in the wilderness,
from our Lord himself one learns and sees that it is his own.
"As Moses lifted up the serpent, so I am lifted up:
let everyone who is bitten come and look on me and be healed by me.
The great serpent bit Eve among the trees,
and lo, I am lifted up; let her look, and if she looks on me, I heal her."
Demons had fallen upon the world and bitten it like snakes,
and it was fitting that he be lifted up like the serpent that Moses made.
The viper bit the mother of the nations among the trees,
and its venom flew through all her race to destroy it.
And therefore the cross was lifted up on Golgotha,
that those who had been slain might look on it and live.

O you who are bitten by Satan, look on Christ,
for this is why he was lifted up: that you might look on him and be healed by him.
O you in whose limbs hidden venom has spread,
by this sight of the Crucified Light you are healed.
O you who are slain by the bites of evil demons,
raise your eyes, look, and be healed, if you will.
O soul bitten by iniquity, do not doubt;
look on the cross, and it will gently heal you.
Sins bite like the bites of serpents,
and if you do not look on the Slain One, you are not healed.
As Moses lifted up the serpent, so your Lord has been lifted up;
look on him, O man, and the wound that pains you will flee.
Behold, he hangs and stands for all the bitten to look on him,
and to be healed by him who is full of mercy for the wounded.
O sinners, behold, he looks to you, that you may look on him,
for in the sight of him is a medicine that heals every blemish.
He hangs like a standard in the midst of the world, for it to gaze on him,
and grace overflows from him, taking pity on whoever looks on him.
The sight of him has been made a remedy for the wounded,
and by him the pains of the soul are healed without medicines.
This is why he was lifted up on Golgotha, that you might look on him,
and that he might heal you from the blows that are devouring you.

"Just as Moses lifted up the serpent, so must he be lifted up":
this is plain to whoever needs healing.
Whoever was bitten by a visible serpent looked on that one,
and whoever is bitten by the hidden viper, let him see this one.
That one drove the visible venom out of the limbs,
and this one pursues hidden sin out of the thoughts.
In Moses' serpent the body of our Lord was being portrayed,
by which all the bodies of the sick are healed.
Except for the venom, that serpent resembled the serpents;
this is the Son, who in all things became like us.
Except for sin, the Fashioner of all became like us,
and by himself he healed us, for apart from him there is no life.
In that serpent there was no venom of serpents,
nor was there sin in the body of our Lord, who became like us.
In the matter of venom, Moses' serpent was sweet,
and as in a mystery it overcame the venom of the serpents.
And the body of our Lord is without sin, as it is written,
and therefore all sinners are healed by him.
O how that serpent resembled the serpents,
yet it was not like them, for it was not bitter and did not bite!
O the Son, who in all things became like us,
except for sin, as Paul the chosen writes!

All the mysteries came to rest clearly on the cross,
and in it all the types were truly fulfilled.
He stood in creation like that serpent in the midst of the camp,
that all who had been struck might look on him and by him be healed.
O soul whom the serpent has bitten, look on the cross,
and by it the hidden wound that pains you is healed.
The sin that bit you — lo, the medicine of life is from Golgotha;
apply it to the wound, and by it the wound is truly healed.
And if by the likeness of a serpent whoever looked was revived,
how much more will the image of the Son heal whoever sees him!
Let these things that have been spoken by me be repeated,
that the mystery of the serpent may shine once more before the hearers.
I will turn my word back over the story with discernment,
for a word becomes clear when the speaker repeats it.
I will raise my voice again over that serpent that Moses lifted up,
for the more the matter is repeated, the more the cross is glorified by it.
When a snake bit a man of the house of the Hebrews,
if he despised Moses' serpent and did not look at it,
the power of the venom killed him, because he was negligent
and did not believe that he should run to the refuge of the serpent.
There was one who despised it, died of his wound and was not healed,

and there was one who believed, drew near, looked on it and forgot his pain.
The one who had been bitten was free to choose what he would do,
for the choice was set before him whether to look or not to look.
The sight was free, and Moses demanded no fee;
the serpent stands, and whoever looks on it, his distress passes away.
It lay in the will of the one bitten what he would do:
he looked, he was healed; he did not look, he died of his wound.
Faith was victorious there among the wounded,
for whoever believed and saw the serpent lived by the sight of it,
and whoever did not believe, the venom of the serpents killed;
he was not healed, since he would not look as was commanded.
And here faith stood, healing sicknesses,
and the healing of the one struck was placed in his own will.
The cross was stretched out, and it never demands a fee from you,
and if you look on it, it freely heals and cures you.
Behold, Satan has made serpents throughout the whole world;
O you who have been bitten, look on the cross, for it will heal you.
Let no one despise a sight that is plain before many,
for if he despises it, he dies by the venom of the great serpent.
The cross never compels anyone to come to it;
whoever wishes to be healed by it, the choice is his own.

The sinner too has freedom and has been given authority
to heal his pain by his own will, without mediators.
Behold, he has before him a healing sign,
which, if he looks on it, truly heals him.
The sin of the body dies through the body of the Son of all;
by this one who did not sin, those who sinned are healed.
As the serpent overcame the serpents at Horeb,
so a body peacefully heals the bodies that cling to it.
By that viper the venom of the vipers was quenched,
and by this body the sin of bodies is wholly abolished.
Its appearance is contemptible, but its healing is very great;
death is depicted on it, and life springs from it every day.
The cross by its appearance proclaims death to whoever sees it,
but on examining it, one finds it gives life to whoever looks on it.
That serpent too, by its appearance, frightened whoever had been bitten;
its name and its sight terrified the one who had been struck.
But when he was persuaded and looked on it, at once his pain was changed,
for its power was not as contemptible as its appearance to whoever looked on it.
And perhaps the one who was bitten was afraid or trembled
when they said to him, "Come, see the serpent and you will be healed."
And he would say, "A serpent has killed me, so why then

should I see a serpent, when even the sight of it terrifies me?
Why should I look at it, when I am tormented by its wound?
Its sight is hateful to me; let it go away from me, since it has killed me.
What use is it to me, when it carries no medicine to heal my wound,
and I can lay no root upon my pain to be helped by it?
Its sight is fearful, and if I look at it, it will add to my pain:
it is a reminder of my wound, a serpent in every way."
This also happens to the cross with many:
they flee from it, not knowing what its power is.
Death is depicted on it, yet it bestows life on those who draw near;
it proclaims slaughter, yet to those who know it it is full of resurrection.
The foolish pagan, who hates his own life, does not love it;
he hates its very name, and who can persuade him to come to it?
When the Church calls the pagan to come and live,
he sees in her the cross, the sign of death, and runs from her.
When she persuades him to come to the life that is found in her,
he looks in and sees a corpse within her, and is terrified.
When she tells him, "If you come to me, you will conquer death,"
he enters, finds a slain man in her, and doubts.
This is what the pagan says to the Church:
"I am made to tremble at death, and lo, the sign of death is set in you.

I see a corpse in you, and I who am slain — who will heal me?
I hoped to live, and lo, the image of a dead man shines out in you.
You called me to life, and how can a dead man give me life?
Death has killed me, so why should I come to death again?
I thought there were bandages for my wound in you, as you announced to me,
and lo, you show me a slain man, swallowed up as I am.
Death is a frightening sign that terrifies me,
and if I see death in you as well, why should I come to you?"
The pagan sees the cross and trembles, not knowing
what power springs from it for whoever draws near to it.
As Moses' serpent terrified whoever had been bitten,
so the cross of death terrifies the pagan by its appearance.
That Hebrew whom a serpent had bitten,
they would urge to come to another serpent, look, and so be healed.
So it is with the pagan whom death has slain and who comes to the Church,
and she brings out and sets before him a sign that is wholly death.
But when the Hebrew had been bitten and was in anguish,
all his kinsfolk would say to him, "Run to the serpent!"
And if he despised the contemptible sight and would not go,
someone who had tried it would warn him not to doubt.
The first who looked on the serpent and was healed
was made a herald among the people to all who were bitten.

And if he saw someone doubting, he would warn him,
and from his own experience he taught him everything.
And so these things would be said to the one who was bitten
by one who before him had also been bitten, had looked, and was healed:
"Come near, do not fear: it is not a serpent just because it is called a serpent;
it is like a root that holds life for whoever looks on it.
It is not like that serpent that bit you; why are you afraid?
Look on it, and see that by its sight you are helped.
A serpent bit me just as it did you, and Moses' serpent
seemed contemptible to me, but when I looked on it my troubles passed.
When you hear 'a snake,' do not be terrified;
it is the physician's work; look on it and test what its power is.
It is a sweet serpent, and it proved to me, when I looked on it,
that by its sight it took all the venom from my limbs."
So too the Church teaches the pagan every day,
that when she calls him to see the cross he should not doubt.
She also says to him: "Look on the corpse on which death is depicted,
and you will also find resurrection springing from it.
The slain one who is set in me — come, test what his power is,
and you will learn that it is he who slew greedy Death.
You see the cross, and you will find that he is also God,

who by the sign of his death abolished death for many.
When you hear 'a slain man,' do not be terrified;
examine the slain one, and you will find that he is not mortal.
The image of death is depicted on the cross for whoever looks on it,
and life springs forth for whoever draws near and clings to it.
See, let the report of a dead man not frighten you when you hear it,
for you will find that in him Death died, while he himself was without guilt.
Look on the Crucified and gaze on him who gives life;
test his work, and do not doubt because of the name of his shame.
Take faith with you when you look,
and lo, shame and suffering will not terrify you when they meet you.
Do not gaze on him with outward sight alone;
look inwardly, and you will find him mighty.
Do not doubt when you see a corpse lying there,
a slain man, a cross, a stripped and embalmed dead man.
Draw near to him, and you will find him Lord and Son,
Mighty One of the worlds, Bearer of creation, Giver of life,
Reviver of the dead, Raiser of the departed, Binder of death,
Deliverer of Adam, and God as well, who is not diminished."
The name of the cross frightens the pagan so that he does not worship it,

And when he goes in and sees what his work is, he takes refuge in him.
While he was far off, he was terrified by the report of the slaying;
but when he drew near to him, he found life, and his soul grew bright with it.
Just as that Hebrew whom the serpent had bitten was healed,
so too the sinner whom death had slain is healed.
There the bronze serpent, and here the Crucified, is victorious;
in the New and in the Old alike, he was made a medicine of life.
That is why our Lord said, when he was teaching:
“See, I am to be lifted up like that serpent which Moses lifted up.”
Moses had set a great riddle among the Hebrews,
and Christ came and explained it plainly to the nations.
The Hebrew fashioned a parable of mysteries in that bronze,
and in the Crucified, light dawned on the hidden things that had lain stored away.
It is our Lord who healed by his power, both here and there:
there by his symbol, and here by his own person, truly.
Today and yesterday he is the same, and he does not change.
Blessed is the Crucified, who gave life to the world that had been struck down!
Here ends the homily on the bronze serpent.
On Aaron the Priest
Homily 5: On Aaron the Priest.

From the beginning, when the Lord created Adam,
he made him a priest, to stand at his ministry.
The Lord set Adam a boundary in truth:
"Of all the fruits in Paradise, Adam, eat,
but the tree that stands in the midst you shall not approach,
for when you approach it you shall taste death."
The Evil One envied Adam, made in the image of God,
and gave Eve counsel, and she plucked and ate from the tree,
and gave to Adam, and he ate and broke the commandment,
and death gained power over Adam, as had been said.
Adam died, and death was carried on through all the generations;
and death came and reached Moses like a captor.
It brought the bond and showed it to Moses, as one who takes all captive;
death cried out and said to Moses, the son of Amram:
"I have a claim against you, I tell you, on account of your father;
you will not pass on from here, Moses, unless you repay me.
Adam ran up a great debt to me among the trees,
and unless you repay me, there is no way for you to pass."

Moses read the bond that his father Adam had written,
and saw that through it death [?], dreadful to all his children.
Thus it was written: "I am liable to death; I shall die,
and because I sinned, I have handed all my offspring over to death.
The debts I have incurred I shall repay, since I was condemned,
and from hand to hand I have consigned all generations to death."
Moses saw the bond that his father Adam had made,
and he drew near and tasted the cup of death in great suffering.
All the upright, and the righteous too, the prophets and the kings,
tasted the cup of Adam, who broke the commandment.
All the priests who bore the mysteries of the house of God
could not cut short or escape that sentence of guilt.
All the prophets and kings and priests, the children of Adam,
were made subject to the decree of the sentence on our father Adam.
Whenever a priest, a prophet or a king arose and was about to pass on,
he saw the bond and surrendered himself to the cup of death.
And as death was carried greedily through all the generations,
it came at last to Aaron the priest, the splendid one of the house of God.
The reason for the homily that urges me on is this:
the priesthood of the sons of Levi, and how it came about.
Adam bore it from the beginning of all generations,
and handed it on from hand to hand to those after him.

That priesthood of our father Adam reached as far as Aaron;
it came to him, and he bore it lovingly and in splendor.
And as he stood clothed in the mysteries of the house of God,
he loosed and bound the things of earth for those of heaven.
And as he stood in the tabernacle over Israel,
no one in all the people transgressed his command.
Moses was made like a god over the camp,
loosing and commanding the sons of Jacob like God.
Miriam was made like the bride of the house of God,
and she held the lyre among the tribes.
And Aaron carried the censer and entered the tabernacle,
burning incense and making atonement for their sins.
He drove dreadful death away from the camp
with the censer he offered, and at once he held back the destroyer.
Moses and Aaron redeemed the people from Egypt;
Aaron the priest was made the forgiver and the atoner.
He burned incense, and a hidden fire received it,
and fire upon fire gave off fragrance before those who looked on.
How does a fire burning from coals appear to you?
Yet here the hidden fire showed its love.
Aaron burned the fire of his heart in the house of atonement,
