and it held back death from the camp swiftly.

In the manner [?] of Mar Ephrem.
Aaron carried two fires
and brought them before God; and God saw his heart
and accepted both. He carried the visible fire in his hand
and the hidden fire in his mind. The fire of his heart pleased Him,
and the fire of his hands was accepted. For had it not been pure,
the hidden fire of his mind, neither would the fire he carried
have been accepted by God. It was because of the fire of his thought
that the fire of his hands was accepted. O atoning fire,
which forgives debts and sins! Through this fire sinners drew near
and received forgiveness. The fire of his hands rose as incense,
and the Watchers above rejoiced in it; the fire of his thought rose as incense,
and the Lord on high rejoiced in it. Where the angel threatened
that he would destroy the camp, Aaron took a censer full of fire,
went out, and held him back from the people. The angel saw the fire
and fled from its brightness. He saw the hidden fire there
and was terrified at the sight of it. The fire put the Watcher to flight,
and the spear he was holding fell away. By the command of the Godhead
the priest held back the bringer of death, and by his incense
he held back the angel from destroying. Yet when the time pressed upon him to die,
he was not spared from death. Between God and the people
Aaron always stood, and at the beckoning of God
he was made the commander of the people.

And Eleazar stood within the tabernacle and watched, to learn how he should stand
at the ministry of God. He watched his father constantly,
how he offered sacrifices, so that he too might offer them as he did,
in purity and holiness. While still a boy he was learning
how to stand in his rank. His thought was bright and fair,
and his whole mind was splendid. He also practiced a modest way of life
in the tabernacle. And Aaron his father stood
clothed in the vestments of the priesthood, the fitting garment of ministry,
the fire that came down from on high. A crown was set on his head
and a turban above his person. He was clothed in the ephod in truth,
and perfect stones were hung on it, and golden bells
on his garment, and he was made priest of God. He entered to atone for sins
in the tabernacle, as it is written. God said to Moses:
"I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be
your interpreter to the great people. And when you have come out of Egypt,
then the priesthood shall be ministered. For it is fitting for such a man
to minister in the house of Adonai, and to administer faithfully
the priesthood entrusted to him." And as he stood in the tabernacle,
with his son beside him in the holy place, the son learned the mysteries of the priesthood
and was perfected in its ways. His father taught him how
to carry the censer of atonement, and how to enter and call
upon God with purity of heart.

And while the boy Eleazar
was ministering in the tabernacle, the debt common to all was stirred up
to claim its due from Aaron. For the time had come
for Aaron to pay what was owed, and the time for Eleazar
to enter and stand in his place. And while Aaron was clothed in the priesthood
and stood in the holy place, Adam's bond was stirred up
to claim its own from Aaron. He who had ministered the priesthood
forty years in the tabernacle could not release himself
from the writ of the common debt. He who had made atonement for the people,
and over whom the angel of wrath had no power, could not [?]
the bond that Adam had written. He who had driven away death
and the angel by his incense, when the cup of death met him,
could not save himself. When the time came
for Aaron to taste death, the Lord called the son of Amram
and spoke with him and said to him: "O Moses, hear what I tell you,
and do not let it grieve you. Do not let your thought be broken
by the news that falls on your hearing; do not let your mind be troubled,
nor distress take hold of your heart. Do not let your eyes shed tears
at the sorrow I speak to you of. Let me not see grief in you
at this mystery between me and you. Do not come to cut off hope
and grow weak like everyone else." Then Moses answered
and said to God: "Whatever Your Majesty wills,
I will do according to Your will."

The merciful Lord said:
"Behold, I tell you, Moses: your brother's time has come
to depart from this world. Your brother's time has come
for another to stand in his place. Your brother's time has come
to take off the vestments of his ministry. Now, Moses son of Amram,
hear what I tell you: Rise, take Aaron your brother,
and take Eleazar with you, and go up one of the mountains,
the one I tell you. The three of you together
complete the mystery among yourselves. Do not weep, O son of Amram,
and do not grieve for Aaron your brother; for it cannot be
that one who drinks the cup of death is not distressed. And tell Eleazar
not to let his thought be troubled when he sees Aaron his father
wrapped in death on the mountaintop."
Of Mar Jacob.
The Lord called Moses his servant and spoke with him:
"Rise and take Aaron your brother, as you have been commanded,
and take Eleazar with him, and let him go with you,
for he is to go up and put on the holy vestments.
He in turn is to enter and stand in his father's place,
and I am making him a shepherd to stand over the flock.
Him I am appointing priest to make atonement for Israel.
Give him charge in these words that I tell you:

let him keep his soul pure and holy from every evil;
let me not see in him iniquity or wickedness of any kind;
and let no hateful deceit come near him and defile him."
These words were spoken by God,
and Moses heard all that He told him with great love.
Moses called Aaron his brother and Eleazar,
and spoke to them words of sorrow and grief:
"A journey has fallen to me and to you, Aaron and Eleazar,
for the Lord has told me that we are to go up together to Mount Hor."
Moses led Aaron and Eleazar,
and they set out to go to Mount Hor, as he had been commanded (sic).
They climbed and reached the mountaintop as they had been told,
and Moses began to encourage Aaron his brother.
Thus a brother spoke to his brother,
in great sorrow and in the grief that had seized them.
Moses said: "I will reveal to you, brother, a mystery I hold,
and I have no choice but to reveal it to you plainly.
Like a limb joined to its fellow, you are joined to me;
in Egypt we did as one what the Lord commanded us.
The wonders too we performed as one among the Egyptians;
when I stood before Pharaoh, you helped me.
And when the rod was changed into a serpent, you cast it down;

when the magicians stood against me, we were as one.
And when their rods became serpents and drew near,
we did not stand apart from each other among the Egyptians.
But now death has come, and behold, it parts us from each other,
and the Lord's command is fulfilled in us according to His will.
You have repaid me, Aaron, with good favors, as was fitting,
and you have shown me a brother's love without blemish.
And now, Aaron, the debt common to all presses upon you,
and there is no way for you not to drink the cup of death.
The writ that Adam wrote has now come due,
and a brother cannot redeem his brother, as it is written.
So now, Aaron, do not grieve that the end has come,
and let there be in you not a single thought of sadness.
See that you do not become a stranger to the Lord through distress,
for there is none born who does not taste the cup of death.
Adam tasted it, and behold, it is carried on through the generations;
do not grieve, for your son stands as priest in your place.
The Lord has willed that the boy enter and take your place;
He told me that Eleazar is to be priest in your stead."
Then the Lord signaled to Moses, saying to him:
"Why are you standing there? Draw near and strip Aaron your brother.
Take from him the holy garments of the priesthood

and clothe Eleazar, the chosen priest, in them.
Take from him all the array of the sons of Levi,
and send your brother away naked, going to meet death.
Naked stood your father Adam among the trees,
and you are to strip him of the priesthood and let him go.
Let him enter the world in holiness, unstained;
and because he has not sinned against me, I lead him away in holiness."
Moses drew near to his brother, as he had been commanded,
and Aaron saw him coming toward him and bowed his head.
Aaron the priest gave himself up to be stripped
of the priest's vestments, and then to go to the new world.
Moses drew near and raised his hands above his head,
and took from him the crown of glory and gave it to his son.
He took from him the beloved breastpiece that had hung upon him,
and gave it to his son, that he might enter and stand at his ministry.
He took from him the ephod that he wore, and the turban too,
and clothed Eleazar in them (sic) before his father.
Aaron stood watching as he was stripped,
and was not distressed that the holy garments were being taken from him.
He was stripped and left naked of the priesthood,
and the boy drew near and received the mysteries of the house of God.

And Aaron stood and watched his son then,
clothed in his garments, standing resplendent as a Levite.
He watched the young priest, the splendid priest,
and rejoiced to meet him, and his heart was glad that he had become his successor.
He was clothed in the crown and the ephod and the breastpiece, with the turban,
and wore the robe, and the girdle over them all,
and the hem and the golden bells arranged on it,
and the twelve pomegranates that depict a great mystery.
Like a bridegroom for the wedding feast was this boy adorned,
to be priest in the tabernacle.
And while the two brothers stood on the mountaintop,
Aaron stripped like Adam among the trees,
and Eleazar clothed in the priesthood of the house of God,
Moses stood and held back his compassion, so as not to weep.
Who has a heart of stone, that he would not weep
to look on Aaron stripped and drawing near to death?
Who, seeing him stripped and removed from the priesthood,
would not bring streams of tears from his eyes?
Mar Ephrem.
The Lord signaled to the son of Amram:
"Why are you standing there, O Moses? Draw near, give your brother the greeting of peace,
and let him go to his dwelling. For behold, the angel is standing
and watching for you, waiting for when you will release him.

Unless you give him the greeting of peace,
the angel will not lead him away. Unless you release him, O Moses,
death has no power over him. Draw near, Moses, and close his eyes,
for you have lingered long on the mountain, lest the people make an idol
to worship him, as is their custom." Moses said to God:
"How shall I draw near and close his eyes? He is standing and speaking with me;
how can his eyes be closed?" The Lord said to Moses:
"Only give him the greeting of peace, and at once the angel will come
and take his soul from his body." And while the son of Amram stood
speaking with God, the boy drew near to his father,
bowed his head and did him homage. And thus
Eleazar said to his father: "Bestow your blessings on me, my father,
and so go from me." Then his father opened his mouth
and lifted his eyes to heaven, and with tears and sighs
offered a prayer to God: "May God, before whom I have stood
in purity and holiness, bless your youth, my son,
and grant you favor before the people. May the Son who is to be born
and will redeem the worlds by His grace grant you a way of life
that pleases the Godhead. May the Mighty One, at whose beckoning
all things came into being, grant you a mind
in which God takes pleasure. May the Judge who will come to judge
His creatures at the end of time

grant you at all times to minister before Him in splendor.
May He who bestowed the priesthood on me, so that I stood before Him in splendor,
grant you to make atonement for the sins and debts of the camp,
and may He accept from your hands pure and holy incense,
and the offering of faith presented in purity.
May the Lord who gave the priesthood to Melchizedek the great priest
grant you fulfillment in the rank you have received today.
May you be adorned in ministry with the power that the heavenly ones put on
in the ministry of fire and spirit, and may you overcome all evils.
May the Good One, who is full of blessings, and whose mercies have no measure,
open the door of mercies and answer your requests.
May the Righteous One, who is full of joys, and for whom the righteous have waited,
grant you joys to rejoice in all your days.
May the Levites obey you and be guided at your beckoning;
may the people fear before you and not resist the word of your mouth.
From you may the sons of Israel receive laws and commandments,
and through all the generations of the ages may the fame of your priesthood go forth.
May the Lord be your companion and keeper at all times,
and may He bring to fruition for you a priesthood that gives rest to His Godhead.
May He be a good hope to you, He who is God, the Lord of all,
and may all your thoughts be made straight, so that they never depart from His care.

May God be your commander and guide;
may you be guided by the word of His mouth and not stray from His commandments.
You are now His servant; do not cease from His service.
See that you do not stray from His way and become like a stranger to Him.
May the prayers of Aaron your father be a good companion to you,
and may they guard your ways before the ark of God.
May the Holy One, whose door is open to all who call on Him in love,
accept, my son, your blessings, your prayers and your petitions.
May the One of heaven and earth, who is in the height and in the depth,
grant you to please Him with works of righteousness.
May the Trinity of the Godhead be your keeper,
and keep you continually, by day and by night."
This was Aaron's prayer over the boy Eleazar,
and God heard his prayer as his mind desired.
Moses drew near to his brother, as God had commanded him,
and embraced him in love and said to him: "Go, and may the Lord be with you."
Of Mar Jacob, of Mar Balai.
Moses said: "Go in peace, brother of truth, who was with me."
Aaron said: "Remain in peace, brother who never kept a grudge against his brother."
Moses said: "Go in peace, beloved priest of the house of God."
Aaron said: "Remain in peace, beloved brother whom his Lord loved."
Moses said: "Go in peace, priest who offered the peace offerings."
Aaron said:

"Remain in peace, brother who performed all the mighty deeds."
Moses said: "Go in peace, priest who fulfilled his Lord's will."
Aaron said: "Remain in peace, brother who brought down manna for the people."
Moses said: "Go in peace, priest who atoned for the sins of the people."
Aaron said: "Remain in peace, Moses, who divided the great sea."
Moses said: "Go in peace, you who were joined to me in all these things."
Of Mar Jacob.
As soon as Moses kissed Aaron, as he had been commanded,
his soul departed swiftly from within his body.
The Lord commanded the soul, and it departed from its companion;
He commanded the bird, and it took flight from within its nest.
He commanded the dove, and it flew off, departed and changed its dwelling,
and the body was left lying on the dust, its kin by nature.
Aaron died on Mount Hor, as it is written,
and in his place a new priest arose to minister in his office.
Moses and Eleazar stood in great sorrow,
and on the mountaintop a wondrous sign appeared.
Aaron was laid out before his brother and before his offspring,
and they took care that no grief should be in them.
What brother, seeing his brother wrapped in death,
would not weep for him as they are parted from each other?

Moses gave no room to distress to take hold of him,
for he knew that God has another world.
The boy Eleazar stood watching his father,
and when he was about to weep, he held back his compassion and his mourning was stilled.
The perfect ones kept the command that the Lord had given;
as they had been commanded, so they carried it out on the mountaintop.
Aaron died, and they rose to minister according to the law,
and the Lord came to be with them, to escort Aaron the priest.
And as they stood, they began the psalms of the Spirit;
companies of Watchers came down swiftly from on high.
They opened their mouths to glorify the one made of dust,
with wondrous voices in their spiritual hallelujahs.
The praise of the Watchers was mingled with that of the earthly ones,
and wondrous voices rang out there over the Levite.
And when that service of the heavenly ones was completed,
the new priest, who had become priest so suddenly, prayed and brought it to a close.
That Levite was escorted with great glory,
and the Lord and Moses and the boy, with the spiritual beings, buried him.
Earthly and heavenly beings shrouded and buried him,
and a sign went forth to the angels to go up.
Streets of flame were trodden on the mountaintop,
for there they escorted Aaron the priest with distinction.

All day long there were companies of fire on the mountain,
and all day long it blazed with flame.
At Aaron's death the angels marveled on the mountaintop
at how greatly his Lord exalted and honored the day of his death.
Lord, who came and by Your blood made peace for height and depth,
give peace to Your Church, for whose sake You died; and to You be glory.
Here ends the homily on Aaron the Priest.
On the Star That Appeared to the Magi

By the holy Mar Jacob.
Homily 6:
On the star that appeared to the Magi,
and on the slaughter of the infants.

Great Dawn, who filled the world with his rays,
make your light dawn on my thoughts, that I may tell your story.
Radiance of the Father, who poured light upon the darkness,
enlighten my mind, that I may proclaim the homily of your glory.
Image of the glory of the great Light that came down to earth,
form in me a word full of wonder, that it may show your beauty.

Glorious Sun of righteousness, who dawned in our land,
shine your light on me, that I may tell your story luminously.
Through you all the ends of the earth that had been darkened were made bright,
and the earth was flooded with your splendid light that was sent to it.
Your rays went out over the corners of the world and lit them up,
and see, the peoples delight in your light, which has gladdened them.
Your rays pierced all the darkness of paganism;
they entered and set up for you an image of light amid the darkness.
To Magianism you sent a letter by a star of light,
and you drew it out of darkness into your radiance.
Your messenger ran to the house of the benighted to bring the news,
and trod a road there for your dawning to walk on.
Hear, you discerning ones, with great love and without distraction,
about that dawning of the star of light that was sent.
See, I bring to light what the subject of this homily is;
let no one grow weary of the story full of wonder.
It is about that divine dawning which shone from on high
and drew the Magi to come and see the great King;
about that Child of the Lord of the heights who came down to earth
and called the far-off to be renewed by his birth;
about the messenger who cast his path in the height above
and stirred Persia with the rays of his might.

It is about the reckonings of astrology in which they were schooled,
which he hunted with its own tools, so that it became his and left its own;
about the preparations of the chiefs of Persia who went up to Judah,
and about the offerings which they offered in love to the Infant;
about Herod, the accursed wolf who sought to kill
the young ram who turned back his charge by his strength;
about the slaughter of the children of Zion who were killed,
and about the Lord's going down to Egypt as a fugitive.
These are the stations the word has set for itself to lodge in,
and it will tow their cargo along the story full of wonder.
The impulses of the mind have taken up this homily,
and they yoke it to the chariot of thoughts, that it may go forth into the world.
This story stoops to be spoken by a poor man,
but the wondrous homily is not poor as its speaker is.
Do not look at the speaker of the word as it is spoken,
but at the beauty of the colors woven into it so wondrously.
It is customary for something great to dwell in a small place,
yet the great does not become less than what is small.
Our Lord himself dwelt in a carpenter's house as one despised,
so now let his stories be told by a weak man.
It is his way to incline his love toward the lowly,
that he may set at naught the greatness of the world wherever it is.

The Rich One dwelt with the poor and lowly,
so here let the glory of his homilies dwell with a poor man.
The King of kings was living in the house of the poor,
for he was devising how to enrich the world by his poverty.
The Child came who governs all even in his helplessness,
and to the far-off he dispatched a messenger to gather them.
By a single letter that he sent, Assyria was stirred,
and it hastened with offerings to see his face.
He showed his command by a sign full of wonder:
that he is the Lord, and height and depth obey him.
He drew one sign of light for the chiefs of Persia,
and they loaded their offerings and brought them to present.
He sent light to kill darkness in its own place,
and to make a road in that dwelling of paganism.
He cast one gleam of his rays into the land,
and with its dawning he pierced the night of error that had thickened.
He had come to enlighten the whole world by his birth,
and he sent first to the head of the earth, that it should come to him.
To a land far from instruction and from preachers
he sent a messenger of light, intending to bring it.
He laid the yoke of his radiance on the shoulder of the unlearned,
and taught them the way to come into his service.

The newborn King was waging war with the darkness,
to show that his side stands firm in victory.
He cast a stone of light into the night of Magianism,
and the hosts of darkness were scattered by the Mighty One.
Of a ray he made himself a fiery arrow,
and shot it and split that gloom of astrology.
With a cord of light he drew the Magi to come to him,
and by his dawning he conquered the ranks of Persia and brought them out.
For he had been sent to enlighten the whole world,
and the nations were worthy of him, as well as his own people.
He dwelt among the people and sent for the nations to come to him,
so that his dawning might gladden both far and near.
The King sent a beam of light into the darkness
to bring them out of that night which covered them.
He wrote a letter and sent it to that land by a messenger,
that there might be peace in the land laid waste by Magianism.
He sent the star to call the far-off by its dawning,
for any man of the earth was too weak to go and bring them.
On a swift road his messenger flew lightly,
and stirred that land with good tidings.
What, then, was the reason for the star that was sent,
and why did he call the Magi by its great dawning?

Why did no prophet proclaim there, as at Nineveh,
or a herald like the son of Amittai announce it to them?
Why did no one like Isaiah go down and teach them
that a virgin conceives and bears a King without wedlock?
Why did prophecy not tread the road to that place
and call the Magi by its divine revelations?
In what manner did a star of light come down to them,
and with what voice did it sow the tidings of the Child in their ears?
A messenger that did not speak, but only dawned—
how did it proclaim its teaching and have it received?
Why was no prophet sent, as I said,
but a star fulfilled the office of preaching?
Here a reason was found for astrology:
it looked into nativities by calculation, not through a prophet.
Through [?] the birth of the King was ascertained by it,
and it granted the casting of nativities its due, that they are, so to speak, true.
The Wise of heart hunted it with its own craft,
yet it did not know how he caught it by its own art.
It was overcome and subdued by a crafty weapon that it had polished;
he killed it with its own, as he did Goliath, mightily.
Teaching lay in ambush within the deceits of astrology,

and it lured [?] and drew it after the truth.
Truth set an ambush and hid among the constellations,
and from there it hunted Magianism and led it away with it.
It dealt with it by guile, as suited it, until it caught it,
and once it was caught, drew it to itself to become its own.
The hunter too sets a snare that he jiggles,
and lures each kind with the food it loves, to catch it.
For he knows that unless he stirs it, he catches nothing,
and so he coaxes each kind with its own kind.
What snare was there to hunt Magianism
except something of the constellations, which it loved?
He gave it its desire until he seized it, that it might come to him,
for it would have fled from its hunter had it known.
Had it not been shown its own, it would not have received him;
therefore he gave it its custom until it was won over.
It would not have received instruction from Isaiah,
nor would it have heard his words had Jonah preached.
For Magianism has books opposed to Moses,
and does not incline toward the teaching of the house of Adonai.
Astrology is the opposite of prophecy,
and had prophets announced anything to it, it would have stoned them.

Its ear would not incline to Moses to hear from him,
so that his words might dwell in it, so intent was it on its craft.
Its labor is on nativities and constellations,
and so truth hunted it by the very thing it studies.
Its mind was bent on gazing at the luminaries,
and from them and through them truth seized it in its skill.
It gazes at the stars and at the tally of their reckonings,
and truth beguiled it to see him there until it caught it.
From the zodiac it claims power over men's fortunes,
and by it the tidings of the Son dawned on it, that it might see his face.
The firmament was its book, and it read daily in its luminaries,
and there the Wise of heart showed it his kingdom.
Its understanding is set on the course of the powers,
in which stations they stand and where they move along their paths.
It established twelve houses and seven governors,
and from them it takes its grounds to speak about nativities.
Truth sat down in its reading and gave itself over to it,
so that by what it had learned it would be caught, and enter, and see the Son.
Had a prophet told it that a virgin conceives in Judah,
it would not have received him unless a constellation persuaded it.
It was rebellious toward the reading of prophecy,

and its heart was steeped in the study of the powers.
And while it was examining and gazing at the portions as its mind directed,
a star of light signaled to it, by a stratagem, of a King in Judah.
Its heart was captive to the calculations of its craft,
and through them it learned that a King had dawned, as we say.
And indeed, my brothers, on the night of the birth of him who saves all,
the whole band of Magianism was watching the constellations.
Truth contrived some occasion and brought them out,
so that a great wonder might be shown to them all together.
And while they were counting the hours of the night and their reckonings,
and observing the times—where, when and what they move—
then the divine Dawn kindled the lamp,
and a new star imprinted itself and appeared to them among the reckonings.
In the well-known place where, as they say, fortunes are made,
the light of the King's birth stood to show itself to them.
By what was not true, truth entered to bring them,
for there was no other net to catch them.
A star stood there, beautiful in its light and great in its appearance;
its dawning was mighty, its splendor blazing, its beauty radiant.
Its burning was kindled, its rays were ablaze, its appearance was wondrous;
it was unique, and there was no other like it.

The new vision stirred them to search it out,
and in their books they found no account of it at all.
They asked much about the wondrous revelation they had seen,
and the books of astrology were not enough to tell of it.
The image of light urged them to depict it,
but all the colors of astrology could not contain it.
And thus the Chaldeans spoke of these things:
“What, then, and how, and who, and where has the Savior dawned?
Something great has come to the world in this new birth,
and he has authority to seize the whole earth.
A mighty man has come to be born, as we perceive,
and all the ends of the earth will obey him once he is named.
A lofty stem has sprung up today among those born,
and the crown of Nimrod will be subject to it once it is revealed.
A mighty man who will hold the world by his strength
is now born; let us search and see who and where he is.
Before this one's crown all crowns fall down;
let us go first, take something and offer it to him.
When he grows up he will subdue all the peoples of the earth;
let us go and show him love while he is still an infant.
All creation rejoices at his dawning, now that it has sensed him;
let us be the first, and see, we will show our love there.

He subjugates kings and yokes rulers under his yoke;
come, let us worship him freely and not under compulsion.
The heads of the earth become servants of his rule;
let us be the firstborn and see his face with offerings.
He governs creation and receives the worship of the peoples;
let us be first and worship, and so our excellence will be seen.
Let us go and enroll our land in his name from now on,
before the peoples clamor at the report of his might.
Let us bring gold and lay it before him as befits his honor,
so that when he grows strong in his kingdom he will be gracious to our land.
Our craft is magnified by this, that we perceived him,
and since we perceived this, it is fitting that we not slight him.
Let us honor him now at his birth as he is,
and in his kingdom, when it is revealed, he will repay us.
Before the kings of the earth come with their offerings,
let ours be the firstborn and be offered to him.
Before the peoples throng to him with their honors,
let us be first to bring a great gift and see his face.
Before gold is held cheap in his treasuries among the treasures,
let ours enter to him as firstfruits.
Before all the distant islands come,
let our land go, take something and offer it to him.

Before the peoples set out to come from every end of the earth,
let our land honor him with tribute from now on.
Before new assemblies crowd his threshold,
let us be the first of those who enter his house.
Before he subdues the [?] of the earth by his strength,
let our company go and fall before him of its own will.
This star's radiance is far mightier than those of other births;
let us search, then, where the King is, and reach him.”
Great beyond understanding is the story of the star of light,
and I cannot help but go down into the sea of its homily.
Mingle your mind with that sphere of the Magi,
and see, it pulls you to go with them on the road they took.
Bind your mind with the cord of love and draw it to him,
as he drew the Magi by his light and led them.
With love, then, hear me as I speak,
for without love a word of wonder is not heard.
One who loves can do more than learning can,
for love opens the door for the word to be received.
To one who is not thirsty, even water is not sweet,
but drink delights the thirsty when it reaches them.
Let everyone who thirsts come and drink of teaching;
it is a sweet spring in which the soul's thirst is quenched.

It is a light that shines on minds and polishes them,
and to the hearing that longs for it, it spreads its beauties.
It is a laborer eager for the profit of all its hearers,
without asking anyone to pay it wages.
For your sakes teaching arose and opened its spring,
so that you may drink, without price, of the sweetness of the great spring.
For your sakes God too sent his Son,
and he came to be born so that you might live by his birth.
For your sakes he sent his light shining into the darkness,
that you might see the way that leads to the house of the kingdom.
For your sakes the star of light dawned from on high,
to announce the great birth of him who saves all.
For your sakes the King sent a new light,
to call all peoples by its dawning and gather you.
In every way he who pities all wished to enrich you,
so that by every means you might live through him.
The Magi saw the dawning of the star of light and marveled,
for with its rays it was urging them on mightily.
They learned from it that a King had come, as you have heard,
and they set their faces to go to him, as was said.
They searched hard to find where his place was and among which people,
and the answer to this question was not to be found in their books.

They questioned one another long and insistently,
and one turned the matter over with another plainly.
It stirred up all astrology and its learning
to see where the place of the King was whose dawning they had seen.
And indeed, as they searched in their writings, they found
what Balaam said to Balak when he prophesied.
“A star shall dawn, they say, from Jacob,” he proclaimed there,
“and a head shall arise from Israel” mightily.
The peoples held Balaam to be a great man;
he was a diviner, and his words were precious to them.
And when a slight breath of prophecy blew upon him,
they reckoned his word among divinations, though it was true.
From him they learned from whom the star would dawn,
and the peoples of the earth believed his word without toil.
That a head would arise from Israel had been heard,
and the chiefs of Persia set their faces to go to him.
They prepared gifts for the King, that he might be honored,
so that they might come to him with offerings when they saw him.
And while they were intent on preparing offerings,
truth arose to teach them what was fitting for them:
“Open your treasures and bring gold, for he is a great King,

and take myrrh for him, for he is to be one who is slain.
Frankincense befits his honor, for he is also God;
bring incense and myrrh and gold to be offered to him.”
They took up their fathers' treasure, gazing in wonder,
to present their offerings to the great King.
They loaded the precious gifts and set out on the road to go up to Judah,
to see the Infant in his place, with offerings.
The messenger rose and urged them on with his rays, so that they would not be delayed
from the journey for which they had prepared.
Persia was made great by the offerings of Magianism,
for they had been prepared from the provisions of the chiefs of the land.
The whole land gave tribute to be sent
to the newborn King whose dawning they had seen in their constellations.
They were provisioned with many caravans
to go up and see the worshipful King who had dawned in Judah.
They became heralds as they went along the roads,
announcing the King's dawning to the whole world.
Their craft, lover of glory that it was, pressed them
not to hide the reason for which they were going up.
So that they might be renowned as wise men in every land,
they spoke much about that dawning which had drawn them.

Truth set them up, by their own doing, on a height,
so that by that means the tidings of the Son would be spoken.
Whether halting or lodging, they spread his story:
“Our road leads to the Mighty One born in Judah.”
Along their roads his teaching dawned,
and at their stations their words were heard.
In every lodging where they stayed they sowed the tidings,
and where they halted too, they spread the story of his birth.
Along the miles of the road their preaching spread,
and at the [?] these stories were murmured.
Cities and their inhabitants were roused by them,
and the peoples of the earth learned the stories by questioning them.
They cast fear on the inhabitants of the cities
as they told of the birth of the great King.
The kings through whose borders they passed lost heart
at the report of the King whose birth they were telling.
They cast down the spirit of the rulers to whom they announced
that a man from Judah is to seize all our lands.
The crowns of the lords trembled at their words,
for they told of his birth with fear.
New tidings were proclaimed in Magianism,
and the birth of the King was spoken of in the lands.

Truth snatched them up to be its heralds,
so that, without being bidden, they told his stories abundantly.
Truth beguiled astrology into praising itself,
and for that reason it sang of the Son in the lands:
“We know, they say, that a King has dawned in the land of Judah,
for we saw his dawning in the constellations by our skill.”
To praise their craft for how much it knew,
they spoke at length of the Son's stories all along the road:
that a Mighty One had dawned whose birth undid their constellations,
and they proclaimed him in the lands with their words.
A Wise One came to wear out the pages of astrology,
and the Magi were made his witnesses, to tell of him.
An Architect rose up against the edifice of Magianism
to pull it down, and they are made laborers to uproot it.
And they praise him, so that even outsiders become his witnesses
that he has come to abolish their reckoning by his birth.
In him the Magi strayed from the error they had held,
and he led them into the way of truth, and so they perceived him.
The unlearned took the yoke upon their necks,
and began to toil in his service on the road they had taken.
They sang of the Son along the roads among the peoples,

and reached Judah, the land that had done wrong in every matter [?].
They saw that confusion and silence had fallen on its wise men,
and they did not perceive the King who had come to save them.
The King's mother was asleep, her heart sunk in slumber,
and the Magi came and called in her ear, and so they woke her.
Persia was stirred at the report of the King who had dawned in the land,
while the children of the land were swallowed up in stupor and did not perceive him.
The mother of the pagans sent provisions to the Bridegroom King,
while the bride sitting in her chamber did not perceive him.
The daughter of the Chaldeans sent gifts to the Savior,
while the daughter of Abraham, in whose house he was, did not honor him.
The uncircumcised were laden with offerings to present,
while to the circumcised the King's renown was held cheap and not spoken of.
The children of strangers hurried along the road to the Mighty One,
while silence lay on those of the household, and they did not answer him.
They came to Jerusalem and knocked on the doors with their questions:
“Rise, show us where the King is who has dawned on the earth.”
She who loved sleep was shaken by their voices,
for she had not perceived the Truth from her own flesh before the far-off did.
She started up from sleep and answered them,
but she would not have perceived it had they not woken her.
The far-off came to announce it to all the near,

about the birth of the One who had dawned in their streets. / The place of prophecy was slumbering, idle of praise, / and through Magianism the tidings of the Son were being sung. / Among these, the scribes, the heads of the people and the elders of Zion, / the sons of Persia stirred up the land about the King in Judah. / From outsiders the tidings came in among the insiders, / so that the nations might be witnesses to His birth by their offerings. / The streets of Zion were filled with tidings from those far off, / and the whole land that had wronged the truth was in uproar at their words. / New apostles from among the nations came in to the People, / and through them the proclamation of the Son's birth dawned. / "Where is the King who has dawned in Judah, that we may go to Him? / We have seen His star, and we have made ready to worship Him. / His great light dawned upon us in our land in power, / and it announced His birth to us in truth." / Herod heard the report of the King, and the weakling trembled; / crown beheld crown, and he shook, for he was afraid of Him. / The One who looses crowns breathed fear into the king of the land, / and in alarm he set about inquiring into His kingdom. / The king was shaken by the tidings of Magianism, / and began to ask how, and how long ago, and when He was born.

He was shaken by the reports, and set his face to inquiries; / agitation took hold of him, and he began to learn about the Mighty One. / He called the scribes and the priests of the whole land, / to learn from them about the Savior, where He would dawn. / He called on prophecy to search out for him concerning the King, / for he was afraid of Him because of the tidings of Magianism. / The wretch's hands went slack over his kingdom, / and he began to ask where it would be and where His place was. / Without inquiries the nations learned of His birth, / but with inquiries the scribes rose up to deny His story. / The nations came with vows and offerings to honor Him, / while the People asks to learn who He is and where He dawns. / These carry the treasures and the blessings of their fathers, / and those wear out the books every day, yet did not perceive Him. / The king asked about the birth of the great King, / and the interpreters of the things to come revealed the mystery to him. / They held up the lamp of prophecy in their interpretations, / to show the way of truth by their expositions. / The feeble king asked them about the Mighty One; / they searched it out for him: the King dawns in Bethlehem. / "For thus it is written in the prophet about Bethlehem: / 'From you shall come forth a king who shall shepherd my people Israel.'"

From the revelations of prophecy they spoke to him, / and his heart was broken by the interpretations shown to him. / From the reading they interpreted to him the undoing of his crown, / and that He is the King and Shepherd of the whole world. / They searched it out for him, that he would truly be replaced, / and that Another was coming whose kingdom has no end. / At the close of the story the undoing of the king was spoken, / and in its interpretation concerning the Son of David it was searched out. / The interpretation came in and took the crown from the house of Herod, / so that they would no longer stand over the kingdom of the house of Judah. / A burning coal rose up from the revelations of prophecy / and scorched the king who had asked to learn about the Savior. / He asked to learn, and in his learning he found his undoing; / he sought an interpretation, and it was interpreted to him that he would be replaced. / Magi and scribes surrounded him as one who was no king, / and between inquiries and interpretations he was being overturned. / The Magi say, "Where is the King?" — you are no king! / The scribes say, "From Bethlehem of Judah He dawns." / The wretch saw his own contemptibility in his eyes on every side, / for Magianism and prophecy undid his kingdom. / He saw offerings passing before him in their array, / and because he was not the King they would not give them to him to take.

They were mocking the haughty one, that he had fallen from his kingdom, / and because he was undone they did not fear to despise him: / "Here are offerings, and you do not receive them, for you are not the one; / keeper of the place, show us the King, that we may present them to Him. / There is another King in the land, and He is its Lord; / to Him we bring gifts to offer: show us where He is. / To the One who made His dawn hasten to us in our land let us go; / Him we long to see and to worship while He is a child. / To the One whose star we saw, whose light was blazing, / and which by its revelation drew us and brought us from our lands. / To the One whose messenger rode upon its course and called us, / and poured out His light, and our land was flooded with His rays. / To the One for whom the heavens are made witnesses to His kingdom, / and the hosts and their powers obey Him. / To the great King whose dominion stretches over the luminaries, / and who in His rays shows the dawn of His might." / Herod was astonished at their precious tidings, / which were spoken without fear concerning the child. / The Magi of Persia sowed new tidings in the land, / and prophecy set its seal of mystery upon their words. / He brought sure witnesses to His story from every side, / for it was spoken both by insiders and by outsiders.

Heaven with the luminaries bore witness to His birth, / and prophecy sang it in mystery, openly. / The Magi bore witness with their offerings that they had seen His dawning, / and the scribes of the People expounded His story in their interpretations. / The star in its dawning, the prophet in his voice, bore witness to Him; / height and depth became witnesses that He is the Son of God. / The scribes were asked where the King would dawn, / and interpretation rose up to show its beauty in the reading. / The beauty of the mysteries that had been hidden was revealed, / for the day had come in which the hidden things would be sung. / The veil of silence was lifted from the reading, / and truth uncovered its face to speak clearly. / Teaching stood upon the high place of prophecy, / and began to interpret to the sons of Persia about the Savior. / The circumcised People shepherded the blind nations, / and began to interpret about that Child who reconciled them. / Those far off came and mingled with those near, / to receive from the True One the one teaching of truth. / For He had dawned who was making the two into one, / and in Him was dissolved the enmity that had been great. / Certainty raised its voice to speak from the reading, / and the nations became hearers who listened to it.

The offerings of Magianism came from among the nations, / and the interpretations of prophecy from within the People. / Offerings came in, interpretations went out; they met each other; / from this side and from that the birth of the King was confirmed. / The Magi say, "We saw His star in our land"; / the scribes interpret, "Behold, His birth is in Bethlehem." / It was spoken in Magianism and in prophecy, / and these two retold it to one another concerning His birth. / Light and voice became heralds of His birth; / prophet and dawn became heralds that He is the Son of God. / But Herod was scorched by their words, / and as if by arrows he was pierced by their words. / The Magi and the scribes were overturning him with their interpretations, / for another King was proclaimed in their sayings. / The despised crown was pained by the heralds, / for they were asking him, as one contemptible, "Where is the King?" / The crafty serpent was embittered by their words, / and the bitterness of his envy sought to pour itself out upon the infants. / The despised king choked with envy over the King, / and plotted a scheme to commit murder in his bitterness. / He planned to kill the King and seize His place,

to overturn the crown, and himself rule over His domain. / He laid an ambush, for a twofold gain, against the child: / to put Him to death and to carry off the treasure sent to Him. / He coveted both the dominion and the offerings, / and set his face to kill the child and take them. / He trembled like a woman before the Mighty One who was proclaimed, / and began to seek a place for murder, to snuff Him out. / The great crown distressed the little crown, / and the weakling began to plan to wrestle with the Mighty One. / He saw that he could not fight Him openly, / and in secret he devised a cunning plot for His death. / He saw that the whole People had perceived that a King was born, / and he refrained from raising a troop and fighting Him. / He called the Magi craftily and questioned them closely: / at what time had they seen the star of light, as they said? / He learned from them about that dawning that had led them, / to make sure from when the King had been born. / "Go, search diligently for the child, / and when you have sought and found Him, come, show me, / that I too may go and worship, as you do, / and with my offerings see His face, once I know Him." / Unwillingly he humbled himself as one who would worship Him;

truth compelled him to count himself among the worshipers. / Whether from craft or from some cause, he spoke the truth: / that he would lower his crown and lick the dust before the Son of David. / "I too will go to worship" — he was being caught in the snare; / truth exacted it of him, and he gave the Son what was His. / Worship in words was taken from him as first fruits, / which was owed to the Son, that the kingdom would pass from him. / The king's word, together with the offerings of Magianism, / was mingled, to enter the treasury of the King. / Yes, Herod, your crown was being subjected to His crown; / your own craft carries what belongs to the worshiped King. / Why then do you fear Him, if He is no king? / Be patient until you see where He reigns. / If even now you fear His kingdom, / by what power will you abolish it when it dawns? / A child has terrified you and cast trembling upon your kingdom, / and see, you stir up bitterness to fight with an infant. / It is made known that He is the great King, so greatly has He shaken you; / wondrous is His dominion, that without battles His report has oppressed you. / The throne of the crown was shaking, about to fall from under Herod, / for there had come to it the One to whom headship belongs. / He called the Magi and questioned them, as we said,

and laid down his terms: "Let us go and worship," as you have heard. / The pure ones heard him, but did not know what his craft was, / and went out to go and search for the King. / But when they went, the star in its dawning received them, / and with its rays moved the King's road before them. / The messenger came who had called them and brought them out, / so that it would again open the door and bring them in. / It strengthened them and took the road at their side, / and came here like a beloved friend to receive them. / It was also needful that they should seek His dawning in the land of Judah; / yet they trusted it and came after the one who called them. / It appeared to them so that they would not be distressed that it had left them, / and so that they might be assured that His dawning was no lie. / They saw it first without the interpretation of prophecy, / and came after it, yet wavered over its revelation. / Then they turned and heard the words of the scribes and their interpretations, / and believed again that the King dawns from Bethlehem. / And after that they saw the star of light a second time, / so that by beginning and by end it might make its truth known. / By appearing to them a second time it taught them / that it was in accord with that interpretation of prophecy. / It began on the road of proclamation with its great dawning,

and came to complete it, showing that it was from the True One. / They saw it, and longed for it lovingly, / for its great light had brought them through their troubles. / They rejoiced at the sight of it and set out to go after its light, / and it led them to the place of the King who dwelt in Judah. / It brought them to Bethlehem, the town of strength, / so that they would not need to ask along the roads. / It became for them a road full of light on which they traveled, / so that they might reach the King's place without fear. / It trod a path of splendor before them, shining, / until it reached the place where the King was dwelling. / With longed-for light it made bright the road on which they traveled, / so that by its embassy it might honor the King's offerings. / It went before them as far as where the child was; / behold a wonder whose story is higher than interpretation! / All the stars run on high with their seasons, / and never has one of them come down into the depth. / In an orderly course they run in the place of their number, / and the fixed course of their conduct is not disturbed. / Which of them, at what time, left its place, / and came down to show the way to a man, against custom? / Where have you seen a star that came out from among the ranks,

and, like the lamps of the great light, led a caravan? / When did this new thing ever rise into thought, / that a star should come down to show a man the way on earth? / At what time did one of the ranks leave the firmament, / and come down and walk with merchants on their paths? / They are fixed in the firmament and run in the course of the height, / but they never descend to the depth to walk. / By the bridle of time all the hosts are harnessed, / and with one even shoulder they have run from of old. / Which of them has slipped its yoke from among its fellows, / and come down and set its way in the depth all alone? / All these are new things that came about by our Lord's hands, / which were never done, neither by nature nor by custom. / Where have you seen a virgin mother, except His? / Or an infant who shakes kings, except Him? / For whom were luminaries messengers, except for Him? / And of what birth were they heralds, except of His? / To whom was a star shown in the depth, except to Him? / All lofty things, and without limit, have served Him. / Let the scribes cease from interpreting His birth, / and the interpreters from inquiries into His glory. / Investigation by speech is found only in praise;

for its word cannot reach to interpret His great story. / Even His messenger is too much for the scribes, and cannot be interpreted; / how then can He be spoken of as He is? / The star in its dawning sets those who examine it in amazement: / it left the height, and in the depth led a caravan. / It moved, and the Magi saw its light and rejoiced, / and it led them on the path of its splendor into Bethlehem. / It went out after them like an attendant from the King, / and brought them to see its Lord with offerings. / It drew them to walk on the path of its light, / and when it reached the King's door, it opened it in radiance. / It went before them as far as where the child was, / and as if with a finger it signaled to the Magi: "This is the Savior." / It became a road for them from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, / and brought them in; they saw the King, and then it withdrew. / These went in and saw there the child lying: / a needy place, a poor dwelling, a little house, / and a young mother without possessions and without kin; / poverty, and a King who lies there without legions. / The Magi gazed at Him and did not doubt His kingship, / and fell before Him, abashed in their honors.

The mighty chiefs of Persia knelt and worshiped Him, / the Head who had arisen from Israel, as had been proclaimed. / The King began to bring back the captivity of the nations that had strayed, / and to fill with amazement the captor who had led them away. / He began to gather the worship of the nations that had been scattered, / even from that land of Nimrod, where wickedness had begun. / The firstborn of crowns fell and worshiped Him in the Magi, / so that other kings might bow down before His honor. / That kingdom of the chief of the mighty fell before Him, / to be a mirror for the world, that it might imitate it. / The great land of the hunter gave pledges, / and with offerings enrolled itself to the King who is its Lord. / That kingdom which is the head of the whole world / bowed before Him, so that through it all creation might be subjected. / The land of Babylon, from which headship began, / truth led to worship that Head of heads. / It saw the stone that had been cut out without hands, / which had struck the great image, and it fell before it. / It struck the head of gold and bowed it to be subject to it, / and like chaff in the wind it drove away the whole image. / The headship of the Medes fell from its honor / before that stone from which the whole earth was filled.

The head of the world was subjected, in the daughter of the Chaldeans, / to the Heir who had come to take back what was His from the plunderers. / The offerings of Magianism came in and were offered / to the worshiped King who had come to His own in poverty. / Because the King was despised among His people by the insiders, / He sent to the outsiders, and they brought Him their offerings. / He came to His own and they did not receive Him; He rebuked them, / for by strangers He was honored lovingly. / From among the nations He sent to bring what befitted Him, / for within the People He was despised by those near to Him. / The last nations became first with their offerings, / and the first People remained at the door and did not come in. / The Magi fell and worshiped Him in wonder, without doubting, / and though, unlike the People, they had seen no mighty works, they did not despise Him. / While He was healing the sick of the People, they reckoned Him mad, / and while He was driving demons out of them, "chief of the demons." / But the sons of the nations, when they brought Him their offerings, / had seen no signs being worked when they worshiped Him: / not when He changed tasteless water into good wine, / nor when He multiplied a little bread and thousands were satisfied; / not when He bound Legion and cast him among the waves, / nor when He cleansed lepers by His word, as Lord of all.

not when He put clay on the blind man and he saw the light, / nor when He spat into the ears of the deaf man and gave him hearing; / not when He trod the waves of the sea barefoot, / nor when He rebuked the winds and storms and they obeyed Him; / not when He called and brought out a dead man after he had decayed, / nor when by His voice He returned a young man to his mother's bosom; / not when He healed the stricken woman of her uncleanness, / nor when He made whole one who was deaf and blind and had a demon; / not when He healed and strengthened those who were sick, / nor when He gave life to the dead who were laid to rest; / not when He cast out demons from lunatics by His voice, / nor when He gave light and hearing to those in need; / not when He restored [?] the hand of the man whose hand had withered, / nor when He withered the leafy fig tree from its root. / While He was lying [?] upon the knees of the [?], / they saw His lowliness and did not doubt His greatness. / In a poor house, without possessions and without greatness, / they saw Him lying, and fell before Him with their honors. / In the despised poverty of all that was hers, / they honored Him, unashamed of His want. / In the destitution in which lords are despised,

the King dwelt, and was honored in it by strangers. / The Rich One disdained the wealth of the world in His want, / by which He bowed kings before Him through their envoys. / By His poverty He trampled down the loftiness of rulers, / and drew them, with their honors, to His humility. / His lowliness compelled crowns to obey Him, / and bent the mighty to labor under His yoke. / Out of His contemptibility fear fell upon the strong, / and with offerings they knelt and worshiped Him without doubting. / In poverty the Son of the Rich One trampled on wealth, / to show that His wealth was His own from eternity. / In a poor house the King's Son dwelt in poverty, / and sent to bring the treasures of kings, hidden away, to His door. / The Magi fell and worshiped the great King in wonder, / and though they did not see His worldly wealth, they did not doubt. / They became a mirror for the world from then on, / that whoever worships the Son in truth should be like them. / They did not scrutinize Him when they offered Him their offerings; / in love they honored Him, unashamed of His smallness. / They did not probe into His birth with their questions, / but gave offerings and did not presume to ask questions.

They did not investigate His birth first and only then give their honors; / they knew He was King, but did not search Him out in their words. / In love they worshiped Him; they did not rise up as disputers against His birth, / so that they might be a model for the children of the house of faith. / A new Church came from Babylon to see the Son, / and did not search Him out, for it was sure to her that He is King. / The noble daughter of the Chaldeans saw Him and did not search Him out, / to be an example, that no one should scrutinize the One he worships. / Magi, who search out hidden things in their inquiries, / kept silence about the birth like discerning men. / Why then is His story not held as precious by disputers? / Instead, see, the scribes pluck at it with their questions! / Why do you not possess that simplicity of Magianism, / which honored Him in conduct and did not search Him out? / Why does not everyone worship the Son of God / as the shrewd Magi worshiped Him, without searching? / Why is silence not spread over His story like a veil, / so that He may dwell within it, hidden from troublemakers? / Why do the scribes not kneel before Him in simplicity, / and not scrutinize Him, just as the Magi did not search? / Why are there rents in His story made by disputers, / and contortions in speech about Him made by scrutinizers?

Why has the inquirer opened his mouth against the faith, / and why does everyone speak in contention to establish his own view? / Why has disputation made itself factions in the assemblies, / and stirred up heresy to probe the Son with quarrels? / Let the Magi be a mirror for whoever worships him, / so that what is spoken among the discerning is not pried into. / The envoys who came from among the pagans with their gifts, / let them teach the story of faith to whoever scrutinizes him. / For only in the land of Judah did they ask, “Where is the king?” / and once they had seen him, they did not go back to asking. / Those true men saw the child lying among the poor, / and they did not waver, or ask again about his kingship. / They knelt and worshipped him and brought their offerings before him; / they opened their treasures and gave him the hoards of their fathers. / They took gold and offered it to him as to a king, / and fine spices they gave in his honour as to the Lord. / They brought him choice gifts after their own fashion, / to the great Crown from whom sovereignty flows. / They knelt before him and begged him to accept them, / and they were not ashamed of his littleness because he was a child. / They fell down and worshipped him with great trembling, in fear, / and begged him not to reject their offerings.

They did not see his crown, yet they believed he was the Lord of crowns, / and with their offerings they sought to please him in great love. / The hidden Crown made them hasten, and they fell before him, / pleading with him to take their gifts from them. / The mighty, the heads of the earth, fell down before the infant, / and with offerings they begged him to accept them. / Words like these were spoken by the envoys / to the King they worshipped as they gave him their offerings: / “Take, my Lord, the gifts our land has sent to offer you; / you are our King: take tribute from your dominion. / The crown of Nimrod, chief of the mighty, has sent a diadem / to pay your kingship its due, for it is glorious. / From now on our land dwells under your name, for you are its king; / accept from us, and release us to go, as we were sent. / The kingdom of Media and Assyria has sent word by our hand / that you are King and that lordships are subject to you. / The great region to which all dominions are subdued / begs by these gifts that you count it among your dominion. / The land of kings, from which sovereignty goes forth, / has now enrolled you as its king from this time on.” / The Magi worshipped the Son and offered their gifts, / in awe of his kingship, without wavering.

The mighty were bowed on their faces, entreating him, / and the virgin mother was pondering wisely in her heart. / And it was as though the blessed woman spoke these words / to the Magi who worshipped her son with their gifts: / “Where did anyone show you a king, and who sent you? / Reveal the mystery to me: who assured you of his kingship? / What retinue have you seen here serving him? / Where is his crown, if he is a king as you have said? / Look, you see the poverty that surrounds him, / and that I, his mother, am needy and destitute. / What ranks of people have you seen around him, / and how many soldiers are at his doors to honour him? / How many armed men are with him, as you say, / and how many ride with him now, as you have said? / How many legions has he sent ahead of him into the lands, / and what troops of his soldiers does he have beside him? / Did you see gold or treasures, as in the houses of kings? / Has he wealth, or power by which he is honoured? / Do servants stand by, or ministers obey him? / Are ranks drawn up, or does a court attend him? / Is his crown mighty, or the chariot in which he parades? / Does his robe gleam, or are seals set in his diadem?

“What is there in him that resembles a king, as you have said? / And who compelled you to come and see his face with offerings? / You have found him in need and in poverty; / who truly brought you the tidings of his kingship?” / They answer: “Mother of the King, your son is mighty, / and he will take hold of the whole world by his strength. / It is no loss to him that the land is dull and does not know him, / and that the people neglect worship and bring him no offering. / The heavens, with the luminaries, bear witness to his birth, / and the children of your own country, in their scriptures, to his authority. / The powers in the firmament have proclaimed his crown: / that he is a great King before whom lordships fall. / The ranks on high have recorded your child as King, / and among the constellations the image of might has risen for him. / On the pathway of the hosts we saw his crown, / and from it we came to understand the authority of his might. / His great image stood above the shoulder of the firmament / and showed us his sovereignty, so that we would come to him. / The image of his glory rose among the luminaries, and we saw it, / and the sun in its brightness cannot compare with his might. / See, the heights carry his authority on their heads, / and his crown outshines the luminaries in their paths.

The firmament with its luminaries bears witness to his might, / for it was by a wonder that it told us of his kingship. / Among these ranks above he is a great King, / and there he has a name more glorious than their courses.” / The maiden says: “The account of your revelations is true, / and I, who am wronged, have long been persuaded of it. / Yes, in truth he is King of those on high, / but those below do not perceive that he has visited them. / To me too a messenger was sent from the Most High, / and he made known to me that the one born is the Son of God. / From the ranks of the hosts the envoy came down, / and with a wonder he revealed his story to me clearly. / I received light from the Most High through hearing alone; / but marriage, I do not know what it is like. / In wonder I conceived him, with no thought of union; / I received his tidings from the Most High, and the infant stirred [?] within me. / I was not wed, yet I became a mother, as you have seen; / my virginity is kept, and I have a child, as you see. / I do not know what union is like, / and yet I have been made a mother in the manner of wedded women. / I do not know what the pangs of women are like, / but I gave birth in holiness, though I had not known a man.

I did not see a man, yet I conceived without intercourse; / I am no wife, yet I am a mother without marriage. / A spiritual being sowed in me tidings full of wonder, / and without the stirrings of a man I conceived, being pure. / I asked him, ‘How can what you say come to be?’ / And he explained to me: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, / and the power of the Most High will overshadow you in holiness, / and you will bear a child whose kingdom will have no end.’ / With that word I conceived, full of wonder, / and I bore a King, and no one has perceived it but you. / I am wronged because of him; be my witnesses among those who wrong me. / I will uncover my face and scorn those who have so oppressed me. / Come, you who are from afar [?], tell his story to those who are near, / and reprove them, so that they may know [?] that he is the Son of God. / Cry into the ear of this sluggish people, so that perhaps it may hear / and grow a little aware through your fair reports.” / They answer: “Mother of the King, do not be dismayed, / for a time will come when the whole world will ring with the praise of your child. / Be patient until he grows to manhood in his kingship, / and all the ends of the earth carry his story to tell it. / The day will come when his crown will dawn over the lands, / and the peoples of the earth and their judges will fall before him.

A time will come for you when you will see crowds surrounding him, / and you will forget the bareness of the little house in which he is being raised. / You will see ranks of peoples falling before him / and honouring him with their offerings and their vows. / In a little while the earth will resound with reports of him, / and his fame will fly over the regions and their inhabitants. / Time passes, and the world awakens to speak of him, / and his gospel runs through all the ends of the earth to take hold of them. / He takes a place that none of the kings has known, / and he shakes all crowns and bows them down before his glory. / He takes hold of a rank where none of the glorious has stood, / and on it he tramples the diadems and [?] of lordships. / He inherits a throne whose height the air does not reach, / and the lofty seats of rulers tremble before him. / In time his story will dawn among the nations, / and creation will resound at his authority, for he is a great King. / Dread of his authority falls upon judges, / and he makes the mighty kneel before him with their gifts. / Above all crowns the standard of his might is set up, / and kings with their dominions become a footstool for his feet. / He shakes the authorities of lordships throughout the lands, / and thrones and those who sit on them quake before him.

He shines on the earth more brightly than the sun in his might, / and takes in the ends of the earth, and no one escapes his authority.” / Mary says: “All that you have said is true to me, / and there is no room for me to doubt your words. / I truly know who he is and whose son he is; / I learned all of it from the angel when I received him. / I have not seen his Father, yet I am persuaded that he is Lord of kings; / his Begetter is hidden, and by his authority the world stands. / By his nod all creatures and their inhabitants hang, / and by him the ends of the earth and those who dwell in them stand. / The prophets bear witness to his birth, that he is the Son of God, / and I, a virgin, that I conceived without marriage. / In prophecy his story was sung openly, / and now you have proclaimed his kingship. / It is fitting for you to begin the preaching, / because the people have shut their eyes to understanding. / It is right for you to speak about my son and his kingship, / for you are strangers to the disputes of the elders of the people. / They are envious and will not believe me that I bore a King; / they are drunk with pride and do not understand what is to come. / The heart of the people has grown fat, as it is written; / it has shut its eyes and stopped its ears against understanding.

Speak, for it is right for you to understand, / since the King has lovingly made you sharers in his mystery. / Let the earth be filled with your fair tidings, / and let the world awaken at the sweet sounds of your rejoicing. / Let the fame of your offerings go out among the nations, / and let creation be filled with the new tidings of your triumphs. / May the King delight in your offerings, as you have loved him, / and receive you, rejoicing in you, as you have desired. / May the honours offered to him please his Father, / and may the gifts you have brought him be to his liking. / May the labour of your journeys please his divinity, / and may he rejoice in the beauty of the offerings that have come to him.” / The King dwelt in the little house of the destitute woman, / and the treasures of kings and their offerings were heaped up before him. / His poverty bowed down the wealth of rulers, / to show that he is the hidden King of all dominions. / In smallness and in greatness he excelled; / over lowliness and over loftiness he was exalted. / In need and in might he went about; / through humility and through kingship he was carried along. / Glory and contempt, from this side and that, pressed upon him:

he was held to be the Son of God and the son of Mary. / In the needy house of the daughter of the poor he was being raised, / and it was he who bowed down the might of the kings of Assyria. / He was despised among the people and not honoured by those within, / but he called those outside, and they answered him with their gifts. / The priests defrauded him and did not bring him their tithes; / the Magi worshipped him and brought their offerings before him. / Zion grew sullen over the praise that was required of her, / but the daughter of the Chaldeans confirmed the worship that was due. / The King’s servants despised the King when he came into the land, / while by those from afar he was honoured with choice gifts. / The scribes of the people, who expounded his story, did not perceive him, / while among the luminaries his new tidings were being proclaimed. / Justice came and would not allow the King to be despised, / and from among the ranks above it called a messenger to prepare his way. / It brought the Magi, and they offered him their gifts, / and by their worship they paid him his due, so that he would not be slighted. / The star by its rising completed the preaching to the nations, / so that the Son’s glory should not be diminished in any way. / It is written that it came as far as the place where the child was; / it seems it stood there over the door, shining. / It left the height and set its light in the depth,

like its Lord, who bowed down and descended to those below. / After the Lord the servants ran to obey him: / angels, and luminaries as well, came down to honour him. / After the King all the hosts follow, / and where he dwells, there his legions too stand. / The Lord of the heights came down into the depth from his Father’s side, / and the ranks on high began to follow in his track. / The angels came down, and the luminaries too began to descend, / for by his birth the earth had become heaven. / When he came down, he brought down with him some of those above, / and when he went up, he took up with him some of those below. / He brought down Spirit and took up body, and fulfilled both; / he became a son of man and made the many divine. / He was born of a woman so that we might be born of the Holy Spirit; / the Son has two births, and we too have two. / He was born of the Father by a birth too lofty to explain, / and again of Mary by a new birth full of wonder. / Though he is God, she bore him bodily, / in a human body, so that he became man without change. / With a pure body, a rational soul and a perfect mind / he came forth from the womb to renew all things by his birth.

He put on limbs over his hiddenness and became one of us, / so that he might clothe us too with spirit and power, and we might be of him. / By his second birth we have been taught what to do: / that we too need another birth, to be renewed by it. / Baptism became the second womb and bore us, / and this birth is truer than the bodily one. / Into the womb of the waters goes an old man, advanced in days, / and becomes an infant by the new birth of baptism. / Though human birth from Adam is real, / from God, through Spirit and water, we have become sons. / Eve, who bore us, is no longer our mother, from our Lord onward; / the Spirit conceived us, and she bore us to be her children. / Eve’s womb bore flesh, from union, / but baptism bears spirit and life, without change. / In himself our Lord showed the pattern, to teach us: / he came to birth though he was ancient in his begetting. / Mary became a baptism for him, and he bathed there, / and he came forth a second time in humanity, to become man. / He received a body from Mary in holiness, / for he had set his course toward the sufferings, to bear them. / The Ancient of Days became an infant by his new birth, / so that the old might learn the way to come to birth.

“How,” it asks, “can an old man return / to his mother’s womb and be born again after his time?” / “From water,” it says, “and from Spirit this comes about”: / so our Lord explained to the one who asked to learn from him. / As the virgin Mary bore him bodily, / so the fountain of life bears the old spiritually. / For baptism is our second Mary, / and by a perfect birth she is truly our mother. / The virgin gave our Lord a body, so that he might become man, / and baptism dipped us in the Spirit, so that we might become gods. / Both we and our Lord have second mothers, new ones: / for our Lord, Mary, and for us, our own, baptism. / He who is spiritual made himself a bodily mother, / and for us who are bodily he appointed a mother of Spirit to bear us. / He took a body, and we took Spirit, from our mothers, / for every mother clothes her child in her own likeness. / This is the road the King laid down for himself to the earth: / he came and brought, he went and carried off, as you have heard. / When he came down, Watchers and luminaries escorted him, / and when he went up, apostles and disciples accompanied him. / Without a body he came, and in the body he was exalted; / he let go and he took up, and by both he completed his way.

So the King came down and made his dwelling among the poor, / and the hosts moved from their place to attend to his honour. / Angels came from the Father’s presence to announce / peace and good hopes to the world at the birth of the Son of God. / The luminaries ran and gave the signal to the lands, / that the ends of the earth might see his rising and bring their gifts. / His rays went out to the land of Persia, which had been darkened, / and there they bound the darkness mightily. / Against all custom his way ran on to triumphs, / and against nature he yoked the elements to his service. / The star and the Watcher and the angels came down to honour him, / and wherever he dwelt, there they stood to minister. / He dwelt in Mary, and the chief of the angels greeted her; / he entered the cave, and it was filled with Watchers and their praises. / He went out into the wilderness, and angels ran to minister to him; / he entered the tomb, and Watchers went down with him to honour him. / Wherever the King’s standard was set up, his legions gathered, / and wherever he dwelt, the ranks of his hosts stood. / He entered the little house to dwell with the poor woman, / and the star ran and stood over its door as in the firmament. / The chief of the luminaries left the ranks, against all custom, / and came down to honour its Lord’s door with its great light.
