she is a mother and she is a virgin, and none can dispute it.

Baptism became a mother to us, and through her we became
sons to the Father, so that we may lovingly call him "Our Father."
This womb prepared us spiritually,
so that from her we might be sons of God in holiness.
For had she not borne us with a second birth,
how could we call the Heavenly One "Our Father"?
From Eve we are made of dust and children of death,
but from this new mother we are children of God.
From her onward we have a Father above in heaven,
and we call upon him, confident that he is our Father.
A Father in heaven—whence or when could we have had one,
since our father Adam lies in Sheol upon his [?]?
If the birth from Eve still stands, then we ought to call
him of Sheol "Our Father," not him of heaven, for Adam is not there.
The serpent bit our first father and dragged him into Sheol,
and there he is in Abaddon, cast down and brought low.
He is rolled in the dust, and rows of worms are wrapped about him;
the worm is his clothing, and he has [?] for a covering.
Worms are beneath him, and above him the moth dwells;
dust is spread beneath him, the clod clasps him, and he wastes away in Sheol.
This is our first father, and this is his place;

and unless he is exchanged through baptism, great indeed is the abasement!
As long as our race remains in this birth from Eve,
this is our father, and we must look for him below, not in heaven.
Flee from him, hearer, from this great abasement,
and seek another Father for yourself, the one in heaven.
Run to baptism, take refuge there, and ask her to be your mother,
and she will make you a Father who is rich and full of good things.
She gives birth to you, and even if you are an old man
you will become a beloved child with a King for your Father.
She teaches you to call "Our Father in heaven,"
and from her onward your Father is above, not in Abaddon.
It is a disgrace to own as yours the one who is in Sheol, for he is very poor;
he is brought very low. Take for yourself a Father who is all riches.
Baptism writes your name above in heaven,
in the church of the firstborn, where the Father sits on high.
Be baptized, hearer, and call "Our Father who is in heaven,"
for from then on your race is heavenly.
The one who is in Sheol has been exchanged for you in baptism,
and from now on look where he is whom you call upon.
The Father who truly became yours from within the waters,

"Our Father" to your Father, by virtue of our spiritual birth.
Since the chosen waters of baptism bore you,
your race is above, where the Father sits on high.
There you have a brother, Christ, whose Father is your Father,
and the brotherhood of the Holy Spirit, who sanctified you.
You were wicked, needy, on the dunghill; mercy took you up
and made you so great that you are called even a son of God.
The waters bore you in place of that bodily birth,
and behold, your voice is raised to call "Our Father who is in heaven."
The Only-Begotten came down and raised you from the dunghill,
and gave you his Spirit in baptism, and made you his brother.
A new mouth and a lofty voice from within the waters
the baptized have gained, and they have become new sons to the Father.
And because in the waters they became brothers to the Only-Begotten,
his Father is truly their Father, and they call him "Our Father."
Therefore, from the birth of water onward,
we have a Father above in heaven, and not in Sheol.
We have forgotten Eve, and we have baptism for our mother;
had she not cast us up to the height, the depths would have swallowed us.
We have left Adam, since God has counted us among the sons,

for Sheol stood [?] over our race, had we [not] left him.
That poor, needy, ruined father of ours, Adam,
we no longer call "Our Father," since he has been exchanged.
We have found ourselves another Father, full of riches,
and that Rich One has taken the place of that poor one.
His mercy constrained him, and in his love he brought in the sons of the poor,
so that he who has riches might fill for them the place of a father.
The Rich One saw that poor man full of woes,
lacking and needy, with sons in great abasement;
and the Exalted One saw that if his sons inherited from him, they would be choked
by the curses among the thorns he would leave to them.
He saw that he had once had a great garden full of good things,
but the serpent stirred up trouble and drove him out of it, and he was left poor.
He saw that he had nothing to leave his sons but thorns
and evil afflictions, and Sheol, a pit that swallows the dead.
And in his love he willed to become a Father and to leave
to all the sons of Adam the hidden treasures he possesses.
So the Rich One sent his Son to the poor,
and chose a virgin and made her mother to his Only-Begotten.
And from within the womb he became a brother to the sons of Adam,

and they enrolled him in the census of men among those below.
And he was called Son of Man throughout his whole course,
so that the sons of men might become with him sons of God.
And in place of the mother he had taken from those below,
he gave a mother who came down with him from his Father's house.
Baptism is a pure womb full of light,
and gives birth every day, divinely and virginally.
She turns human beings into sons of God,
and receives the bodily and makes them spiritual too.
In her race is mingled with race in holiness,
and she makes those below to be of those above.
She makes the house of Adam kin to God,
so that they may call him "Our Father" by nature when they call upon him.
The Holy Spirit dwelt in the waters and brooded over them,
so that by birth they might become brothers to the Only-Begotten.
In baptism he became for them a Father who does not suffer,
in place of that father who had been bitten by the viper.
The Father sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts,
and by it we truly call "Abba, our Father."
The Son of God became Son of Man bodily,

and human beings became sons of God spiritually.
Mary gave the Word a body, that he might become incarnate,
and baptism gave man spirit, that he might be renewed.
Because he became our brother in the womb, he made us sons
in baptism, to call the Heavenly One "Our Father."
And because our race has drawn near to that great kinship,
nature moves us to call him "Our Father," though he is in heaven.
We have become kin to his Godhead by birth,
and from within the waters we have truly become sons.
And from here we have come to call "Our Father"
the hidden Father who gave us his Spirit in baptism.
Come, you outsiders, enter as sons: the door is open,
the house is rich, and the Father is glad to receive you.
Come, you who are far off, be brought near in baptism;
there is room in God's house for all who come to it.
Come, you strangers, become members of the household from within the waters;
gain a new Father on high and call him "Our Father."
Come, you debtors, enter, take back your bonds free of charge,
and in the waters blot out the debts of your persons.
Come, you poor, grow rich in spiritual baptism,
and forget the abasement of poverty in the great treasure.

Come to baptism, lamb that strayed from the Lord of the flocks,
that through you that complete number of a hundred may be made full.
Come, sinner, weary, crushed and full of turmoil,
and cut off from yourself the burden of iniquity in baptism.
Come, you blind and darkened, who became so by your own will;
be baptized and be opened and enlightened by her, the daughter of day.
Come, you lost: the Good Shepherd has gone out seeking you,
and has set himself a meeting place by the spring to gather you.
Come, you who were scattered after the worship of dead idols;
be baptized and be sanctified from the uncleanness of iniquities.
Come, you who strayed and were enslaved to wickedness,
and from within the waters learn the way to God's house.
Come, you old ones who grew aged and worn out in paganism;
gain renewal in the new womb of baptism.
Come, you unclean of the earth, be sanctified in the pure waters,
and receive purity from the spring of holiness.
Come, come, great coin of the Godhead,
for see, the master of the house is lovingly seeking you.
Come, penitent, whom mercy has drawn to baptism,

so that at your coming the heavenly hosts may rejoice.
Come, daughter of the peoples, church who played the harlot with gods;
put on your betrothed and be with him in a pure union.
Come, harlot, give your hand to the Only-Begotten,
and he will make you a virgin in the waters in holiness.
Come, dark woman, whose colour the sun has marred by its risings;
put on splendour in the merciful waters prepared for you.
Come, you darkened one, who reeked with the smoke of sacrifices;
be lit up by the radiance, and let your scent be made sweet with chrism.
Come to baptism, old woman grown aged in idolatry;
become from the waters a girl, glorious and praised.
Come, go down and put on the garment woven divinely,
and come up, show us your sweet beauty, that we may rejoice with you.
Come, be dyed from the spring that overflows with light,
and let the world see you in the embroideries of the Holy Spirit.
Chains of gold for the bride who has come up from within the waters!
Let silver spangles increase the beauty of the lady of radiance.
Let them bring pearls from Cush for the exalted head,
and from within India rows of precious stones.
Let the sea bring what is fairest of the purple shellfish,

and its companion, the dry land, flawless and shining stones.
Let the mountains offer all their emeralds and fine seals,
and the depths send up jacinths from their treasuries,
stones of glory from among the springs of [?],
and from Ophir, too, gold for beautiful ornaments.
Let her rich betrothed multiply her adornments in all their forms:
wrought necklaces and chains for the neck of the perfect one.
The bride says: "I have the Cross instead of embroideries,
and by it all my beauties are arranged upon my limbs.
He dyes my garments with his blood and adorns me,
and I have no need of what the sea of purple shellfish gives.
He sets his sign between my eyes and makes me radiant,
and I have no need of chains of gold and pearls.
With his chrism he gladdens my face and sanctifies me,
and silver spangles are not needed by me.
Instead of jacinths and fine seals he has given me his nails,
that from them I may forge all the adornment of brides."
How beautiful you are, daughter of the Arameans, how beautiful you are!
Your whole countenance is like the morning that adorns its dawn.

Upon your eyes rests a light so great
that even the sun, if it gazed on it, would at once bow down.
Your pure mouth is like a scarlet thread,
and it seems to me that your lips are dyed in blood.
In two colours your beauty shines in the assemblies,
in blood and in water, which flow to you from the Fair One.
Your bridal chamber is in the waters, and your dwelling in the cloud of the Exalted One;
the Cross is your beloved, and your hope is at the right hand of the Father.
You are clothed in adornment like a high priest of atonement;
fire and Spirit weave for you a garment that is all light.
O daughter of the peoples, betrothed to light from within the waters,
guard your bridal chamber from the darkness that would strip you.
You have an enemy full of envy: beware of him,
lest by his wiles he bring a blemish upon your watchfulness.
O bodily one who became spiritual in the waters,
sanctify your soul to become a temple for the Godhead.
Son of the poor, who became brother to the Son of the Rich One,
see that you do not lose your great wealth through lusts.
Baptized in the waters, you have become brothers to the Only-Begotten;
let him not be grieved by your bodily deeds.

Do not join his member to a harlot;
he has joined you to his Father: keep your soul pure from licentiousness.
Do not defile baptism, which is all light,
with deeds unworthy of God.
Whoever has put on new clothes takes care
that neither mud nor filth comes near him.
You have put on baptism, O man: flee from iniquity,
lest your garment, which is beyond price, be torn from you.
Freely the Son of God has given you a splendid garment;
do not despise it, lest it be soiled by your sins.
The serpent is wont to steal garments by his hateful counsel,
and to bring their wearers to great disgrace.
The robe of glory that was stolen among the trees
you have put on in the waters, and the evil enemy envies you for it.
And if you lend him an ear that listens to lusts,
he will expose you, as has been his habit from the beginning.
Daughters of Eve, keep the purity of baptism,
for that bond of Eve was torn up in the living waters.
Let the serpent not come again and enter as is his custom,
and find his opportunity in the whisperings of the lovers of the world.
Not for you, then, even that fruit of lust, which is all death,

and most hateful both to God and to your husbands.
In baptism you have been betrothed to God,
and if the thief finds an opening, he makes a rent.
Baptized one, who has found that glory which Adam stripped off,
do not lose it again through sin, now that you have found it.
Soul betrothed to the Son of God in baptism,
do not give yourself to Satan, lest he torment you.
Snatched from the demons, the Father sanctified you and gave you to his Son;
keep faith with him, lest they corrupt you after your sanctification.
O soul, who paid off her debts in baptism,
do not begin to write another bond.
You were baptized and pardoned; leave sin behind, let it depart;
let the sore not return to its place through hateful iniquity.
You have put on the High Priest who cleanses leprosy;
let uncleanness not turn back again upon your purity.
See, iniquity is strangled in the chosen waters of baptism;
do not bring it back to life through unseemly lusts.
Soul who rose from the pit into which the serpent dragged you,
do not fall again into the hands of your enemy; stay pure and steadfast.
Baptized one who has put on the robe of glory full of light,

flee from filth, that you may shine among the angels.
Do not cast your splendid garment into the stinking mire,
lest your enemies, who envy your watchfulness, laugh at you.
This garment you have put on, O man, from within the waters:
its warp is fire, its weft is Spirit, and it is [?].
The Father prepared it, his Firstborn wove it, the Spirit spun it,
and you went down into the waters and put it on divinely.
The Trinity kindled a fire in baptism
to burn up iniquity and let the soul live with God.
In baptism our race found what it had lost;
blessed is he who gave us a womb of waters in which to be renewed.
On the prayer that our Lord taught his disciples: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name"
By the holy Mar Jacob. Homily 50, on the prayer that our Lord taught his disciples: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name."

Son of God, through whom all who speak are made rich, / give me a word with which to speak about you. / Lord, who came to become a brother to servants so that he might redeem them, / enable me to sing you pure praise with a loud voice. / Yours are the discourses, the words and the songs; / from what is yours, my Lord, accept praise from a weak man. / Yours, my Lord, are the mouth and the word, and the tongue as well; / grant the mouth, unworthy though it is, to stir up your praise. / Yours are the mind and the understanding, and thought as well; / grant the mind to gaze on you and tell your story. / Yours are the movements of the soul and its thoughts too; / grant the soul to see your beauty and to speak of you. / Give me your word, the Word who came to become flesh, / so that by it I may speak of your coming, which is full of wonder. / You came to us, yet you remained with your Father; you are above and below. / Heaven and earth are filled with you, Son of God.

Fill my mouth with praise, as you said: “Open it, and I will fill it.” / Open it and fill it, for even when it is open it is a feeble man's mouth [?]. / You are the one who opens shut mouths so that they speak, / for who can open his mouth without you? / Once even a she-ass spoke, so that everyone might know / that it lies in your power to give speech even to a beast. / Open my mouth, which I have shut by the wrongdoing of my hands, / for it befits you to do good things. / Open it and fill it, for you are the one who opens all that is closed; / shut mouths are opened by you to give praise. / Who, my Lord, opened a door in the rock in the wilderness, / so that rivers flowed out of it for a great people? / Who opened the dry bone that Samson held, / and brought fresh drink out of it for the one who was thirsty? / Who opened the jar and the horn in the widow's house, / and gave plenty in a time of famine, to great amazement? / By you all the doors that had been closed were opened: / the eyes of the blind, the ears of the deaf, and the mouth of the mute. / The blind came to see, the deaf to hear, the mute to speak; / so open my lips for me too, that I may speak. / Open my ear as well, that it may hear your story with discernment,

for you are the key, and by you all creatures are opened. / Let the soul see you: if it gazes on you, it shines with your light, / and speaks of you radiantly, made radiant by you. / The world darkens everyone it has bound with desires, / but whoever gazes on you lovingly shines with your light. / The human eye has no light within it by which to shine, / but it is well suited to receive light. / It receives light either from the sun or from fire, and the source / from which it has received it becomes its own, and the eye becomes that source's. / So it is, my Lord, with the soul: when it has seen you, / it receives a word from you and goes out telling your story. / It is not luminous, yet when it gazes on you it shines with your light, / and through you it sees you and speaks of you richly. / Nor does the eye see the sun except by the sun itself: / it is the sun that gives it light to see it lovingly. / The sun gazes on the eye and clothes it with its own radiance, / and in that radiance the eye shines so that it can see all creatures. / Gaze on the soul as the sun gazes on the eye, / and it will put on light from you, and speak of your revelation. / Come, go, my mind, and see the Messiah as he stood / among the crowds, like the Gihon full of mercies,

flowing, pouring out every cure in abundance for the stricken, / and flooding the land of Judah with his help. / Great grace burst out of him like a flood, / sweeping away illnesses and pains to remove them. / Through him the blind saw, the deaf heard, the dead lived, / and the whole earth, which had been darkness, shone with his light. / Everyone who met him received healing as he passed by, / and to all who came he gave help as he went on his way. / Through him the fallen rose, the outcasts were [?], the hungry were filled, / for he came for this: to raise up the ruins of the world. / He walked the earth to uproot the thorns from its corners, / and to sow peace in the place the curse had laid waste. / He chose apostles to send out to the regions, / so that through them he might bring the whole creation to his Father. / The Messiah, the Sun, took for himself twelve hours, / to gather them and make one day of great light: / twelve steps on which the sun rises and sets, / spreading its dawn over darkened lands; / twelve rays from the orb of righteousness / that went out like lightning after a night that had covered the earth. / He took from the world twelve men of renown,

upright, simple, pure, and without malice. / He chose fishermen, neither rich nor wise, / for the way of the Son has no need of wisdom. / To overturn the wealth of the world and its wisdoms, / he chose unlearned men to carry his preaching out across the earth. / They loved him, held fast to him, and clung to him; / they were lit up by him, were joined with him, and grew rich through him. / They left the world and came after him for love of him; / they hated possessions so that they might gain him lovingly. / They gave up family, children, brothers, and fathers, / home and kin, and went with him as he wished. / They heard his word in everything, however he spoke, / for they had no life in which to walk except in him. / He taught them not to own gold or silver, / and they seized his command as a great possession. / He taught them not to worry about what they should say, / and they did not wish to speak except through him. / They said to him, “Teach us to pray, my Lord,” / so that they would not utter even a prayer at all without him. / They held back even from the speech that is natural to us, / and lived on nothing but what was his alone.

He commanded them not to worry about speaking before judges, / and they went further than his command: / they resolved not to speak, before his Father or before him, / in prayers made without him. / “Teach us to pray, my Lord,” they said to him, / “so that we may not offer even a prayer to your Father except from you.” / The disciples asked him to teach them to pray, / and their request shone and was beautiful with love for the Son of God. / And the great Scribe began to teach the children of his mystery / how one ought to pray when praying. / So that nothing superfluous would be said in prayers, / he set what was needful in the prayer he taught them. / For first he commanded them that when they pray / they should say nothing superfluous. / He taught them carefully not to make prayer long, / so that prayer would not grow tedious with lengthy words. / In this discourse which urges me to speak, / the beautiful prayer that our Lord taught shines out. / A discourse needs a hearing that is clear of evils, / and love of the Lord, which is the sum of all good things,

and love, the great bond of faith; / and amid these a discourse pleases its hearers. / Even if a discourse had every lofty beauty in it, / if the hearer does not love it, it does not please him. / The prayer that the Son of God taught the children of his mystery / will be explained to you, if you listen lovingly. / The disciples asked him to teach them to pray, / and since he knew they had asked well, he did not hold it back from them: / “Pray like this when you pray: / Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, as it is holy. / May your kingdom come to us from where it is, / and may your will be done on earth as in heaven. / Give us the bread we need for the day from your treasury, / and forgive our debts and pardon our sins, as we have forgiven. / And do not bring us into temptation, for we are weak, / but deliver us from the Evil One, for your power is great. / For yours are the kingdom and the might, / and the dominion with the glory, for ever. Amen.” / The Son of God placed great armour in this prayer, / and gave it to his apostles to break the battle line of the Accuser. / Ten thousand times ten thousand prayers a man might pray, / the Son of God summed up in ten words.

The whole force of all the petitions of all who are in need / he packed into this short prayer and gave to his apostles. / In the very first word he taught us, to say “Our Father,” / the whole power of the enemy is brought to nothing. / For our mighty Lord knew our enemy: / how shameless he is, and how much he hates human beings; / how envious he is, how he wars, how he corrupts, / and how, wherever he can find room to prevail, he works ruin. / Eager for destruction, devoted to corruption, a lover of wickedness, / killing comes easily to him, he delights in blood, he stirs up strife. / He is a teacher of the sword and skilled in combat for battle, / and as soon as anyone stands in prayer, he stands beside him. / If he could, whenever anyone prays, / he would shut his mouth with iniquity so that he would not pray. / He hates prayer, hinders it, and throws it into confusion; / he overturns it, and if it were in his power he would put an end to it. / Wounds and arrows do not so terrify a man who is unarmed / as prayer terrifies the Evil One, who hates to see it. / Therefore he stirs up thoughts that are not good, / and troubles the soul with anxiety over all kinds of affairs. / He sprinkles his smoke over the mind so that it cannot become clear,

so that by every device prayer may lose its purity. / He stands there while the one who prays is praying, / and watches to see which way the stirrings of his soul are leaning. / If he sees that the man is full of contrition and discernment, / alert and standing to ask for mercy earnestly, / he schemes and plots and contrives / how and by what means he might trouble his soul and draw it from its petition. / He casts into his heart something the man greatly hates, / and holds him back so that he prays no longer. / And once he has thrown evil thoughts into his mind, / he turns and accuses the man of having thought all those wicked things. / With distressing thoughts he seems to mock him, / and seems to rebuke him: “Why are you thinking these things?” / He overturns him and silences him in the middle of his petition, / so that, though he has done no wrong, he suffers as one who has done wrong, / and through that pain the prayer, which was beloved, may cease; / for it torments the Accuser unless it ceases. / If he were dying, he would not be so afraid to look on death / as he is afraid to look on prayer before God. / Nor does he move away from the side of the one who prays / until he sees him leave his petition. / He also throws him into confusion through the affairs of the evil world,

and once he has drawn the man's mind to himself, he leads it off and goes. / And if he meets a soul that is free of worldly affairs, / he lures it, reminding it to do some good deed, / and makes it brood over that good deed, as if it were prayer; / and if it becomes occupied with that, then prayer is neglected. / Whoever comes forward to pray stands in battle, / and Satan too stands with him to fight. / The prophet saw Joshua the priest, son of Jozadak, / praying in the Holy of Holies before God, / and he saw Satan standing at his right hand, / seeking to cast down the spirit of the priest in the house of God, / and seeking to throw the high priest's petition into confusion; / and had the angel not restrained him, he would have confounded him. / This is the Evil One's custom with those who pray: / if he can, he betrays them even in the house of God. / Therefore, at the very beginning of the words of the prayer, / our Lord taught us to call on “Our Father,” and gave this to his apostles, / so that as soon as you come forward to pray you say “Our Father,” / and the Evil One, who is fighting you, may hear who your Father is, / so that at the start of the battle he may not come at you in his arrogance,

not knowing that you have a Father above in heaven, / and, despising you as one of weak stock, make / war on you and mock you in his arrogance. / That is why you have learned to call the Father “Our Father”: / so that from the start he may know who your Father is. / As soon as he hears that you have a Father above in heaven, / he is shaken, and his foot trembles as he fights. / You are like a weak child who has a mighty father, / and who, when he is fighting, calls his father into the battle; / and his enemy, as soon as he hears him call his father, / lets go and flees, for he is weak before the mighty one. / So you too are commanded to say “Our Father,” / so that the Evil One may flee as soon as he hears who your Father is. / “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name,” you say to him: / “We are hallowed, my Lord, for your name has hallowed us. / Your name has been called over us; may it be hallowed in us for your sake. / You are holy; may your name be hallowed in us who are weak.” / The prayer that the Son of God taught is full of riches, / and from it you can learn who you are and how great you are. / It teaches you that you have a Father, a great King, / and your soul grows so great that no humiliation can reach your rank.

The Son of God came down from the height and became a man, / and raised you up from the depths to become a son of God. / He became your brother from a womb full of holiness, / and made you his brother from the womb of baptism. / He became a man for your sake, though he was God, / so that, though you are a man, you might become with him a son of God. / He became poor for your sake, though he was rich, / so that you, who are poor, might gain riches for his sake. / He made you a son of God with him from the water, / so that, though he is the Only-begotten, he might gain brothers by a second birth. / For since he too became a man by a second birth, / by that second birth he made you a son of God. / And so that you would not forget who your Father is when you pray, / he taught you to say “Our Father in heaven” at the head of your petition, / so that your soul might grow great at the remembrance of its noble lineage, / and your enemy might fear because you have a mighty Father. / If he despises you because Eve is your mother, / let him in turn be afraid because baptism gave you birth. / And if he is confident that he can defeat the lowly son of Adam, / let him tremble when he hears that you have a Father above in heaven. / And when he fights you, meaning to defeat you in his arrogance,

let his foot shake in the battle at the name of your Father. / Let him tremble before you because of your Father, who is too hard for him, / and you, be eager to do good deeds every day. / Flee from deeds that are not good, / because God, who is full of beauty, is your Father. / Be pure and without blemish, because you are a son, / and turn aside and pass by evil things for your Father's sake, / so that when you sin he may not be grieved because of you, / he who was pleased to be your Father, though he knew you. / See to whom you are saying “Our Father” in the place of atonement, / and purify your soul for his sake, so that he is not grieved. / Look, you have risen to great honour because of him; / let him not come to great grief because of you. / Through him you are great; let him not be made small through you, if you have discernment. / Guard the honour of the Father, for he is great, and through him you are great. / That is why our Lord taught you to call the Father “Our Father”: / for a great lineage demands a very good name. / Since you call God “Our Father,” / take care to be beautiful, as one who has become a son of God. / So that your enemy would tremble before you, he taught you how

to say “Our Father,” whose name makes creatures tremble: / courage for you, as you learn who your Father is, / and terror for the one who hears that you have a mighty Father. / He wanted to remind you of the birth of baptism, / reminding you that you were born spiritually, / so that you might have great hope toward God, / who became your Father, while you became his son by a second birth. / When you pray, you call on the Father to come and redeem / his children, who long ago were enslaved to the Accuser. / You say to him: “I have been taken captive, and I am being sold; / I have become a slave, and look, I am enslaved among strangers. / Sin sold me, and I fell from freedom; / they led me away from you, and I became a slave to wickedness. / The evil master I came to belong to has put me under a hard yoke, / and look, he mistreats me in a house of slavery full of sufferings. / I sold myself, my Lord; how can I return to freedom? / For I went of my own will with the evil master. / The cunning serpent took a pen from me, and I set my hand to it, / and in Eve's house they wrote the deed, and I was made a slave. / I gave my word and became a slave, I who had been freeborn, / and the Accuser who bought me has imprisoned me in his wickedness.

But you, Father, did not set your hand to my deed; / you did not sell me, so do not abandon me to the wicked one. / Let the bill of sale that the serpent wrote without you be produced, / and see that you cannot find your hand set to it. / Now, as if with a son acting without his father, / that rebel dared to make a purchase, and was not afraid. / If a child goes and sells himself without his father, / who will buy him, trusting that the sale will hold good for him? / Let the bill of sale be produced, and if the father has not set his hand to it, / then let both the seller and the sale be void. / I was sold, my Lord, without your knowledge, since you are the Father; / let the transaction that took place without you not be confirmed. / Let not the Evil One rejoice over me, who thinks he holds me by right; / you did not sell me, so do not let me go, since I am yours. / Your hand is not set to my deed; let it not be confirmed. / Tear up the bill of sale that the serpent drew up with great cunning. / I bore your name, which is your image, and it was defiled: / “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” for your own sake. / Father, do not leave in the house of slavery the children who have fled to you; / come, rescue them from the rebel who enslaves them. / Nothing that has happened without you will stand,

because you are the Father; let your word stand, and take back what is yours. / Without her husband, Eve sold her children to perdition; / in a judge's court a woman's deed is not accepted. / The serpent is the scribe, and the one who sells is a woman, / and I have come to suffer evil at their hands in the house of slavery. / Their deeds are not valid; let them not be accepted. / Tear them up, destroy them, and undo all the falsehood. / You are the master, and there are servants who bear your image; / a deceiver hunted them down and sold them, / and took them out of your lordship, which is full of beauty, / and led them into a house of slavery full of woes. / Do not reward the one who sold your servants without you; / take them for yourself, and do not let him possess them. / He wanted to be master over your possession by robbery; / take back what is yours, and cast the robber into perdition. / You are Lord and Father; come, redeem what is yours from the rebel / who wants to take wickedly what is not his.” / When you say, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name,” / you have gathered up all these movements as you pray. / That is why our Lord taught you to say “Our Father”: / so that you may obtain every benefit from your petition,

that you may take pride in having an exalted Father, / and the Evil One may fear the greatness of your exalted Father. / And let all the earlier and later dealings / that were done to you without the Father come forward, and he will undo them. / Since you were a child and were sold without your Father, / let the bargain of the sale be void, and you be set free. / And sin, which sold you into the serpent's hands, has come to know / that the bargain made by the curse is being undone. / For the Father wished his children to return to him, / and look, they call on him, and who can hold them back? / That is why the Son of God taught you to say “Our Father”: / so that in the Father's name all good things may be yours. / When you say, “Hallowed be your name,” he is teaching you / to be holy for the sake of your Father, who is full of holiness, / and that sin should give way, in the soul that is not holy, / at the fearful report and the great name of fatherhood. / “Hallowed be your name, and may your kingdom come to us”: / for if the kingdom shines forth to come, the rebels tremble. / That is why our Lord taught you to call on that kingdom: / because of the troops of fierce demons that surround you, / setting traps, hiding snares and nets,

and shooting arrows of iniquity at the soul to strike it. / So that you may not be overcome by the camp that thirsts for blood, / call on the kingdom, and at once the unclean demons flee. / The hosts of the Evil One are trying to strike your soul, / and they surround it like a walled city to break it down. / But as soon as they hear of the kingdom of the house of God, / that it is shining forth to come, the legions of darkness flee. / That is why our Lord taught you, when you pray: / call on the kingdom, and look, rebellion is defeated. / The Evil One hears that you are calling on the kingdom of the Father, / and he realizes that he cannot shatter the kingdom. / It is not a righteous man you call on in prayer to help you, / nor a prophet to come and support you as you pray, / nor an apostle to drive your enemy away from you, / nor one of the captains of the hosts to deliver you, / nor Gabriel, to come to you as he came to Daniel / and assist you in that petition, / nor Michael, to draw his sword, as he did when he went with Joshua son of Nun, / against those who surround you. / You pass over the hosts, the captains of hosts, and the rulers, / and call on the kingdom itself; you call it to come against the rebels.

Not angels, nor the just, nor the righteous / did our Lord teach you to call to your help when you pray, / but to call on that kingdom of the house of God, / before which all the enemy's hosts tremble. / Call on the kingdom to come to you full of light, / and at once all the demons, the children of darkness, flee. / As soon as the demons hear you calling on the King to come, / they do not wait for him to come and find them; / they flee at the report of him. For who can face the great King, / or come near where he is coming to give help? / Had an angel or a righteous man come, / the Accuser might have fought, or he might not. / But if that kingdom is shining as it comes, how / could he have the strength to break the brightness of that majesty? / Therefore, so that that kingdom would come to you, / the Son of God taught you to call on it when you pray. / And since you have invited it to come to you, you too must prepare / a place fit for that encampment to be honoured in. / Look, you are calling on the kingdom to come: prepare a place, / a house that is swept and full of holiness throughout. / The door of the house, which is the mouth: hang [?] over its doorway,

its door-leaves [?], unpainted, yet adorned in every way.
The middle of the house, which is the heart, sprinkle with purity:
all the thoughts that love beautiful things every day.
In the soul, which is the court of the house of the King who is coming,
burn spices as incense, good works, on every side.
On the floor of the house spread the fair carpet of love,
for where love dwells, there He wishes to be seen.
You have called in prayer for that kingdom to come to you,
and since you have called, it is coming: prepare a place where it may be honoured.
The one who was ranged to fight against you, see, he flees;
the King is coming to you, to take His lodging where He will lodge.
See whether you are angry, see whether you are troubled, see whether you are agitated;
see whether your soul has loved money, or greed.
See whether there is falsehood in you, a foul stench,
or fornication, the filth from which the King flees.
See whether there is deceit, and speech that turns two ways,
or whisperings, and an ear that leans toward the Accuser.
If these are there, drive them out, for the King is coming;
for if He comes and finds these, He will not dwell in you.
And if He turns back once you have brought Him in, then back too comes

the rebel, and he will ravage you with his tyranny.
Let your soul be a place worthy of the King's lodging,
that He may come and dwell, as you called Him to come to you.
This is why you were taught to call that kingdom
to come to you: so that you may make ready a clean place for it,
so that when it comes in splendour the Accuser may flee,
and you may shine with joy and receive it in holiness.
For you call: 'Your kingdom come to us, my Lord;
and may Your will be done on earth as in heaven.'
'Let Your will, my Lord, be served by us,' you say to Him,
'among human beings as among the spiritual Watchers.'
This is fitting for one who prays before God:
that he should yield all his requests to His will.
Our Lord Himself prayed in this way,
and said to the Father, 'Not my will, but Yours.'
So He taught you to plead in your prayers:
'May Your will, my Lord, be done on earth as in heaven.
As the angels continually carry out Your will,
so may human beings also obey You.
Let the earth thunder with congregations that praise You,
as heaven teems with troops that minister to You.'
Pray that Your will may stand above our will,

so that our will may be surrendered to Your will.
Desire that we may desire in You whatever You desire, we too,
so that we desire nothing more, but that all Your wishes may be done.
'Your will, my Lord, be done on earth as in heaven:
let human beings praise as the angels also praise.
As those ranks of Gabriel's company minister,
so let the churches on earth also minister without strife.
As those hosts of Michael's company shout aloud,
so let Your jubilation stir in our congregations with true love.
As that radiant assembly of the seraphim sanctifies,
let the throng of humankind sanctify You throughout the earth.
As that chariot, shimmering with visions, blesses,
let the Church cry out with trembling, "Blessed from His place."
As all the orders of praisers that are in heaven
obey You and serve You spiritually,
let the whole earth fulfil all Your wishes,
as heaven never departs from Your commandments.
Let the priests of earth, like the angels who are in heaven,
obey You and serve You in holiness.
In all forms, in all patterns, and in all ways,
may all Your wishes be done on earth as in heaven.'

This is the prayer that is able to grant every request
to the one who prays, from its divine provisions.
Whoever wishes to be among the perfect of God's household,
let him stand in this prayer with discernment.
This is the prayer of the Receiver of prayers:
He Himself taught us how the one who prays should pray.
The Son, who brings every petition in before His Begetter,
taught you how to speak to His Father when you pray.
According to the mind of the hidden Father He composed the petition
and placed it in your mouth, that you might pray to Him according to His mind.
He wished to show you how He wants you to speak to Him,
so that you would speak according to His will when you pray.
And as you have also learned, so it is right to pray,
so that everything that is needed is found for you in prayer.
'Give us the constant bread of the day': ask this of God;
for what does the life of the day require but bread?
Gold and silver and pearls, and beryls too,
precious stones, and fine linen, and handsome garments:
these lofty riches are no part of life,
for the body needs only the constant bread of the day.
And if you give it pearls from Cush and from India,

and withhold bread from it, it grows faint, dies, wastes away and crumbles.
Bread is what the body needs in order to live, and nothing else;
but because the world is empty, it asks for superfluities.
For the body does not eat gold if you give it,
nor jacinths, nor precious stones either.
A pearl has neither taste nor smell;
it is neither eaten nor drunk, and yet it is precious.
Why is it precious, except that the world is empty and lacking
in knowledge, and eager to acquire superfluities?
The king takes the day's bread from his kingdom,
and the labourer takes the day's bread from his labour.
The body's need, its want and its sustenance,
king and labourer receive alike, and they are equal.
And though the king has the produce of the whole earth,
they give him from it only the day's bread.
And though the labourer has only a day's wage,
that same constant bread of the day they do not withhold from him.
And what does gold or produce profit the king,
since he takes from his kingdom only a labourer's bread?
Nature has sufficiency and bread to live on,

and the poor man has sufficiency, and has bread.
And the gold he has acquired does not profit the rich man,
for only the constant bread of the day suffices him.
And so a measure is given by God to each person as a ration,
an equal share for each day, on its day, to live on.
If nature is forced to eat greedily,
to take more than the measure that is appointed,
its ration is cut short; it is weighed down and burdened,
and it stops and holds back from eating because it took too much.
It ate two days' ration at a single time,
and therefore for a day it falls short of food,
so that the day's ration is cut off from it, for what it ate was already the full amount;
and so it takes its food in order, as is fitting.
Nature stands like a creditor over the glutton,
and if he is greedy for food and eats too much,
it demands from him whatever surplus he has eaten,
and it also makes him sick and shakes that surplus out of him.
And so it gives him only the constant bread of the day,
for this suffices for a pleasant life.
This is why our Lord taught us to pray:
'Give us the constant bread of the day to live on,'

so that no one should seek gold and silver when he prays,
nor possessions, nor pleasures, nor advantages,
lest he be enticed and seek these superfluities:
in the bread of the day He set the limit of the prayer that asks to receive.
He set it as the prayer of the rich and of the poor,
so that it might rebuke us if we are greedy for more.
For if the poor man seeks anything else
but bread, he will be accused by the Giver.
And the rich man, again, when he prays 'Give us bread,'
is put in a strait, because he has a great deal of bread.
And he comes to know that the surplus laid up with him
is not his, but belongs to the hungry outside.
The day's bread that is lacking in the poor man's house
is laid up in his house, as though he were made steward for his fellow.
And if he does not bring it out and give from it to the one who hungers,
he is bound to be swallowed up by judgment before Justice,
when it accuses him: 'Why did you hide your brothers' ration,
while they went hungry and you grew proud in what was not yours?'
Therefore, 'Give us the constant bread of the day':
He taught him to pray so that he might give away the surplus he has,

and make himself equal with the poor in his possessions,
and eat with them of what God gave him in abundance.
And let him pray, 'Give us the constant bread of the day,'
openly, with the poor who are his brothers.
How beautiful is the prayer that the Son of God taught!
Blessed is he who has set it in his soul and shines with it.
All the beauties of righteousness and of perfection
are found in it by the one who learns it and prays it.
All fair and precious requests
are granted through it to the soul that asks of God.
All the gifts that fill with riches all who are in need
are given through it from the treasury of the Godhead.
'Forgive us our debts': the Son of God taught you to say this,
for He wishes to forgive; that is why He taught you what to say to Him.
For if His hands were not set on forgiving,
He would not have taught you to say, 'Forgive me my debts.'
But because He longs to forgive debtors,
He taught them also to plead for forgiveness.
'Forgive us our debts and our sins, my Lord': He taught them,
the children of His mystery, to say this to His Father when they pray.
He has given encouragement, because He wishes to forgive debtors,

and that is why He taught them to plead with Him for forgiveness.
Who would not rejoice in a creditor who teaches him
what to say to him when he goes in to see his face?
'Forgive us our debts': He wishes to hear it from the debtors,
so that He may give His justice a reason for forgiveness,
lest, when He forgives, He be blamed by His justice:
'Why do You forgive, when they do not plead for forgiveness?'
The paralytic too He questioned in this way as He was healing him,
so that He might learn from him whether he wished to be made whole.
And the debtors He taught to pray to Him,
'Forgive us our debts,' so that He would not forgive while they were not asking.
He wished to forgive, and He wished them to ask mercy of Him,
so that the gift too might be the more beautiful through the asking that takes place.
He requires discernment of them when they pray,
so that His mercy may not be mere laxity when He shows mercy.
See, your bond lies with God, before His justice,
and unless someone pleads, she does not release it from her hand.
And because He does not wish to distress His justice when He forgives you,
He taught you to plead for forgiveness when you pray,
so that His justice too, when she hears you pleading with Him,
may be stirred with love and pour out mercy on the debtors.

You say to Him, moreover, 'Forgive us, my Lord, as we have forgiven';
here He teaches you that unless you forgive, He does not forgive you.
He has given you the measure and agreed with you that as you measure,
so you too will be measured: take for yourself what you receive.
'How much forgiveness I give you, you know:
as much as you forgive the one who needs your forgiveness.'
It is a great fear for one who needs forgiveness,
that unless he forgives, he is not forgiven when he prays.
His judgment comes from himself, and his judgment rests on his conduct:
he has pronounced the sentence, and so it comes about as he said.
'Forgive us our debts as we have forgiven,' you say to Him;
and so He answers and deals with you as you prayed.
He knows how much you have forgiven; do not deceive yourself about it:
that is the measure, and by it He measures out to you what He gives you.
So be bold: ask forgiveness of God
as much as you have forgiven your fellow, if he has wronged you.
And unless you have forgiven, with what face do you ask Him
to forgive you, when the condition is laid down for how He will forgive?
Forgive your fellow, and forgive him abundantly, however much he owes;
then come and ask the same of God, and you will receive it.
Let the poor man too hear here what he should forgive,

for the word is common to rich and poor alike.
Let everyone forgive, for that prayer taught it to everyone,
the Son of God, who wishes everyone to live always.
Let the one who has gold forgive gold to his debtors,
and let the one who has bills [?] or accounts forgive these.
If he holds bonds of others, let him tear them up,
and let him go in and plead for forgiveness with a loud voice.
And so that they may tear up the great bond that stands against him,
let him not hesitate whether to tear up the small one that he holds.
But the poor man, who has neither business nor accounts,
neither debts nor claims, let him also forgive.
If someone has despised him, if someone has driven him away, if someone has struck him,
whatever cause there is that distresses him, let him forgive it.
If someone has cheated him of the wage for the work he did for him,
and he wants to curse him, let him forgive him instead, and not curse.
If someone quarrelled with him, or ever dragged him off by force,
let him put these things out of his mind and forgive as well.
If a poor man, his fellow, owes him a single obol,
let him forgive it, like the one who forgave a well-known talent.
And if no one owes him even a single word, let him forgive;
and if he has heard a word spoken maliciously by someone, he must be one of the forgivers.

The Son of God taught this prayer
to all human beings, so that all might be enriched by His teaching.
Let each one forgive: this one debts, that one accounts,
this one anger, that one a grudge, another an insult;
if his fellow strikes at him with some other mocking word,
for everyone is required to forgive when he prays.
Glorious and great, and full of the beauties of righteousness,
is the prayer which the Son of God taught that a person should pray.
Everything that nature needs to receive from God
He placed in the prayer, and gave it to the apostles of the world to teach.
'Lead us not, my Lord, into temptation' is in the prayer,
because all of nature is weak if it is put to the test.
Here the word calls for no ordinary hearing,
for among the learned it ranks far higher than its fellows.
That temptation which a person prays not to enter
the children of discipline consider with great understanding.
Yet for the one who listens I will tell
what kind of temptation the Son of God placed in the prayer.
When the Accuser struggles with a human being,
there is help from God beside that person.
Like a guard who neither slumbers nor sleeps,

so a hidden power guards human beings.
And when Satan stirs up a contest against a person,
there is an angel who helps him without his knowing it,
as happened with Joshua son of Jozadak,
the high priest, who was helped by an angel.
For without his perceiving it, the angel rebuked the Accuser,
and the prophet saw what took place, but the priest did not see it.
So it is always: beside every person there are angels
who drive hosts of demons away from him, so that they do him no harm.
And when a person wishes to please the Lord by his conduct,
the Accuser sets himself to fight against him.
And without his perceiving it, an angel too comes in secret
and helps him to overcome the evil one, if he is good.
And as long as a person stands in prayer before God,
Satan too stands there to mock him.
Then the angel also comes, like a guard,
and rebukes the evil one and drives him away from the person.
And when Satan has been defeated many times,
and the godly person has prevailed and won the victory,
the wicked one pleads, as he pleaded concerning Job,

that the help which guards him be taken away from him.
And in his wickedness he asks this of God:
that the Lord should let that person go, without help,
and that he, the evil one, should go down alone into the contest with him,
with no one to help or support him in the contest.
This is the temptation that our Lord taught
a person to pray that he might not enter.
This is the great contest unto blood,
of which Paul says, 'You have not yet reached it.'
In this contest the soul either conquers or is conquered,
for it is a contest in which it either kills or is killed.
For it goes down without help into the contest with Satan,
and the struggle is fearful because it is stripped of help.
This is the temptation which a person prays
not to enter, as he has learned from the One who knows all.
Into this contest Job went down when he struggled
with Satan without divine help.
That righteous man even perceived it, and said:
'See, His help is not in me now that I am being tried.'
For this contest is very fearful,

and few are those who come up from it victorious.
That is why our Lord taught a person to pray,
'Do not lead me into temptation, to be tried in it.'
Satan asked God concerning Job
that He take away from him the hidden power that helped him.
And the Lord said to His adversary, 'He is delivered into your hands,'
for He knew that the athlete would not give way.
And one man entered the contest with Satan,
while the Lord withdrew from the two of them like a spectator.
The Lord led that righteous man into temptation,
and from the great contest unto blood he carried off the victory.
Because the struggle is very hard, our Lord taught
a person to pray that he not be tried by temptation,
and that no one should seek to conquer without divine power,
lest he boast of the victory.
The one who flees from temptation humbles himself,
and hands the contest over to the One Victor, that He may fight it.
For he says to Him, 'Do not lead me into temptation,
but deliver me from the evil one, whose power is great.
Do not hand me over to the Adversary to struggle with me,
for without Your help [I cannot]; rather, You conquer him in me, the weak one.'

'Let not Your hidden help be withdrawn from me, that help which is
the power that goes down with the athletes into their contests.
Do not test me, for I know that I am weak;
let the whole contest be Yours, and You be the one who fights.
Yours are all the victories of all the victors:
conquer, for it befits You, and do not lead me into temptation.
Deliver me from the Adversary who struggles with me,
for without Your help I cannot overcome him.
Do not look to me to conquer in the great struggle unto blood:
take the contest for Yourself, and take the victory, for it befits You.
Deliver me from him, and Yours be the crown and the name,
and do not reckon to me either victory or triumph.
Deliver me from him, and let all the glory of the athlete's struggle
rest with You, for it is You who conquered the Adversary.
Deliver me from him, and let guilt run after me,
as I confess that I was a sinner and You acquitted me.
Apart from You I cannot conquer in the contest:
let me not be tried; deliver me from him without temptation.
In mercy deliver me from Satan who struggles with me,
for all victories befit You, that You should take them.
Deliver me from him, for Yours is the power,

and the kingdom, and the dominion, and the glory.
Even when someone conquers, whoever conquers, conquers through You,
for Yours is all strength and might.'
The prayer which the Son of God taught the children of His mystery
is set against the throng of demons to put them to flight.
And so too against all the powers of the evil one:
by it a person fights with the ruler who holds the air.
By it he calls on the Father to come down into the struggle with him,
to drive away from him the demons who hunger for the soul's blood.
By it the children of the Spirit are emboldened to call Him 'our Father',
and they make the Accuser tremble with the great Name.
By it a person calls for that kingdom to come to him,
to put to flight the powers of the evil one that surround him.
By it a person confesses that he submits to the will of the Father,
that it be done on earth as it is in heaven.
By it a person asks for the day's bread without greed,
and leaves aside all the superfluities that are not needed.
By it a person also seeks forgiveness from God,
having promised that he too forgives his debtors.
By it a person flees from the temptation of the great contest,
beseeching God with supplication that he may not enter it.

By it a person calls on the Helper to come to him,
to deliver him from that enemy of humankind who fights against him.
It teaches you that all power and glory
and dominion belong to the Lord: to Jesus be glory.
Here ends the homily on “Our Father who art in heaven,” composed by Mar Jacob.

By the holy Mar Jacob.
Homily 51.
On the young man who said to our Lord,
“What shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
(Matthew 19:16; Mark 10:17; Luke 18:18. E. N)

Dark and cunning is the evil world, and full of snares,
of slippery places and every evil for those who journey in it.
You, our Lord, are the good companion and the great light,
and the road full of life and blessings for whoever walks in it.
Blessed is the one who has hated wealth and possessions,
and has bowed his shoulder and taken up the yoke of your poverty.
Whoever owns nothing in the world, if he possesses you,
is far richer than all the rich of the whole world.
And if a man possesses the whole world but does not possess you,
he is poor and needy, ashamed and despised, and full of woes.
You are the great possession, our Lord, Son of God,
and the pearl that is never stolen from those who acquire it.
The world is false, and whoever trusts in his possessions
deceives himself, for the wealth he has found is not real.
The shoot [?] filled out and grew rich for a day, and tomorrow it is gone;
and where is the wealth, when its owner is not there to delight in it?
In the wealth of a dream only a fool rejoices,
and a possession that lasts only a day no one should love.
A man lies down rich, and when he wakes there is no wealth;
why then does he rejoice? He is only deceived by falsehood.
If possessions do not pass away, O possessor,

you, the possessor, pass away from your possessions.
Either they leave you while you look on, and pass from you,
or you leave them to others against your will.
There is no way for all your wealth to remain yours
unless you have hated it and scattered it among the needy.
If it is yours, then give it to whoever is in need,
so that what you need may be found for you as true gain.
Why does it deceive you, entice you and trouble you,
so that every day you run after a gain that does not last?
Look, you run to add to your possessions every day,
and once you have gathered them all, in a single hour—
look, you are wise, you are bright, you are quick,
you are capable, you provide, you gather in;
and capability and wisdom and brightness
have filled your house with many good things—
yet if only a slight attack of fever should come upon you,
all that capability and brightness come to nothing.
And the wisdom that loved wealth comes wholly to nothing,
and all these things that were dear to you become hateful to you.
You become an obedient slave to sickness,
and you let your possessions slip from a hand that cannot save you.

Where is your running? Where is all your wisdom?
Where is the care that kept you busy over profits?
Look, you are weak, you are dazed, you are helpless;
look, you are burning with fever, and who will bring you relief?
Call your possessions, bring your gold, gather your wealth;
if they rescue you from distress, then they are yours.
But if wealth cannot put out a fever,
how does it profit you? Or what, then, is its profit?
Do not wear yourself out over what does not love you as you have loved it;
it is not yours, so why do you exhaust yourself over what is not yours?
Look, it is laid up and guarded, and you watch over it lest it slip away;
yet it stays, and you are carried off, and what are you doing?
If you wished, it would be easy for your wealth to be yours,
by sending it on the King’s road by the hands of the poor.
It would go before you to the lofty place full of blessings,
and it would all be yours, since you had sent it on ahead.
Why do you hurry to furnish a house that is not yours?
Your dwelling is a tent, and you are very anxious over its affairs.
It is uprooted and folded away because of the seasons;
for that great building of yours, which is everlasting, it is folded away [?].
Do not toil too much with your skill for strangers,

for everything of yours that stays here is not yours.
Why are you mistaken, though you are wise, O capable one?
Why are you skilled in empty things, O wise one?
Why do you love a house that falls, O man of knowledge,
while your soul has fallen into iniquity and you do not raise it up?
Build, build up the soul that you overthrew by the iniquity of your hands,
and then take care to build a house that is not yours.
This is iniquity: that a house is built and full of good things,
while the soul, which is the King’s fortress, lies in ruins.
What is yours you have ruined, and with what is not yours you are so capable:
the soul uprooted, and the house prosperous and full of good things.
I do not seek to become a teacher to you, good friend,
for no one lacks the knowledge of how he may live.
Every wise person knows what profits him,
and in every human being there is the knowledge of what to do.
Everyone knows, but not everyone is willing to do it;
for what is lacking is good will, not knowledge.
Level is the road that leads to life, and full of light,
and all the commandments are set along it like lamps.
Whoever wishes to enter into life, the door is open;
and if he is willing, nothing is demanded of him, and he enters at once.

It is not teachers that are lacking in the evil world;
it is the world that has hated the teaching of God’s house.
God himself became a teacher to humankind,
and by the commandments he set down in the scriptures he made them wise.
He gave a law full of light from Mount Sinai,
and by its observances he marked out the road to the kingdom.
He sent his Son like a day of great light,
and the whole world shone by him, grew fair, and gained life.
And after this teaching full of wonder,
by which the whole world learned and shone like daylight,
a certain lacking man was asking the Son of God,
“What shall I do to inherit the life of God’s house?”
A proud, empty young man, full of arrogance,
asked wrongly, when there was no need for the question.
With a haughty spirit and a mind full of pride
he framed a question to show himself a man of knowledge.
Yet from his very words one can tell he was no man of knowledge,
for had he known, he would not have asked, “What shall I do?”
Tell me, wretch: are you wise, or are you simple?
Do you want to learn, or do you wish to be a teacher?
The road of life, for the whole race of humankind,

God has revealed, so that they may walk in it without concealment.
But if the road of life is still not visible to you,
why, when it is revealed, is it hidden from you, if you are wise?
If you know and still ask, you are presumptuous;
and if, again, you still do not know, you are simple.
Either way, your question shows that you are lacking,
for wealth has puffed you up, and look, you speak extravagantly.
“What shall I do to inherit life?” he was asking
of the one who sees all that is in the thoughts of the heart.
He justified himself and went up and stood on high ground,
and began to talk with our Savior like a man of discernment.
He wanted to show himself to the crowd as a wise man,
one who had gone out in search of new life to gain it.
He was rich, and he spoke with confidence in his wealth,
for the spirit of wealth has a loud voice in gatherings.
The mouth of poverty is stopped wherever it is,
and it is given no place in the world to speak.
The poor man is silent, and no one listens to him at all,
and even if he is wise, they do not let him speak.
But the rich man, though he be simple, is high-spirited;
his speech is bold, and he has room to speak.

So as a rich man he sought to speak with our Savior,
the foolish young man, thinking he would win praise.
“What shall I do to inherit life?” he was asking him—
an obvious matter that needed no question.
Our Lord heard him, and knew beforehand what he would say,
and in his humility he bore patiently with that haughtiness.
Our Lord said, “If you wish to live, keep the commandments”:
the first bandage that Moses had applied, he left on his wound.
He did not change the bandage, for he saw that he had not yet been helped
by the first bandage that the great prophet had applied.
Moses brought down a great bandage from Mount Sinai,
and with it he bound up the wound of the people who had been struck.
Like a healing herb full of grace for the wounded,
he applied the law to the people, bound it on, and it healed.
And when the wound of iniquity had been rid of its swelling,
the Son of God came and changed it (for another bandage.
Moses commanded that no one commit adultery, and he held back adultery;
but his Lord said, “Do not even look upon a woman with desire.”
The Son of God, by his wondrous teaching,
held back from people the very thought that gives birth to adultery.

This bandage, which does not leave even the scar of the wound,
the Lord of Moses applied to the soul when he bound it up.
Moses commanded that no one covet what is not his,
and taught the soul not to be greedy for more.
But our Lord came and taught people
that even what is their own they should give to whoever is in need.
For the wounds of the world the Son of God changed the bandage,
but the physician’s mind was one and did not change.
Little by little he treated the wound as he bound it,
so that the sick man would not run from him if it hurt.
Had he said to the adulterer, “Do not desire,”
the man would not have listened, for the word would have been too hard for him.
Nor, had he said to one who plunders his fellows,
“Go and give away what is yours,” would he have responded.
First he restrained wickedness in those who practiced it,
so that they might first cease from the evils being done.
And by the law, as with muzzles and fetters, he bound
the evil world, to make it cease from evils.
Then, once people had been trained to learn what is fair,
he raised them another step toward the good.
And like a teacher full of love (toward his disciples,

he would draw them little by little toward his teaching.
A skilled scribe does not write out something new for a child,
but goes over with him again the first reading he took up.
And a good physician does not change the bandage on a wound
unless the wound shows that it has healed.
Therefore our Physician, our Scribe, the Son of God,
did not add further teaching for that rich man,
but required of him that by that first law
he should train himself, and then be raised to spiritual things.
Stay, young man, with the commandments of the great Moses;
read the law and do all that is written in it.
Unless you have done it, I will not go further and teach you what to do.
It is that law that brings you in to new life;
read it, read it, and it will teach you what to do.
“If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.”
The fool says, “Which are they, that I may keep them?”
That lacking man did not even know what they were,
and so he asked to learn which they were.
He set himself up as a righteous and wise man,

and showed that he was both a sinner and a simpleton.
He had no sense of righteousness, nor even of what it is,
nor had wisdom ever met the fool who was so presumptuous.
He did not even know the divine commandments,
which they are, those by which the world lives.
Without reading them or keeping them he came up to our Lord,
to be a questioner in the assembly before many.
He tripped himself up and was exposed as no man of knowledge,
but a fool who meddles in a matter he does not understand.
The wretch asked, “What shall I do to inherit life?”
and was told, “Keep the commandments,” and he did not know them.
He began to inquire which they were, so that he might keep them,
and the skilled Scribe went over them again and did not weary of him:
“Do not steal,” he said,
“nor bear false witness at all in the world.
Honor your father and honor your mother, and you will have life,
for whoever keeps the commandments lives by them.”
Then the proud man began to resort to contradiction,
saying, “All these I have kept.”
Greatly he lied, greatly he presumed, and greatly he erred,
and from the height he fell into the pit of falsehood.

Because he presumed to ask without knowledge,
he was confounded and fell back on contradiction.
He claimed to have kept all the commandments,
and insisted, moreover, that he had kept them since childhood.
But since that young man did not know which they were,
how could he have kept them all as a child, as he claimed?
In his youth he was simple, worthless, and full of confusion;
in his childhood what did he know, except how to sin?
Our Lord did not wish to cut him off from his teaching,
that Spiritual One, because he saw that he was carnal.
So he left him in the hands of Moses the scribe to train him,
and would then give him the book of perfection to read.
But he began insisting about the commandments, that he had kept them,
that he had done them and fulfilled them since childhood.
And with that lofty horn the fool began to butt,
raising his voice and piling up words of falsehood:
“The commandments, I tell you, I have kept since my childhood;
add something new for me from your teaching.”
Tell me, young man: have you made light of Moses and his observances,
and do you now seek more from me, that I should tell you?
All the commandments of Moses are kept, as you say,

and now you seek other, new commandments.
So you are higher than the law and the commandments,
and above Moses who laid down the law.
You are perfect, you are spiritual, as you say,
and you wish to hear a word of perfection in a spiritual way.
I too have a great and spiritual word,
but I am sparing you, because I see that you are carnal.
The wound of your soul is not healed enough to come to perfection,
and so I have left you to Moses, the physician, to treat you.
That reading which Moses left you, you have not finished,
and so I have not given you the great book.
You fall short in the old, which you have not completed,
and yet you are set on reading the new with brilliance.
It is not that I lack a lofty word to offer you;
it is you who have no ear that hears spiritually.
But if you wish to be perfect, as you say,
go, sell all your possessions and give to the needy.
Do not keep for yourself anything in the world of all you have acquired;
if you leave yourself two garments to wear, you are not spiritual.
All that you have on earth, scatter among the poor,

and do not keep back for yourself anything of your possessions.
All the property you have, sell it, and your holdings [?],
and your goods too, and give to the needy without sparing.
To the poor give all that you have, and do it gladly;
treasure will be laid up for you on high—and come, follow me.
And once you have stripped off the affairs of the evil world,
I will teach you how to live with my disciples.”
The young man heard a word that rose higher than the law,
and he shrank from the matter, because he saw he was not equal to it.
The lancet cut into his swollen wound, and the weakling fainted;
he could not bear the cutting, for he was sick.
His heart was broken by the spiritual teaching,
because he was held fast by that bodily possession.
He saw how lofty is the step of perfection;
he looked, he fell back, and he could not climb it.
He was troubled with anxious thoughts,
and could not return a word to our Lord.
Distress rose like smoke from his mind,
and dimmed and put out the light of his face with grief.
The pain within had gathered and stolen the beauty without,
and the whole assembly saw that he grew ugly and his flesh [?].

The color of his face, which had been glowing, changed,
and the lofty speech of the man who was rich was put to shame.
He bowed his head, who had walked with his neck held high,
and his spirit fell, who had thought himself righteous.
He saw the road on which the perfect walk,
and he turned back, unable to walk on it.
The whole assembly saw and recognized him for a liar,
a talker, a proud man, and not genuine.
And the humility of the Son of God shone out,
and his wisdom and his teaching, how bright they were.
The assembly realized that he had indeed been sparing the rich man,
and had not cut him off from that teaching at the outset.
His compassion and his gentleness were seen:
how he wants every person to live, wherever he may be,
and how he heals without exposing people,
but bears patiently with them and binds them up gently.
The young man asked him, “What shall I do to inherit
life?” and he knew that he would not accept the teaching.
Yet knowing this, he did not rebuke him before many,
for it is not his way to expose anyone who comes to him.

He did not say to him, “You cannot; you are not equal to it;
you are not genuine, you are a liar, you are mad—go away.”
Instead he received him, listened to him, and heard him out gently,
and applied a bandage that would have healed him had he heeded it.
Had he listened when he was told, “Keep the commandments,”
and gone and kept them, he would not have come to that exposure.
But he tried to snatch a step that was not his,
and he fell, and became a laughingstock in the assembly (for how he had presumed.
Love of the world had taken hold of him like a fever,
and it silenced him so that he could not speak.
He was bound by his gold and his possessions, and because
the Son of God sought to set him free from them, the weakling faded.
Very lofty for those who travel it is the road of life,
and few are those who journey to the high place.
It has its milestones and also its inns of righteousness,
and for every rank there is room on it to walk.
If someone gives a cup of water to one who is thirsty,
he is walking on it, and has a reward for his uprightness.
If he speaks only a good word about his neighbor,
he is close to the road of life and walks on it.

And the more he adds to his good deeds, the more room he has
to travel the road and go up into life in brightness.
That rich man, had he stayed with the commandments
of the great Moses, would easily have inherited new life.
And had he sold all he owned, as he was commanded,
and given to the needy, he would then have lived by the running of his course.
To the height of that higher road he was not equal,
not even had he scattered all his wealth among the poor.
Our Lord had another word to tell him,
and that is why he was saying to him, “Come, follow me.”
For when a man has distributed all he owns to the poor,
he has not by that alone become perfect and spiritual.
A man is indeed rid of his affairs
when all that he owns has been given away, so that he may gain his life;
it throws off the world’s burden from him, so that it becomes light for him,
and he may run unhindered on the road of righteousness.
“Go, then, sell, give to the needy, and come, follow me,
and I will show you the whole road of perfection.”
And had he sold and followed him, as he told him,
he would have heard yet another word, higher than the first.

He would have said to him, had he wished (to follow him:
“If you can stomach it, make ready your cheek for the one who strikes you.
And if evil men take your tunic from you,
leave it in their hands (and let them take your cloak as well.
If they hate you and persecute you, bless them,
and pray for them while they strike you, and love them.
If they bring you to judgment, do not worry about what to say,
and if they persecute you, be mad with love, without murmuring.
Take no staff for the road, and no bag,
no purse, and no provisions for even a single day.
In short, do not worry about what you will eat, if you are my disciple;
and anything beyond these things comes from the evil one.”
That rich man, without even hearing these things, lost heart;
he took fright, and did not even stay to hear them.
He heard the call for his possessions to be sold, and was confounded,
for he did not want to sell anything of what he owned.
He loved that possession, which is bounded by time,
more than the whole great road of perfection.
And because he heard that it was to be distributed to the poor,
he did not stay to listen, for love of wealth had filled him entirely.

When a man sells all he owns and gives to the needy,
he still has to begin walking the road of perfection.
It is like a tree: when it is uprooted from one place,
it takes labor to plant it in another.
So when a man has scattered all he owns among the poor,
he has only just uprooted himself from the world like a tree,
and he needs labor to plant himself in the new world;
he needs watering and all the cultivation of righteousness.
(If he does not love those who hate him, as he was commanded,
(if he will not consent to offer his cheek to the one who strikes him,
if he grows slack and worries about tomorrow, he is not fit
to be planted there, in the land of life, like a tree.
He is uprooted from here when the poor have taken his possessions,
and is planted there, and needs much care to grow.
And if divine husbandry does not water him,
he will not be allowed to bear fruit in the new world.
Nor is he fit for that place merely because he has been uprooted from this world
and has scattered his wealth, unless he lives spiritually.
Nor, even if planted in the land of life, will he bear fruit
if his mind wanders about the world after its affairs.
Nor can one who owns nothing in the world inherit

new life if he longs to acquire anything.
That is why our Lord spared the rich man,
and did not show him which is the road of perfection,
for he knew he could not walk on it,
since he was tightly bound by his possessions, and they would not let him go.
The young man tested our Lord, and he taught him what to do;
but once he had learned, he would not do as he was commanded.
Love of wealth strangled his soul, which was dark.
May they possess you, my Lord, for you are great wealth to those who possess you.

Here ends the homily on the young man who said to our Lord,
“What shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
composed by the blessed Mar Jacob the teacher.

By the holy Mar Jacob.
Homily 52.
On the son who squandered his property.

Your word, our Lord, is light through and through to the one who loves it; / by it I am given light to tell your story in the world. / You are broad daylight, our Lord, to the one who journeys by you:
