by your light I will set out to walk without stumbling. / The world is dark, and you are radiant, Son of God; / by your light I will walk with you, in you, toward the One who begot you. / The road of the world is full of every stumbling-block and snare; / be a smooth road for me, our Lord, and I will walk in you. / Your company is light, and you are the Sun of righteousness; / with you I will journey in a land cleared of stumbling-blocks. / The earth is full of pits and snares and slippery places, / but whoever holds on to you is lifted up and raised above falling. / Peace and light and a smooth road are you, our Lord; / give me your hand, that I may walk in your peace and see your beauties. / See, the creatures set your praise in motion by their forms; / open my mouth too, to praise your might. / See, the days and the nights, within their bounds, / open and close to carry your story out to all the earth. / Evenings and mornings at their watches, in their seasons, / rouse humankind with discernment to glorify you. / Summers and winters, with their changes and their fruits, / teach the earth that you are the one who changes their seasons. / Cold and heat, which come and go in their courses,

tell of you, how skilful you are in your works. / The hours of the day, and the four watches of the night, / all offer distinct praises to your creative power. / The sea, with its ships, its storms and its [?], / tells in wonder how awesome is your workmanship. / Raging waves together with mighty winds / sing your story: how wondrous is your might! / The great abyss, and Leviathan with the dragons, / in the depth of the seas, are upheld by you within their bounds. / All the dry land of the earth, its mountains and its heights, / praises you, for you carry it so that it does not fall. / The heavens, see, tell your glory by their nature, / and the firmament shows the work of your hands, how mighty you are. / The great tent that your creative power stretched out and spread, / see, stands stretched over every border and is full of your praise. / The sun and the moon, with their settings and their risings, / in their great course rouse the world to your praises. / Through me too, Lord, set your praise in motion, like a rich man / who freely gives every need to those who ask him, / so that my word about you may be for your praise, / in plain words, without the twistings of presumption.

Mute natures praise your name richly; / stir me boldly, more than them, to glorify you. / It befits your image to sing your praise with discernment, / better than these that are not free, which are driven by you. / To me alone among creatures belongs freedom, / while they praise you in the driven courses of their natures. / Not by its own will does the sun shine and the moon grow fair; / bound is the course, driven by forces. / Your great power compels all of them to praise, / and it is not their freedom that chooses to praise your majesty. / For me, a free being, it is fitting if I choose praise, / for my will has authority, and I neglect or am stirred to praise. / And if I neglect it, justice swallows me up, / for justice demands that free sons should praise with discernment. / Therefore I will praise you, my Lord, while I tremble, / for I am not worthy; see, I am bold, though I am not sufficient. / All mouths are bound to praise you, / and who is worthy to sing praise? / You, my Lord, are worthy that all creatures should praise you, / with word and voice, and without voice, in their forms. / Stir up the discerning to praise on behalf of the creatures,

the silent ones, whose due it is to praise. / The Son of God, who came into our world for our sake— / who can repay him, even if he is never slack in praising him? / For sinners the Son of God went up on the cross, / to turn them to repentance, and see, they are idle. / His loud voice, which split rocks and tore open tombs, / did not urge us to seek his face in repentance. / The love of the world, like a fever, see, clings to us; / the Physician touched us and gave health, but it has not left us. / Love of gold, a fever more bitter than pains, / has taken root in our soul and will not yield to health. / Sins lay in wait for us on the road of the world like brigands, / and we do not cry out for deliverance to escape them. / Our soul has grown dark from the possessions it loved, / and the light has dawned, but it does not open the door for it to enter. / The Chastiser struck with rod upon rod like a judge, / but our hard heart has not been corrected of its evils. / Like thieving slaves we were thrashed for our folly, / and from the blows we rebelled all the more. / That we might hate the world, he afflicts and overturns us in it, / but because its love is woven into our soul, we have not let it go.

That we might flee from the world, he shakes us with upheavals, / and because we loved it greatly, see, we are worn down by this world. / Evil has grown strong, and see, the love of money is glued fast / to people like a live coal, and see, they burn with it. / It has ruined the world and destroyed its beauties and its works, / and see, it is overturned and troubled and full of falsehood and lies. / Love of gold has ruined the road to the Kingdom, / and see, it has laid a hand on the saints to corrupt them. / Into the bright place where the Trinity is served / it has entered like the serpent into Paradise, and see, it troubles it. / It has led priests astray to acquire gold, and who can be found / to be sound, when the salt of the earth has lost its savor? / At the head of the spring Satan has stirred up the waters by his hateful counsel, / and who can drink, when all creation has been muddied for it? / We were commanded not to own two coats in the world, / and see, many things are heaped up for us—what shall I say? / He did not allow us shoes or a staff to carry on the road, / and see, we carry beds along with their coverings. / He commanded us not to go about with a bag from place to place, / and see, purses of gold are laid up for us—who would not weep? / We do not have that teaching of the household of John,

or of the household of Simon, for gold has ruined all its beauty. / That disciple of Paul has now been corrupted, / for see, the disciples have acquired villages and their hamlets. / They have become shearers of the sheep and flocks of the Christians, / though they were commanded to shepherd the sheep of the Son of God. / Instead of souls, see, the disciples have acquired cattle, / and when the Lord of the sheep comes, what will they say to him? / 'Give away what is yours,' your Master taught you, O disciple; / how then are you now rich from what is not yours? / Possessiveness in disciples is theft: / Judas taught it, and its master is not Simon. / Ananias stole from his property and from its price, / and when Simon Cephas perceived it, he struck down his body. / What then will become of one who steals what is not his, / when see, Simon's Lord sees him—will he let it pass? / The Just One has by no means neglected his demands; / he kindles fire to cast the greedy into Gehenna. / He sends his Spirit to bring them to repentance, / and if they do not come, see, a burning coal pursues them in judgment. / Examine people in the light, O disciple, / and teach and stir the one who does not fear Gehenna.

Do not acquire possessions, and so teach the one who hears you, / that the wealth of the world is a noose for the one who acquires it. / The Tishbite, who acquired nothing, see, is in heaven, / and Gehazi, who acquired, see, is clothed with leprosy and a foul name. / Simon Cephas, who left what was his, became master of the house, / and Judas, who took a bribe, bought himself a noose. / Judge now between the one who acquires and the one who does not: / who has grace, and who has a good name? / The great serpent who drove Adam out of Paradise / is the one who teaches you to acquire gold, O disciple. / From that bitterness that dripped from him in the garden of trees / he is ready to give you to drink when he teaches you to acquire gold. / That teaching which he cast into Eve's ear / he casts into your heart when he leads you to mammon. / The love of wealth is the fruit full of death / that Eve plucked from that tree of knowledge. / The Tree of Life seeks to give life only / to people who acquire no excess. / Christ teaches: 'Hate gold, and come, acquire life'; / and the serpent whispers: 'Acquire gold and take pride in it.'

And see, the teaching of the Son of God is despised and overturned, / while after the serpent's teaching the whole world runs. / Wealth is beloved, and even the disciples are corrupted by it, / who ought to have acquired nothing but our Lord. / See, they have gone out after wealth without discernment, / and the love of money clings to them like a live coal. / The serpent's counsel is greatly loved, though it is murderous, / while the doctrine of the Son of God is despised and trampled. / No one makes room for the word or for teaching, / for evil has multiplied, and teachers are swallowed up in ruin. / Pupils do not wish to profit from teaching, / nor does the teacher lay money on the table. / In the love of gold, as in a sleep, teaching slumbers, / so that everyone grows rich as in a dream that does not come true. / Everyone knows that wealth does not profit its owners, / and everyone says that the world and its wealth pass away. / The one who acquires nothing in the world is praised, / yet no one wishes to hate wealth as he hated it. / Everyone loves and praises righteousness, / and everyone runs away from it and does not practice it.

Sin is hateful, and no one wishes to run from it; / they insult it while serving it in their deeds. / When the lofty story of one of the righteous is told, / everyone says, 'Who will grant me to be like that?' / He is buried in sin and yet drawn toward righteousness, / and he belittles himself, though had he not willed it he would not sin. / Righteousness is easy for the whole world to acquire, / and if the whole world wished, it would acquire it. / Wealth is not easy for everyone to acquire, though he loves it, / nor does everyone who wishes become rich as he wishes. / But with God, whoever wishes becomes righteous, / for no one is prevented from acquiring righteousness. / For God has given freedom to human beings, / and by his freedom a person acquires righteousness. / In the same way freedom also does wrong, / and it is not prevented, for if it were prevented it would not be freedom. / And that human beings have freedom equally / you may perceive from the teaching of the Son of God. / If this were a time when doctrine was loved, / I would also speak of freedom, that it is equal for all. / It is not that one is unfree and another free, / for everyone is equal both in nature and in freedom.

For God gave equally limbs, / and a constitution, and freedom to human beings. / Whoever wishes to do evil has the power to do it, / and no one stops the one who practices righteousness. / And that human beings have freedom equally / you learn from that parable of the younger son. / Full of light is the doctrine of the Son of God; / O you who are darkened, shine in the daylight of righteousness! / In the story of the younger son who squandered all he had, / you have something to learn about freedom, that it is equal for all. / 'A certain man,' he said, 'had two sons,' / an elder son and a younger son, of one father. / In the parable he called God the Father 'a man,' / and the two sons the whole race of humankind. / And because it contains both the righteous and sinners, / he named them the elder son and the younger son. / He called the righteous the elder son because they were / with God and loved him greatly from the beginning, / and the son [?] those who only at the last drew near to God. / The younger son, who said to his father, 'Give me my portion,' / is as though a person should say, 'Let me do all my will.'

The father divided and gave the property to the two brothers; / by the property that was divided he meant freedom. / 'He divided his property between them,' he says, as if to say: / he made that freedom equal and divided it among human beings. / The righteous and the sinner have one freedom, / and the Lord gave it equally to the one and to the other. / That property which the father divided between the two brothers / is the freedom he gave equally to human beings. / And the sinner, who was named the younger son, / took freedom as his portion from his father's house. / He went out and went to a country far from his father's house, / and lived there in wantonness, with reckless revelry. / And that property his father gave him when he divided it / he spent wickedly, and became needy in an evil life. / The far country to which that sinner went / is the evil will that is far from God. / A person removes his heart from God and then sins, / as if he had gone off to another country to sin there; / and as though the Lord were not there and did not see him, / he sins, and the Lord is not in his thoughts. / That is why it is written that he went to a far country

and squandered his goods while living in wantonness. / He removed himself from God while he sinned, / and enslaved his freedom to the service of vanities. / Virginity, the great treasure that nature possesses, / he ruined with adultery and fornication, and it passed from him. / He also despised the holiness of the state of the married, / and did not order himself to live chastely. / He enslaved himself to the love of the belly and to frivolity, / and lost all his freedom in his folly. / When a person is far from God, he does these things, / as though the Lord were not there to see his wickedness. / But this one, while he lived in wantonness, / was overtaken there by want and poverty. / Whoever is far from God is very poor, / hungry and weary, and can find no life at all. / Whoever hears the word of our Lord clearly / fears to sin, lest he remove himself from God. / That evil will which the younger son acquired / placed him far from God while he sinned. / And when he was brought low, and sin had ruined his freedom, / he went to one of the lords of the country to become his slave.

The lords of the country the Son of God calls demons, / for through error they became lords and gods. / In that very country where people removed themselves from God, / gods and lords came in to be worshipped. / The lofty horn of idolatry was raised up in it, / and people were enslaved to the service of vanity. / Devils came in and stood at the lofty head of idolatry, / and became like lords to the world, to be worshipped in it. / And in that country where sin is served in great measure, / demons and devils are its lords, as has been said. / And the younger son, when he had removed himself from his father, / went out to one of the lords of the country and became his slave. / The sinner went astray when he removed himself from God, / and enslaved himself to a devil who loves vanities. / The devil of love of the world, to whom he enslaved himself, seized him / and handed him over to the evil passions of desire. / He sent him, it says, to feed swine, and he longed / to be filled with the carob pods, and no one gave him any. / By swine our Lord in the parable meant the passions, / and the desires of the evil world are like carob pods. / Let everyone tremble at the meaning of the great parable,

and let no one sin, if he hears it clearly. / The parable teaches, beyond dispute, the one who perceives / that when a person sins he is far from God. / It also makes known to us that when a person has fallen into sin, / he attaches himself to a devil who inflames him with desires. / And that very devil, who loves vanities and is devoted to them, / uses them to provoke the person who serves him. / And as a herdsman made to tend swine runs about, / so he serves vanity for nothing, without profit. / Woe, sinner, how cast down you are when you sin, / in a country far from God, where he is not! / Woe to you, wretch, to what kind of lord you have enslaved yourself— / to a devil who has entangled you in vanities so that he may drink your blood! / Hate sin because of the devil who is its master, / for he makes desires look beautiful before sinners. / Do not enslave yourself to one of the lords of the country of wickedness, / for see, you have the Lord of all countries. / One is your Lord; do not go off to lords; / the Lord is your Lord—renounce the devil, who is not your lord. / Hate sin, because it is beloved of Satan;

you are free; do not enslave yourself to vanities. / Do not ruin that freedom which was given to you / by God, by enslaving it to desires. / Do not leave your father's house through the wickedness of your hands / for a country far from freedom and from integrity. / By the fearful parable that the Son of God set down in his book, / tremble at the wickedness by which people ruined freedom. / The weak son attached himself to one of the lords of the country, / to the demon who leads people astray from God. / And he sent this one to feed swine, and he longed / to fill his belly with carob pods, and could not. / For desires produce hunger, not satiety, / like carob pods, which are not wholesome food. / He longed, and they did not let him fill his belly, / for no one can make his deeds run as his desire would have them. / The one taken captive by love of money desires gold, / but he cannot acquire as much gold as he desires. / The adulterer wishes to defile his neighbor's wife, / but she runs away free, and the fool is ashamed that he did not get his way. / With hateful desire he wishes to commit fornication with many,

but not all of them yield to his wantonness. / He wishes to wear fine garments, and they are not to be had, / and he already craves food, and he has none. / For he cannot fill his belly with carob pods, / nor do they let him carry out his will as far as he wishes. / He desires greatly, and his desire is never fully satisfied, / and every day he needs to be sated with desires. / There is no way to be satisfied with carob pods, / nor to be sated when a person desires vanities. / The sinner grows weary, and his soul gains nothing from its weariness; / he feeds swine—hard is the labor and shameful the wage. / He wanders over mountains and heights and stumbling places, / and the flock is unruly and harasses the one who tends it. / Evil are the brutish passions, and full of death, / and the fool runs after desires without being sated. / Sins are snares, and love of gold a noose; / lechery is a desire full of stinking dung. / The lust of the eyes is slippery ground in a smooth place; / anger is a serpent that spews bitterness that kills the soul.

Great is the weariness the sinner suffers in the labor of his road, / and if he does not turn back from stumbling, at the end there is fire. / Sin wore out the younger son, who served it much, / and he was exhausted by the desires he had loved. / The wretch saw that he could not satisfy them, / nor did they let him have them as he wished. / The wretch was distressed at his stumbling and his affliction, / and at his slavery, as he remembered that he had been free. / The sinner reflected that had he not willed it, he would not have sinned, / and had he not wished to serve wickedness, no one would have forced him. / And as if from the sleep of desires he stirred and wailed, / for he saw that he was living in these contemptible conditions. / He came to himself—come, listen and marvel, O discerning one: / whoever sins becomes far even from himself. / When, it says, he came to himself, he said this: / 'How many hired men in my father's house have their fill of bread!' / He came to himself, for he had been far even from himself / while he was far from God and served wickedness. / Whoever knows what the soul is finds it hard to sin, / lest its lofty and natural beauty be corrupted. / And when a person forgets God, he forgets himself,

and remembers neither the soul nor God. / He came to himself, he who wished to come to God, / and at once he knew who he was, whose son, and in what state. / He saw himself, and became clear to himself in his own person, / and he trembled because he had sinned, and turned back to come to his father's house. / He saw that beautiful nature which had been his possession, / how corrupted it was by ugly desires. / He saw that God had created it beautiful and without blemish, / and by its own will it had fallen into sin and become hateful. / He came to himself, for while he sinned he had not been with himself, / and he knew what it was, and grieved for its beauty that had been corrupted. / As soon as he came and saw himself, he saw God, / and perceived from whom he had removed himself while he sinned. / He remembered his father's great house and his servants, / and his halls and his beautiful things. / He remembered that great table of his father, / full of plenty, while he himself received only in want. / The wretch thought of his father's servants and hired men, / and of the table at which even outsiders have their fill. / For repentance, as soon as it draws near to the sinner, / remembers God, and his greatness, and his servants,

and the saints, how near they are to God, / and the righteous, how beautiful their rewards; / how much beauty there is for the chosen in God's house, / and in what rank the perfect stand, victorious; / and how many righteous ones God has who are near him, / while he is cast out and far from God by the wickedness he has done. / As soon as a person turns to come to repentance, / he ponders all these things with groaning, / embittered over those beauties he has lost, / grieved for his freedom, how cheap it has become, / while shame stands over him like a creditor, / so that he bows his head, ashamed of the wickedness he has done. / The sinner is contemptible because he has lost these beauties / which nature possesses, and has become hateful, bearing trembling. / He sees others in excellence and perfection / and righteousness, and he is humbled. / Everyone who drew near to God has won and been praised, / while the sinner is ashamed and hateful, and everyone rebukes him. / He bows his head, and is not even permitted to look up to heaven, / and his mouth is shut, and he has no strength to pray. / He sees that he has spent the greater part of his days in vanity:

and sinned greatly, and corrupted his soul, which had been beautiful. / He is wretchedly far from God because of his wickedness, / while other people are near to Him through their discernment. / Though freedom is the same for him and for the righteous, / he fell into sin, and because he willed it he became a sinner. / In the Gospel God called the younger son a son, / because he was late and came to God at the last. / He came to himself and began to say, groaning, / words that bring back love and a father's compassion: / “How many hired servants in my father's house have their fill of bread, / and here I am, perishing of hunger in the house of strangers!” / As long as a man has not fallen into sin, he is a son of God, / fair and beloved, with a nature full of beauties. / God saw that His creation was very good, / and the offspring is beautiful like its begetter as long as it does not sin. / The whole of nature is beautiful and full of righteousness, / and because of its beauty it is worthy to be a son of God. / But when love of the world falls upon a man and he begins to sin, / he loses the lofty beauty that belongs to his nature. / He is brought down from the height that belongs to sons, / for that beauty which nature has has been corrupted in him.

When a man begins, with labours of righteousness, / to heal these wounds that sprang from his freedom, / then, like a hired servant who works to fill his belly with bread, / he must be diligent in the work of righteousness. / Little by little, from here and from there, / and then again with the soul's repentance, in tears of suffering and supplication, / he clothes the naked, feeds the hungry, visits the orphans, / in the hope that he may find mercy to return to the house of God. / So the younger son asked to stand at this rank, / not at that coveted honour of sons. / A son who does not sin, whose seed is in him and who is not enslaved— / would he do wickedness, when he is pure like his begetter? / But when he sins, he goes down to the rank of hired servants, / so that he may run after righteousness and save his soul, / and by labour, petitions and alms / may enter within the door of the house and not be lost. / Because he was a son and corrupted the beauty that belongs to sons, / he became a hired servant and toils so that by it he may live in the house, / until he draws near to repentance from among strangers— / he who sins and is no longer running on the course of his way.

He is enslaved by passions to one of the lords of the land, / and there he serves emptiness in the house of strangers. / But when he wants to return and come to the house of God, / the lords of the land do not hold him back to remain there. / If God did not stop him from going when he wanted to go, / how could the Evil One stop him when he wants to come? / The sinner wanted to sin, and sinned as much as he pleased; / he wanted to return, and nothing can hold him back. / He fell as he willed and rose as he willed, for he is his own master; / freedom is not compelled in what it shall do. / The younger son willed to turn back, to come and see his father, / and the whole slavery of the passions could not stand before him. / Satan, who wrestled with him, did not hold him back from his way, / nor could demons bring his good resolve to nothing. / Nor did love of the world hinder him, as it usually does: / when he willed to come he came, and no one restrained him. / O sinner, when you will to come, you come, / and there is no power that can keep you from what is to your gain. / Only will it, and leave that pasture whose wage is shame: / swine, husks, wretched sufferings—all of it error.

Come to yourself, as that wise heir came, / who, when he came to himself, grew wise and called upon his father. / See that you do not forget the great house, the house of God, / for you are far off and cast out of it like a stranger. / In it the upright take delight in the course of their conduct, / and the perfect are glorified in the beauty of their ways. / All the righteous fill its banquet with their honours, / while you are far away, abased and ruined in the house of strangers. / Come, sinner, come, see your father who is waiting for you; / you have delayed long—come in before they close the door. / By repentance the soul is restored when it has been defiled, / and through it regains all the beauty that had been corrupted. / Take on that resolve of the younger son, the penitent, / which the Son of God told for your instruction. / Come to yourself and ask for mercy as he asked, / for the Father is ready to welcome and draw near to whoever asks Him. / Take, O sinner, that resolve of the younger son, / and it will bring you in to be an heir in your father's house. / Come to yourself as he came back from his offences, / and with a penitent mind ask for forgiveness. / The hunger of the passions has gripped you—passions that are not yours,

and they do not let you have your fill of them: why do you stay? / Come to the table of the house of God, which is full of plenty, / and fill your belly with its spiritual delights. / Consider, sinner, that everyone who has drawn near to God / has his fill of His good things and grows fat on His abundance. / The younger son was emptied by hunger and want, / and so he turned to go back to his father's house. / He remembered the splendour in which he had been raised, / and his soul was distressed, and with weeping he began to speak: / “How many hired servants have their fill of bread in my father's house, / and here I am perishing of hunger—what shall I do? / I will go back to my father, and weep and wail and plead with him, / and I will say to him: I have sinned against heaven and before you, my father, / and I am no longer worthy to be your son, / for I have sinned so greatly as to be beyond forgiveness. / I am not a son, for my profligacy is not that of sons; / let me be a hired servant—it is grace enough for me to live with you. / If from now on I may have my fill of bread among your hired servants, / the bread of your house, so full of plenty, will be splendour to me.” / So he turned to come, a penitent son, and see his father, / and while he was still far off, a father's compassion went out before him. / He wanted to come, and because he wanted it, his father ran to him

and went out to meet him while he was still far from his father's house. / His father was deeply moved, because he saw the dead one alive, / and he rejoiced in the life of the one who had returned from perdition. / He received that lost one as if from the bosom of Sheol, / and rejoiced as at the resurrection of the dead, that he had risen from the grave. / Rejoicing, he fell on his neck and embraced his son, / and kissed him as though he had brought wealth into his house. / He did not reproach him for going away, nor demand of him where he had lingered, / nor press him about his property and what had become of it. / He did not ask him to bring back the portion that had gone out with him, / but welcomed the heir who had returned to his father's house. / He was not grieved over the property that had been squandered, / nor did he trouble him to account for the wealth he had lost. / He welcomed him as one who had gone out and brought back with him / riches and treasures and every kind of goods to his father's house. / He rejoiced in the heir and was not grieved over the possessions / that he had wasted in profligacy to no purpose. / The sight of his son, and the love that stirs in sons, / filled the father in place of wealth; it was the son he was seeking. / The boy said: “I have sinned against heaven and before you, my father; / I have served wickedness, and I am not fit to be your son.

Let me be a lowly hired servant in your house, labouring, / suffering, being beaten, and enduring. / No one can measure the heavens, how high they are, / and my folly has no measure, so great is it.” / That confession of the returning heir was precious, / and his father welcomed him like a very great possession. / He welcomed him without reproach and without murmuring, / and loved him as though he had never strayed from uprightness. / He embraced him, kissed him and honoured him, / and the deeper the son's guilt, the more his father loved him. / Then he commanded his household and servants / to bring the first robe that the father had, / to put a ring on the hand of the returning heir, / and to shoe the boy's feet with sandals from his father's house. / The father commanded, and the fatted calf became a sacrifice for him, / and the servants did as the master of the house commanded. / The house resounded with the sound of praise and songs, / and with the rejoicing held for the returning heir. / The father's house rejoiced in the dead one come alive, and the shouts of joy rang out, / with songs and the blended sounds of great praise. / While they were feasting, the elder son, who had been in the field, came,

and heard the sound, and began to ask about the rejoicing. / “What is this?” The servants say: “Your brother has come, / and your father is rejoicing because he is safe and well; come, rejoice too.” / When the elder son heard this he was angry and turned away, / and did not want to go in and rejoice over the returning heir. / But the father, whose compassion is never divided, / went out after him as well, to bring him in to rejoice with him. / The elder son began to try to undo his father's compassion, / and argued about what seemed unjust, saying to him: / “Look, how many years I have served you, my lord, as a slave, / and you never gave me a kid to feast on.” / His father said: “My son, you are with me all your days; / I do not send you away or remove you from your father's side. / Everything that is mine is yours, for you are the elder, / and you are the heir; your brother comes in by grace. / You are here with me, but your brother who has come was not with us; / he was dead and has come alive, and because he lives, come, let us rejoice in him. / Because he was lost and I have found him, let us rejoice today: / who would not rejoice over something he had lost, if he found it? / Your brother was lost; do not be grieved that I have found him. / Your brother was dead and today he lives—who would not rejoice?”

Who would not marvel at the Father, wholly full of grace, / who is wholly a sea of compassion without limit? / He welcomed the younger son who came, so that he would not go away, / and with love he entreated the elder not to be angry. / So wide was his love that both the younger and the elder / he would hold in his compassion, and abandon neither. / The People is jealous over the peoples who had been lost, / and because God received them, it was angry and went out. / But God wishes to win all the peoples, / and He wants all the peoples to be His heirs. / He wants to save both the last and the first, / for they are one to Him, and He wishes to bring them all back. / So too with the righteous and the sinners: / He opens His door and calls them all, to save them. / He wants sinners to come to repentance, / and He admonishes the righteous and lovingly makes them heirs. / Because of His love He bears the weight of both sides, / for His compassion is enough to save them both. / But the righteous man is with God all his days, / and that is why he was the elder son and the first. / To him it is said: “Everything that is mine is yours,” / for the righteous inherit the earth, and it is theirs.

Yet the sinner too, if he comes to repentance, / finds mercy and inherits life in the Father's house. / “Look, how many years I have served you as a slave, my lord; / I am righteous, yet like a sinner I am made to plead. / I have not sinned, yet like one who has sinned I am made to entreat every day, / and you have not let me think that I have any rest in your way. / I have feared you, your tablets and your commandments, / your warnings and the laws of your strictness. / You did not allow me to take two wives, as you teach, / and if I look at a woman, my desire for her, they say, drags me down. / If I call someone ‘Raca’, I fall into Gehenna, / and if I say ‘fool’ to my brother, the judgment is harsh upon me. / If my tunic is taken from me, I must let my cloak go too, / and if I do not do these things, the depths below swallow me. / Look, how many years I have been made a slave to the fear of you, / and you have not let me loosen or disregard a single one of these. / Never have I transgressed the commandments of your strictness, / nor diminished your words to loosen them by the smallest amount. / I have kept them all, however hard or strict, / and I have met with no rest in your way since I came to know you.

Yet you did not give me even a little kid for all this— / that I neither diminished anything nor made the smallest reduction.” / These are the words the perfect man has before God, / openly, raising his voice and demanding his reward. / He has no need to ask for mercy at the judgment before justice, / for he was not tried by sin so as to need to ask for mercy. / That is why, when a sinner comes into judgment, / the perfect man does not think there is any way for him to live. / And that is why the elder son wanted to be angry: / because he saw that the penitent came in through mercy to inherit. / And the elder son said to the father in a loud voice: / “I have never loosened your words or your commandments. / But this son of yours, when he went mad in debauchery / and gave his whole inheritance to harlots, / and squandered and lost all he had acquired on uncleanness— / look, you have honoured him with the fatted calf to feast on!” / But God rejoices in the one whose face is open before Him, / and He wants to give a hand so that whoever has fallen may rise. / And if the sinner wants to come to repentance, / He makes a place for him in His mercy, so that he may live there.

And the sinner, once he becomes one of the penitents, / reclines with the righteous and sits at His table. / When the younger son came back from his offences, / they clothed him in the first robe that the father had. / There was one robe for the last and the first, / for it is not torn so that each of them takes half. / That first robe was given to the younger son, / and there was no other for the elder son to put on. / Faith and baptism are one with God, / and one is the garment He gives the baptized from the water. / One is the sacrifice by which all sinners have been pardoned, / and with one ring the treasures of God's house are sealed. / One is the sandal of the bride who came up from the water, / the shoe of fire with which she treads on serpents. / The Son of God is a lover of repentance: / come, sinners, recline at His banquet, that He may delight you. / A gracious Father—His compassion is spread over sinners; / who would not come, except one who hates his own life? / He made the younger son an heir with the elder, / for repentance raises the dead at the Father's sign.
He was dead and came alive, and became a hope for all sinners / that they can live through repentance. Blessed is He who has pity on all!
Here ends the homily on the son who squandered his possessions.
By the holy Mar Jacob. Homily 53: On the Pharisee and the tax collector, of whom our Lord said that they went up to the temple to pray.

The teaching of the Son of God is full of life;
you who love life, come, take delight in his instruction.
All his words are light to those who discern;
O discerning ones, shine in the gospel that is full of light.
From his lips rivers of living waters
have gone out to creation, to water the earth that had become desolate.
On his tongue are blessings and riches beyond comprehension,
and he distributes them to the hearers in the assemblies.
When he opens his mouth to speak, death flees,
and his power gives resurrection to the dead, to awaken them.

From his sayings life dawns upon souls;
even those bitten by the serpent are healed.
When he speaks, his voice falls into the ears of the dead,
and they stir as though from sleep and rise to give praise.
He carried remedies and brought them to our land from his Father's house,
and distributed them freely to the afflicted and healed them.
He dawned upon diseases like the sun upon shadows,
and drove them out of all the bodies of the afflicted.
By his teaching he healed the soul that had been sick,
and his word bound up the body of the dead man that was afflicted.
He drove from the soul sin, the blemish that was killing it,
and from the body too the pain and the sore that wore it down.
The sins of the soul and the pains of the body, which were many,
were wiped away like smoke before a strong wind.
Wherever he saw sin in a soul he gave forgiveness,
and when the pain of a body met him he gave healing.
While teaching, he gave a 'woe' to the scribes and Pharisees,
a cautery for the pain that had resisted healing.
He saw pride and had pity on the soul that was slain by it;
he gave it an incision and applied a cautery to heal its sore.
He saw the poor who are distressed in poverty,
and to the poor he gave a blessing to encourage them.
He saw the rich who show no mercy to the poor,
and revealed the story of the rich man and of Lazarus.
By him who asked for a drop of water and was not given it,
he taught them to show mercy to the poor.
Over against the iniquity of the soul, which is a hidden sore,
he revealed and showed the fire of judgement, that the soul might become good.
One event among the events of the new world
he recounted, to help both the rich and the poor.
By the drop that the one who asked sought and was not given,
he cast fear upon the rich, that they might not grow proud.
And by Lazarus, who was reclining beside Abraham,
he gave encouragement to whoever is bowed down by poverty.
While teaching, he portrayed the ten virgins for the world,
and revealed and showed what becomes of the foolish and the wise,
so that the soul might prepare good works for the Messiah;
he showed it how the wise enter with him.
He made the soul afraid that unless it shines with good deeds,
they will not open to it to enter beside him when it pleads.
Again he portrayed himself as a shepherd who takes care to separate
the goats and the lambs, to the right and to the left.

The lambs he set in light and the goats in darkness,
for indeed the goat's colour is dark to anyone who looks at it.
While teaching, he revealed something he will one day say
to those he sets at his right and at his left:
'Depart, you cursed,' the children of the left hear from him,
and 'Come, enter and inherit,' the children of the right hear from him.
These words of the end he spoke beforehand
in order to help whoever hears his teaching,
so that, before he goes to the place of judgement, he may know
what the judgement is, and prepare good works for himself.
In every way he takes care to profit humankind;
the Son of God fills one with wonder by his teaching.
In one place he spoke in parables and proverbs;
in another he showed the soul threats and scourges.
At other times again, by gifts and by praise,
he would stir the soul to love good deeds.
There he spoke about the tax collector and the Pharisee,
and told a story that greatly profits whoever hears it.
Concerning pride and humility he wished to show
who is guilty and who is innocent before the Judge.
He wished to strike down both boasting and arrogance,

by which the soul is brought low and found guilty before justice.
In his love he wished to rescue it from pride,
and to rebuke [?] with reproof the soul that practises good deeds,
so that after its toil it would not be emptied of its good deeds
and lose its labour through a haughty spirit, should it have one.
He cast fear upon the righteous man, that even while he is righteous
he is never permitted to recount his good deeds.
And the sinner he encouraged and sustained: if he humbles himself
and asks for grace, it is easy for him to receive it from God.
For this reason the One full of light set out the story
of that tax collector and Pharisee as they prayed.
He said that two men went up to the temple to pray,
one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
Among the Hebrews the name 'Pharisee' means something like 'righteous';
hear now that the Pharisee was righteous.
And that the tax collector was a sinner is plain;
and these two went up to pray in the house of God.
They went up to pray, one righteous and one a sinner,
Pharisee and tax collector, before the Judge of all the earth.
And the Pharisee began to speak in a haughty spirit,
because he trusted in the good deeds he had done.
He looked at himself and saw that he was pure and without blemish,

and because of his purity he was confident to stand and pray.
And he began to say: 'O God, I thank you
that I am not like the sinners or the plunderers.
I thank you that I am free of reproach;
there is no iniquity in me, and I am not like evil people.
There are adulterers, there are fornicators, there are extortioners,
and I have never been like these, nor am I.
I am not like the workers of iniquity and the wicked;
I am pure and set apart from evils.
I thank you that I have not been a liar, unjust or contemptible,
nor am I like the doers of iniquity in their conduct.'
O righteous man, what are you saying in your prayers?
This speech you are speaking is not prayer.
O Pharisee, this is not how one who prays behaves,
nor does he dare recount his good deeds before the One who knows all.
You have praised yourself; you have not offered praise to your Lord;
by recounting your good deeds now, you yourself have made them void.
This is not the kind of prayer that enters before God;
rather, in suffering it begs mercy from the Judge.
This is not how the soul stands before God,

but bowed, trembling, shaken and full of awe.
How have you come, and why have you come to pray?
For look, you have not prayed; you have praised your good deeds.
But if you need to receive something from God,
there are needy people: why do you not plead for sinners?
Or if your soul wishes beauty to be added to it,
there are needy people: pray for them as a good man would.
This man looked at the beauty of his own soul and was carried away [?] by it,
and did not know to look at God and see how good he is.
Whoever gazes upon the beauty of that Majesty
finds his own soul hateful in his eyes, however beautiful it is.
If a small lamp is brought into the great sun,
its light disappears, for the daylight covers it over.
So too the righteous man, when he is dazzled and gazes at God:
his righteousness grows faint and small before God.
For Abraham, who gazed at the greatness of God,
called himself dust and ashes, though he was just.
Simon Peter said to his Lord, 'I am a sinner';
and who is righteous when he speaks with God?
If Abraham called himself dust and ashes,
and Simon Peter was a sinner, as he said,

who would dare to let his good deeds appear before him
and recount them when he speaks with God?
This Pharisee was righteous in his own person,
but he did not perceive in God how good he is.
That hidden vision which gazes on hidden things
he did not have, to look upon the beauty of that Majesty.
He did not have the great mind and lofty knowledge
that dares to ascend and enter the abode of the angels,
that boldly uncovers the face of the gate of the creation of light [?],
where the waves of the splendour of that Majesty overwhelm it,
and its vision is dazzled by those beauties beyond comprehension,
and it despises itself if ever it thought it had beauty.
Had the gaze of his soul been clear when he looked
at the lofty beauty, he would not have seen his own beauty.
Whoever sees his own beauty is not beautiful,
for if he were beautiful he would consider himself all blemishes.
The soul that is lovely does not see that it is lovely;
it gazes on the beauties above and is dazzled by their splendour.
Whoever is truly righteous considers that he is not righteous,
like the disciple who cried to his Lord, 'I am a sinner.'
This Pharisee had been made righteous by the law,

by observances and bodily commandments,
for he did not know another degree of righteousness
above his own, by which one draws near to God.
Love of the Lord is commanded by the law,
and it does not look to a reward to be repaid for it.
And the more beautiful the soul, the more it considers itself not beautiful,
for the lofty beauties of the Godhead make it tremble.
But the Pharisee, who was righteous by the law,
was pleased with himself and stood up to recount his good deeds.
He looked at the tax collector, who had also gone up to pray,
and despised and scorned him, and spoke as if to his reproach.
He thanked the Lord in a spirit full of boastfulness,
and compared himself with the tax collector and saw that he was greater than he.
'I thank you that I am not like this tax collector,'
he said to God, forgetting that it was a prayer.
He did not look to Moses, nor to Elijah, nor to Jeremiah,
but to this man, and in comparison with this man he was righteous.
He belittled his soul while he thought he was praising it,
for he compared it with the tax collector, and it seemed to him beautiful.
He did not compare his light with the light of the Beautiful One,
to see which beauty is beautiful and which is ugly.

He compared his meagre light with the tax collector's darkness,
and from the darkness, not from the light, he judged that he shone.
He did not look at Joseph, the youth who conquered lust on its own ground,
nor at Daniel, who refused the king's delicacies.
He did not look at Job, a sea of beauties and of trials,
nor at Jacob, who wrestled with the angels.
He looked at the tax collector, and his own righteousness grew great to him,
and because he saw someone hateful, he thought himself beautiful.
Therefore whoever wishes to profit his soul by his righteousness
must look at what is beautiful and lofty.
And if he attains the measure of the perfect, let him look at God,
so that, comparing himself with him, he may be ashamed before his greatness.
When a rich man sees wealth greater than his own,
he sees himself as a poor man and does not grow proud.
But if he looks at someone who lacks his daily bread,
he is misled into thinking there is none in the world greater than he.
If the soul looks at the perfect and the spiritual,
it descends a long way into humility, which is full of beauties.
But if it looks at evil people, it vaunts itself,
and arrogance brings harm to whoever acquires it.
It becomes hateful while it thinks it has become very beautiful

by comparison with the wicked, and it falls into the pit of arrogance.
This is what happened to the Pharisee while he prayed:
he saw the tax collector and reckoned that he was greater than he.
He began to revile him and point him out to the Lord, saying,
'I thank you that I am not like this tax collector.'
In a haughty spirit he committed two evils,
and in both there is loss, for those who discern.
That a man should look at his neighbour's sins is an evil,
and that he should be pleased with himself is an evil too.
Let no one look too long at a sore that is not his own,
but let him attend to his own sore, like a wise man.
Let no one dwell too much on his good deeds,
but rather let him forget them once they are done.
As it is written: 'What lies behind, I forget,'
he says, 'and I strain forward to the good things ahead.'
'If I did a good deed yesterday, it is finished,
and see, I run to do another, if I can.
I forget yesterday's good deed along with yesterday,
for if I dwell on it, I make myself lose the good deeds by it.'
The good deed he has done, once it is finished, he puts behind him,
so that he may run forward again after another good deed.

'Let yesterday's good deed be kept in yesterday's life;
as long as I live, let today have its own day.'
So the sun too forgets and casts off the times that have passed,
and runs after those that are coming, to pass through them.
If the sun were to stop and count yesterday's course,
today's course would be held back from its journey.
Day by day it casts behind it the courses that have passed,
and seeks again to run forward, like a diligent man.
Paul resembles the sun on the road of apostleship,
for he forgot yesterday's course and did not count it.
Why recount the good deeds that have been done,
so that they become a reason for others not to be done?
For the Pharisee, his good deeds became a cause of evil,
for when he sought to count them, he was not justified.
Yesterday he had longed for good deeds and done them,
and today he stood up to count them, and they were lost to him.
All good deeds are laid up in the hands of the Lord,
and he does not forget them: why are you anxious to count them?
Why do you leave off the labour of righteousness
to reckon up what you have to your credit with God?

He does not forget; do not you cease from good deeds.
Do not remind him of what you have done, for it is written down with him.
Deeds and words, events and thoughts,
the impulses and stirrings of the soul he knows, and watches over them.
Yet though he does not forget, you have thought him somehow lacking,
so that you remind him, see, by recounting your good deeds.
It is needful, my brothers, that no one dwell on his good deeds,
for because that righteous man dwelt on them, see, he is reproached.
Whoever sins, let him set his sin before his face,
and if he becomes righteous, let him cast his righteousness behind him.
Look at sin, for if you look at it, it is wiped away for you;
and do not look at righteousness, lest you undo [?] it.
Forget righteousness if you practise it,
for if you forget it, the Lord keeps it so that it does not perish.
For if you dwell on sin, God forgets it,
despises it and lets it go, when he sees that it wearies you.
But if you forget sin once you have committed it,
the Lord does not forget it so that it goes away, but requires it of you.
Look at sin as you would at a sore, while it is in you;
for who can forget his sore while it pains him?
The more someone with an evil sore complains,

the more the sound of his groaning rouses him to seek his physician.
But if he does not complain, how can he make known that he has a sore?
He neglects the physician, and does not bind it up, since it does not pain him.
So too the sinner: the more he looks at his sin,
the more God attends to his sore and heals him.
But if he neglects it and does not look at it, the bandaging is abandoned,
and the sore remains without remedy and without help.
If a man remembers his sin while despising himself,
a contrite spirit obtains mercy from the Judge.
Like that tax collector, who had set his sin before his eyes
and could not look at heaven because of it.
He did not wish to raise his gaze from his folly;
he looked at it, and dared not look above.
The sins he had sinned he set before his face,
and it was not easy for him to look at the heaven that was over him.
He looked only at the iniquity his hands had done,
and could see nothing else beside it.
Bowed down, he stands like a thief before the Judge,
and because he was despised in his own eyes he could not lift his eyes.
He feared and dreaded the justice that sits on high,

to raise his eyes toward it, lest it be angered
and raise the rod and strike him to destruction because he had dared,
and had looked boldly into the place of judgement while guilty.
And therefore he did not dare to look at heaven,
toward the fearful Judge whom sinners dread.
He looked at his sins and was moved to ask for great grace,
for the sore of iniquity, nothing but grace can bind it up.
He stands ashamed, praying, and despised in his own eyes,
but God did not despise him, because he humbled himself.
His soul shone; he saw his sins and beat himself with his hands,
all alone, trembling, as he cried out before the Judge.
He called on God, saying to him, 'Have mercy on the sinner;
your grace is life: revive the dead man whom iniquity has killed.'
Strengthen me [?] for the account of this tax collector and Pharisee,
for it is a great awe to speak of its story with wonder.
Though I do not dare, though I am not able,
I will tell them as they were to those who hear me.
His good deeds became a cause of evil for the Pharisee,
for by them he darkened his soul with boasting and pride.
But that tax collector, through the very fact that he had sinned, his soul shone;
it trembled and longed to ask grace from the Judge.

The righteous man grew dark because he counted his good deeds;
the sinner shone because the iniquity he had done stirred him.
The just Pharisee went astray so far as to reproach even God,
while the tax collector knew the Lord, that he is full of mercy.
Yet it is not said that evil sprang from good deeds,
nor is it heard that good dawned from evils.
What then shall I say? That the Pharisee, from his good deeds,
was puffed up with boasting and praised himself, and see, he is reproached;
and the tax collector's sins opened his soul before the Judge,
and he asked for grace and is praised as a wise man.
Let us then accuse not the good works that were done,
but the error and the pride of the Pharisee.
And let us praise, in turn, not the sins the tax collector sinned,
but his soul, which looked and saw how hateful it was.
In his story he became like a mirror for the doers of iniquity,
that they should stand in great humility in the house of God.
He urged the soul to ask for grace from God,
and it came to know that if it asks him, he gives to it.
Our Lord spoke this parable to help by it
both sides, if they hear it with discernment.

Both the righteous and sinners profit from it,
for the Son of God wishes to profit them both.
O righteous man, never despise the sinner;
he is the image of God even if he sins, and he is your fellow.
Do not boast if you do good deeds,
lest you fall from that height of righteousness.
You gave to God from what is his; you did not give from what is yours,
that you should reproach him with the tithes you give him.
When you fast, do not boast and recount the fasting,
for Daniel fasted in humility when he fasted.
Humble your soul in the house of God when you pray,
for your prayer is not accepted from you if it is made in pride.
Ten thousand beauties, even if they were stored up and arrayed in you,
are not beautiful unless you put on humility.
Even if you are more righteous than Job in your deeds,
your good deeds are not accepted with a haughty spirit.
And you, sinner, from the story of the tax collector that has been told,
gain profit, and stand in prayer with a face full of shame.
Do not look at heaven; justice does not permit you,
for the place of judgement is a great terror to those who are guilty there.
Tremble in prayer and ask for grace in humility,
and you will receive from the Giver of good things.

Be silent and humble yourself if you are rebuked by the righteous,
for that tax collector too kept utterly silent when he was reproached.
He said to God, 'I beg you, my Lord, have mercy on the sinner,'
and he has mercy on you because of the abundant mercies in him.
Our Lord's parable is all life to whoever hears it,
and it can help both the righteous and sinners.
This parable was not merely a parable;
it really happened, just as it was told.
At one time they met and stood in prayer,
Pharisee and tax collector, and spoke these words in the house of God.
And the Son of God listened to them with his Begetter,
for it is he who receives all petitions and prayers.
No prayer enters to his Father apart from him,
and no gift goes out from him except by his hands.
He receives, brings in, takes, and brings out from the Father's house,
for he is our Mediator in his Father's house, to make atonement for us.
The sacrifices of Levi and the tithes of just Jacob
he received and brought in to his Begetter.
He received the prayer of Hannah in the holy temple,
and brought out for her the merciful answer to her request from his Father's house.
He listened to the prayer of Jonah from inside the fish,
and brought it in to his Begetter like first fruits.

Choice sacrifices and the incense of priests and whole burnt offerings,
prayers, petitions, all tithes and all vows,
the words of the mouth and the thoughts of the heart:
it is he who receives, listens, hears, sees and remembers.
It was he who heard the Pharisee and that tax collector
as they stood in prayer in the holy temple.
And though he was hearing the petitions of the whole world,
he did not forget to tell them exactly as they had been heard.
And since it was an event that happened in time, just as it was told,
he made it a parable to help whoever hears it.
Because the tax collector, praying in humility, pleased him,
and the Pharisee, praying out of pride, did not please him,
he kept the story and made it a parable full of profit;
he set it in the gospel so that all who hear it may be helped by it.
He taught the world that whoever exalts himself is humbled,
so that everyone may flee from pride, which is abhorrent to him.
Whoever is lofty in his heart, it says, is abhorrent before God;
and who would not tremble at pride, if he is discerning?
Many are the faults that do not please God,
yet of pride alone has it been said that it is abhorrent.

He hates all of them, and wishes that none of them be found;
but of this one alone it is written that it is abominable before God.
He does not merely hate it, as he does its companions;
rather, it is [?] exceedingly abominable to him.
All sins hang back from God in utter shame,
but pride seeks to come as close to him as it can.
The Lord is lofty, and wishes to dwell with the lowly,
and whoever exalts himself before God has dared to be proud.
And because it is written, “The Lord reigns, he has put on majesty,”
he hates for a human being to exalt himself or be proud.
That is why it is written of pride that it is abominable
before God, so that whoever hears may plainly understand.
That is why the parable of the Pharisee was written:
so that whoever does good works may grow wise by it,
and flee from speaking of his own good deeds,
and from pride, lest he be abominable in the house of God.
It is good for you to flee from every passion;
it is good for you to hate every fault;
it is good for you to hate sins in all their forms;
but flee far from pride, because it is abominable.
And humility is full of the beauties of righteousness,

so that even a fault, wherever it may be, is covered by it.
The tax collector was hateful, and his faults were many,
but because he humbled himself, see how well he is spoken of.
The Pharisee was righteous and possessed virtue,
but because he wanted to recount his virtues, see, his case became hateful.
With one root our Lord healed two wounds,
and clearly he bound up both the righteous and sinners.
From one parable he made a cure for two sides,
so that whoever sins and whoever is righteous may be helped by it.
On the righteous he laid a fear, so that he would not boast,
lest his good deeds be stripped away by his boasting.
And the sinner he taught to feel pain and to be humbled,
to know himself and find mercy before God.
The Son of God wishes to benefit everyone by his words;
blessed is he who wills that everyone should live, even in his negligence [?].
Here ends the homily on the Publican and the Pharisee.
By the holy Mar Jacob. Homily 54. On the parable our Lord told about the laborers whom the owner of the vineyard hired.

See, your sweet taste stirs my tongue: I will cry out praise
to the Father who sent you, so that everything bitter might be sweetened by you.
Jesus, the honey that came forth from the carcass of the lion, Death,
came forth to sweeten the palates of the world, which had been bitter.
The Star ran, and by its rising called to the lands
to bring gifts to the Father who sent it, great praise.
Let the whole earth be moved to praise you, my Lord,
for all of it has shone with your divine rays.
You are living water for all who sought you and drank of you;
they delight in you and are filled from the fountain full of mercies.
Your teaching welled up from Golgotha, the Eden of God,
and went out to water all creation, which had been laid waste.
The parched and ravaged earth was filled from you;
it flourished and became like a paradise full of good things.
Your stories went up into the world like channels of rivers,
and see, the whole of creation meditates on your teaching.
Pishon, Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates have ceased from watering,
for through your disciples a channel was made for the world to drink.
The Cross burst open a single fountain from Golgotha,
and divided itself into four heads, and see, it gives us drink.

He stood on a height and opened a well facing the deep,
so that by its lofty waters it might overwhelm the whole earth.
He laid channels toward the peoples and the lands,
and they all drank and were filled with your sayings, spiritually.
The whole creation, which had been asleep, heard your voice;
it stirred, rose up, and clapped its hands in praise.
Come, let us delight in the teaching full of life, beloved children
whom the womb of baptism has borne.
Bring with you the assemblies of your thoughts,
for this is what the story of the Son demands of whoever hears it.
Let the whole of you come, if indeed you are coming to the teaching,
for Christ wants the whole of you to live and to be with him.
The Gospel is a light for souls in darkness;
by its rising it gave light and life and delight.
The sayings of the Son are laden with life to distribute
throughout the whole world to whoever listens with love.
He carried good things and riches and brought them to us from his Father's house,
and made the poor treasurers over his treasures.
The Lord of kings became poor because he willed it,
and see, the whole creation is rich through his poverty.
He spoke with us, since it pleased him to become one of us,

and by his teaching he seasoned souls that had been insipid.
He became our physician and bore the pains of our sickness;
he became our shepherd and gathered the sheep that had been lost.
He became our bread and drove hunger from our souls;
he became our water and quenched the thirst that was choking us.
He became our way, and we walk in it to come to his place;
he became our door, and through it he brought us in to his Begetter.
He became our brother, that we might be his kin and be with him;
he joined us to himself, mingled us with himself, and became one of us.
He dawned in our world like a day full of light,
and put an end to the darkness in which the whole creation had been groping.
He spoke in parables and created clear similitudes,
so that through the exercise he might make the soul wise to seek out his stories.
In likeness after likeness he portrayed his kingdom as he taught,
so that by its images the whole world might be drawn to it.
In one place he portrayed it in ten virgins,
in a wedding feast, and in the lamps of the wise.
In another place he likened it to a talent and to its profits,
the great wealth that comes back doubled to the householder.
There is also a place where he portrayed it as a small seed that became
like a tree, and the bird made its nest in it.

And again he likened it to the bit of leaven that
a woman hid in the dough [?], and it leavened all of it, and it was sweetened by it.
And besides these he also portrayed his kingdom in a householder
who went out and hired laborers for his vineyard, to work with him.
Let us now speak about this parable that he made,
the Son of God, when he portrayed his kingdom in laborers.
He said that the kingdom of the house of God is like
a man who went out to hire laborers for his vineyard.
He called laborers at the dawn of the day and agreed on a denarius
for each one of them, and brought them in, and they worked diligently.
At the third hour he saw other laborers and called them,
and brought them in to his work beside the first.
At the sixth hour, in his zeal, he hired still others,
without settling how much wage they would receive from him.
At the ninth hour he again saw laborers and brought them in,
for his vineyard was wide enough for all creation to work with him.
After this the lord of the vineyard went out at the eleventh hour
and saw other laborers standing idle.
And the lord of the vineyard began to speak, reproaching
the laborers who had been idle from work the whole day:
"Why, men, are you idle and empty-handed,

wasting the whole day without work?
Why do you not work alongside your companions
in the vineyard that can give life to whoever works in it?
Why has your idleness stayed with you the whole day,
and evening has come, and you stand there as if ashamed?"
The laborers say: "No one has hired us to work with him;
nor has the lord of the vineyard called us to his work."
He says to them: "You go too; the vineyard needs
laborers at this hour, for there is work for everyone who comes to it."
The laborers came, and evening fell, the time to receive their wages,
and the householder called his steward and said to him:
"Rise, give a good wage to the laborers who worked with us,
and to the last give a denarius each when you pay.
Begin with them, and give each of them a denarius,
and so treat them equally, and pay the last and the first."
The steward rose to pay the wages as he had been commanded,
and gave to the last, to each one of them, one denarius.
But the first, who saw the wage he had given to the last,
supposed that they would receive something more than their companions,
and they reckoned: "If he gave the last a denarius,
how much more will he give us, the first, what is our due!"

But the steward gave to the last, and to those after them,
and to those in the middle, a denarius, adding nothing.
All of them passed through, and the first came in to receive their wage,
and again he gave in the same way one denarius, with no addition.
But when that first laborer saw the denarius,
he closed his hand on it in his grief and would not take it.
His wage had been agreed, but because he had hoped for more
he forgot the agreement and was ready to be angry over the wage.
And he began to speak, accusing the householder
for having made them equal and paid the last like the first.
He said: "It is I, after all, who worked the whole day,
from dawn, look, in toil and weariness and exhaustion.
I bore the heat and carried the burden of the whole day,
and what have I gained, if my wage is the same as the last?
These worked one hour, and look, they received one denarius;
twelve times as much is owed to me, if you are just.
For one hour a denarius, and for twelve one denarius:
it is not justice that I should be paid as you say.
No, master of the wages, do not go beyond what is fitting,
so that the one who works and the one who does not are equal in your eyes.

It is not because you have been generous to the last laborers that I complain,
but because you have wronged me that I am embittered.
You were generous to these, and without toil they received a denarius;
look at me, who toiled, and be generous to me too, if you are good."
Then the lord of the vineyard, in his uprightness, began
to rebuke that first laborer, saying to him:
"Your wage was agreed; why do you hope for more?
See, I have not wronged you; do not blame me as if I were in want.
I agreed with you on one denarius when I took you on;
here, take the good denarius. Why do you complain?
If I gave more to your companion, what do you lack,
since I have not cheated you of the condition we made between us?
If I am good with what is mine, what of yours have I kept from you?
For as I covenanted, see, I have given you one denarius.
I did not agree on two, for I have only one,
and I give it both to the last and to the first.
I have not deprived you, I have not lied to you, I have not shortchanged you;
the agreement is known and the word stands. What is the complaint about?
Is it perhaps that your eye is evil, and you grumble
because I made your companion equal to you in the good wage?

Or do you suppose I have no power to do as I will with what is mine,
to treat them equally and pay the last and the first?
Take what is yours, as was agreed with you; and if I wish
to make your fellow equal to you as well, that is not your affair."
The mercy of the lord of the vineyard gave the wage
to the last laborers as to the first, with a good heart.
Now we must turn to the spiritual meaning
and to the interpretation, which clothes the word in beauty.
The scriptures of the Son are like the sea, and in the sea
pearls lie cast and hidden for the merchants.
The interpreter, like a diver, goes down after them;
he searches the depths and brings up a pearl with him.
Once it has come up, see, it is carried to the merchants,
and all who have acquired it gain greatly from it.
Like a diver, the mind goes down into the reading
to bring up with it the word of life, a pearl.
O hearers, receive the word as merchants do,
and gain from it, all of you, and grow rich spiritually.
Whoever buys a pearl pays a price;
come, take freely the word of life, which is full of wealth.
The mind went down and dived into the scriptures, though it is not worthy,

and searched and seized the pearl of the house of God.
And see, the tongue carries it, to cast it before the hearers:
hang the daughter of light in your ears and adorn yourselves with it.
Our Lord opened his mouth in parables, as it is written,
and on his lyre sang riddles to the whole world.
He veiled his words, so that whoever gives himself to gain
might uncover and see the hidden beauties of his similitudes.
Let us now hear who the householder is,
what the vineyard is, and what the laborers hired for it are,
and why at dawn, at the third, the sixth and the ninth,
and also at the eleventh, the lord of the vineyard took on laborers,
and why that steward was commanded
to pay the wage to the last laborers before the first,
and what that denarius is which the steward gave
both to the last and to the first, with no addition.
God, who established the worlds, is the householder,
and the vineyard is the labor of righteousness.
The laborers he hired are the human race, whom he called
so that they might live well and become heirs of the kingdom.
The first laborers were those of Adam's house, whom in the beginning,

at the dawn of the world, he brought into Eden to labor.
And that denarius which he agreed to give the first
was his beloved Son, whom he gave to the last at the end of the ages.
These laborers of the third hour, if you look closely,
are the house of Noah, whom he set to his work.
Those of the sixth hour are the house of Abraham in the land of Aram,
who again put on righteousness like the first.
And these laborers of the ninth hour are Moses the great
and Joshua son of Nun and the whole company of prophecy.
All the laborers of the house of God went in and fulfilled their labor [?]
in the vineyard of the Lord, which is the course of righteousness.
The way of the just went on and came down from Adam,
reached Noah, descended, and drew near to Abraham.
The way passed on and rested upon Moses the great, of the ninth hour,
who ran it mightily in the observances of righteousness.
They toiled diligently in the vineyard of the Beloved,
those whom he hired at four times and brought in.
All of them ran, working in righteousness:
those of the house of Seth and Enosh from the beginning of the great world;
those of the house of Noah were added and lived righteously;
and Abraham and Isaac arose and worked diligently.

Then Moses came, and with him the divine prophets,
and they became good laborers in the vineyard and were diligent in it.
They stood like fences [?] and put on the love of the new life,
and toiled well in the vineyard of spiritual fruits.
Through their revelations they bore the heavy burden of the world,
and endured the disgrace of the love of the idols of vanity.
They uprooted the thorns and the thicket of error from the lands,
and cleansed souls, the vines, of evils.
In chastity, purity and holiness
they planted their lives and produced the fruits of faith.
After these, when the world was drawing near its end,
as one might say, when the day was about to set,
the lord of the vineyard went out at the eleventh hour from Ephrath,
and saw the peoples empty, dissipated and without labor:
abject, prostrate, idle and slack as well,
loose-living, who had slept the whole day without work;
men who had lived in the whole world without knowledge,
without the course of righteousness and uprightness.
They had not gone in and served the house of God in faith,
nor produced good fruits for the glory of the lord of the vineyard,
but they spent the time of the world in evil lives,
and in error the time of the world in evil lives,
and in the error of the love of the idols of vanity.

The lord of the vineyard saw them idle,
and began to reproach them, to rebuke them and to scold them:
"Why, men, are you idle the whole day,
and empty of the work of righteousness?
Why are you so asleep to good things,
and no one calls upon righteousness and faith?
Why, when the ages have run out and lifetimes have come to an end,
are you asleep to labor and to understanding?
The day has set, the world is ending: rise up, you idle ones,
be diligent in the beloved hour of repentance.
Why were you idle while the ages of the whole world passed,
and did not work in the blessed vineyard of the house of God?"
The peoples say: "No one hired us to toil
with him, and that is why we are idle and dissipated.
No law, no commandments, no observances,
no prophets, no revelations of truth.
No one hired us, no one taught us or made us wise,
no one required us to go in and work in the house of God.
They called Abraham from Aram to the land of Canaan,
and they called Isaac to be a sacrifice on the mountains of Jebus.

They called Jacob to the ladder of heaven,
and Joseph, so that his grain might give plenty to all Egypt.
Moses was given authority over the revelations of prophecy,
and Aaron the priest enters confidently before God.
The Most High comes down on Mount Sinai to the Hebrews,
and the people eat bread freely from the thick cloud.
The congregation drinks blessed water from the rock,
and the Jordan is split so that it may enter and dispossess the Amorites.
Joshua son of Nun uprooted lofty walls before it,
and compelled the sun, so that gates might be opened before its entry.
David leads it after him, to bring it to God,
and Samuel adorns it and ministers to it in the house of atonement.
Elijah is zealous, laying waste the land as he teaches it,
and the prophets of the Most High are made like servants to it.
The prophets taught it, made covenant with it, and agreed its wage,
and by their persuasion brought it in to work in the house of God.
But as for us peoples, none of the seers hired us,
and no revelations were sent to us from on high.
No prophet arose among us to prophesy to us,
no herald to show us the vineyard to work in.
And see, we are left like orphans and outsiders,

and we are idle and empty and dissipated.
No one to hire us, no one to require of us, no one to counsel us,
no master of wages to entice us to toil with him.
There was no one; but if there were one to hire us,
see, we stand ready to work like diligent laborers."
Then the lord of the vineyard opened his door to the peoples of the earth,
and the whole creation entered and worked in the house of God.
At the end of the world, at the close of the ages and seasons,
all the peoples entered the great house at the eleventh hour.
They began diligently on the course of fair deeds,
and wove and put on righteousness in bodily form.
They smashed and threw away their carved images and their idols,
and took hold of the swift course on the way of faith.
They came to know the Father, believed in the Son, and honored the Spirit,
and all of them became chosen temples for the Godhead.
They entered at the eleventh hour, and in justice received the denarius,
which is our Lord, the wage of all righteousness.
The first, who sowed and fell asleep with their generations, were left behind,
and see, the last carry the sheaf full of plenty.
The last peoples have become first in the body of the Son,
for they put him on from within the waters of baptism.

Enosh, Noah, Abraham and those of Moses' house are far off,
and the last laborers have received the denarius, and see, they are rich.
The tax collector is justified, and see, the robber triumphs in the Garden;
even the harlot kisses and embraces the Son of God.
Moses is far off, and see, the sinful woman clasps his feet
and anoints him with ointment and tears, lovingly.
Abraham, who longed to see his day, was left behind,
and see, all the peoples gaze on him in his crucifixion.
When all the lives of the world had been brought to nothing and come to an end,
the peoples perceived that there is a God, and at once they clung to him.
They entered at the eleventh hour and were diligent in repentance,
and see, they are clothed with the Son of God bodily.
They came at the end, when all the ages had been completed,
and see, they have become first in the Gospel full of life.
The last laborers are the peoples who entered at the eleventh hour,
following the pattern of the five times at which the lord of the vineyard hired laborers.
The human body is sustained by five senses;
the Law has five books, full of mysteries;
the Lord established five covenants with humanity;
five times the lord of the vineyard hired laborers.
The first covenant he established with Adam among the trees,

the second with Noah, the righteous son of the ark,
the third with Abraham, the good friend,
