the fourth was that of Moses, and the fifth that of the Son of God:
at dawn, at the third, the sixth, the ninth, and also the eleventh.
For yet another covenant there is no place in the world,
just as a human has no senses other than five,
and the right hand has only five fingers.
Nor is there any teaching after the commerce of the crucifixion,
for with the fifth the world is completed and comes wholly to its end.
A human being too, by five measures, as by steps,
is able to ascend, and so is completed and becomes a man.
He is an infant, and after that a child,
and after boyhood he becomes a youth, and becomes a man.
See: infancy and childhood and boyhood,
and youth, and so he reaches the full measure of a man.
And after this fivefold measure there is no room
for anything more to be added to the measures of human beings.
The world has reached that fivefold measure, that of the Crucified;
it is completed, it has become a man, and it grows no more.
The time of the infant has passed, the first Adam,
and of the child, Noah the righteous, who inherited the earth,

and of Abraham the boy, who ran with God,
and the time of Moses the youth, watchful and divine.
The last time has come and stands, the fifth, that of the Messiah;
the ages are completed, and for anyone who considers, it is now the end.
The dawn has passed, when the laborers entered the great vineyard,
and the time of the three bright hours has passed.
The sixth has passed and gone, and the hot ninth as well,
and see, in the cool of the eleventh the world is running.
Noon has passed, and the love of humankind has grown cold;
evening has drawn on, and see, the world is ebbing toward its end.
O you of the eleventh hour, quicken the race with repentance;
last peoples, become first in righteousness.
The word of the Lord is very like a pearl,
its face all full of light for whoever looks on it.
To whoever has spent most of his days in emptiness,
the parable of the Son of God lends a hand;
to whoever sinned in his boyhood and his youth,
and the web of his life reached its cutting while he was squandering it.
O you old man, aching and bent with age,
who wish to turn back and enter at the eleventh hour: you are accepted.

The hour of life lies before you, and if you are diligent
in it, you can find the whole of life without end.
The Evil One enticed you with desires while you were sinning;
see that he does not block the door before you if you repent.
He will say to you: "How now is there any way
for you to be accepted in repentance, you who were idle?
There is no strength in you to bend your soul to supplication,
nor is fasting easy for you, to hold to it like a diligent man.
Nor does your body lend a hand to toil and weariness,
and you have sinned much: by what will you find favor, if you repent?
Your strength has failed, your sight is dimmed, your body is weak;
how much less [?] are you fit for the labor of righteousness."
These are the counsels the Evil One gives to whoever sins,
to cut off his hope so that he does not draw near to repentance.
But you, laborer who entered at the eleventh hour, do not be divided in mind,
for your wage is prepared along with the first, if you repent.
The Son of God loves the last laborers,
for he too came at the end of the ages and visited the earth.
The ardor of youth carried you away when you were sinning,
and in idleness and an evil life your days passed by.
Give that remnant of a little life to God:

for He is willing to accept even one hour that a laborer gives. / It has been shown how our Lord pays the wage, / and He bore witness in the last laborers to how dearly they are loved. / He gave encouragement to whoever turns to repentance, / that if he works at it for one hour, he becomes first. / O sinner, who has spent the whole chain of his years in great wickedness, / behold the Lord of the wage, whose door is open and who scatters His treasures. / Even at the end of your whole life, if you repent, / at the hour of the wage He counts you among the idle. / And if you have no strength for the labor of righteousness, / give your will to God, and it is accepted. / Hate sin, which has worked great loss for you, / and give yourself to righteousness, which has never yet seen you. / Turn away from iniquity, even if your days have now come to an end, / and be a last laborer who receives a good wage. / Turn your soul back, then, and be your own accuser; / while your conscience reproves you, be ashamed of your evil deeds. / Say to your soul: “O wandering ewe that has gone astray, / signal [?] to the shepherd, even with a sign, and he will find you. / The wolves of sin have set about tearing you apart among the mountains:

enter the fold of the One who heals the sick.” / “The day has declined, and see, the shadows of death surround me; / be a sun to me in the evening, our Lord, and let me see Your light. / Let not the day of death set upon me outside Your vineyard; / Your eye is good: accept the hour of repentance. / My times are spent, while I have labored for emptiness; / accept the end of my life’s time, that it may be Yours.” / For repentance there is no time that is not its time, / and unless a man has reached the gate of Sheol, he does not lose it. / As long as the soul remains and dwells in the body that sinned, / there is hope of repentance for all sinners. / As long as blood runs in the veins and limbs, / there is room both for sin and for righteousness. / As long as there are tears for the eyes to shed upon the face, / there is mercy to deliver whoever has sinned. / As long as you can weep, you can ask for mercy, / and if there is weeping, there is grace for all sinners. / Even the sick man who lies on a bed of pains, / if he pleads for forgiveness, can receive it. / If in a single hour a man draws near to God, / that hour is far better than a long span of life. / Unless a man has entered and the bars of Sheol have been shut in his face,

he is not far from the reach of repentance. / Unless the ship of life has come to rest at the silent grave, / the cargo of riches is not taken away from penitents. / As long as you live, you are a penitent if you wish; / but if death meets you, it snatches away your repentance. / In the grave alone is the door of repentance shut, / for the dead are not allowed to repent in the house of destruction. / Even in the very hour of death there is room to repent, / and good works too can be done in it, if you wish. / Even when the soul is stirring to go up out of the limbs, / if it acquires a good will, it will find life. / When death has entered and stood at the door and shot its arrow, / hurry, order your affairs justly. / If there is anyone you have plundered, give back the plunder, and so depart, / lest the one you plundered bring a complaint and distress you by it. / If there is a laborer who has not received his wage, pay him what is his, / so that you are not accused at the crossing, if he meets you. / If a widow has been wronged by you, call her and make peace with her, / before her voice shakes the door of the judge’s house. / If you have taken anything from an orphan, give him what is his, / for at that door the complaint of orphans is readily received.

If a time of slackness has overtaken you in sins of the body, / send gifts to the solitaries and the holy ones. / Plead and weep, lay bare your soul and reveal your distress, / and ask them to ask mercy on your behalf. / It is the hour of life, and there is still room for righteousness; / at the eleventh hour you have entered: quicken the race of good deeds. / Look into the house you were gathering for yourself with such care, / and with it buy water for the fire that is prepared for you. / Bring out and scatter: to one a cloak, to his fellow a garment; / to this one clothing, to that one a covering, to his fellow bread. / Call the poor and the beggars, and by their hands / send a bribe to the fire, so that it may forget what you have transgressed. / Ask your heirs, plead with them and persuade them / not to be distressed if you take care to save your soul. / And whoever is distressed, regard him as a great enemy to you, / who wants you to burn while he inherits your goods. / Rouse your soul to generosity in the hour of death, / that with every [?] you may bind up the many afflictions within you. / Tear up the bonds of debt and throw them into the fire; it is accepted from you; / and if you give up the bonds, the one who would demand them of you [?] will not come near.

You have run about in the world and toiled much for emptiness; / provide for your soul before the door is shut in your face. / You have no excuse to say, “No one hired me,” / for behold, the Lord of the wage is stretched out on the cross and waits for you. / See, His hands are spread out, and He stands on Golgotha / and calls everyone to come to the vineyard of righteousness. / He cried out with a loud voice on the cross, and the earth trembled, / and He roused all the idle to repentance. / See, the denarius is placed in your hand, His body that was broken, / and He has appointed you to work for a good wage; why are you idle? / Your Master is generous to the first and to the middle ones; / be wise in the hour of life that remains to you. / Make friends for yourself with the mammon of iniquity you have acquired, / so that they may receive you into their shining tents. / Pay your debts while you are in your own place among your acquaintances, / for in that place all debts are demanded with fire. / Look at the cross as at that bronze serpent, / and seek from it the medicine that heals your wounds. / It is the hour; it is yours: ask forgiveness in faith, / for faith never returns empty but obtains all it asks.

Even the robber was fixed with nails and pinned fast, / and the arrows of death were striking him beside Golgotha. / And in that very hour of death he asked for mercy and found it, / just as he asked, because he asked in faith. / By the good wage He gave to the last, He gave encouragement / to whoever comes to repentance at the end of his days, / so that the world may learn that He receives whoever comes. / Blessed is the First, who gave the last a good wage!
Here ends the homily on the laborers whom the owner of the vineyard hired.
By Mar Jacob. Homily 55, on Zacchaeus the tax collector.

For the sake of the wicked our Lord set out on His way into the world,
to gather those who had strayed from His Father's house.
He directed His journey toward sinners to bring them back,
and sought out the strays to find them, for they were lost.
He let go of the found and sought the lost in His care:

He left the perfect and went about with penitents.
A harlot kissed Him, and He received her;
sinners invited Him, and He took delight in it.
He was called the friend of tax collectors and harlots;
He carried bandages, and none but the broken love bandages.
The good Physician did not come down to bind up the healthy,
for none but the sick are in need of His help.
One who is not dead has no need of resurrection,
and for one who has not sinned, forgiveness is superfluous.
Whoever is broken wants a bandage brought to him,
and whoever is struck calls for the physician to come to him.
A medicine for sores is never put on anything but sores;
a remedy for diseases is needed by none but the diseased.
Only the broken-hearted need encouragement,
and only the distressed in spirit are pressed for comfort.
Whoever has sores is in need of medicines,
so that by being healed he may find relief from his wounds.
One who has made his debt to his lord very great
hangs his soul on forgiveness, because he needs it.
One whose soul has been struck by iniquity and who feels its blow,

it is he who needs the medicine of mercy to be brought to him.
Whoever is bitten by sins and wails aloud,
he is the one who needs a dresser to bind up his wound.
One who has swallowed the arrow of wickedness into his limbs
needs grace to draw out the barb [?] of his pain.
One on whom sin has fallen like a lion
needs mercy to rescue him from destruction.
Fittingly, then, our Saviour came to sinners,
to visit them as one who binds up the stricken.
In Zacchaeus the tax collector He set up a market for repentance,
so that everyone may come and trade in it without hindrance.
Through that plunderer He gave encouragement to the children of iniquity:
if they repent, they are not driven away from righteousness.
He set him up like a mirror for eyes to gaze into:
if they turn back, their offences are not remembered.
Who will cut off his soul's hope when he looks at him,
at the companion of tax collectors who became a companion in the apostleship?
Who indeed will think that his debts will not be forgiven,
when he sees a robber mixed in among the disciples?
Who will not run to take refuge in repentance,

which has the power to make doves even of hawks?
Who will not come after this good Shepherd,
who hunts wolves to make them lambs within His flock?
Who hates his own life so much that he would flee from Him,
from this Physician whose power triumphs over wounds?
He mixed the tax collector in with the disciples for a purpose:
to hold out to robbers an incentive to become like him.
Who will not marvel at the one the Son of God caught:
a greedy tax collector, to be an apostle to the penitent!
This man had filled his house with plunder taken from the oppressed,
and had carried off a great deal of spoil that was not his.
This man had seized everything he found on merchants,
and did not know how to walk without plunder.
This man had sinned shamelessly all his days,
emboldened by the law and by the authorities.
He sinned and was confident, and the authorities made use of him;
he worked iniquity, and worked it barefaced.
His sin was open, yet he was not condemned by judges;
his wickedness was known, yet no one rebuked him for doing it.
What tax collectors and harlots do is open wickedness:

such a one does not sin by stealth, so as not to be exposed.
He snatches openly while they look on, and is not ashamed;
he plunders while they watch him, and is not abashed.
It is a sin that has rebelled against shame and [?] the law,
and does not hide from onlookers what it does.
The tax collector's iniquity cries out loudly against the one who practises it;
his spoil is renewed every day in every form.
This man heard that Jesus was passing through the land of Judea,
and went out after Him in love, to see Him clearly.
He was sick with iniquity, and he heard of the fame of the Physician who had come;
he took up his pain and went out to see Him, so that He might bind him up.
There was a great sore in his soul that had grown stubborn,
and he hastened to bring it out to our Lord, the source of life.
Greed saw that Son of Righteousness and shut its mouth,
and with good thoughts rose up to gaze at Him.
The plunderer heard: "Look, the Judge is passing by!"
and gave up the habits in which he had spent his life.
A light dawned by grace in the soul of Zacchaeus,
and he recognized the Son who forgives debts, to take refuge in Him.
He entered into repentance as into a walled city,

to hide himself in it from that raiding band of plunder.
The stray lamb heard of the fame of the Shepherd who had come,
and ran after Him to cast himself into His flock.
He saw the crowds that surrounded Him in great numbers,
and the ranks of people running vigorously before Him.
His soul was set on seeing the Son, but they would not let him,
the crowds pressing in from every side to cling to Him.
His stature was small and the people were in the way: what was he to do?
His pain was pressing, and the Physician he longed to gaze upon was hidden.
He was pressed hard by his sins, and longed to see the One who visits.
A small man in a great crowd, he was hindered,
and could not see the Son whom he loved.
Yet Zacchaeus was not as small as he looked:
small as he was, there was something in him wider and broader than the world itself.
His height was shorter than that of the many around Him,
but his mind in its love passed even beyond the clouds.
If you look closely at this man,
he was a giant of renown in his lofty mind.
A great soul was seen in a small body,
whose measure rose above created things and all their adornments.

His limbs were short, but his thoughts reached far;
small in appearance, but greater than many in searching.
He saw that he could not see the Son as he wished,
and the wise man ran to the fig tree to carry out his plan.
And this is what Zacchaeus said to the fig tree:
"Provide me with a means, as you helped in the beginning.
You clothed Adam with leaves when he was exposed;
through you let my need now be met, that I may see the Son.
Lend me your height, that I may climb and stand on your branches
and gaze upon the Lord of Eden who has come to visit us.
Make me a place at your lofty top to stand and see Him
who, together with His Begetter, made all the trees spring up.
Bear with me a little while I look and gaze
upon the Fruit of life that has been sent to us from on high.
My stature is small, and unless I stand on your height
I cannot see your Lord among the crowds.
I have no height, and you have no fruit that satisfies:
be height for me, and I will be fruit in you.
Supply for me the stature I lack,
and I in return will fill the place of fruit in you."

The wise man climbed and stood in the fig tree, and there he gazed
at our Lord as He came, with the crowds around Him.
His small stature had not been enough for his faith,
so he added a borrowed height to himself to see the Son.
Love lifted him, and he climbed and stood on the tree,
so that his whole sight might be filled with the Son of God.
He saw that he was low and could not see the Son,
so he seized a height not his own and stood gazing at Him.
His faith gave him a new stature,
so that in a single hour he grew taller than the whole crowd.
The lowly man climbed and stood on high upon the tree
to see the Exalted One, how far He had come down to lowliness.
He was lifted up to gaze on the One who had humbled Himself;
he climbed to the heights to look on the One who had come down to the depths.
The great tax collector gazed on our Lord and was justified;
he saw Him from afar, and loved Him as though from near at hand.
Zacchaeus, chief of robbers, had been bitten by a hidden serpent;
he gazed on the Son, and the venom subsided from his limbs.
The blow of the bite had pained him once he felt it,
and he ran to see the One in whose mystery the Hebrews looked and lived.
In place of that bronze serpent, our Lord was there

for the chief of tax collectors, whom iniquity had bitten like an asp.
Sin was in his soul like a swift-spreading venom,
and when he gazed on the Son it subsided from him, and he was justified.
The sight of our Lord made the tax collector a new creation,
for the moment he looked at Him he was changed from his evil ways.
He only looked at Him, and found all righteousness;
for wherever love wishes to look, it does its work.
Whoever gazes lovingly upon something with desire
shares in it willingly, even when it is not near.
The movements of desire create, as God creates,
either building up or tearing down the one who has it.
Hateful desire works iniquity even by its gaze,
and the desire for truth is wholly mingled with God.
Zacchaeus saw God with desire from the tree,
and the ardour of his love mingled him with Him in fellowship.
Whoever desires in his soul something to gaze upon,
however far away it is, it is near to him because of his love.
There is no mountain that can keep desire from mingling,
for as far as it looks, it is wholly mingled with what it looks upon.
Zacchaeus was standing far off from the whole crowd,

yet because he gazed on Christ with desire, Christ mingled him with Himself.
The fire of love burned fervently in him,
and he gazed on the Son and lifted Him up in desire upon his thoughts.
Had love not done its ministry there,
who would have been farther from our Saviour than Zacchaeus?
Outside the crowd he stood on the fig tree to gaze at Him,
and love brought him nearer than all who were there.
He gazed lovingly and saw the Son, longing for Him;
and who was as near as he was?
And as with blessed sight he thirsted for our Saviour
and drank from Him as from a spring full of life,
and as with his eyes he snatched the Son away from among the crowds,
so that he alone might delight in Him, the sweet Fruit,
and as he rejoiced to have found a place to his liking,
high enough to see from it the One he loved,
then our Lord, as He passed by, looked at the tree
and saw Zacchaeus standing on its branches.
He looked at him with love and began to speak to him:
"Come, Zacchaeus; I have seen you as you have seen Me.
Come, tax collector, be My apostle to the penitent,

and teach them that I have mercy and forgiveness too.
Come, sinner, go out and proclaim Me with My disciples:
that I receive anyone who repents of his evil ways.
Come down, plunderer, and run on the road of preaching,
and call the wicked to hope with a loud voice.
Come, I will send you to the wicked to teach them
that I have grace and receive whoever seeks Me.
Come, let Me fashion a fitting image of repentance,
so that the whole world may long for you and become like you.
Come, be an advocate for My mercy among sinners,
for I greatly desire to forgive the debts of those who seek Me.
Through you peoples, worlds and regions will learn of Me
that I am the Shepherd, and the stray lamb is dear to Me.
Come, come down, Zacchaeus: I must be in your house today.
Come down, make ready for Me, for I delight in your hospitality."
This is the Guest who came of His own accord, by His own will;
though they had not invited Him, He was pleased to dine.
He did not ask him, "Shall I lodge in your house?"
He saw love in him, and was very glad to go with him.
O the Husbandman who tilled the land that had been rebellious,
until He found He could turn even tares into wheat!

On evil thorns He poured the water of His teaching,
until they yielded sweet fruits throughout the world.
From the harlot He took tears as firstfruits,
and the chief of tax collectors, whom He only looked at, He made an apostle.
Even from rocks He brought forth fruits by His crucifixion;
even dry stalks [?] gave Him [?] when He sought them.
In the desert, bread; in the vine, good wine;
for the hungry, plenty; for the ailing, every kind of help.
He passed through no place without taking a gift from it,
for He sought fruit even from a barren fig tree, that it might give it to Him.
From the depths of the sea He took a stater, against all custom,
and from that wood stripped of fruit, a sweet fruit.
Beloved is the fruit of this fig tree, which had been barren,
for Christ plucked it from its branches as He passed by.
He saw Zacchaeus in the tree like a first-ripe fig,
and hastened to pluck him, to enjoy his sweet taste.
Not even in Eden was there anything found as sweet as that fruit
which He plucked from that fig tree as He passed by Jericho.
He was not like Adam, who fled among the trees
and took from that fig tree leaves and nothing more.
This man longed from the tree to see the Son,

not like Adam, who hid himself from the Creator.
He ripened in love and was full of the taste of repentance,
until he grew so pleasant that he was offered even to God.
From Jericho and from that fig tree that had been barren
Christ in His diligence produced this fruit.
A ruined city and a wood stripped of produce
gave a sweet kind of fruit to the Gospel, that it might be honoured by it.
Great is the power of repentance when it shines forth,
for by its power it can build up even ruins.
On what has no produce at all it makes fruit:
on a barren, desolate wood in Jericho it hung a beloved cluster.
The Son of God did new things on the way He set out on,
and by every means He caught the world for repentance.
He took Zacchaeus as firstfruits from among the sinners,
to be a sign for those who come to repentance.
"Come, come down, Zacchaeus!" And he hurried and came down wisely,
with a good heart, to receive the Lord of kings.
He hastened to bring in the great wealth he had come upon,
for he had never imagined he could find a treasure like that.
The greedy tax collector cast his eye on the Merchant,
and meant to bring Him in and plunder great wealth from Him.

He saw a load of mercies passing along the road there,
and dragged it in, so that it might rest entirely in his house.
A caravan had come down bearing grace from on high,
and Zacchaeus seized it to take it as his own, and would not let it go.
The chief of tax collectors held fast the company full of blessings
that had come down from that hidden place to the earthly.
In love he laid hold of that Merchant of mercies who had come,
and brought Him into his house, to grow rich from His treasures.
O Zacchaeus, robber of earth and of heaven too,
plunderer of men, you lodge God Himself in your house!
All the merchants on their roads have been plundered by you;
orphans and the oppressed groan over you in their reckonings.
All travellers complain of you in their inns;
even those who dwell there murmur against you in their [?].
Mercies came down to earth and were walking about, and you seized them;
grace was journeying from on high, and you took it in.
Goodness came to pass through your region as well, and you held it fast,
goodness that brought forgiveness to the world, and you boldly plundered it.
The gift that brings peace to the earth has come, and see, it is in your house;
you dared, and diligently acquired heaven and earth.
You have conquered me, Zacchaeus, and I do not know how to speak of you;

I marvel at you, O victor full of victory.
Shall I call you a tax collector? You are an apostle to the penitent;
you are a disciple, O plunderer, along with robbers.
In everything you are a paradox, and I am too weak to speak of you:
chief of the tax collectors, brother and companion to the apostles.
In the world, your wealth; in the apostleship, a triumphant name;
you lack nothing, and your praise is mingled with that of the disciples.
You rely on possessions and are diligent with your revenues;
you have it in you to plunder, and to give away is no hardship to you either.
It is yours, and it comes easily to you, to gather and to scatter;
you have the power to be greedy, to plunder, and to be justified.
On one side your hand is full of plunder and spoil;
on the other it pours out every kind of alms to everyone.
Iniquity was in your life, and the Son of God in your house;
and so you have conquered me, and I give up on praising you.
The Son of God invited Himself to the house of Zacchaeus,
to give life to those who were in need of forgiveness.
The Physician went in to drive out the sicknesses of iniquity,
and the blind crowds blamed Him while He was healing:
"Why has this man gone into the house of a tax collector full of evil?
Why does He mix with sinners and love them?

Why does He not turn away from the wicked and leave them alone?
That is why He mixes and keeps company with the unrighteous.
Why does He not loathe the workers of iniquity, if He is true?
Why does He eat with the wicked, and they love Him?"
The Shepherd was blamed as He sought the lamb that had strayed,
while by His seeking He was shown to be diligent.
The surgeon worked zealously and cut away the hateful sores of iniquity,
and they murmured against Him because He was healing the stricken.
There was hope for the wicked and for sinners at that banquet
at which the Forgiver of debts reclined in the house of penitents.
Zacchaeus saw the great wealth that had entered his lodging,
and despised his possessions so as to acquire this treasure he had found.
His soul was enlightened, and he saw that the wealth of the world is iniquity,
and he began to want to cast it from himself upon the many.
He saw that the Lord of the world had reclined at his banquet,
and he despised the world and began to flee from his evil ways.
He came forward wisely and worshipped the Son, saying to Him:
"I worship You, Physician who visited me when I was stricken.
Thanks be to You, my Lord, that a soul ruined by wounds
has been cleansed by Your grace, so that it sees Your beauty clearly.
The stricken man with his many sores is ashamed before You,

that You did not scorn to bind up my pains in Your kindness.
My feeble mouth gives thanks to Your mouth, which spoke into my ears
sweet words, that I might turn to You from my stumblings.
Let my lips kiss Your heels, Physician full of help,
for since You visited me my limbs, which were sick, have found relief.
Let me lick the dust from Your holy footsteps,
for by Your coming You have driven out the iniquity that dwelt with me.
Let half my possessions be the fee for Your feet, Physician,
for I was not worthy that You should come to me on Your visit.
Whatever I have robbed I repay, my Lord, with joy,
and the iniquity I practised I turn into righteousness.
What I plundered, I return with interest,
and all that I snatched I will give back many times over to the one who was robbed.
Far be it from me that iniquity should henceforth come in through my doors,
or that hateful wickedness should be practised within my palaces.
The door by which the great King entered to dwell with me
I will never again open for sin to enter by it."
Christ did a great work at that banquet,
for He who needs no harvests was not hungry to eat bread.
There He held a great wedding feast for repentance
in the tax collector's house, and He invited all sinners to it.

It was a feast at which righteousness was gained,
and our Lord went to rejoice there with the penitent.
The Son of Truth came in and drove out the iniquity that was there,
for darkness cannot dwell with light.
Zacchaeus began to scatter his possessions on the needy
and to distribute all his property to the distressed.
He carried alms in his right hand and in his left,
and diligently gave out with both his hands.
He was as quick to scatter as he had been quick to gather,
for on every side he was diligent in whatever he took up.
His doors were open, and he carried things out to those outside,
and raised his voice: "Whoever has been plundered, let him come and take!
O you who have been robbed, come and take what is yours from the plunderer;
let no one come forward against me on the day of retribution.
Come, you poor, take alms from the wrongdoer;
you needy of this place, help me quickly scatter my possessions.
O you who are in want, be my labourers for a good wage,
and carry out this iniquity that has multiplied my debts."
It was fitting for him to run to give alms
and scatter his possessions on all who came from every side.
The spoil that had come in little by little, while he rejoiced,

in a single hour he brought out and gave away, exulting.
He had seen the Son, and his eye was filled with His beauty,
and he could no longer look lovingly on the world.
Christ yoked him to the light yoke of the apostleship,
and it was fitting for him to bow his shoulder away from [?] mammon.
He made over half his possessions to the Gospel when it met him,
and did not delay to go out and give what he had pledged.
His hands carried righteousness to share it out;
his eyes called out to the poor to receive it;
his feet ran along the roads to the passers-by,
to share his possessions in love with whoever was in need.
This was the work performed at that banquet,
and fools complained, "Why does He eat with sinners?"
It was no greater a thing that He raised a dead man after he had decayed
than this great thing, that a tax collector should become an apostle.
Yes, truly this wonder was full of astonishment,
that a greedy man should share out and scatter all he had acquired.
It is a greater thing for a soul to come alive again from its evils
than for a body to rise from destruction.
This is a great sign that the Son of God performed,
that from a sinner He made a righteous man in a single moment.
Where are those crowds who complained when He went in,

into the tax collector's house to eat bread with sinners? / They did not know how to see what he was doing: / he was wise of heart, and he was reckoning up gains. / The fisherman cast the hook with gentle comfort, / and by his mercy he caught the ruler of the whole town. / He shut up the chief of the tax collectors in the net he had cast there, / for no one has ever caught such a catch except our Lord. / Into the sea of the world the Son of God cast his net; / it shut in the tax collector and dragged his possessions along with him. / Had our Lord not gone in to eat bread there, / this fish would not have entered this net. / Had he passed by and not chanced to come to him, / this find of repentance would never have been found. / For he knew what he was doing, being who he was, / and so he did not fear reproach. / Our Lord saw Zacchaeus and rejoiced in the lamb he had gained, / and he began to call him a son of Abraham because of his love. / "Today life has come to this house," he said, / for life shone in it, and the death that had reigned in it fled. / Here is encouragement for all the wicked and the sinners, / that through repentance they can become good.
See the new things the Son of God did on his way! / Blessed is he who proclaimed good news to humankind.
Here ends the homily on Zacchaeus the tax collector and the meal.
Next, Homily 56, on the rich man and Lazarus.

To You, O Giver, I quickly bring my petitions as I worship,
and from You I shall receive all the needs that I ask.
Trusting in You, my Lord, I will set out my request with discernment;
by Your will fill up my lack richly.
Will in me, that I may will to bring my life to Your will,
and that to You, my Lord, I may live, even now, as I should.
Make flow in me a spring that gushes living waters,
that the flocks bought with Your blood may drink from Your fountain.
Let Your mystery strike the rock that gave birth to rivers;
let Your Cross stir the soul with wonder, so that it may make Your stories bear fruit.

The barren soul is like the barren rock as well:
let it bring forth Your words, as the rock brought forth rivers.
Your glory, which is Yours, is easily spoken even by stones;
how much more by souls that perceive You!
Let me not, my Lord, fall silent from the praise of Your Godhead,
lest the stones fill my place for You if I keep silent.
It is written that if you keep silent the stones will cry out; so I will cry out,
that the stones need not be required in my stead to give praise.
To the rock silence, but to me, my Lord, give speech as is fitting,
that the speaking mouth may stir up Your praise with discernment.
It is not to God that our praise brings profit, O discerning ones,
for as He is, He is exalted, glorious, and full of good things.
Whoever is eager for His praise is the one who is helped;
let us then fill our mouths with praise, by which we shall profit.
To those who praise Him He gives a great reward,
and though praise brings Him no profit, He buys it at a price.
Though the one who praises gains more than anything else in his life,
the reward for his praise is besides the kingdom, which is his due.
But for the one who withholds praise, Gehenna He has appointed,
threatening him so as to catch him for the life of the spirit.
For the slothful one who kept his talent without trading,

[He decreed] bonds and [?], and drove him out into the fearful darkness.
He threatens much and raises a commotion against the idle,
so that, as He contends, He may profit them when they draw near to Him.
By every means He seeks to win every person for His life,
that by every device He may gather the worlds to their Begetter.
He opened the kingdom to entice by it the one who is weak,
and set up Gehenna to frighten by it the one who is slack.
With enticements and with threats, lo, He contrives
to bind mankind to Himself in love.
For the one who loves, neither kingdom nor Gehenna
becomes the reason to bind his love to God.
Love needs neither enticement nor threat,
for without any cause it is bound to God wholly.
Whoever stands at that degree of great love,
for him both kingdom and Gehenna are superfluous.
He is not stirred by wages to labor with God,
for he fulfills his desire; it is not to a wage from Him that he looks.
Nor does fire frighten him into fleeing from evils,
for with hatred he hates evil deeds, without fear.
And whoever has thus brought his love near to God,

Him He neither entices nor frightens, for he belongs to Him.
But when someone slips from that degree of love and falls,
God hastens to entice, support, and encourage him.
He opened the kingdom, set out promises, and multiplied good things,
so that, even if by the wage promised him, He might win him back to Himself.
And for one so sluggish that he does not even wish to be a hireling,
He kindled fire, heated Gehenna, and lo, He threatens him,
so that by threats, rebukes, and warnings
he may fear Him and not draw near to evils.
So then, there are three orders of righteousness,
and in all three runs the road to the house of God.
One is from love, the second for the sake of a wage,
and the third, that a person may escape from Gehenna.
The one who loves is an heir, for he does not labor for a fixed wage,
as it is written: 'All that is mine is yours.'
Then he who desires the kingdom of God
is a true hireling who receives his wage openly.
And he who fears Gehenna while being righteous
is a good servant who keeps himself from punishments.
There are three ranks in the Father's house who are dear to Him:
hirelings and servants, and sons, who are His heirs.

The servant fears blows and does very well,
for as long as he fears he does not fail in his work.
The laborer rejoices in a good wage and takes heart from it,
and because of it he labors very diligently.
But a son whose love is bound to his father from the soul
loves him with affection and cherishes him lovingly.
Nature moves him to love his father without his knowing
why he loves his father, except that he is his father.
And even if he has neither kingdom nor Gehenna,
the son loves and honors him because he is his father.
God is loved because He is God, O discerning ones,
and without any cause they labor with Him for His love's sake.
Another toils for the good things kept for him,
and this too is fair: it is the second in the house of God.
Another does well because of the fire that he fears,
so that he may not burn, and he does not draw near to evils.
But we now, in which degree are we known,
and in which rank have we any beauty to show of ourselves?
[?] let us run after the things that are fair.

Sons love, hirelings labor, servants fear;
we neither love, nor labor, nor fear.
For we are not near to that love of the sons,
nor have we entered into the labor of the hirelings.
Nor are we afraid like servants who fear blows;
whom do we resemble within the house? Not one rank.
In that high degree of the sons we did not remain,
and in that labor of the hirelings we did not persevere.
Even the fear of servants has been taken from us and gone into exile,
so that we have not even a place in the house in which to remain.
Evil deeds have set us far from God;
they have made us strangers to Him, and where shall we go?
He called us sons; we made ourselves hirelings and servants,
and all three ranks have let us slip, and we are cast out.
In His image He formed us: this is the portion of the sons,
that we should be with Him, inherit what is His, and become like Him.
And because we abandoned Him and forgot the love of His fatherhood,
He came down and roused us to labor with Him and receive our wage.
And when He saw that even in this we were sluggish,
He threatened us with fire, that in fear we might turn to Him.

The pit of fire and the great chasm of flame
He revealed and showed us, that in terror we might run to Him.
The Only-Begotten of the Father in His mercy made us His brothers, and all
the mysteries that are in His Father's house He revealed and opened to us.
He told us about Gehenna and about the rich man,
and about Lazarus and the kingdom of the house of God.
He wished to tell us of that chasm which lies between,
and how the two sides look upon each other in great suffering.
He revealed to us the mysteries of what is there before we go,
to show us the heat of judgment for rebellion.
Reports of terrors He brought to our place when He came to it,
to warn us by His tidings of the great judgment.
The custom of the place from which He came He wished to teach us,
that we might be prepared for the fire that threatens us.
He saw the rich man burning within Gehenna,
and came and revealed it to us, to deliver us from his torment.
One event among the events of that place He laid open,
so that when we hear it our heart may turn away from evils.
He multiplied His love for us, and to make known how much He loved us,
He brought out the mystery of the new world for our sake.

In our evil world He would not have brought out the mystery of His world
had He not shown us His love clearly.
He revealed the hidden things in His Father's house to assure us
that He has made us children of the mystery, friends, and His brothers.
What was done there in His place He showed in our place,
so that before we go we might learn its workings.
Who would have known the fearful story of that rich man,
had our Lord not revealed his story to warn us?
Or who would have known the account of that Lazarus,
had He not told it to encourage whoever is in need?
Because the new world was hidden and not seen by us,
He came and showed us its whole story in one event.
Through that Lazarus, afflicted with sores, whose story He told,
He taught this: that whoever is in need should not complain.
And through the proud rich man whom He showed, He also made us wise
as to how fiercely the fire of judgment threatens the rich man.
That no one should acquire gold He taught when He was teaching,
and then He showed it in the rich man as he was burning,
so that from what took place there everyone may know
that fire is made ready for wealth and its owners, if they acquire it.

Once also He spoke woe to the rich,
and it was not made plain what the reason for the woe there was.
But through the rich man who was tormented, whose story He told,
He showed everyone why there is woe for the rich.
He also gave a blessing to all the poor, and it was not made plain
why He said, 'Blessed are the poor.'
But when it was heard of Lazarus how great he became,
in him the blessing He spoke over the poor was explained.
The word of our Lord is all light to the one who hears it,
and it is full of hope and life and every benefit.
Let us then gain much profit from His teaching,
that His word may be for our benefit, O discerning ones.
Concerning Lazarus and the rich man, whose story He told,
what need was there to bring their events to light,
except that people might profit from their stories,
and that all who hear might be helped by their disclosure?
Let us then direct our discourse toward profit,
and for this alone let us speak, that we may help.
In the fearful story of that rich man in Gehenna
there is a great fullness of every benefit for the one who tells it.

Let us all then listen now with discernment,
and let the story that is told be for our profit.
It is written in the Gospel that there was a certain rich man,
who was clothed in fine linen and purple, and was proud and haughty.
He took his pleasure, he feasted, he exalted himself,
and lived every day in all pride and arrogance.
And a certain wretched poor man lay at his gate,
needy and oppressed, despised and abject and full of pains.
And he longed to fill his belly with the crumbs
that came from that rich man, and they would not give him any.
And that poor man was full of pains and wounds,
and the dogs kept licking his sores.
Hear, O discerning ones, about the rich man and about Lazarus,
about their lives and the differences in their conduct.
That poor man was not only made poor,
but he was also wasting away with pains, as we have heard.
He was battered by poverty and by sicknesses;
the two worst things in the world were with him.
Want and sickness surrounded him,
and by both he was torn, yet he did not grumble.
For one who is poor and healthy is better than a rich man who is sick,

since one who is rich and sick is put to shame even by his wealth.
Let the hearer set healthy strength against gold,
and compare and weigh poverty against sickness.
Wherever one of them befalls a human being,
he bears it with great suffering, growing embittered.
But when the two come together, whoever is able to meet
them without grumbling is far more victorious than the victors.
Lo, Lazarus was poor and he was sick,
lacking bread and full of sores and pains every day.
When there is suffering, if there are friends, they are a comfort,
for they support the heart, and in their care the suffering abates.
But Lazarus had not even friends in our place,
and for this reason the dogs became his caretakers.
Our whole world has its hands dyed with partiality,
and it knows how to love the rich man deceitfully.
For its love is for sale, and whoever gives it a price
it greatly loves and honors, wickedly.
But the poor man has neither friends nor kinsmen,
for the world's love is not of God but of appearances.
But if one is poor and cast down, who knows him

except the dogs, these that gathered around Lazarus?
He was full of sores, and no remedies reached him,
for he had no fee to give, since he was in need.
Stripped of friends, of food, and of health,
he had sores, poverty, and dogs as his companions.
No possessions with which to comfort himself and forget his sufferings,
no health by which to take heart, since he was in need,
nor friends to support his heart in his troubles:
dogs, pains, and want, and nothing more.
There was no one to bind his sores, though they were many,
nor anyone to support his heart, broken by need.
He was in pain, hungry, and full of woes; and what was he to do?
Yet though it was so with him, he did not complain, for he was discerning.
But the rich man, at whose gate he lay prostrate and cast down,
hear also how he exalted himself and was full of good things.
His body was healthy, and in his possessions he was rich;
his clothing was splendid, and his foods were fine.
His table was full, his house resounded, his place was feared;
rich and healthy, and everyone loved and honored him.
Desirable clothing, a healthy body, a full purse,

luxurious living, and every good thing without harm.
He rejoiced in his wealth, was haughty in his garments, and was all elegance;
delighting and healthy, he paid no attention to the poor man.
But Lazarus was at the gate of this proud man,
full of woes, seeing good things, yet not complaining.
He longed only to be filled with crumbs,
and the abundance that was there he did not seek.
Not for clothing, nor for wealth, did he [?],
nor for the foods on the table, many as they were.
For the crumbs the dogs eat, only for these was he in need,
for nature too demanded this, and so he longed.
Had nature not stirred up great hunger,
[?] his discernment, and he would not have longed for crumbs.
Desire is hateful when a person asks for superfluities,
but what nature demands as its own is fitting for it.
That a person should long for daily bread comes from nature,
but foods that make the appetite vary are excess.
That discerning man did not long even for a whole loaf,
but only to be filled with crumbs and ease his hunger.
When nature rose against him and pressed him like a creditor,

he longed for small things to offer it.
He longed to fill his belly with crumbs,
and not even this was given him, so that his beauty might increase.
He longed, yet he did not blaspheme,
nor did he grumble against the Giver of poverty.
From God the portion of poverty came to him,
and he knew that it was from God that he received it, and he was silent.
He was long-suffering in hunger, sickness, and need,
and bore his pain like a discerning man, without murmuring.
So he carried poverty without complaint,
as a gift that had been given him by God.
He recognized that it is God who distributes wealth and poverty,
and because He gave him poverty he did not grumble.
He perceived of the Distributor that He is upright and discerning,
and did not think Him unjust, but upright in His distributing.
A sick body and a needy house had come to the afflicted man,
and he did not seek to change anything, for what had come to him was right.
He saw that in his portion there was neither wealth nor possessions,
and for what was not his he did not long to acquire it.
He saw the crumbs that were utterly wasted by the rich man,
and so he longed for these, that they might be given to him.

If those of the rich man's house had been compassionate or helpful,
would he not have [?], so as not to be condemned by justice?
After they fell from the table he longed for them,
while they were trampled underfoot so that the master of the house would not be troubled.
He longed for the ones that were wasted, and they did not come to him,
and once more he endured his need without grumbling.
He did not envy the rich man, nor his table,
nor his clothing, nor his health, nor his comforts.
His desire was bent on the crumbs, to seek them,
and since they did not come to him he was silent and let even these go.
But the rich man took his pleasure, was proud, and paid no attention
to the wretch who lay prostrate at his gate, full of pains.
His eyes were lofty, his heart at ease, and he was all joy,
and he despised the afflicted man, though he was not far from his gate.
He went out puffed up, came in haughty, sat proud,
stood elegant, walked cheerful, came in skipping.
He reclined and took his pleasure, he leaned back and feasted, adorned in garments,
he reclined over delicacies, relaxed in comforts, busied with vanities.
His house was secure, his belly full, his body healthy,
and all the good things that are in the world were abundant for him.
But Lazarus was miserable, poor, abased, and needy,

sick and hungry, oppressed and forsaken, despised and abject.
His belly was empty, his life barren, and he was full of sores;
he had pains and a wretched life, and he endured shocks.
His misery grew strong, his oppression increased, his torment dragged on,
and his end arrived, to depart from the world and its evils.
Since his existence in the world was pursued by pains,
he leaned toward death as toward a harbor where there is rest.
Poverty rose against him like a tempest,
and pains pursued him like waves on the great sea.
And because he was a wise sailor, without harm,
from the house of sufferings he gathered the trade of great wealth.
On a certain day the evil life came to an end,
and like a merchant he entered the harbor full of rest.
He passed through the years of sufferings and afflictions,
and they all passed like a shadow and were not noticed.
He gathered up his labors, and with sighs he endured his seasons;
his journey through existence was completed, and he entered into rest.
The months of his pains leapt past and slipped away one after another;
they trod upon one another and departed, hastening to the end.
Evening and morning, this one after that, carried him and bore him along,

and brought all the [?] and their pains to the end of their time.
The wheel of his life turned toward the end,
and from the house of sufferings it carried him off and set him in a high place.
Lazarus died, if indeed his death was truly rest;
but the righteous would rather say that he came to life who had been dead while alive.
The poor man fell from the dunghill into the house of the kingdom;
he slipped from his place to the splendid place of the good life.
He fell from the depth, and the height of Abraham's house received him.
The man of pains died, so to speak; rather, he who had been dying came to life.
Lazarus died, and the children of light gathered to honor him,
and the ranks received him with a great procession to do him honor.
The angels spread out their holy veils,
and crowns of light they set upon him on the way to the kingdom.
The heavenly hosts drew up their ranks,
that the man of pains might come to the house of the angels.
Clouds of light, like white sponges, passed
over his sores, and he forgot his wounds.
Sicknesses fled, pains and poverty came to an end,
and the man went in and stood in the place of good things and glories.
The angels came out, and as for a bridegroom they bound a crown on him,

and in procession they brought him in to see the bridal chamber of Abraham's house.
He passed boldly through fearful places, rejoicing,
and at the fearful crossing of fire he did not shrink back.
Companies of light became his escort as he journeyed
by the fearful sea full of darkness, and he was not afraid.
The swift troop of Gabriel's house passed over with him
through the place of death, and he did not shrink back like a weakling.
Over the great pit he passed by the hand of Michael's house,
and they carried him off and set him beside Abraham in the house of the kingdom.
He had gone down to the degree of poverty like a diligent man,
and without complaining he won the victory in it and went up like a victor.
He stood in the contest of hunger and pains and succeeded in it,
and the Watchers marveled how strong he was, without murmuring.
And because he had won, the angels came out with their crowns
to receive him, honored, from their dwellings.
He had gone into the furnace of poverty as choice gold,
and when his beauty shone they took him and set him in the house of the kingdom.
On the bed of pains he fell like gold upon the anvil,
and the pains hammered him until he became a great crown.
The poor man came to rest in the bosom of Abraham in the house of the kingdom,
and the time came for the rich man too to die in truth.

The rich man died, whose death was indeed death;
he died and was buried, and his burial bears witness that his death was death.
Of Lazarus it is written that he died and they carried him to Abraham,
and of the rich man that when he died he was buried and went down to Sheol.
There is great need for discernment along with reading;
but if a person does not discern, let him not even read.
To read, everyone truly knows how to read,
but discernment you will find among few.
There is great need for reading to be lessened a little,
and for the soul to dwell clearly in discernment.
The sound of a word even animals hear,
but its discernment belongs to a person of mind and understanding.
Let the mind then open its ears to instruction,
for it is able to see the beauty that is in the reading.
Of the poor man it is not written that he was buried, and why so?
Only because his beloved death was not death.
From evils to good things his departure brought him,
and as one living he lived; it is not written that he was buried, for he lived.
But the rich man, of whom it is written that he was buried, because in his death
woe, a narrow place, and a great pit awaited him:
when this one died, they buried him as [?]

and went down to Sheol—which did not happen to Lazarus. / This one they buried, and did not carry off, as we have heard: / one was sent to heaven, and one to the abyss. / It is written of this one that while he was tormented there in Sheol, / he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham and Lazarus. / From what is written, that he lifted up his eyes, it becomes clear / that he was in the depth, and that poor man in the height above. / So the wretch died and was buried, as was said, / and went down to the burning pit of fire in great pain. / Like a fleeting evening shadow his good things passed away, / and all evils without end came and surrounded him. / As in a dream he grew rich and proud, and his soul was deceived, / and he woke and saw that he was crushed and oppressed and full of pains. / Like a blossom fair of colour he shone in his clothing, / and suddenly the heat of the fire reached him; he withered and was ruined. / He grew fat on delicacies and wines and luxuries, / and when the fire of judgment struck him, he shrank and was brought low. / Time threw him down from his lofty couch and he fell / into a hollow pit that has no bottom and is full of fire. / His proud and crowned bed was overturned, / and he went down from it, and coals of flame received him.

Death swept away that man whose table was full of good things, / and in Gehenna, where there is no water, it made a place for him. / The wretch left behind the clear drink in his proud dwelling, / and went down to the place where they will not give him a drop of water. / The world, which he greatly loved, caught him with its enticements; / the fire loved him, and he became bread for the flame. / He went down to the abysses and inherited darkness in the dwelling of Sheol, / and tremblings and pains and sores and all afflictions surrounded him. / And while he was tormented there in Sheol he lifted up his eyes / and saw Abraham and Lazarus in the kingdom. / He saw the needy man who used to lie at his gate every day / now exulting richly in a lofty place. / He saw the lowly one, on whom a crown was set among the victors, / exulting on high, full of heavenly blessings. / He gazed at him reclining at the table of Abraham's house, / eating light and drinking splendour to his fill. / He saw him reclining beside a basin full of life, / and licking from it all delights in the spirit. / He appeared to him in a place where pains do not enter, / and sores never come near those who dwell there. / He saw him in the bridal chamber which the Father had prepared for his friend Abraham,

where a feast was being held, and he too was there with the saints. / It became clear that he was that needy man who had been thrown / before his gate, whom he used to look upon and not pity. / He recognized him: he was that sufferer around whose sores / the dogs had gathered and licked them with their tongues. / The Gospel is an eye full of light in all its words, / and on every side it has faces that shine brightly. / It teaches us about the revelation of the new world, / about its forms, its affairs, and its ways. / Through it we are able to know clearly here / what there is beyond, and what the great judgment is like. / If the Gospel had not shown us, who would have known / that the two sides see each other in the new world? / From what happened to the rich man and to Lazarus / we perceive the whole view the two sides have there. / They see and know, and the one hears the voice of the other; / otherwise there would have been no speech, nor questions from one to the other. / The Judge is just, and because his great judgment is upright, / for this reason the two sides will see each other there: / so that the orphan who was wronged will look out from the kingdom / and see in the fire the one who wronged him, as he is tormented.

The widow will be standing on high at the right, / and will look upon her plunderer cast into Gehenna. / So that Abel, who was slain, will look upon crafty Cain at the left, / while he himself reclines and shines at the right. / So that the wronged may see those who wronged them being repaid, / and give the Judge his due, because his judgment was upright. / For this reason the two sides look out at one another, / so that the Lord's judgment may not be hidden from his creatures. / And whoever saw here that he was wronged and it grieved him, / let him rejoice there when he sees in the fire those who wronged him. / And whoever thinks here that something was a trifle, let him see [?] there / that even for a small word of the mouth there is retribution. / And let the peoples know that the Lord is just in all his judgments, / and in uprightness judges every man according to his deeds. / For this reason he raised up, turned, set opposite and arranged / the lofty place of the kingdom facing Gehenna, / so that he should not judge men in secret; / he revealed his great judgment like light before the creatures. / He gave his uprightness faces, so that by it / the peoples and the world might look upon it—an uprightness that will not stoop to respect of persons. / All hidden things come out into the open at his great judgment, / and for this reason the two sides are arranged one facing the other.

So that when the judgment is laid out and goes forth in uprightness, / both sides may cry out: Just is the One who judges all! / How just it was that this proud man should see / that poor man in the greatness in which he now dwelt; / and that, as the one had longed to fill his belly with the other's crumbs, / this one should now long for a small drop from the other's splendour. / For justice weighed their deeds equally, / and repaid their debts in the upright measure of their doing. / Against the crumbs she set a drop of water in the balance, / to repay the debts there equally, as in scales. / That one longed for crumbs, and this one longed for a drop; / and since that one did not receive, this one did not receive, lest it be unjust. / He saw him from afar in the kingdom, just as he had once seen him from afar; / and again from afar he was struck back by justice [?]. / That hidden Seer, who saw that poor man / longing for crumbs while they would not give him any, / pressed that rich man so that he would long / for a drop of water, and those of Lazarus's house would not give it to him. / He spread for him a bed of fire in Gehenna, / in place of the bed of sores on which he had seen that poor man. / In place of his purple and his fine linen in which he gloried, / he gave the needy man splendour and glory to wrap himself in.

And in place of the proud life that this one lived, / Lazarus received that kingdom which never passes away. / In place of the foods of that rich man he gave the needy man / a table of good things whose provisions have no end. / Now he weighed the flame against the sores, / and the fire of judgment against the fever of that poor man; / and the great thirst that surrounded that rich man in the fire / against the great and hard hunger of that poor man. / And as the needy man had asked here for crumbs, / so the rich man asked for a drop of water in great pain. / He was cast into the fire, and the flame surrounded him, / and the wretch wailed, and those of Lazarus's house did not pity him. / The fire clung to him, and he bellowed in anguish, / and his friends stood far from him and did not answer him. / There in the coals the thirst for water pressed him, / and he began to cry: My father Abraham, have mercy on me! / He saw the refuge of the just dwelling on high above, / and from Gehenna he made his petition in great pain. / He saw Lazarus, known and beloved among the saints, / and asked that he come to him in the fire and quench his thirst. / He saw that if that poor man were sent, he could, / from that company, bring him relief from his anguish.

He saw that if he came and stood [?] in the fire and listened to him, / the flame surrounding him would die down a little. / And therefore he bellowed in entreaty to Abraham / to send him, so that he might give him a little relief. / “My father Abraham, have mercy on me,” he begged, / “and send Lazarus to me,” he implored, / “and let him bring with him a drop of water from your side, / and moisten my head, which burns with thirst.” / Woe to the proud rich man of the drinks and wines— / to what lowliness he came down, to ask for only a drop! / Woe, woe to the one proud of his delicacies and luxuries— / what great thirst surrounded him in Gehenna! / Woe, from what height to what depth he fell from his pleasures, / to be in need of a drop of water and not receive it! / Woe to the wretch, how proud he was in the life here, / and he went and found an evil life of every torment! / Woe to the lofty one, how exalted he was above many, / and time swept him away into a river full of flame! / Woe, he was proud and pampered and sated, / and it overtook him, and look, he is dragged across the coals! / Woe, he was desirable and fair and beloved like a blossom, / and the fire of judgment blazed up and quenched all his beauty!

Woe to the rich man who used to change every kind of wine; / he asked for a little drop and they withheld it, and his pain grew great. / Woe, he was arrogant with his cupbearers and his stewards [?], / and he thirsted for water in the fire and called out, and no one heard him. / Woe, he was used to a crowd of servants and attendants, / and he begged the poor man to give him water to drink. / “Father Abraham, send my brother Lazarus to me”— / of course he recognized him, that he was the one who used to lie before his gate. / As a man might say: He knows me and I know him, / and who I am and what I was, he knows. / The rich man saw that the people of his own side, of his counsel, / and of his rank were not in the refuge of Abraham's house. / The companions of his table he did not see there, nor his dear ones, / nor his friends, nor the fine companions of his conversation. / Of these acquaintances of here he saw none there, / but only that poor man who used to lie before his gate. / Had he seen his friend or relative in the kingdom, / he would have asked for him to come to him instead of Lazarus. / And because he was hard pressed, and there was no one of his own there, / he asked that the one who used to be always at his gate every day should come. / His friends, it seems to me, were with him;

that is why he saw no one of his company with Abraham. / Of that whole crowd that used to be at his great gate, / he saw only the downtrodden one, there in the kingdom. / And as a confession he asked for him by name to come to him— / for this very announcement of his showed that he had greatly wronged him. / In reproof of his own soul he began to call him, / so that by this very cause he might be accused by justice. / For when he lay prostrate and cast down at his gate, he did not know who he was; / and once he had been removed far from him, how eagerly he called on him! / He asked him to come to him in the fire as a friend, / and that he was no friend, his lowliness and downtroddenness bear witness. / Before his gate he lay in sores and in need, / and he did not know him—so whom is he calling now? / He trampled him going out, crushed him coming in, despised him while making merry; / and now that he has come to rest, look, he too is called upon [?]. / He endured sores and pains and need with strength [?], / and the other stands calling him to come, so as to plunge him into Gehenna. / When his table was full of all good things, he did not know him, / and once the sea of fire surrounded him, he made him his companion. / When he exulted in his delicacies, the other was far away, / and once he was brought low among the coals, the other became near.

“Father Abraham, have mercy on me,” he begged, / “and send Lazarus to me to relieve my anguish.” / The rich man bellowed cries of pain from Gehenna, / and Abraham answered him from the kingdom, saying to him: / “Remember, my son, that you received your good things, / and Lazarus endured his evils in abundance. / And now, look, here he is at rest and you are tormented; / yours was there and his is here—and what do you ask?” / The Gospel needs no interpretation among the discerning, / for it is all light, and the interpretation of all mysteries as well. / The sun grows dark, yet its light does not change; / the moon sets, yet its dawning shines on the creatures. / Only let the eyes of the heart, which are closed in us, be opened, / and see, it appears clearly in its beauty. / See, it shows us, if we look with discernment, / that this world is the opposite of that one in every respect. / For its good things are truly evils, / and its evils in turn are surely good things. / All the good things of this world are full of death, / and from its evils life overflows for the one who endures. / Whoever is at ease in it, afflictions await him and are kept for him, / and whoever is afflicted in it has rest in the new world.

Thus the Gospel of our Lord teaches mankind, / and whoever wishes not to heed it—it is still His. / He said openly that whoever finds his life shall lose it, / and whoever loses his life shall find it again in the world to come. / For he loses his life who is wearied and persecuted and crushed, / and crucified every day in the face of sufferings and desires; / and he dies every day for the hope of the world to come, / and lives in abundance in a world he does not love. / And whoever loses his life here goes and finds / a desirable place and a life of light without end. / And he finds his life full of good things in the great world, / and peace be upon him, for he finds his life when he loses it. / But the one who is proud and pampered and sinful and arrogant, / to whom the life of the world and all its splendours come readily, / who loves wealth and whose soul is bound up in possessions, / who hates afflictions and flees far from troubles, / and finds his life in a proud life free of afflictions— / this one loses it and condemns it, because he found it. / And he goes and inherits the sea of fire like the rich man, / who here received all his good things, as was said. / O the comforts of this world, how bitter they are,

for from them all troubles spring up for their owners! / O the garments and the pleasures and the possessions, / which beget pains and sores and death and every torment! / O the foods and the delicacies and the wines— / what thirst they bought for that rich man! / O the great table full of every splendour, / from which all afflictions spring up after a little while! / O wealth, which honoured its master for a short time, / and then carried him off and swept him into a sea of endless fire! / O possessions, what did you do to that wretch, / who acquired you as in a dream and is tormented forever! / O gold, how it deceives and goes unnoticed, / how it puffs up and makes arrogant, and in the end casts into the fire! / O honours, which passed like a shadow and vanished, / and from which sprang envy and contempt and every evil! / O the banquets and suppers of the proud man— / what pains they bought for him in Gehenna! / O the good things which a great storm carried off, / and in their place time brought every evil! / O the world, how much it deceives men, / and with its desires entices, strangles and destroys them!

I renounce you, world, for how hateful are your beauties, / and how evil, how full of woes, are all your good things! / It is you that must be feared; blessed is he who utterly detests you, / and reckons you with his great Adversary, as indeed you are. / Woe to those who loved you, woe also here to those who hate you; / for whoever loves you burns, and whoever hates you is crushed and wearied. / The evil world therefore drowns men by means of your good things, / for in them one finds the scourge and the fire and the great judgment. / Let everyone fear your gifts, if he is discerning, / for within honey you place bitter things, whatever you give. / You are sweet and you strangle, for even your sweetness is bitterness; / your good things are evils, as it is written. / From now on, then, let no one fear your evils, / but let him fear your good things, if he is wise. / For through your evils, those which that poor man endured, / he found that kingdom with Abraham. / And who can set his heart on your evils / and love them, except a valiant man like Lazarus? / But if a man loves the evils of this world, / it is clear that from them he inherits every good thing. / For a man receives here, and there they will not give to him; / in one world only is a man at rest—whichever he loves.

Whoever's soul has gone out here to this world, / and has loved it greatly, has no place in that world. / For whoever has his face set with discernment toward what lies beyond / reckons the comfort of here a thorn that strikes and wounds. / And these things you can know clearly / from the words that Abraham spoke to the rich man: / “Why, you received all your good things, and he his evils, / and in place of these, look, he is comforted and you are tormented.” / The word is very hard to hear, and who can bear it / except one who hates pleasant comforts? / That rich man is tormented because he lived at ease, / and because he was proud in this life the fire swallowed him. / It is not written that he sinned, but that he lived at ease and was proud, / and that he made merry and gave nothing to the poor. / He was not accused by justice of plundering or robbing, / nor of doing wrong, nor of wronging his fellows. / No orphan cried out against him that he had seized and taken his property, / nor a widow that he had brought her possessions within his gate. / In this alone was he accused before the Judge: / that he was proud and did not look upon the poor. / When the reproof went forth for him from Abraham,

the just man recounted to him, recounted all his passions and his deeds. / Had there been anything else of which he was guilty, / the just man would not have kept it from him and hidden it. / With what was truly his, truth rebuked him without wronging him, / for he said to him only: You received all your good things. / He did not reproach him for robbery or plunder, / for had he been guilty of these, he would have exposed them to him. / He did indeed remind him of the things that had been, / but said nothing to him except that he had received all his good things. / What then will befall the man who does wrong and inflicts wrong, / not only being proud but wearing down his fellows? / This man burns because he neglected the poor; / what then will become of the one who even plunders the poor? / That man was tormented because he took his pleasure in his possessions; / how great then the burning of the one who took the bread of the hungry! / Because he wore splendid clothing, he was clothed abundantly with coals; / what then is the judgment of the one who stripped even the widow? / Why was this man's story told at length, / while of the plunderer and the robber there is no story? / This proud man they swept into the fire because he was proud; / then what place will be the plunderer's lot there?

If because he lived at ease he became known in Gehenna, / where shall we look for the one who crushed his fellows? / It seems to me that the plunderer went down to the bottom of the pit, / and the flame covered him down in the abyss, / and did not allow him to see Abraham and Lazarus. / This man, who did not plunder, saw Abraham and Lazarus, / but the robber was cast and sunk to the bottom of the pit. / The fire swept him away and brought down his treasure [?] to the abysses below, / and there is no story of him, for he was covered by the flame. / He was buried in the coals, and his story was forgotten and not told; / the pit swallowed him, and every word and account of him ceased. / But this proud man is known and his great judgment revealed, / and his story, his words and his changes of fortune are written in the Gospel. / Let the account of him cast trembling on the rich, / and from his story let fear fall on everyone who is proud. / Let great pain move my words to tell his story, / and let the mouth recount him with groans, for great was his suffering. / He bellows in the fire and raises his voice from Gehenna; / he knocks again and again, but the door is shut and they do not answer him. / Where there was no door for mercy, he asked for mercy, / and after the door had been shut in anger, he knocked to enter.

Oh, what the world did to that wretch! / It bound him with its love, and because he rejoiced in it, he bore afflictions. / Because he lived at ease and filled his belly with bread in it, / look, he is crushed and downcast and thirsty and wailing from the burning. / He asked in entreaty for a drop of water from the King's house, / and it was too costly for them, because he did not ask for it in its time. / The great door of the kingdom had been shut against him, / and it was no longer the time for ears to incline to requests. / The Bridegroom's chamber was honoured, and he had entered within it, / and at that hour he would no longer receive another wedding feast. / The bride entered her chamber to be wedded, / and whoever then knocked was turned away and they did not answer him. / Noah's household had entered, and the door of that ark was shut, / and those who remained outside were from then on not permitted to enter. / Whoever did not enter, the sea and the flood of waters swept away, / and he could not enter the ark of life. / Because of the great flood of fire the door was shut, / and those inside, who had been saved, would not open. / It is not that God is stripped of mercy in his great judgment; / it was the hour of that rich man that was without mercy. / Evil brought it on itself and went out against the wicked,

and they entered; / the beloved were honoured there in the kingdom. / Once the Judge has taken his seat and pronounced the sentence, he asks nothing further; / for the guilty is guilty and the innocent innocent, and there are no questions. / That rich man, after the great judgment was finished, / awoke to entreaty, and therefore they did not even hear him. / His flight had ended in the mouth of the flame, / and the Judge no longer wished to hear his word. / The questions were over and the judgment had gone forth in uprightness, / and there was no room either for petition or for entreaty. / That is why that just man did not send / a drop of water to the one who had delayed and only then asked for it. / “Why, you received your good things,” he said to him, / “and Lazarus you did not know when he was with you. / Had he been used to sitting with you at your table, / he would not now be so far from your company. / Had his soul been delighted with you at your supper, / it would have been easy for him to come to you as a friend. / Had he drunk from your basin that used to overflow, / long ago, look, a river would now have broken the flame. / You did not delight him with you there with delicacies, / and he has no way to come to you—so why do you call him?”

And besides all this, a gulf is set between the two sides,
and there is no crossing for anyone to go and come to his fellow.
There is no crossing from here for one to come to you,
nor is there passage from there for you to come to us.
The bridge is cut, the gulf is deep and full of fire,
the stream is fearful, and no one is able to walk it.
Wrath has cut the road between the sides so that it is walked no more,
but each must stay in his place, where he is.
One place no longer allows another place to have dealings with it,
nor can any visit cross to one side from the other.
My son, why did you put off seeking mercy for so long,
forget and neglect supplication, and only now draw near to it?
Until now, where were you idling, far from entreaty,
that now no one hears your voice or what you say?
The season for repentance was squandered in the time that is past;
it has been taken away and is not accepted from now on.
Up to this point it was grace that heard the cries,
and from here on, see, justice carries the scourges.
Why did you waste all this long time,
so that the time of repentance passed, and only now do you draw near to it?

The regions are cut off from one another,
and an unbridged gulf lies between — what will you do?
Burn in the fire, wretched man, and cease your wailing,
for no one crosses from here to there, as you ask.
Great is the suffering for anyone who hears with discernment
the fearful word about the fire of judgment, how harsh it is.
But who will grant me to weep, and to make those who hear me weep,
for without tears the story of the wretched man cannot be told?
His story is a groan; I cry out in pain, and so I say:
How fearful was the hour when he spoke with Abraham!
When his request was flung back in his face at the great gate,
and his plea remained rejected, spurned and not received.
That sentence full of wrath was returned to him,
and the wretched man knew that there was no place for asking.
