He saw that time would not give him a hand to repent,
and he was convinced that there was no mercy to rescue him.
He began to cut off all hope within Gehenna,
and his cries ceased from supplication to Abraham.
His soul grew small in his own eyes, and he gave up entreaty,
and he pondered in his heart that Abraham's household had no pity on him.
A cloud of fire surrounded him on every side,

and coals of flame beat upon him in a narrow place.
He learned and saw that there was no place to escape,
and he perceived that his torment had no end.
He cried out much, and it was settled for him that they would not answer him;
he asked for a drop, and was told that they would not give it to him.
He came to know the place where requests are of no avail,
and saw that the sides are separated from one another.
No one from there is allowed to cross over to him,
and the road is barred, so that it may not be walked.
The bridge is cut, and no one crosses as he had supposed,
and the gate is shut, and they do not open to the one who knocks.
The place is bounded within its place and no longer admits
any going in or coming out at all.
There is no physician to come and touch his great pain,
nor any visitor to do anything for his wounds.
He learned that his suffering is forever, without healing,
and in his heart he gave up supplication, no longer to draw near.
At that hour he hated his wealth and his goods,
and despised and scorned even his comforts and his pleasures.
He heaped reproach on all his gold and his possessions,
and loathed bitterly his fine robes and his delicacies.

There he learned what he had not wished to learn here:
that desires kindle fire upon those who own them.
The flame became his teacher, and it made him wise:
that it would have been right for him never to despise the poor man.
He was beaten with flames of fire, and learned from the Judge that He hates
it when a man turns his eyes away from the poor.
Gehenna became like a school, and in it he grew wise
in how the owner of wealth ought to conduct himself in it.
And now he was uttering these cries in Gehenna:
"Blessed is he who has seen wealth as I have now seen it!
Blessed is he who wore rags in the world and went begging,
for the fine linen that I wore kindles flame upon me.
Blessed is he who was needy like Lazarus,
and reached his place and inherited the bliss of Abraham's household.
Blessed is he who was hungry and thirsty there,
for here they would give him water if he asked.
Blessed is he who did not have his fill of bread in the evil world,
for I, who had my fill, see, I burn bitterly.
Blessed is he who did not exult in life there,
and came here and lives in comfort like Lazarus.
Blessed is he who was sick and hungry like the poor man,

and was placed beside him, to live with him without torment.
Blessed is he whom pains pursued in the world beyond,
and who here does not see the coals of fire that wrap around me.
Blessed is he whom pains and need wore out,
and who was not tormented, as I am, among waves of fire.
Blessed is he who did not glut himself on his daily bread,
and here escaped the burning that consumes me.
Blessed is he who was a slave to poverty,
and was not called a master of wealth, and did not burn as I do.
I renounce robes and possessions and delicacies,
the pleasures and the goods of the world beyond.
Who would make me there an owner of pains every day,
and grant me here to draw near to the place of Lazarus' household?
Who would have had dogs surround me in the world and lick my sores,
and rescue me here from the bites of the flame?
Would that there were a way [?] to death within Gehenna,
that I might depart from it as I departed from pleasures!
All my goods have passed like a dream and like a shadow,
and here my wounds have no end — what shall I do?
Who will grant me that someone from the dead might go and say
in the world beyond: 'In these torments I am overthrown here'?"

In such agonies the wretched man was tormented in Sheol,
and he raised his voice with groans, and they did not answer him.
He begged for a small drop, and they did not give it to him,
yet had he received the drop, how would it have helped him?
O great rich man, proud son of pleasures,
why is your request so small when you ask?
A drop of water against a sea of fire, what could it do?
In that wilderness of flame, how far would it go?
A small drop against that burning which has no bounds [?] —
if what you asked for came to you, what would it do?
Small is your request, though your need is very great;
why then do you make it so small, asking from the King's house?
The wretched man said: "If even so, see, I receive nothing,
had I asked for something great, what would have happened?
If, when I ask for a drop from there, my request is put to shame,
had I asked for more, what would they have said to me?
By something small I tested the customs of the place, that I might learn,
and see, I have learned that requests are of no avail in it.
Loans are repaid, and whoever has laid out good loans
receives from justice by the measure with which he measured.
My loans are evil, for I never had pity on the poor man,

and that is why the just have no pity on me."
The wretched man said: "Since my case has been settled,
and there is no room for mercy to come and rescue me,
Father Abraham, send someone from the dead to go
and tell my brothers about the torment into which I am cast.
Send to my father's house, to my loved ones and my companions,
that I am in such sufferings and overthrown.
Let someone from the dead go and proclaim in the streets
to the whole world that every man should fear luxuries.
Let him take from here a letter full of terrors and afflictions,
and carry it to the rich of the world.
Let him paint a picture of my great torment in words of suffering,
and go and set it up in the houses of the rich, that they may look upon it.
Send to them, that they may not resemble me in their deeds,
nor trust in the possessions of the world as I did.
Let them hate wealth, for because I loved it, see, I burn,
and let them not delight either in comforts or in robes.
Inform them about Gehenna, how harsh it is,
and how consuming the fire of judgment is upon the rich.
Counsel them that if they see a poor man in the street,
they should bow down before him and embrace him in their arms.

Teach them that very great is the boldness
given here to the poor in the great world.
Show them that whoever neglects a poor man
will come to ask for a drop of water, and they will not give it to him.
Let them grow wise by me, so that the world does not ensnare them and lead them astray
with its enticements, as it led me astray, and here overthrew me.
Let my plight be like a mirror in the houses of the rich,
that they may look at me, and not resemble me, and burn like me.
Let them be told of the burning and of the blaze,
and of the torments of the lords of gold, how bitter they are.
Let me become a theme, a saying and a proverb full of sufferings
in the houses of the rich, and let them speak of it trembling.
Let them remember me and withdraw their hand from their possessions,
for from them the flame flares up that will burn them.
Let me be like a tale full of terrors,
and let them tell me over to one another with great reproach.
Let me be a warning, and keep them far from what deserves blame,
and on my account let them be turned away from rebellion.
Let someone from the dead go now, as I have pleaded,
and tell them there what is here, so that he may profit them."
See, you who discern, how wise that rich man grew,

turning from rebellion to the point of teaching, had they let him.
The fire of judgment makes all rebels wise in the end,
and teaches them the way of truth that they had not learned.
Whoever did not grow wise through words and teachings
is beaten with rods of fire and learns, like the rich man.
Whoever rebelled against commandment and law
learns in the flame of judgment what was fitting.
Like the rich man, who here neglected teaching,
and once the fire reached him, was eager to teach.
While he was in his wealth he did not consider what lay before his eyes;
once he was tormented, he looked to the course of what was fitting.
Then he learned, when learning was no longer of help;
for if a man sows upon fire, what will he reap?
In Gehenna his soul was stirred for his loved ones,
and he was eager to send them instruction.
While he had it in his hands, he did not relieve the needy,
and when all he had was gone, he would teach, though no one asked him.
He wanted to send a messenger from the abode of the dead,
to bring instruction to the world from Gehenna.
And Abraham answered him like a teacher of truths:
there are prophets and Moses in the world to teach
them.

From this, further, there is profit for mankind:
that they should not pry into that world, how it is,
so that no one may say, "Who will grant me someone from the dead
to tell me what is there and how things are,
to speak to me about Gehenna and about the kingdom,
and explain to me at length about that judgment?"
This is what the rich man asked: he would have sent
a dead man to the world, had they heard him as he asked.
And so that no one should seek what he sought, it was made known
that it is superfluous for a dead man to teach mankind.
See, there are Moses, and with him the prophets, and preachers too;
from them let the whole world learn what it needs.
Whoever wants a dead man to come and tell him
about that world, his heart is like the rich man's.
It is superfluous, as Abraham told him,
for a man can find every explanation in the prophets.
The Scriptures are medicines for the soul in the world:
for every pain you find every cure in them.
They teach mankind the way of life,
and by their revelations open the gate into the kingdom.
They are set in the world like lamps of great light,
and chase error from souls like darkness.

In them one finds height and depth, breadth and length,
and all the wealth and all the treasures of God's house.
In them one finds even the mind of the Godhead,
and attains that exalted knowledge of the divine Being.
See, in the Scriptures is the whole life of mankind,
and they teach how you may draw near to God.
If there had been need for a dead man to be sent, he would have been sent,
as that rich man pleaded.
For God wished by every means to help
mankind and bring them to repentance.
And had the rich man's request been profitable,
it would have been accepted before God, and He would have sent.
He who sent His Only-begotten, who came to the house of the dead,
would not have withheld sending a dead man, had it been of benefit.
What would the dead man have had to tell mankind,
if they had sent him and he had come to our place from them?
The Scriptures have left us lacking nothing of teaching,
and everything that needs to be spoken of, they have said.
It is written in Moses that no one should neglect his kinsman,
but should give alms to the poor and the sojourner,
and that a man should not glean his field to the end when he reaps,
nor strip his vineyard bare, for the sake of the needy.

"Break your bread for the hungry" is also written in the prophets,
"bring the stranger into your house when he is driven out."
They also pronounce blessings on the one who considers the poor,
and He promised to deliver him in the evil day.
Had that rich man listened to all these things,
they would have sufficed for him to live well by them.
Moses taught that a man should love his neighbor
as himself — so why did that rich man not listen?
The poor man who lay beside him was his neighbor,
and it would have been easy to bring him in and seat him at his table.
And because he neglected his kinsman who was at his gate,
justice neglected him and did not give him the drop he asked for.
He had heard: "Blessed is he who considers the poor";
had he considered him, they would have pitied him, and he would not be burning.
In the evil day the Lord will deliver him, as He promised,
and the one who did not consider did not escape torment.
The evil day is the day of the great judgment,
and whoever considers the poor escapes on it.
Therefore that man did not escape the fire,
because he did not consider the poor.
All these things are written in Moses and in the prophets,

and he lacked no teaching in the world by which to live.
It was superfluous for a dead man to come, as he wished,
for he would be of no help where Moses teaches in the world.
And Abraham answered him justly, saying to him:
"See, there are the prophets; let them listen to them."
The wretched man said: "I do not want that, father Abraham,
but let a dead man go to the world and teach them."
The Just One said: "If they do not listen to the Scriptures,
neither will they hear his teaching if a dead man goes."
If they despise there the prophets, sons of the mind of the Godhead,
who is able to teach them?
If the eloquent harp of Moses is not received,
who is sufficient to make them hear teaching?
If that great one, full of revelations, is despised when he teaches,
what will they do to the lowly one who goes, when he speaks?
If they wrong Moses, whom then will they listen to when he speaks?
My son, it is superfluous for a dead man to go, whom they would not heed.
Well did that righteous one speak to the rich man,
and justly refuse his request, so that it was not accepted.
At that hour afflictions surrounded the miserable man,

and he dwindled and shrank and was crushed, and came to an end in great suffering.
At that hour all his words were cut off,
and there was no longer room for him to speak again with Abraham.
At that hour his petitions and his pleas came to an end;
his voice fell silent, his tale faded, and his fire burned.
At that hour, when his speech with Abraham was broken off,
the flame already clung to him all the more.
At that hour, when his two requests had been offered
and they had rejected them, his woes surrounded him with great pain.
At that hour the sea of flame roared against him,
and he was tormented in the great storm of fire.
At that hour wave upon wave struck him,
and coals upon coals were heaped on him to increase his suffering.
At that hour, when all his pleas were closed off,
and there was no conversation with Abraham's household to comfort him.
At that hour, when the Just One fell silent and spoke to him no more,
and he heard only the voice of the fire, roaring loudly.
At that hour, when wrath turned back his words at the gate,
and he had no recourse but to say, "Woe is me alone!"
At that hour, when he grew bitter within himself,

and bellowed in pain, and his voice mingled with the burning.
At that hour, when he turned his eyes away from Abraham,
and did not look at him, nor see him, nor hear him.
At that hour, when to the right and to the left
he looked, bellowing, and there were no loved ones to rescue him.
At that hour, a lament full of terrors
he raised for himself in cries of suffering, saying:
"Where are they, the friends and companions and loved ones,
that they do not rescue me from the burning of the flame?
Where are my counselors and the companions of my circle,
who fanned me with [?], so that I went astray in my life?
Where is the wealth that ensnared me and did not stay with me,
that kindled a great fire in me, and departed, and now is gone?
Where is my table, that was full of all good things,
for see, I ask for a drop of water and they do not give it to me?
Where is the gold that I ran after to gather,
for if it could be exchanged for a single drop, let it all go!
Where are the garments of fine linen and silk,
for here I am clothed only in a cloak of coals of fire?
Where is my authority, where my possessions, where my confidence,
where the world that brought me disgrace and a foul name?

O you fire, kindled forever, what shall I do to you,
for there is no place on any side to flee from you?
O great Gehenna of judgment, how bitter you are,
and no breath of mercy blows in you for a man like me!
O burning, which wealth gave me, depart from me;
let me rest, if it is possible, even a little, and have relief from you.
O torments, which I acquired from delicacies,
in what place can I escape from you? I do not know.
The Judge did not pervert judgment against me; it was I who acted wickedly,
for I withheld my mercy from the poor man and did not help him."
To this story let whoever wishes open his ears,
all the more because it is entirely full of suffering.
By it one learns about the kingdom and about Gehenna,
how desirable the one is, and how fearful the other, to those who discern.
Who hears of the torment of that rich man
and is not terrified by his burning into hating his life?
Or who learns of Lazarus, how greatly he was exalted,
and does not love poverty, if he is wise?
Yonder is wealth, and here poverty,
and there is no change there, but permanence in all things.

Here the seasons are mounted on wheels to change,
and every day wealth and poverty are carried along by them.
For the one rich today becomes poor tomorrow,
and the one now poor is rich again after a little while.
The sick man is made whole, and the healthy one falls sick,
for this world and its works are woven upon changes.
The child grows, the man grows old, and the old man dies,
for in the world there is no perfect standing without change.
Morning passes, noon comes and then declines,
and evening comes and takes the place of them all.
The day is lovely, its light beloved and its beauty fair,
and night creeps in after it and destroys it.
Yonder it is not so: the seasons do not roll on wheels there,
nor are the times subject to changes, to vary.
There is no passage for evening to follow after morning,
nor for night to take away the place of day.
On the right is day that has no evening,
and on the left dwells night that has no morning.
They do not turn, but stand without change,
for in the middle is a great gulf that has no
bridge.
The way is cut off before the seasons, so that they do not turn,

and the axle of the wheel is broken, and it rests from changes.
Light has no bridge to cross over to darkness,
nor darkness to set its way toward the light.
Whoever has works and righteousness there,
all his wealth is his own and stays with him.
And whoever is poor there is truly poor,
for time does not change there and alter his lot.
That rich man, then, they will call a poor man,
and Lazarus a rich man of renown.
The names of this place a man leaves behind here in this world,
and there he acquires a true name by his deeds.
Light has dawned upon creation from the teaching,
and has driven from us the darkness of the world that blackened us.
That new world, which we had not seen because it was hidden,
Christ came and revealed, and showed it to us clearly.
He revealed to us the woes and the blessings in that place,
and the conversation between the sides and all that took place was told to us.
That rich man pleaded with Abraham for a dead man to come,
and something greater than that was fulfilled for our sake.

He who was God became man and came to our place, / and revealed the whole story of the new world as it truly is. / Instead of what that man begged for, that a dead man should come, behold, there came to it / the Lord of the dead, and He told us everything to help us. / In His mind He saw that if it were told, it would profit greatly, / and the Lord of all did not wish to let it drop, as He had promised. / A dead man was not sent to come, since that would not have profited there; / behold, the Comforter of all the dead came and spoke to us. / So that this too should not be lacking from the help given us, / He recounted it as it happened, to help us. / The Lord of all places moved from His place, / and came and revealed to us what was spoken in that place. / And though the request of that rich man was not heard, / what he had asked for was fulfilled through our Lord. / He was pleading there that his story be told in our place, / and he had begged Abraham that his torments be recounted to us. / Not because he persuaded him, but because the Father willed it, / He sent His Son, who came and recounted the whole story to us. / Since a dead man could not cross over and come to our place, / behold, the Living One came and laid open the mystery of the world. / He brought to our world the voices that came from Gehenna,

and the speech that went out from the kingdom to the rich man. / He brought to our place a picture of the sufferings of that place, / and spread it out in the marketplaces of the whole world for everyone to see. / Instead of paints, He set up a great image in words / of the world beyond, drawn from the thoughts of that rich man. / And He spread out his story in the hearing of all the living, / so that they would know what was spoken in that place, / so that no one else would ask again, as the rich man did, / that a dead man should come out of Gehenna and come to teach. / And do not say that if one had come, it would also have profited, / and if the world had heard him, it would have been helped by the story. / Heavy is the charge, and it is not right, to say against God / that there is another remedy that would profit, and He withheld it from us. / What did He have that He hid and loved like His Beloved? / And He gave Him to us — what then could He withhold from us? / All the mysteries in the Father's house the Son brought out to us, / and now the Father has nothing hidden from us. / Even about the drop of water that the rich man asked for, / our Lord gave us a revelation, to show us how merciful He is.

Even what he begged for, that a dead man should come, when they did not answer him, / was fulfilled for him entirely by His own coming. / The rich man showed his love from Gehenna, / for he was pleading that word be sent to us by the hand of a dead man. / Come, let us all now plead on his behalf, / as he pleaded with Abraham on ours. / Our Lord, who came and recounted his words to us — go and say to him: / "We have heard of your burning and of your torment. / We have learned too that you were begging for a dead man to come, / to tell us of your distress and to help us." / We do not ask this, my Lord, that You send someone; / go Yourself and tell him, as You came and taught us too. / For You alone the way is open to come and go, / and both to Gehenna and to the kingdom it lies open to You. / The chasm does not prevent You from crossing to those places, / and visiting them, and supplying their needs. / The gulf that is set between the two sides does not daunt You / from making Your way from here to there if You wish. / Go to him, my Lord, as it pleased You to come to us,

and if You command it, You can relieve him even with that drop. / For Lazarus could not carry water, / and leap the chasm, and visit a road that was not his. / For us, behold, You have filled the place of the dead man who was not sent; / fill for him too, with water, the place of that Lazarus. / Because You humbled Yourself and did not spare Yourself, so that we might find mercy through [?] it, / for You came and brought it — go, my Lord, and carry good tidings, / and to those here and as far as the world beyond, stretch out water in mercy. / Abraham also decided about the dead man, that he would not be sent, / and about the drop as well, that it would not be given to the one who asked for it. / Let what happened to him become this for us: through You all live, / so that in both these things You may be praised here and beyond. / My Lord, have pity on me too, and let me live in mercy at the right hand, / and let me not be tormented there with thirst like the rich man. / Through thousands of waters let me cross the sea of fire, / so that the place of flame may not weigh heavily upon me. / Let baptism shelter me there from the burning, / and spread its wings over the coals while I pass over. / Let this spring of living water go with me,

and let me not, my Lord, be in need of a drop in the house of the thirsty. / Let me not, my Lord, ask Abraham for water there, / for I have learned that to the one who asks they do not give. / If my path falls into the fire through the wickedness of my hands, / let me see You there, as Hananiah saw the fourth one. / If my sins cast me there beside the rich man, / let me be there like Azariah with that angel. / If justice commands that I enter the furnace, / through You let me forget the fire and come out like Mishael. / You are the living water, our Lord, and I have taken You / as provision for the fire, so that I may drink from You if I thirst. / Be a bridge for me over the gulf that is set between the two sides, / so that over You I may cross to Your Begetter and live with You. / Behold, take from here the tears that are dear to You, / and give me living water there, and let me not be tormented. / Behold, from now on I beseech You, my Lord: accept my petition, / and let me be driven far from the Gehenna that terrifies me. / Let the fire be put to shame before my limbs when it meets in me / the fragrance of Your body and Your holy blood that is mingled within me. / Good One, who has authority over the kingdom and over Gehenna, / through You may I be saved from Gehenna into the kingdom.
Let Your great grace cut off the fire that is set against me; / blessed are You by all, You through whom all live in the great world.
Here ends the homily on the Rich Man and Lazarus, composed by Mar Jacob.
Again by him, that is, by the holy Mar Jacob: Homily 57, on the Canaanite Woman.

The great Light that dawned on earth in the days of our Lord
to slay the darkness of the world's blindness where it lay.
The Shoot of the Father dawned, His radiance upon those below,
so that the darkened road might be lit by His rising for those who walk it.
The Sun of righteousness came down and walked upon the earth,
and at His beauty the shadows, which had been many, fled.
He spread His rays over the corners of the earth and gladdened them,
and the world, which had been dark until He dawned, was filled with light.
He drove out the error that had grown great among all peoples,

and showed the world the way of life, to walk in it.
He sprinkled healings on humanity, which was sick,
and the pains of the afflicted, which were many, were quenched.
He poured out His healing on the sick and made them sound,
and on the afflictions of the oppressed He breathed and quenched them.
He poured out His gift to enrich the world with His help;
He opened His treasures, and all who were in need plundered them and grew rich.
The blind were seeing and the paralysed were being healed;
demons were driven out, and the bent were made straight.
He gave hearing to the deaf and light to those without light,
cleansing to lepers and forgiveness to sinners.
He came down like rain on the land of Judah, which was sick,
and like sick roots they sprang up from their beds.
He drove away the remnants (that had held sway over humanity,
and by the breath of His mouth He rebuked harms from many.
Like a physician [?] who gives freely, He was not angry when they wronged Him;
He bound up their sufferings while they mocked Him with their questions.
The people hated Him, though His healing was mighty,
and though His help was abundant, He was despised.
The uncircumcised peoples believed in Him and in His help,

while the circumcised people were divided over His healing.
For the Canaanite woman the report was enough to make her believe in Him,
but the daughter of the people not even the Scriptures could make wise enough to believe.
To Tyre and Sidon the fame of the Son of God sped,
while Jerusalem mocked that He was the son of Joseph.
In the land of the pagans, as He passed by with His disciples,
His faith was being sung in the Canaanite woman.
He passed through the region of Tyre and Sidon and gave them light,
and their empty gods began to tremble.
By His rising He tore apart that darkness of unbelief,
and His light began to spread through the world over the lands.
The leaven of life fell into the dough of the pagans and took hold,
and the lump began to draw its sweetness into itself.
The Farmer of truth passed through the borders of the Canaanites,
and sowed His seed, and began to gather a sheaf from it.
The peoples received the good seed warmly,
and quickly it bore fruit in abundance.
In the woman whose daughter a demon had seized and was tormenting,
faith was being sung for all the peoples.

An evil demon had seized the young girl to rage in her,
for he always longs to destroy what is beautiful.
The murderer of mankind had taken the girl to make sport of her,
and in his cruelty he tormented her bitterly.
He snatched a pure virgin to ruin her,
for he greatly longs to corrupt the race of mankind.
The strong one broke in like a raider upon the daughter of the pagans and carried her off,
and dragged her bitterly through stumblings.
The whole earth was pictured in her in a mystery,
and resembled her in her sickness and in her healing.
Satan had captured the earth too, driven it mad and made it pagan,
and dragged it about at his will, crushed it, and multiplied its pains.
He filled it with madness, and brought in and set up in it the worship of idols;
he poured falsehood over it so that every day it would serve emptiness.
The evil demon crushed the earth with every kind of error,
until the great Savior dawned and rebuked him away from it.
Grace became a mother to the earth and pleaded for it,
like the woman whose daughter the demon crushed, with a loud voice:
"Lord, see the earth, a young girl who has gone mad like this;
come down and save her from the error that has grown great in her."
From grace a plea entered before the Majesty,

and the merciful Physician was sent to the afflicted.
The Mighty One came and bound the strong one by His power,
(and restored the mind of the earth, which had gone mad with idolatry.
The good Physician walked through the world and visited it,
and gave healing to every pain that came to meet Him.
And as He was going through the land of the pagans, as we have said,
the report urged the Canaanite woman to come to Him.
She saw that the demon was tormenting her daughter and tearing at her,
and she ran after Jesus, hurrying to make her request of Him.
She heard the report that the Judge of the world was passing by,
and she went to lodge a complaint against Satan, for she had been wronged.
The One who does justice and righteousness passed by her place,
and she went out to complain against the plunderer who had seized her daughter.
The Mighty One in power [came] to the region of the [?] woman,
and she cried out before Him: "A raider has come and carried off my daughter!"
The Hunter who drives out demons was walking through her place,
and she implored Him to drive out that demon from her daughter.
The Good Shepherd had gone out to seek the lost,
and she told Him that the wolf had snatched a pure lamb.
He came to the region of Tyre and Sidon, as you have heard,

and the Canaanite woman went out after Him to make her request of Him.
The reports stirred the woman, who was full of courage:
Jesus was passing by, and she hurried to take refuge in Him.
She began to cry out among the crowds and to plead with Him:
"Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me, for I have been robbed.
My daughter is being cruelly driven by Satan,
and this request is Yours to grant, if You will.
The hater of mercy has seized a young girl, and see, he crushes her;
snatch her from him, and through her healing she will be Yours.
The wicked one has taken a lovely young girl, and see, he oppresses her;
rebuke the madman in her, and her mind, which he troubles, will be restored."
With mournful cries she went out after Him in distress,
and with groans she pleaded with Him for her daughter:
"Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me and heal my daughter;
a demon has seized her and will not let her go until he has crushed her."
By the daughter of the pagans He was confessed as Son of David,
while among the people they called Him the chief of demons.
To the Canaanite woman He was truly the Messiah,
but envy blinded the Hebrews, and they did not believe in Him.
The pagans perceived that He was the good Physician who drives out demons,
and the priests of the people that He was the good Physician who drives out demons [?];
and the priests of the people said it was by Beelzebul that He did it.

The daughter of the Arameans sang among the crowds that He was the Son of David,
and by her story she proclaimed to the Jews how much they had wronged Him.
New tidings were being uttered in the Canaanite woman,
and prophecy was being wronged by the daughter of the people.
The scribes despised the revelations of prophecy,
and the idol-worshippers became the first to preach.
The pagan woman knew that He was the Son of David and drove out demons,
while the believing synagogue wronged Him as He was healing it.
The Aramean woman cried out among the crowds, raising her voice,
so that the faith of the peoples might make known how great it was.
The nation of the pagans despised the idols of emptiness,
and to drive out demons it pleaded with none but Jesus.
To the King she complained about the rebel who was crushing her so,
for He was able to bind the strong one by His power.
She did not run to the gods of the Canaanites,
for she knew that Jesus destroys their idols.
She became a harp of undivided faith
as she cried, "Son of David, have mercy on me!
That rebel of evil ways has made a raid
and carried off my daughter; come, bring her back from her stumblings.
A demon who strips beautiful girls has burst into a young girl

and driven her mad; command the madman to leave the wretched girl.
The tyrant who has hated mankind since Adam
has driven my daughter mad, so that she loses her mind, which was sound.
King of the land, drive the stranger out of Your domain;
You are the Son of David: be zealous and kill him, as He did Goliath.
Do not let the uncircumcised one make my daughter a plaything and mock her;
snatch her from him, and she will be Yours once You have redeemed her.
David Your father saved the congregation and became king,
and removed the Philistine's reproach from the camp.
That David, too, killed a wolf for a lamb's sake,
caring for his sheep that they might come to no harm.
Care for Your flock, Lord, more than David did;
command the demon to release the girl he has carried off."
Mercy drew the Canaanite woman after Jesus,
and she pleaded with Him in entreaty, but He did not answer her.
He knew that the woman was not divided (about the truth;
while she cried out He disdained her, so that she might win.
Though He loved her, He held back from her and did not answer her,
so that through her endurance her faith might grow great.
The voice of the believing woman's love was sweet to Him,

and He let her cry out among the crowds that He was the Son of David.
He did not answer her at once, so that she would not give up from the start;
He disdained her so that she might add to the victories of her faith.
He disregarded her and passed on, as if neglecting her,
to show that true love is not divided.
And when she disturbed the apostles with her loud voice,
they came to our Lord to plead with Him about her.
(Because her clamour was a disturbance to the whole crowd,
they pleaded with Him to send her away, so that she would stop following them.
And to add beauty to the image of her faith,
once again He disdained her and her plea before the disciples:
"The Father sent Me after the lambs of the house of Israel,
and it is right that I should now seek them and find them.
I came out to seek the lost sheep of the house of Abraham,
and by every means I wish to gather them.
I was sent only after the lambs that went astray
—as if to say, all the peoples are forgotten.
As soon as the peoples sense that I have come, they come;
it is for the lambs of the people that I came out to seek, who do not seek Me.
The peoples are saved, for they come to repentance;

it is after the people I have now come out, for it is stiff-necked.
The calling of the peoples is easy, as soon as they are bidden;
the people is hard for Me; I weary of bringing it back.
It is a small sign the peoples need, and they come;
with the people there is toil, for it is very much [?].
I was sent only after the lambs of Jacob;
it is them I seek, because they strayed from the truth."
Our Lord gave the people no pretext to be angry with Him;
He bore with them all as with the sick, and gained nothing.
He spurned the faith of the peoples while He loved it,
so that it might become great, not small, through its hope.
He rebuked the Canaanite woman to make her stop raising her voice,
but her faith was sound and would not be rebuked.
She pressed in among the crowds and pleaded with Him:
"Lord, help me, for I am in need of Your help."
He said to her: "It is not good to take the bread
that belongs to the children and throw it to the dogs, who are unworthy.
Let the heirs eat first and live from the table,
and so the dogs, which are not loved, are fed from it.
Let the dogs be left, and let the children receive the provisions;
let the children eat, and let not beasts trample the bread."

She says to Him: "Yes, Lord, and the dogs eat
of the crumbs that are the children's, and live along with them.
For where else is a dog to eat or be fed,
if the bread of its masters' children does not sustain it?
The heirs give to the dogs so that they may live along with them,
for who keeps a possession alive but its owner?
The Lord feeds both souls and beasts;
along with the heirs He keeps hired servants and dogs alive and glad.
The children eat from the table as heirs,
and the dogs gather from the crumbs as property.
Children and dogs live from the Father's bread;
He feeds them all from His table, for they are His.
Even the crumbs the dogs eat are bread;
it is one leaven that keeps alive both dogs and children.
A son, as heir, eats well from the table,
and the dog gathers the scraps of his bread to live along with him.
No one forbids the dogs to eat of the crumbs;
there is room in the house for both children and property.
You, Lord, are able to give life to dogs and children alike;
the peoples and the people are satisfied by You, for they are Yours.
Your table is full for both those within and those without;

You are wholly (fullness for those far and those near.
You are able to feed both children and hired servants,
and the dogs eat of the crumbs and live along with them.
Your treasury is able to enrich the people from Your treasures,
and the needy peoples, too, to be sustained by Your provision.
You are a great sea, and though all peoples draw from You,
they take but little from Your divine fullness.
You are the Bread of life; flocks and thousands are satisfied by You,
peoples and the people, troops and crowds, and You never run out.
You are the good Physician, and all help flows from You,
and the least of Your power heals thousands, and it is little to it.
You are able to drive out the people's demons and heal their sufferings,
and the afflicted of all the peoples may be healed by You.
The overflow of Your power gives life to the dead, if You will,
for Your treasury cannot run short of treasures.
From the crumbs of Your healing, Lord, give to my daughter,
and through them she will live and be truly Yours.
You beckon, and the demons flee in terror;
You will a thing, and like smoke the sufferings vanish.
By the breath of Your mouth, if You command, demons come to an end;
You are a great treasury, and every help is found in You.

Your bread is not too scant to feed only one people;
all the peoples eat of it, and still it suffices.
Your medicines, Physician, are not short of remedies,
that You should heal sufferings in one people and not in another.
Your wealth is not something that runs out or diminishes;
it is a great spring, and the more one draws from it, the more it increases.
Give Your people bread to be satisfied, like children,
and from it throw crumbs to the peoples, as to dogs.
I have not come to ask You to withhold help from Your people;
You are able to give to me, and to them, and to many.
Who can exhaust Your wealth, O King, or lessen it,
when the overflow of Your treasuries surpasses all peoples in power?
Who can drain You, great sea full of good things,
whose waves of love could flood the whole world?
Storehouse of the hungry, who can empty You,
when You are able to feed all the ends of the earth, and they are little to You?
Hold out one crumb of Your help to my daughter,
and by it she will be satisfied and gain strength and health."
In the Canaanite woman the faith of the peoples grew;
in her a foretaste of them all was taken from that time on.

She asked and was spurned, and again (she pressed on for her help;
He rebuked her to be silent, yet she cried out for her need.
The crowds troubled her, yet she did not cease from her plea;
the disciples were disturbed, yet she was not held back from following them.
She was counted even with the dogs, the [?] woman,
and still she pressed on in her plea without ceasing.
It was made plain to her that she was not reckoned among the children,
yet she did not agree to be silent and turn back from the Savior.
He answered her insultingly and called her a dog,
yet it did not grieve her into turning from Him, for she was true.
The apostles rebuked her, but they could not silence her;
her voice drowned out the whole crowd, and hers prevailed.
Though insulted and rebuked by many,
she pleaded against them all and won boldly.
While the crowds troubled her, she spoke gently;
she paid no heed to any of them, though modest, with a loud voice.
Even His insult became fullness for the blessed woman,
and from it she gained the strength to win in her replies.
From His reproach there sprang up for her something that made her win,
and with it she argued against our Lord with discernment.
His spurning urged her on, so that her faith grew,

and from His rebuke her discernment increased.
By the very fact that she was reckoned with the dogs and not to eat,
by that she argued that He was bound to let her too be fed.
"Even the dogs eat of the crumbs!" she said,
and she won acquittal out of the very bosom of guilt.
Rightly she showed that He was bound to grant her mercy,
since justly she asked to receive what was her due.
The Lord, then, is bound to feed the dogs as well,
and while He lavishes His love on the children, He keeps the dogs alive.
In the very argument by which He had set out to write her guilt against her,
she was found standing with her foot upon victory.
When truth had bound her by His words, so that she would be condemned,
from that same argument she won in the contest of verdicts.
"Even the dogs, then, take life from the crumbs":
truth acquitted her, for He was bound to let her too receive.
Like a claimant she held the Son to account, to receive from Him,
and she showed Him that He was bound to give mercy to her as well.
"I accept being a dog, so long as You are my Lord:
feed Your own from the crumbs that You have in plenty.
The dogs eat and are satisfied from what belongs to the children;

it is Yours, Lord, to give life (to heir and possession alike.
Who gives a dog its life but its master?
It too eats from what is the children's and lives along with them.
If I am a dog, You are the Lord,
for all my life is given me by You alone."
The one who loves is not despised, nor does he presume;
whatever love says is welcomed by its own.
It was love that drew the Canaanite woman to our Savior,
and that is why even her boldness was welcomed.
No one ever answered Him back when He was teaching
but this woman, full of love and faith.
The scribes of the people and the teachers He refuted by His words,
but when love rose to speak with Him, He was defeated, and rejoiced.
Love put on the woman, as it were, and entered the arena with our Lord,
to show that it can win even through the weak.
There love answered back to the Lord of the worlds;
in the Canaanite woman, to what He said she did not say "Yes."
"No," she said to Him; "yes, even the dogs eat."
She did not concede to Him that it is not good for the dogs to eat,

but He conceded to her, as He magnified her faith.
He saw that she was burning with the fire of love and arguing with Him,
and He accepted that the woman should defeat Him with her replies.
"It is not good, then, for the dogs to eat of what is the children's."
She says, "Yes, Lord, of the crumbs they eat."
He saw that her boldness was wise and loving and full of love,
and rejoicing He granted her to win and to receive mercy.
He marvelled at her, that she had brought what was fitting and had said it to Him,
and before the crowd He praised her: "Great is your faith!"
The Wise One wove a great crown full of beauties,
and before the eyes of the crowds He set it on her faith:
"O woman, great is your faith;
from now on let it be to you truly as you wish."
He saw how close her will was to the truth,
and He set it as steward over all His treasury.
"Let it be to you, then, as you wish," He said to her;
to her will He granted that she should receive as much mercy as she asked.
And what she wished was that the demon should leave her daughter;
for there was nothing else that troubled her.

Love granted her that all she wished should be done for her,
for He is able to enrich in all things those who call on Him.
Here is proof that pleading is full of profit for the one who perseveres in it;
but without love no one draws near to God.
Faith can conquer lofty fortresses,
so that not even demons stand before it when it dawns.
It rebukes demons, and they flee from it in a frenzy;
it breathes on sufferings, and all who are distressed find relief through it.
For it holds our Lord's healing, since He magnifies it,
and no one can see Him except through it.
Draw near to God by faith and cling to Him,
and whatever you wish you may receive, if you love.
In the Canaanite woman a likeness is shown to you;
for she is a mirror: if you look into it, you will find beauties.
You too have a soul to love more than a daughter,
for there is already in it a pain worse than the evil one.
Her daughter the demon was crushing, and she was distressed;
your own soul sin is oppressing: do not neglect it.
The suffering of the soul is worse than the girl's evil demon;
pray for it, and see, it will be healed as hers was.

It is Jesus who answered the woman who called on Him,
and today too He answers, and is able to give to those who ask Him.
If pain crushes you, press the Physician boldly,
and as He drove out that woman's demon with ease, [so He will drive out yours].
Do not let the evil pain be pleasant to you while it dwells in you;
call on Jesus the Physician: He does not hoard His medicines.
Complain against wickedness as that woman complained against the demon,
and He breathes on it, and it flees from you as that one fled.
Pray for your soul as she prayed for her daughter;
it is dear to you, for it is single and only-begotten.
You have one soul, and if sin carries it off from you,
come to Jesus; He breathes on it to cure its madness.
Take for yourself the faith of the Canaanite woman and her love,
and Jesus drives out the evil pains if they trouble you.
And if He seems to neglect you, do not stop pleading;
He wants to be overcome by you; do not weary of asking.
There are times when He seems to neglect and disdain the one who loves Him,
not to neglect him, but to magnify his faith.
Boldness opens His treasuries (and it comes easily to it,
and it draws as much wealth from His treasures as it wishes.

Had the Canaanite woman fallen silent when she was rebuked, / the boldness of her faith would never have been praised. / Jesus rejoices when you knock boldly at his door, / and if you do not grow weary, he can make your faith great. / A woman cried out after him among the crowds with a loud voice, / and when they rebuked her, she did not let go of her plea for help. / Nor did she heed him and turn away from him before she had received; / she cried out after him in love, and so he relented and granted her requests. / She contended with him, and he praised her because she had overcome him: / for love can be bold and still not be blamed. / “O woman, great indeed is your faith!” / So he made her known to the crowds, so that everyone might be bold and follow her example. / Take for yourself, O man, her boldness, so full of wonder, / and by it you can drive out passion if it enters you. / When you ask, do not be of two minds about the Giver: / he is a great treasure from which all who are in need grow rich. / He is the way by which a man runs to see his Father, / and the door of life through which those who enter overcome death. / He is the physician from whom help flows, / and the spring that pours out life on those around him. / By him devils and demons are driven out from among humankind;

he heals the pains and blemishes of the afflicted. / By him the life of the soul is made bright, and the soul shines from him; / by him the sins of the world, which were many, are slain. / He justifies tax collectors by the power of his preaching, / and makes hardened sinners into the forgiven. / He drove out the demon of the Canaanite woman who sought him, / and he will quench the passion of your soul if you look to him. / He it is whose might bears the weight of the world; / on him all creatures lean, and in him they exist. / He is the Sun of righteousness and the great Light; / he is the physician, and the healer of all who are sick. / He is wealth, and the Son of the Rich One, and he makes all rich; / he is the strength of all the weak, and by him they are made strong. / He it is who binds up pains and diseases and drives out demons: / blessed is he who sent his help down to the world and healed its pains!
Here ends the homily on the Canaanite woman, by the holy Mar Jacob. Amen.
Next, Homily 18, on Palm Sunday, composed by Mar Jacob.

Fountain of life, from which the dead drank and lived,
open your spring to me; quench my thirst from your fountain.
Drink that came down to the thirsty earth so that it bore fruit,
let me drink from you and cry out openly how sweet you are.
New Well, which they dug with spears on Golgotha,
give drink to my mind, which has need of your springs.
Son of God, who called himself living water,
give me to drink; let me be filled from you, and I will speak of you.
Fountain that came down from the summit of the height to the earth,
with your drink my mind will pour out fruits of praise to your Father.
Grant me to speak of you, not to set a limit to you, for you are boundless,
but to proclaim to the one who hears me that you cannot be comprehended.
For who could grasp how to speak of you, our Lord, as you are?
Yet it is love whose story is higher than words.
As far as there is room for love, let it speak of your revelation:

give me a word to recount the beauty of your humility.
From the chariot to the colt, the borrowed foal of an ass,
your love brought you down; and who is able to recount your story?
From the legion of the cherubim, which cannot be searched out,
a lowly rider in our land: how did you come down?
From the house of wheels and faces and wings of flame,
mercy took you, and behold, the foal of an ass carries you in procession.
From that majesty of the throne full of light,
to the lowliness that held out its love to the children.
From that back full of eyes as they turn about,
to this mount, than which nothing in the world is more despised.
From the house of the ranks and troops that stand beside the chariot,
to the little crowd that carried branches in the streets of Zion.
Where now shall the speaker tell your story,
and in what place shall the mouth speak of you, if it speaks of you?
Behold, your splendor dazzles the heavenly beings,
and a weak and despised colt carries you among the earthly.
You are blessed in the tumult of the speaking wheels,
and you are praised with palm branches in the assemblies.
You are above and below, in majesty and in lowliness;
in height and in depth, who is able to speak of you?
Emmanuel, for our sake you became like us,

and you are like your Begetter; for his sake you are like him.
Behold, the cherubim of fire bless you with their wings,
and the children too praise you with their hosannas.
Every place, behold, bears you in triumph in its own manner:
the height with its light, and the depth with branches from its trees.
Above, the Mighty One, before whom the flame is afraid;
below, the Humble One, who has put on all poverty.
The Watchers of the height tread his path with lightnings of fire,
and the children of the depth throw down their garments before him.
The Mighty One came down from his Father's house to visit our land,
and of his own will came to the utmost of poverty.
He who binds on crowns borrowed a colt for himself to enter Zion,
that by his humility he might break the strength of the rulers.
He destroyed the horse and also the chariot of the kings of Ephraim,
and carried peace and brought it to Zion, which had been troubled.
He scorned and rejected the adorned mounts of lords,
and rode a colt, to travel his way in humility.
The children of the Hebrews saw the humility of the great King,
and took branches to honor him as he entered.
The elders withheld the praise of the King who had come to the place,
and the children of the place were stirred with wonder to praise.
The youths paid the debt of righteousness that the elders of the people owed,

and there the praise that was required was made ready.
The priests and scribes shut their mouths and did not praise,
and the little children banded together like young cubs to shout their hosannas.
“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” cried the innocent,
and the path of the King who came resounded with new praise.
The trees bowed down to give branches, that his path might be adorned,
for the blessed [?] had given the sweet fruit to the world.
The children wove a crown of praise as they rejoiced,
for the Ancient of Days, who had become a child in their company.
The Elder of the ages came and became a youth in our land,
and for this reason the youths were stirred to praise.
Zechariah the prophet took up his spiritual lyre,
and ran before him, singing and rejoicing in prophecy.
He tightened its strings and raised his voice as he sang:
“Rejoice, daughter of Zion, shout and cry out, for your King has come.
Behold, he has arrived, riding a colt, the foal of an ass;
open your gates to him, for he comes to you humbly.
Rejoice greatly and cry out praise with a loud voice,
for behold, he comes, as I promised you in prophecy.”
Zechariah sang to the daughter of the Hebrews that she might rejoice with him,
but the despised bride did not dance as she had been called to.

She was defiled, and she was distressed that the Bridegroom had come,
and for this reason she did not dance when she received him.
Her heart was captivated by the calf she loved, and she was devoted to it,
and she did not listen when the prophet told her to rejoice.
She was entangled with the detestable image of four faces,
and could not open the gates to the King who had come.
She was eager to serve her idols,
and cared nothing for the service of her Lord's praise.
She worshiped Astarte and made mourning for Tammuz;
she loved Milcom and offered sacrifices to Baal, her companion.
To Kewan and Chemosh and Ashima she openly bowed down,
and for the gods of all the nations she held feasts.
She was occupied with Egyptian songs,
and had no leisure to sing praise with the disciples.
She was eager to prepare sacrifices for demons,
and did not go out to carry branches with the children.
Children bless and praise the King who has come,
while the old woman polishes her images and renews her idols.
The prophets knock at her high gates and rouse her,
but she lies asleep in love of the many companions she has.

“Rejoice, daughter of Zion!” But she, the companion of calves, did not dance,
for she was distressed that the Father's heir had come.
She knew that he would expose her, and she hated him,
and she was not pleased that he should be praised by children.
In her heart she was envious; she grew mute and fell silent from praise,
and she was eager to silence those who praised.
It was not enough for her that she would not praise;
she was anxious to stop the praise of others too.
These praise, and she is angered at their voices,
and threatens them to cease from praise, but they would not cease.
Isaiah cried, “Awake, awake, and put on strength!”
and Zechariah cried, “Rejoice greatly and be glad, for your King has come!”
The children cried, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!”
and praise resounded richly along the King's path.
But the Hebrew woman would not listen to them,
neither to Isaiah, nor to Zechariah, nor to the children.
She heeded neither the prophets nor the youngsters,
but was distressed and angered at their voices.
In her great impudence she was eager that they should stop,
and sought a way, by every pretext, to silence them.
But those who praised did not cease from praise,
for manifest truth stirred them to praise.

The way of the Son was a marvel to the Pharisees,
yet the praise of the worlds and their inhabitants is small for him.
In great amazement stood the troops of Michael's house,
seeing the Son riding a colt in the streets of Zion.
The heavenly ones looked, and they saw the Only-Begotten,
humble and quiet among the crowds of earthly beings.
The fiery ones trembled lest he had come down from the chariot,
and all of them bent down to see whether he was there.
They saw him exalted on the throne in his high place,
and they saw again that it was he who rode the foal of an ass.
The angels marveled as they gazed at him in both places:
in height and in depth he was not two, but one.
They gazed at him, and the throne had not been emptied of him,
and they saw him among those with the hosannas.
He rode the cherubim and he rode the colt, and it was a wonder,
that he dwells in the height and travels in the depth and is not divided.
The heavenly ones bow low on his path with lightnings of fire,
and among the earthly ones he was honored with palm branches.
The cherubim tremble as they bless him in his high place,
and the youths praise him in the depth with their hosannas.
But the daughter of the people was envious; she raged as he was praised,
452
and she was eager that praise should cease from every mouth.
She would allow neither the heavenly nor the earthly ones
to praise the path of the Son, which is full of wonder.
She toiled greatly to silence those who praised,
but because truth filled their mouths, they were not silenced.
The elders of the people envied the children and their hosannas,
and the priests murmured and the scribes grumbled at their voices.
The Watchers praised the Son in his high place,
and in the depth the simple youths with the disciples.
The Jews, haters of everything beautiful, set to work,
and drew near to him and urged him to silence them.
“Do you not hear what they are crying out?” they said to him,
as though he had taken borrowed praise that was not his own.
It was from the abundance of his great praise that he was praised,
yet they envied him as one who had snatched the praise of others.
They cried hosannas that fell short of his praise,
yet the scribes envied as though he had never earned praise.
They told him to tell them to cease from praise,
as though, if the children stopped, his praise would come to an end.
O Jews, haters of light, how can they cease
from the praise of him whose praise fills heaven and earth?

If you silence the youths who took up branches,
behold, he has hosts in his own place that never cease.
Myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands of heavenly beings
praise him; and who could silence them?
Even if this small crowd were ordered to stop,
who can give orders to that legion of Gabriel's house?
They told him to tell them to cease, and he answered them:
“Even if they cease, the stones will cry out in praise.”
And so it is, as the Teacher of truth said:
had they been silent, the stones would have spoken, as he said.
It was the time when praise was owed to the Son,
and had they withheld it, the stones would have paid him praise.
Had the children not praised with palm branches,
the dumb rocks would have praised him in their assembly.
The Lord of kings rode a colt, the foal of an ass,
and nature was moved to raise praise for his humility.
The priests and scribes and heads of the people were obliged
to utter that praise which was required.
And because the elders withheld the praise whose time had come,
the children leapt up to raise praise with their hosannas.
And had they been silent, praise would not have ceased there,

for the stones in tumult would have sung that praise.
Nature was hastening to pay its Lord praise,
and had the speaking not spoken, the mute would have spoken.
And had they too been silent, there were stones to raise praise.
At that time praise could not cease;
it would have been uttered either by men or by stones.
Creation marveled at the humility of the Son of God,
and was eager to raise praise with a loud voice.
Had the children not shouted, the stones would have spoken,
for there was no way for praise to be cut short then.
Who now can make plain to us these hidden things,
whether the stones would have cried out praise, as was said?
For us who know, the word of the Son is true,
that, as he said, the stones would have paid him praise.
Let us now speak to whoever needs a demonstration,
since from things revealed he must learn about hidden things.
At the crucifixion those who praised were silent;
stones and rocks cried out the praise that was required.
In place of the disciples, who did not throw their garments before him,

the dead came out and gave him praise in their assembly.
In place of the trees, which did not send him their branches,
the sun cut off the fringes of its light to honor him.
In place of the crucifiers, who were blaspheming the Savior,
dumb natures praised him in their own ways.
Friends fled and enemies remained at Golgotha,
and it was the time for praise to rise to the crucified Son.
And because men fell silent, the stones were moved to praise,
for the King should not remain crucified without praise.
And through these things which then [?] at the crucifixion
it was made plain that, had they been silent, the stones would have spoken.
Had the children not praised there with branches,
he would have been praised as he was praised at Golgotha.
And the matter stands clearly before the hearers,
that had they ceased, the stones would have cried out, as was said.
Natures never withhold praise from the Lord,
for all creation is moved by him to praise.
Even by stones, even by wood, he can be praised,
for his hidden sign moves natures to raise his praise.
Creatures sing praise in their own ways,

speaking and silent alike, in all their variety.
The sun with its light and the rays of its heat,
how much it gives praise in the running of its course!
The moon with its rising and the changes of its waning
stirs up praise to the Lord of the seasons, who does not change.
The firmament with its expanse and the luminaries set in order in it
sings praise night and day to its Creator.
Earth and seas, with high mountains and with hills,
give praise in the ways in which they were created.
All the forests, and the trees with their fruits, and the cedars
give praise every day in great wonder.
Heaven and earth are full of his praise, as it is written,
and everything, as far as it can, murmurs praise to its Creator.
All his creatures sing praise in their own tongues,
but how, and how much, you can never hear.
That all natures praise him, truth bears witness,
but how, no one can grasp so as to tell it.
No one knows with what mouth and with what voice
the earth sings the praise of its Lord when it is required.
That it praises, David bears witness, for he demanded

even of the elements that they raise praise by their natures:
fire and hail, ice and snow, and the sea monsters too,
all the deeps and the earth, and the mountains and the hills too.
On these David knocked for praise as on a door,
that praise might rise to the Maker from his creatures.
“Let the winds and the storms praise,” he urged them;
and had he perceived that they did not praise, he would not have urged them.
By the Holy Spirit David was moved, and he stirred them up,
and the heavenly ones to praise [?].
The sun and the moon and the luminaries in the firmament,
the earth and the mountains and the hills, and the trees too:
“Praise the Lord,” David said to all of these,
and because he knew that they praise him, he roused them.
But how, or in what manner, they give praise,
do not ask of me, for it is too hard for me to explain to you.
The hidden mysteries of God and of his creatures
are his, and he hears how they praise in their own ways.
Stones cry out his praise when it is required,
and he alone knows how to hear their language.
And they were ready, when he was borne in triumph on the colt,
to praise the path of his humility.

And because the youths took up branches to praise,
there was no need for the stones to raise praise then.
And had those who took up branches there been silent,
the stones in tumult would have praised the King who came.
And when the Jews were eager to silence the Son's praise,
he answered them that the stones would cry out for his sake.
And they would indeed have cried out, as he truly said,
for there is no way for his praise to cease from creation.
Speaking mouths praise you, my Lord, with their tongues,
and mute natures sing your praise in their own ways.
All nature that was renewed in you gives thanks to you, my Lord,
for all of it is bound to give thanks in wonder for your humility.
The height worships you, who humbled yourself among the earthly,
and the depth praises you, who are higher than the heavenly.
The redeemed congregation of the church of the nations shouts to you, my Lord,
for you set her free from the weights of the ruined idols.
The daughter of the Arameans dances on your day and rejoices in you,
while the daughter of the Hebrews, who grew gloomy, scorned and was angered.
Behold, the youths praise you with branches from the trees,
and the voice of praise of the elders is mingled with that of the children.

Behold, the shepherds and their flocks worship you,
in place of that flock which crucified its shepherd on Golgotha.
Behold, the assemblies of the nations in every place bless you,
because you were rejected by that band of Caiaphas's house.
Behold, they cry to you “Holy, holy” in the congregations,
in place of the people's assembly, which cried, “He deserves death.”
Behold, all voices from all mouths sing your praise,
in all the tongues which you stirred up to praise you.
Seraphim of fire, with the voices of the hosts of holiness,
stir up your praise as they veil themselves from your radiance.
The glorious cherubim who bear you in the chariot
bless your majesty every day with a great tumult.
Thousands of thousands of heavenly beings sing your praise,
never ceasing from the praise of their wings.
Behold, she exults in you, is enriched in you, and rejoices in you,
the virgin Church, whom you, my Lord, brought back from the captors.
All things give thanks to you, for by your coming all things were renewed;
blessed are you by all; to you be praise in all tongues.
Here ends the homily on Palm Sunday.
By the holy Mar Jacob. Homily 59, on our Lord's question, and on the revelation that Simon received from the Father.

Father, Merciful One, who redeemed us by the blood of His Only-Begotten,
from You I take strength for the discourse on Your Only-Begotten.
Glorious Son, who came to us to set us free,
through You I will speak of Your revelation, for Your sake.
Holy Spirit, scribe of the wise and of the simple,
through You I will grow wise and stir up a discourse that is wholly wonder.
Begetting Father, give me a word about Your Offspring,
that I may tell His story with love and in abundance.
Begotten Son, reveal Your beauty in me concerning Your Father,
that my mouth may speak with lifted voice in new praise.
Advocate Spirit, through whom the whole Gospel is sung,
through You let my tongue become a lyre for Your praise.
Father, who sent His beloved Son to be a brother to us,
open my lips to speak of Your Only One.

Only-Begotten, who gave us all the wealth of His Father,
by the wealth of Your mysteries let my words stir before the hearers.
Spirit, who went forth and leveled the obstacle before the disciples,
smooth the path, that the wondrous discourse now stirring may shine from me.
Father, from whom are all things, and all that came to be through Him,
from You I take the occasion for a discourse without limit.
Son, by whose hand are all things, and without whom is not anything,
by Your hand I will sing to Your Father a praise full of discernment.
Spirit, treasury of prophecy and of apostleship,
from Your treasures give me wealth for speaking.
Father, who in His love delivered up His Son for sinners,
speak in my stead about Your Offspring before the hearers.
Son, who humbled Himself to become one of us, though He is our Lord,
shine in me with wonder, and let Your light dawn from my words.
Spirit, who brings low all the haughtiness of the dull,
prepare a path for my feeble words.
Who will give me a love that stands like a claimant
before the hearers and draws them toward teaching?
Who will give a thirsty ear to the voice of instruction,
to which the sweet drink free of strife is pleasing?
Who will make the rivers of great love flow

from speaker and from hearers in one will?
Who will make everyone run to the one will of God,
which wills that everyone should profit from it without lack?
Let each one strive to gather profit,
whether speakers or hearers of the faith.
O you who speak, take care, and profit while you speak;
and if you make no profit, keep to silence.
And you, hearer, profit too while you listen;
and if you do not profit, why are you idle before the speaker?
Let us bring love, for love also moves me to speak,
since profit is gathered by nothing but love.
Do not listen to my words cunningly, to ensnare them,
for love is never caught in a snare.
The word is pure of cunning and of worldly wisdom;
let your hearing also be pure, then, for simple things.
Come down from the height of wisdom where you stand,
and be humble toward me, and I will speak to you plainly.
Had the Son of God not come down and humbled Himself for us,
who could have reached Him to speak of Him as He is?
Had He not lowered Himself to poverty in love,

who could have told of His spiritual riches?
Had He not willed and come and put on weakness,
what mouth could have recounted His might?
The Exalted One came down and gave Himself to us, that we might speak of Him;
not in loftiness, then, should one listen to the account of His revelation.
On the great road that the Son of God laid out in the world,
unless a man puts on humility, he does not walk.
Unless it be in love, which is the fountain of all beautiful things,
no one can speak of the Only One.
O you who hear me, hear my words as I speak them,
with the love of a soul that knows how to love simple things.
Know from the soul of the one speaking, if you are discerning,
that the discourse he has begun to speak is higher than he.
The Son of God, who cannot be told by those who speak—
who speaks of Him, except with a word free of dispute?
What scribe, or wise man, or disputer
can explain the wonder that cannot be explained?
Who will claim to know the Son so as to explain His name,
when, apart from the Father, no one knows who the Son is?

Or who will undertake to speak about the Father,
since the Son alone knows the Father, who is like Him?
And you, hearer, how can you demand, if you are fair,
that one speak within limits of that Offspring who is without limit?
Your ear has no room for the measure of the Son,
nor can a speaker tell of Him as He is.
Do not claim that you have a hearing that grasps His story,
for I have not claimed to have a word that reaches Him.
Whoever thinks he can circumscribe the Son of God
is gravely mistaken, whether he is hearer or speaker.
He who thinks he reaches the measure of the Son has denied knowledge,
and reason too, if he thinks he has grasped Him or can grasp Him.
If you wish to grasp His measure, do not hear it from me,
for I have no word that reaches the height of the Son.
For who can stride up steps that cannot be climbed,
to go up and speak a word that is above all speakers?
The Son is in His Father—and who can measure the height of the Father,
in whom is His Offspring, hidden in His bosom in His being?
Who can speak of Him who was hidden in His Father's bosom,
and, without changing, dwelt in a Virgin full of wonder?

Hidden in the Father, and in a virgin mother, is the glorious Son;
and whoever would explain Him has only this: to fall silent and marvel.
He came down without moving and came to us without changing;
He was in the height and He was in the depth—and who can equal Him?
For while He dwelt in the depth, the height did not lack Him,
since He was wholly in all, both in Mary and in His Begetter.
He came not to be circumscribed or explained,
but to visit the sick flock and bring it back to its place.
The world saw the Great One in the measure of littleness,
and those who speak were confounded and could not find how to tell of Him.
They saw Him as a man who had come in the flesh, while He is God,
and what to say about His coming they did not know.
They saw that He was full of power and strength and might,
yet His appearance was lowly, while His powers were beyond tongues.
He opened the eyes of the blind, cleansed lepers, made the deaf hear,
healed the sick, and raised the dead, divinely.
When they saw Him in weakness, like a son of man,
they turned and saw Him in might, like God.
At one time He hungered like a man full of sufferings,
at another He fed others like God who has compassion.
And in the midst of this new way, full of wonder,

the onlookers marveled, and could not tell who He was.
They stood in the middle, between greatness and littleness,
and could not say without confusion who He was.
To say of Him that He was God was no small thing,
for they saw Him like a man in their streets.
Yet they would not let go of regarding Him as a son of man,
though the mighty works He did bore witness that He was God.
He mingled with men and performed mighty works divinely,
and no one among those of earth knew how to say who He was.
And not knowing, they went searching for names,
to say who He was, though their wisdom did not know.
One said He was Elijah because of His miracles;
another said He was Jeremiah, because that prophet had been chosen.
One was confused and did not know what to call Him,
but called Him one of the prophets whose name is not known.
And they went on calling Him one [of the prophets] whose name was hidden.
O onlookers, do not give Him a name that is not His;
do not call the Son of God by a foreign name.
Call the Son neither Elijah nor Jeremiah,

nor a prophet whose name was kept by his Begetter.
They chose borrowed names and set them on the Son of God,
and these did not please Him; He was ready to flee from them.
He took pity on the world, which was confused and seeking His name,
and He willed to teach it what His true name is.
Our Lord, the Light, led His Twelve,
to teach them clearly what His name is.
He brought them through the whole country, and they came to the region
of that knowledge which reveals divine mysteries.
They reached the region of great light and of revelations,
and the Great One began, as it were, to question His disciples.
"Who do men say that I am?" He asked them,
that there a door might be opened for mysteries to be spoken.
Like a scribe who leads children and teaches them fine things,
He questioned them in order to teach them wisely.
He became a questioner, not because He needed teaching,
but to reject the borrowed names the people had given Him.
He saw that the disciples were not asking to learn His name,
and so in their place He asked, in order to teach them.
Wrongful names, confusion and talk He wished to silence;
for this He asked what was being said by the many.

When a teacher asks a child for an explanation,
he trains the child and teaches him so that he may become enlightened.
He did not ask them in order to learn from the disciples,
but so that they might truly learn from Him.
In this too, in His asking, He resembled His Father,
so that not even in this would He be less than His Begetter.
The Father asked among the trees, "Where are you, Adam?"
From Mount Sinai: "What is this that you have in your hand?"
The Father asked Moses and Adam, and so His Offspring
also asked, "Who do men say that I am?"
He looks upon the minds and thoughts of the whole world,
and searches all hearts and their reflections.
No heart can stir a thought without Him,
nor can a mind be troubled by a notion without His perceiving it.
And since both hidden and open things are alike to Him,
and things past and things to come are one to Him,
the Father asked at one time, and His Offspring too asked,
so that the one asked might come to know from Him who searches all.
"Who do men say that I am?"—though He knew
what they were saying, even when their thoughts were silent.

Much beloved was that hour, and that question,
by which the Knowing One was moved to speak lovingly.
The Sun stood and spoke with His rays,
and filled with light the great region of faith.
Twelve lights with the Day of righteousness,
the hours of the day, in whose dawning the world shines.
Twelve had sprung from the sphere of the Sun, our Lord;
they stood beside Him, that He might teach them what His name is.
A company full of light and life and gladness,
of truth and hope and peace and love and faith.
Twelve dawns that overthrow the night so that it departs,
to gladden the lands that the Light had betrothed.
Twelve captains of hosts who went out with the King's Son,
to establish the realm of peace for the faith.
Twelve signets that the Son of God set in His crown,
and before Him fell the crowns and diadems of vanity.
Twelve men whom the good Heir chose,
by whom all the ruins that had been overthrown would be rebuilt.
Twelve laborers whom the Son of the Diligent One led with Him,
to fence the breaches of the world with diligence.

The Bridegroom set about building a house for the betrothed Bride,
and brought twelve stones to lay her foundations.
He looked over them all, to see which He would choose to set first,
and waited for His Father to show its beauty by revelation.
In the region of life He fastened a bridal chamber for the Church,
and with promises He crowned her lovingly.
He marked out the house with the Twelve, full of light,
and chose one stone for its priestly foundations.
He waited for the Father's mystery to be the occasion, then,
for that stone with which the Church was being built by the Son's hands.
And He began to ask, though He knew what He was doing,
so that by occasion of that question the Church might be established.
"Who do men say that I am?"—as if He did not know;
and they began to tell Him the talk of those outside:
"My Lord, some say You are Elijah, and some Jeremiah,
and some have reckoned You another of the former prophets.
The people are divided into many parts,
and Judea is full of rifts and talk about You.
Each one reckons You as he thinks, for they are many,
and there are disputes and divisions about You."

The disciples recounted the sayings of all the people,
and what is spoken among the assemblies about our Savior.
Our Lord said, "Behold, the outsiders have spoken as outsiders;
they have all spoken—now you speak as those within.
Behold, you have told Me what is said by those far off;
tell Me now your own word, as those who are near.
Behold, I have heard what is said among those who hate;
you who love, reveal to Me now your thoughts."
