The question slid from the starting point where it had stood,
and went inward to the disciples to search them out.
See how our Lord had no need to learn that talk of the outsiders,
but He made it an occasion for His own story.
If He had asked them in order to learn what was being said,
why, having heard, did He turn the question upon the disciples?
Behold, He had heard the people's talk when He asked;
and had He asked in order to learn, He would not have turned back.
He showed openly that the question about the outsiders
was a demand He brought in to those within, to search them out.
For the preachers of the faith He laid out a road,
that as true ones they might say what His name is.

A great demand was laid there upon the disciples,
to say who is the Hidden One whom the people do not know.
He left aside the opinions spoken by the Jews,
and demanded of the sons of His house that they tell Him what He is.
He left and scorned that Jewish notion,
and began to ask about the mind of the apostleship.
Of them He demanded that, as true ones, they say who He is,
for upon them was the key of the treasury of God's house.
"Who do you say that I am, O My disciples?"
And the disciples were shaken by the wondrous question they heard.
Our Lord set them between death and life,
to know who He is, or else they would be put to shame.
Simon heard, when the glorious Son demanded of him
that he call Him by His name, and he trembled to speak without His Father.
And the head of the disciples sent his mind flying to the height above,
and in his thought he rose up to the place of His Father.
He ascended from the earth and from the visible creatures,
and left behind him the airs and the worlds and all that is in them.
In his mind he strode out from the building of the temple of the world,

left the lower heavens behind, and rose higher still.
And above the air he stood in the hidden Holy of Holies of the Existent One,
before the Father, and began to entreat Him with a pure heart:
"My Lord, who dares to give a name to Your Only-Begotten?
You begot Him; teach me how I should call Him.
This belongs to the Father: to give the name of His Son.
It is Yours, my Lord; command me to call Him according to Your will.
It is not mine to give a name to Your Only-Begotten;
reveal to me who He is, and I will go down and reveal Him from what You have taught me.
For I do not know how I should call Him;
call Him by His name, and command me also to call Him so."
The entreaty of Simon, the head of the apostleship, entered
before the Father, and He revealed His mystery to that true one.
A revelation went out from the Father's house to that disciple,
and he took it and came down like a herald from the king's house.
In the hand of the hidden Father a seal appeared,
and on it was written: "You are the Christ, the Son of God."
And he raised his voice, as he had been commanded by the revelation,
before our Savior: "You are the Christ, the Son of God."

His true name was hidden in the Father, and Simon learned it,
and came and showed his Lord that he knew His name.
He learned it and declared it, the worshipped name of the Son of God,
to which there is no room to add or from which to take away.
The Father revealed to Simon, the chosen one, the truth about His Beloved,
but hidden from Simon was who had revealed this great mystery to him.
And the Son, who knows the hidden Father and His revelations,
showed Simon who had revealed to him what His name is.
Simon called Him as if of himself when he called Him so,
and our Lord showed him that the revelation was not his own:
"Flesh and blood has not revealed to you that you should say this;
it is not from yourself that you have brought this unrevealed name.
It is not your own knowledge that has taught you to call Me so;
it is My Father who revealed it to you, for otherwise you would not know Me."
With the beloved name that Simon brought from the Father's house
he called his Lord: "You are the Christ, the Son of God."
And at once, as from the hand of a king, he received a crown:
a great blessing for the faith that does not stray.
He gave him blessedness in return for the confession of that disciple,
so that everyone who confesses as he confessed may receive blessedness.

For this too our Lord asked when He asked:
that He might give blessedness to everyone who holds the faith.
Simon brought the name by revelation from the Father's house,
and received his reward, a divine crown of blessedness.
He gave him blessedness as the seal of the faith,
that this confession might take hold as the law throughout the whole world.
He showed Simon that when the Father revealed to him He Himself was with His Father,
the hidden mystery, to bring the true name to the world.
He showed that He is equal to His Begetter in revelations,
in hidden things, and in the interpretations of all wisdom:
"O disciple, I was with the Father when He revealed it to you,
just as even now the Father is with Me and not far from Me.
The Father did not give you the revelation apart from Me,
nor do I give you blessedness apart from the Father.
The Father revealed it to you, not without My knowing,
and I gave you blessedness, not without the Father's consent.
Your soul is worthy of revelations and of confession,
full of truth, and not inclining toward divisions.
You are the Rock, and in the foundations of the great house
I set you, and upon you the Church that I have chosen.

Truly your place will bear honor and will not be shaken;
you I will set first in My building, as a sure one.
Be a foundation for the holy temple that I raise up in it,
and upon you I will open all the dwellings of the Daughter of Day.
I have betrothed the Bride and prepared a great wedding feast for Myself;
you lie first, as a sure support.
To you I will entrust the summer of the Daughter of Day,
and upon you I will build her, and your building will rise above disputes.
Your truth is rock; therefore you are the Rock,
and upon you I will build the Church that is higher than divisions.
You are the Rock, and upon you I will build the Church,
and the bars of Sheol shall not prevail against her with their schemes."
And what are the bars of Sheol, O hearers,
but death and Satan, who laid waste the earth?
High gates within which they imprisoned Adam,
and there all the captivity dwells in the house of darkness.
Bars that barred the path of life so that it could not be walked,
and fenced off the crossing so that no one might pass over to God.
Gates and bolts that had been barred against Adam,
so that he might never again come out of the darkness in which he was wasting away.

Because of these the Bridegroom promised the Bride
that they would not imprison her in their palaces nor overcome her.
Light betrothed her, and she is not imprisoned in darkness;
Life redeemed her, and so death does not prevail against her.
He began the house, chose a stone, and laid a foundation,
and gave her the exaltation to conquer death and Satan.
He promised her that the bars of Sheol would not prevail against her,
so that without fear she might give herself to be with Him.
The great apostle became the foundation for the great house,
that the Bride might enter into an adornment that does not perish.
He fastened a bridal chamber for her and promised her that she need not fear,
for destroyers have no power over her adornments.
He began to build her, and upon that great stone that He found
He set her building, that her height might pass even the clouds.
He set twelve stones in order in the fortress of light,
and chose one on which the whole house would rest.
He shaped it, marked it, and carved the great stone He had found,
and set it deep in that great building which He founded.
The Bridegroom chose it, and His Father carved it by that revelation,

and the Spirit perfected it and set it in the foundations of the Church.
Revelation drew from the hidden knowledge of the Father,
and came down to prepare a house in which the Son would be served.
The Bride was betrothed and did not know who the Bridegroom was,
and the Father revealed it to her, and she began to tell of her betrothal.
The Bridegroom demanded of her whether she knew Him, and because she knew Him,
He gave her blessedness, for she had proved equal to the Father's revelation.
He promised her that she would not be overcome by destruction,
and invited the peoples and the regions of the earth to rejoice with her.
From the house of snares and stumbling-blocks He took up the Bride;
He broke the snares, prepared a way, and led her to Himself.
She had two adversaries who hated her,
and He granted her that they would not overcome her.
The tyrants of Sheol were trampling her within their borders,
and He bound them and set her feet upon their necks.
He set her in light and swept the darkness away before her,
and drove the shadows of death from her paths.
He built her on the great stone, chosen and full of beauty,
and established her foundations on His Twelve, full of light.
He opened gates for her toward the dawn of the apostleship,

that she might dwell in the splendor of light, mightily.
He set His cross for her like a pillar bearing creation,
and drew up and [?] the stones of light for the great house.
With the upright wood of righteousness He completed her dwelling,
and with its arms, reaching here and beyond, He set her roof straight.
With the nails of His hands He fastened her priestly sinews,
and to adorn her He dyed colors in His blood for her honor.
He gave her blessedness as a gift full of riches,
that every day she might delight in His divine light.
He rebuked death and swept Satan away by His passion,
and the Bride rejoiced in the Bridegroom's blessedness and in His promises.
Because that disciple had called the Son by His name,
He gave him blessedness and built the Church upon the apostle.
He made him a rock and set him in the foundations of His house,
for He saw that he held firm in every place and was not shaken.
"To you I give the keys of My kingdom," He promised him,
so that he would be the foundation and the steward of the house.
"If you bind on earth, it is bound also in heaven,

and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” / In the height and in the depth he gave authority to the apostleship, / so that above and below it might command with lordly power. / The rich one was betrothed to the daughter of the poor and wrote her in his name, / and he gave her the keys, so that she might be mistress over his possessions. / The wealth of the depth and the treasure of the height he quickly gave her, / so that above and below she might be a mistress who takes no orders. / Her lineage was despised, and so that she would not think he despised her, / he let all his keys go into her hands, for great was his love for her. / All the doors his Father has, he gave her to open, / so that she might see and rejoice, and her heart be glad at how rich he is. / He made her mistress over those above and over those below, / so that height and depth might obey her in their ranks. / He saw that she loved the good Heir and did not turn aside, / and at once he gave her all his treasures and their keys. / Though her lineage was poor and wretched and her stock hated, / he gave her his keys, because he saw her truthfulness. / He lifted the daughter of the poor from lowliness and from the dunghill, / and she seized the height, so that she now commands the abode of those on high.

The lofty doors of the holy of holies of the Most High / he empowered her to open, because he saw that his Father loved her. / He had seen the Father give a revelation as to one who was faithful, / and he himself gave the signet ring and the keys in full, to be in accord with the Father. / He saw that his Begetter loved her, the praised one, / and he too gave her the keys and the goods of the whole house. / There was a mystery in his Father's house, and he saw that the Father revealed it / to the Church, and at once he made her mistress of his house. / The Bridegroom saw that his Father had given his name to the bride, / and he wished to do the will of the Father, who had loved her greatly. / He saw that by that revelation she had received him from the Father's house, / and he gave her the keys of great wealth and of the whole treasury. / The Father loved her because she loved his Only-Begotten, / and she received his Firstborn, for she saw that his Father loved her. / Come, onlookers, marvel at the deed of the Bridegroom King: / he saw that the poor woman was true, and he gave her a crown. / He built her a house upon the disciple who loved him, / and gave her the keys of height and depth because of his love.
He empowered the free woman to seal treasures and to break seals: / blessed is the Rich One, by whose coming the poor have become rich.
By the holy Mar Jacob the Teacher. Homily 20. On Simon Cephas, when our Lord said to him, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew 16:23; Mark 8:33).

In all my homilies I call upon you, glorious Son;
let all my words give praise through you to your Father.
Let the voice of thanksgiving rise to you from me in songs,
as I recount a homily of your praise in your congregations.
Let my mouth be a censer of voices for you, Son of God,
and instead of incense, receive praise from a weak one.
Let my mind boil over to speak with the fire of your love,
as the beauty of your story glows toward the hearers.
Let the homilies of your faith be a peace offering,

and receive them in mercy as an oblation.
Let my tongue honour you with songs instead of sacrifices,
and with every voice let all thanksgiving be offered to you [?].
You are the sacrifice, and blood [?] is not fitting for you;
let my voices of praise be the fat that pleases you.
Son, for whom it was fitting to become a sacrifice for sinners,
let my mouth sing clear praise to you with a lofty voice.
Your story is loftier than speakers [?];
let praise draw me on, so that I may stir my voices to your glory.
I cannot climb to the height of your homily to measure it;
let it come down to me, for it is able to resemble you.
Let it humble itself, and in its humility be spoken through me,
for I cannot climb to where it is.
If your story had not come down to the great depth,
who could tell it in its own place as it truly is?
Let your homily look at you, how you came down to the earthly ones,
and let it come to its place—and lo, it has been spoken by the weak.
From the high heights your Father's love drew you down,
and set you beneath the depths and the lowest regions of the earth.
And because you came down, the earth grew strong through your humility;
lo, the creatures of dust tell your story, though they are weak.

You came down from the heights, and lo, the depths are enriched by you;
enrich me too, that I may proclaim your story within the depth.
Mercy drew you, our Lord, to the lower parts of the earth,
and therefore the dead have spoken of you in their regions.
Who could have risen to your lofty place,
and spoken of you among the legions of flame?
Who would have strode among those troops in Gabriel's house,
and cast your story among the ranks of the heavenly ones?
Who would have drawn near the awesome chariot of the wings,
and stirred your homily [?] with the motion of the great height?
Who would have travelled the path of coals that cannot be touched,
going, seeing, and coming back to tell your story to the earth?
[?] where you are with your Father, who would have stood
and opened his mouth [?] that are many for you?
No one there stirred up your story; you came down
to sinners, and lo, they sing to you in their tongues.
In the depth of the dead your mind knocked and raised its voice,
to cry out with a stirring of how great your wonder is, Son of God.
In the lowly assembly beneath the earth my thought saw you,
and lo, it stirs up praise to the height of your Father because of you.

My mind saw the hollows of the graves that shine with you,
and it too shone, to tell your story in your neighbourhood.
Here among us, with us, in our place you walked,
and as the Father willed, and you with him, lo, we speak of you.
Nor do we see you here within bounds, Lord of bounds,
for you were with us and with your Father—and who is sufficient for you?
The whole path of the Son of God is beyond bound,
and whoever supposes that he grasps it does not walk in it.
His revelation is lofty, yet faith sings it;
with plain voices there is no mouth that can recount his story.
If anyone draws near him by knowledge, he is confounded;
but if he seeks him by faith, he finds him.
Knowledge was condemned and all wisdom was brought to nothing,
and his teaching shone forth through simple fishermen.
The scribes were put to shame and the interpreters became of no account,
for through untrained men his gospel ran to the whole world.
The wise boasted of what they had prepared about his coming,
to speak of him; they fell from the truth and became deranged.
The philosophers were astonished and confounded and became fools,
for they saw untrained men teaching wisdom.
Those who held nets have been filled with power:

lo, the might of the world is bowed and bends its head to hear them.
The ear of the earth inclines to hear the Galileans,
and scorns the scribes of Beirut and the wise men of Greece.
Needy men, without buildings and without possessions—
the lords of gold bow before them with their offerings.
The Great One of power was slain, and his servants proclaim victory,
and through him who was slain they took hold of the earth, which became settled in his name.
Vessels empty of knowledge he chose for his knowledge,
so that he would send them not with what was theirs but with what was his.
He commanded them to let go of the possessions of the world,
so that the whole world would be theirs while they were poor.
With what was his he enriched them and made them great,
while of their own nothing at all remained with them.
Yet in his death his powers were not overcome,
and whoever is ashamed to confess his death is not his.
As for Simon the chosen, because he said to him, "Far be it from you to die,"
he called him Satan, and did not spare him though he loved him—
that disciple who became the rock for the church he was building,
and to whom he gave the keys of height and depth because of his love.

Because he saw that his death did not please him, he rebuked him,
and as if in anger he called the head of the disciples Satan.
If I had a love that searched into teaching,
I would now stir up this story: why was it spoken?
The chosen apostle whom he had even made the foundation of the church—
why, a little later, was he calling him Satan?
It is love that keeps one from inclining one's ear to contention;
and if there is love, there is speech full of beauties.
Let us say now why that disciple was grieved
when our Saviour called him Satan, as we said.
The hater of mankind was envious of Simon because he had grown great,
and he set out to put a blemish on that fair one.
He saw that he was chosen, fair, pure and full of light,
lofty in his truth, and his faith full of beauties.
He heard that he had received that revelation from the Father's house,
so that, as a son of the mystery, he learned the name of the Only-Begotten.
He looked at him, that he had received a great blessing from our Saviour,
and had become rich and reigned through blessings and revelations.
He heard that a fair name had been given him, that he should be the Rock,
and that he had become the foundation for the building of the house of the kingdom.

He saw that his Lord had given him the keys of the whole treasury,
so that he might command height and depth with lordly authority.
He heard that the decree had gone forth concerning the apostle,
that even in heaven he should have power to loose and to bind.
He saw that the one who had been a fisherman was filled, and today reigns,
and he envied and burned and beat his hands in bitterness.
He heard that the church, which had been overthrown, was being built,
and that he and death were being driven from it, so that they could not enter it.
The enemy learned that Sheol was being uprooted in its treasury,
and that the church of the firstborn was being built upon the disciple.
He heard that the bars of Sheol fall, are defeated and brought to nothing,
and that the church holds the heights and the depths and the whole world.
The perception came to him that the way of Eden was being opened,
and that Adam's return was taking place, that he might go back to his inheritance.
From the promises of the Son that wicked one learned
that whoever has stumbled is restored and so exalted.
The Evil One was distressed at what he heard about Simon,
and the vile one set himself against the apostle to destroy him.
For he said: "If I lay waste the great foundation,

lo, the whole building that has reached the height will shake.
If the disciple slips a little, as if to fall,
the church shakes—and if it shakes, great is our [?] bringing low.
If this one who became the Rock wavers or bends,
the building that stands on him also slackens.
I will set a snare for Simon so that he falls, and if he falls,
lo, the whole company of eagles that surround him is caught.
They are twelve, and if I take captive the first one,
all his companions come with him into darkness.
If I seize the head of the company, it scatters;
but if it gathers, my tracks are wiped out from the regions.
If I bind that head of the apostolic band,
the whole gospel is uprooted and ceases from the regions.
If Simon, the head of the disciples, stands firm in his truth,
lo, that is my downfall and the death [?] of my beloved band.
If the disciple remains in the beauty of that confession,
the whole earth learns from him and forgets my teaching.
If I do not somehow snatch his keys,
he will bring out wealth from the Father's house and mock me.

He goes in and stands over the treasury of the Godhead,
and provides for the world with wealth, and forgets me.
All my images in the lands become a mockery,
and the high horn of idolatry is broken.
My feasts, my festivals and my assemblies cease from the lands,
and my priests turn back, or are led to God.
The whole camp of the gods becomes a mockery,
and the high idols I set up on the earth fall to the ground.
If Simon does not slacken from his confession,
I cannot stand, and I will have to flee from his teaching."
With great envy Satan envied that disciple,
and he set snares and hid nets for that true one.
And if against his Lord the foolish dragon stirred up a struggle in his error,
how much more would he threaten to confound the servant!
If with God—God himself—he waged a battle,
how much more would he scheme against a man in his insolence!
He began with the Master, and then came again to the disciple,
for the dim-witted one was contriving to rule [?] by all his schemes.
Darkness stood up against the light to fight it,

and as far as it could it raised up a faction, so as not to be exposed.
The Evil One was insolent and made a struggle with our Saviour,
and when he dared, he fell like lightning before the eyes of the angels.
He trembled and was confounded and let his hands drop from victory;
he knew the Son, who he was and whose son, and gave up on him.
Then he began to lurk among the assemblies of the Jews,
teaching stumbling blocks to the priests and scribes and Sadducees.
He went in and lay in wait among the slanderers and the respecters of persons,
so as to take delight in their blasphemies against the true one.
Whenever our Lord performed mighty works, he was stirring them up,
so that instead of praise, divisions would be roused among the onlookers.
And from the signs our Lord performed he was snatching away the credit,
saying it was by Beelzebub that he cast out demons, and not as the Only-Begotten.
At one time he made the priests his companions;
at another he brought the leaders and rulers to his aid.
With blasphemies and with outcries he set them ablaze,
so that through the struggle to bind the innocent one he might rouse divisions.
But the sun was prevailing over the shadow,
and wherever it went it drove it from the roads.
With rays of light it exposed it and laid it bare,

and gave room for light to take hold of the whole world.
In all the mighty works our Lord performed he was watching,
and was eager to stir up the assemblies against whoever obeyed him.
He found an opening, and for a time fell upon a disciple,
and through greed he corrupted his soul away from freedom.
He cut Judas off from that band of discipleship;
he whispered falsehood and made him his partner in hateful deceit.
The great snare of the love of money he set for Judas,
caught him, and threw him into theft and strangling.
And if he could, he would have scattered them all, since they were gathered together,
for he had feared them from the very beginning of their deeds.
The great serpent bit the apostolic band on its heel,
but it cut off that limb and gave it to the earth.
It bound it and tied it off, so that the venom would remain in one limb,
and the whole body was kept safe so that it would not be corrupted.
Judas fell into the noose that cut him off from the disciples,
and because his inside was full of venom, his belly burst [?].
Another limb entered in his place with the disciples,
and the body of the apostolic band stood without blemish.

It was not with Judas that the Evil One began to lay snares,
but with the Master and Lord of all lords.
And when he suffered a fall in the dreadful struggle he waged,
he remained ashamed before the innocent one who exposed his falsehood.
After this he barked at Simon, the head of the disciples,
and one by one he felt out all the good servants.
He went down and found the one who carried the open purse,
and in the purse he set a snare for him and caught him there.
Theft and great deceit and treachery
he taught the chosen one, and made him vile among the disciples.
Hear now: it was because of the deeds of that stranger
that Christ called Simon, the head of the disciples, Satan.
It was he who envied him, and he who drew near him to whisper to him,
so that, if he could, he might cast him from his greatness into a snare.
He came to him with the cunning of the serpent, his kinsman,
so that if he gave him room, he might snatch the keys from him—
because he had received that revelation from the Father,
and had taken and gone out with a great blessing from the Son,
and had been set as a true one for the foundation of the church,
and the Son had given him keys to manage his Father's house.

Satan set out on the track of that disciple,
and ran after him, to see if he could put a blemish on him.
Our Lord began to speak about his passion,
and to reveal to his disciples the mystery of his crucifixion.
Our Lord spoke about his killing and his suffering:
when and how he would bear all these things from the Jews.
Before it happened, he told them what would happen, to teach them
that by his own will he mounts the wood of crucifixion.
He recounted to his apostles what would befall him from the crucifiers,
and for this reason Satan drew near to show what was his.
He counselled Simon, as a lover of the Son of God,
to grieve greatly, and, as a beloved friend, to be swallowed up in distress.
For he could not set any other snare for him,
since he was true and would not exchange his Master's love.
The head of the disciples would not stoop to the love of money,
nor to stealing, nor to lying, nor to changing sides.
So in that very love in which he stood he set a snare for him,
to find in love itself an easy way [?] by which to swallow him.
The demon of distress entered and stood before his mind,

and clothed him with grief over the story of the crucifixion.
Simon was distressed as a kinsman would be, and weighed down;
but that distress which was in him belonged to Satan.
As a lover he grieved at the tidings of suffering he heard,
and he feared and was distressed for his Master as a kinsman.
The disciple became merely compassionate instead of true,
and began to give weak counsel to the Son of God:
"No, my Lord, no, my Lord, do not bear the sufferings of the cross,
and let suffering and death not come near you in any way.
Far be it from you to die or be mocked by the Jews;
far be it from you to suffer or be tormented by the crucifiers.
No, not so! Let suffering not touch you, our Lord.
Ever-holy one, far be it that you be reviled by madmen.
Life and glory befit you, for you are the Son of the Living One;
death is hateful to you—far be it from you to die, you who give life to the dead!"
With these troubling counsels of a feeble love
the head of the disciples was trying to keep him from suffering.
But he who searches the heart saw his soul, and who was troubling it,
and, as one who knows all, he knew the speaker and where he came from.
In secret he struck at that thought which was stirring in the apostle,
for it was the serpent's seed and not that disciple's own.

At once he grew angry with Simon, though he loved him,
and as if in wrath he called him Satan—yet he was an apostle.
It was the weak counsel that came from Satan [?],
while the apostle himself, in what was his own, stood with our Saviour.
That anxious thought that was in Simon
he called Satan, for it did not agree with the crucifixion.
The serpent that brought death to Adam among the trees
was giving counsel that the Son should not suffer on the cross.
And because he knew who had given counsel to the virgin,
he rebuked his lover on account of the enemy who was troubling him.
Our Lord did not, like Eve, accept the weak counsel,
for he had come for this very purpose: to crush the head by his crucifixion.
He did not let himself be persuaded by the disciple he loved
to give up the cross by which life is found for the world.
Because he wanted to rid him of it, he called it Satan,
for the death of the Son of God was distressing to Satan.
"Go, Satan," and "Turn behind me," he said to him;
"do not block for me the road I have set toward Golgotha.
The Father sent me to become a sacrifice for sinners;

why do you withhold the great sacrifice, so that it should not be offered?
Flee from before me; let me reach the death prepared for me,
by which I loose the captives of Sheol from darkness.
Come behind me, for the road runs straight toward the sufferings,
and no one can stand against me and stop me.
You are a stumbling block to me, for you want to block the way of death;
it will not be blocked—turn behind me, O Satan.
A little road remains for me, and I reach Golgotha;
who persuaded you to block the way that is full of life?
It pleased me, and I was in the womb, conceived, born in a manger,
baptized in the river—and now would you hold back the cross, and would Adam live?
Why far be it from me to die and give life to the dead of Sheol?
For lo, they are watching for me to enter and loose their bonds.
If you had held me back from the womb, or from birth,
or from the river, you might have been able to hold me back from Golgotha.
The Father who sent me gave me an appointment with the depths of Sheol,
and unless I go down and search the abyss, I do not turn back.
The corrupter has sunk the Father's image, and lo, I am going down
to draw it up myself, and unless I take it up I do not ascend.

The serpent cast Adam from paradise into the grave,
and for this I came: to enter and bring him out from perdition.
If you say to me, 'Far be it from you to bear sufferings,'
then far be it from the world to live, as you say.
This word of yours means: 'Let me keep far from Golgotha,
and let the great image remain in Sheol, unrenewed.'
This is your counsel: that I leave the cross and not go up on it,
and that Adam waste away there in Sheol where he is.
If you hold me back from death, you hate life,
for unless I die, life is not found for Adam.
The captives are imprisoned in the clefts of the graves, and lo, I am going
to bring back the captives—why do you hold me back from redemption?
The tyrants of Sheol have plundered my possessions—flee from before me!
I will go and bring back my possessions, plundered by thieves.
The sons of perdition have bound Adam in the house of darkness;
let me go, to enter and loose the bound, and then I return.
The serpent and Eve took counsel together and overthrew Adam;
your counsel, which resembles his, is void if it is accepted.
Why far be it from me, if I do a work in Sheol,
and break the doors of death that are barred,

and cut down the lofty bars of the daughter of darkness,
and demolish the fortress of death so that it is not inhabited again,
and lay waste the stronghold that swallows generations,
and uproot all its walls with the shaking of my cross,
and become a guest of the dead for three days,
and proclaim to the captives of Sheol that it must let them out,
and roll in the dust of the dead and search in it
for the precious coin which bears our image, which had been ruined,
and with the lamps of the crucifixion search for
the image which the deceitful serpent ruined among the trees?
Why, Simon, do you say, 'Far be it from you to do these things'?
For if I do not die, they will all be void, as you say.
Your word stands against the mysteries of prophecy,
for if I do not die, they are not fulfilled as they were spoken.
If they do not hang me on the wood before the people,
Moses is made a liar, who saw Life hanging on the wood.
Unless they pierce my feet and hands, as you say,
David is put in the wrong, for he would be exposed as not true.

And if they do not give me vinegar and gall to drink,
the mystery of prophecy is void, and you are believed.
Unless the people divide my garments, as was sung,
who would vouch for King David that he was a prophet?
If I am not among the dead, as was prophesied,
why did he cry, 'Lo, he is among the dead,' unless I die?
If they do not lead me like a lamb to become a sacrifice,
Isaiah too, who called me a lamb, is made a liar.
Unless I am silent like a ewe before the shearer,
it is great distress for the prophet, who would not be confirmed.
If the marks of the nails are not seen in my hands,
what will Zechariah the prophet say to the one who asks him why?
Unless the sun darkens and then shines at the crucifixion,
why was it said that there would be light at evening time?
Unless I am in the heart of the earth three days,
the figure of Jonah is confounded among the revelations.
If indeed, as you urge, far be it from me to taste death,
then all the prophets are void from now on, as you say.
This persuasion, that the way of the crucifixion should be made void,
is from Satan, who wants to confound what is fair.
You are a stumbling block to me on the road that runs toward sufferings;
get behind me—go! I will run ahead to Golgotha."

It was at that great redemption he wrought by his crucifixion
that our Lord was looking when he called the apostle Satan.
"Far be it from you to die" is as much as to say "Far be it from you to save,"
and therefore he rebuked him, spurned him, and greatly scorned him.
He looked and saw how many bonds he would loose by his death,
how many closed doors he would open for the imprisoned,
how many debts of the people he would pay off for the generations,
how many hidden snares of the accuser he would break,
how many above and below he would reconcile,
how far he would abolish the enmity the serpent had cast,
how many dead would be revived by him when he died,
and how many imprisoned would see light when he descended to Sheol.
Looking at these things, when it was said, "Far be it from him to die,"
he rebuked his lover and cast him behind him in great anger:
"You are a stumbling block to me if you say to me, 'Far be it from you,'
for you are thinking not of the things of God but of the things of men.
Because the Father revealed to you in his love that I am his Son,
you suppose it would be a disgrace to me if I die.
Because you know whose son I am, death troubles you,
as if there were no way for the Son of the Immortal to die.
You do not consider that if I will it, I am able to die:

and if I die, my own life is kept safe within me. / You are thinking human thoughts when you look, / that a bound man is led away to become a corpse. / Though he does not want it, death subdues him by a sentence of judgement, / and his end brings him low and drags him off to the dwelling of Sheol. / His spirit departs, and he returns to his earth to become dust; / he sees corruption, wastes away and perishes, for he is weak. / Moth and worm divide him up within their borders, / and nothing at all is left of him there in the darkness. / His story is forgotten, and he never again returns to those he loved; / he leaves his dear ones, and they never again have their fill of talking with him. / This is the human way that you are thinking of, / and you do not think of the divine way by which I walk. / Since you have learned that I am God, the Son of God, / do you not consider that if I die, my death is like me? / When I die, the bars of Sheol do not hold me back, / and death cannot look me in the face when I come out. / I do not see corruption there in the house of the departed, / and death is given no power to shut the gate in my face. / No one says to me, “Since you are dust, to dust you shall return,” / and the devourer and the moth do not trample me as they are used to doing. / I am not forfeit to destruction in the house of the departed;

death does not bind me in its pit as it does the rest. / Devouring Sheol does not imprison me when I go down into it, / and the worm does not sink its tooth into me to corrupt me. / I do not perish from my loved ones like a man, / nor do my kin [?] say, “He is no more; he has decayed.” / You did not consider that if God draws near to death, / life is hidden in Him, and even when He dies He gives life to the dead. / You are thinking human thoughts, O disciple: / that men die and perish, and what remains of their memory ceases. / You did not consider the divine way: that when He enters / Sheol, it trembles and spews out the dead it has swallowed. / You did not consider that when God goes down to the grave, / throngs of the dead come out of destruction to meet Him. / You are thinking human thoughts: that in their death / men's lives came to an end and they became dust inside their graves. / You did not consider that the Son of God, who enters Sheol, / uproots it, empties it, and returns to His place. / You do not consider that if God consents to die, / He sees no corruption in Sheol as a man does. / So you are thinking human thoughts and not God's. / My way is my own; look at it as mine, if you are going to look.

For I told you that I will die and that I will also rise: / rejoice in the resurrection, and do not let death grieve you. / I have a swift journey to the depths of Sheol, / but without the sufferings of crucifixion it cannot be trodden. / Wait for me here three days until I come back, / for when I go, it is not a human departure. / I will go and keep vigil with the dead for three days, / and open for them the gates of Sheol that were shut. / I have two halting-places to go down to on the road of death, / and on the third day I will come back; do not be grieved. / It is easy for me to die and easy to live, and I have the power: / I go and come as I wish, and nothing holds me back. / The gates of Sheol are not shut when I enter it: / at once it falls, and the dead imprisoned in it rise. / For I am able to lay down my life if I wish, / and when I wish I take it up again, for I have the power. / No one else takes it from me when I die, / for of my own will I place it in the Father's hands. / Yet you do not consider the divine way, that it has such power, / but you look at it in terms of human death. / Through Simon the church learned from our Savior

that when the story of His death reaches her, it should not grieve her. / The death of the Son of God is the slayer of death, / and His suffering makes sufferings bearable for whoever knows Him. / Sufferings suffered in Him when He suffered on Golgotha, / and death died in Him when He died, but He did not. / He taught the church through Simon, the chief of the disciples, / that the news of His slaying should be dear to her whenever it is told. / With rebuke and with a reproof full of anger / He drove fleshly thoughts away from the disciple. / And He drove Satan away from the church with a rebuke, so that he would not sow in her / the feeble thought that is afraid to confess the Son's death. / And He took the disciple back to Himself from Satan's side, / when he was afraid to hear the news of the crucifixion. / The one who was vexed at His name departed, for he was an alien, / and took with him the feeble thoughts he had brought. / Satan fled behind Jesus, and the disciple remained / before the Son, taking refuge in His crucifixion. / “Get away, Satan” — not “Get away, Simon” — was what was heard, / and the evil one went away, while the apostle stayed to confess his Master. / The feeble counsels that came from Satan fled from Simon, / and Cephas remained, being the rock in the building. / By the rebuke He hurled, the Son of God held fast to His friend,
and the enemy fled, so that he could not hinder the Son's way. / He set His face toward sufferings without wavering. / Blessed is He who by His death gave life to all who lie in Sheol.
Here ends the homily on what our Lord said to Simon: “Get behind me, Satan.”
Next, by the holy Mar Jacob: Homily 21, on the denial of Simon.

Where even the disciples were afraid and stayed away from you,
a word enters to speak of the beauty of your humility.
Where Simon Cephas denied that he knew you,
there a feeble mouth seeks to confess your judgment.
Let my mind put on your love, our Lord, with discernment,
and speak with it of the story of your judgment lovingly.
Only by love can a mouth speak of you,
for it was love that drew you, too, to suffer for our sake.
The great sign of the Father's love is the slaying of his Son,
for he so loved the world that he gave up his Only-Begotten.
See how much he loved us: he gave his Son to death and redeemed us;
with that same love, then, let us speak of our Redeemer.
Love has great force wherever it is,
so that no strength is stronger than it in those who possess it.
Who could have compelled the Father to give up his Son,
if not love, which is greater than all, as it is written?
In this way a person draws near to God,
for in this way he too drew near to us and became one of us.
For who can love as he did,
or who is able to love the Son in return for his redemption?

Who went in with the Son to judgment and endured sufferings?
Love alone accompanied him as he was humbled.
When the crucifiers armed themselves against him with murderous fury,
his friends abandoned him, and in his great love he stood in the contest.
The lambs had fled, and the Lord of the flock remained alone,
so that the sign of his love for his flock might be revealed.
At the hour of slaying, friendships went down to the combat there,
but save the Son's, no love among all the friends prevailed.
The hirelings fled, but the shepherd did not flee from his flock,
so that by this the sheep might learn who loves them.
Truth weighed the Son's love against his disciples',
and the disciples' was found wanting, and the love of the Son of God outweighed it.
The chief of the disciples denied the Messiah, swearing he did not know him;
where, then, is love to be sought, if not in the Son?
Come, see Simon as he swore and denied again and again,
raising his voice that he did not know the Son of God.
The denial of Simon, the crowned one, magnified the Son's love,
for he alone endured sufferings on behalf of many.
By the very fact that the great apostle denied, this was taught:
that there is no love that can attain to the love of the Son.
As he swore before the eyes of many that he did not know him,
he painted an image of the Messiah's love, which is greater than all.

And his denial, too, is a great witness to his preaching:
that the love of the Son of God has no comparison.
The steadfast one denied, so that the Lord of truth might be believed:
that his love is greater even than worlds and creatures.
Cephas was found wanting; who then can weigh heavy beside our Savior?
This is plain: there is no love that can be compared to his.
At the time of the trial Simon went in to see his suffering,
but he did not stay to bear the great burden with him.
They seized the Son, and trembling confounded the apostleship;
sufferings and death drove them in flight from the Savior.
And since Simon had been honored far above his companions,
he alone longed to see the spectacle of his trial.
But when the ordeal was stirred up against him, he turned his back,
for none but our Lord was equal to that combat.
The disciple looked and saw his master standing
with a band of enemies surrounding him to torment him.
The master was being devoured, and the servant could not speak;
the teacher was being judged, and the chief of the disciples stood far off.
Wolves surrounded the lamb on every side
and drove him on to come to the slaughter in great suffering.
The sword was sharpened and the spear stood ready against the Savior,

and he drank sufferings and bore the tumults of the many.
Pain and insult and mockery from the wicked surrounded him;
he was silent and humbled, and those on the left struck him.
The mighty one was bound, and the lowly threatened him with death;
the assembly raged, and he was silent and did not speak.
That disciple groaned softly in his suffering,
and was afraid of the crucifiers to raise his voice.
The lamb bleated toward the shepherd who was being mocked,
and feared to come near because of the wolves that surrounded him.
His soul was wrung with grief for his master,
but he could neither weep nor let the people see him.
He made his face look cheerful while his mind was troubled like the sea,
to show them that he was a stranger to the Savior.
He looked on furtively, afraid that they might see him,
until the Son's trial was ended, and so he kept far off.
He held back his tears lest they flow before the outsiders
and they perceive from it that he wept for one who was his own.
He was silent though he loved, and stood apart though he was a friend,
and could not show his love openly.
He stifled his groans lest they be heard as he groaned,
and he too be taken into the sentence of death with the innocent one.

He mixed himself among the crucifiers by cunning,
so that in this way he might stay and see his whole trial.
He put aside mourning and sat warming himself with the wicked,
to see the end, though he kept far from the court.
And when he had thus deceived them by every device,
they recognized who he was, whose he was, and where he came from.
For they were saying, "You too are one of them;
your speech, too, is very like a Galilean's."
A storm rose against the steadfast one, and he was torn in two,
and as in a sea, he sank into denial in the house of the crucifiers.
The scribes beat upon him again with waves that were stormy,
and covered the ship in the whirlpool of denial.
The priests blew like whirlwinds with their threats,
and Simon was afraid and let himself go under.
They were saying to him, "You too are a man of his,"
and at this he ran lightly into denial.
He began to swear, "I do not know this man;
I will not be held to account [?] for what I know nothing of," he said wickedly.
"I came in here with the many to see the trial,
though in truth I do not know the man."
He hid himself in falsehood and covered himself,
and the threat that had been stirred up to mock him subsided.

His soul was covered with wickedness without his noticing,
for it is a great disgrace to deny the Son, that he did not know him.
Sin entered and spread a veil over his mind,
so that he did not see who our Lord was as he denied him.
Error entered and seized [?] his whole soul,
and he did not think he was lying as he swore.
In place of truth, falsehood filled him,
and he did not perceive that he was lying as he denied.
He had utterly forgotten that Jesus was the Lord as he denied him,
and truly, too, he swore that he did not know him.
The eye of his soul was blinded by terror,
and he did not know who Jesus was as he denied him.
He was dazzled by the threat and could not see clearly,
and he forgot the Son and did not know who he was.
Many times he swore that he did not know, and it was true,
for in that hour he did not know, because he had forgotten him.
He feared death so much that he became one who did not know;
he trembled before the assembly and set his face to deny.
Death terrified him, and he fled by the road of falsehood,
and forgot the Son in the trembling of his heart, and stood denying him.

And when the tumult had died down around him and he was at ease,
another wave was stirred up against him bitterly.
A woman of the crucifiers saw him and said to them,
"This one too is truly one of them."
And when the crucifiers looked threateningly at Simon,
again he set his face to lie as before.
He began to swear as he had sworn, that he did not know him,
and shook out his garment as though he had never seen the Messiah.
A second wave rose up against him and shook him again,
and since he was already sunk in falsehood, he sank once more.
"Oh, why now? I do not know this man;
I have not seen him and I am not persuaded by him—why this injustice?
Judge rightly; do not condemn me when I have done no wrong.
I do not know who the man is whom you have seized;
chance called me to come in and see—why should I die?
I swear it is not that I know him, as you have said;
for I have not seen him, so why should I suffer for his sake?"
Into the great pit of falsehood Simon sank,

and the more he struggled to climb out of it, the further down he went.
The abyss of denial surrounded that steadfast one,
and he was covered by turbulent waves at the Son's trial.
The friend of truth denied his friend, that he did not know him,
for a fearful ordeal met him there, and he forgot his love.
The good servant saw his master being mocked,
and was afraid to show himself lest he be swallowed up.
The disciple trembled when he saw his master being mocked,
and swore that he neither believed in him nor knew him.
Simon, who hated the world and followed the Son of God,
openly denied him: "I do not know this man."
Fathers and brothers and nets he left when he commanded him,
and went after him; but when the ordeal arose, he denied him and fled.
Terror entered and broke a breach into that fellowship,
and in place of love came denial and breach and hatred.
And just when he was about to win out in the lie that he did not know him,
again he was caught by those who saw that he was his disciple.
Into three snares the light one fell and was entangled,
and with all three snares they caught him as he trod on them.
The first net and the second bound him,
and he was caught again in the third, like the others.
Falsehood wrapped itself around him and battered him,

and he did it a second and a third time, swearing that he did not know him.
He had put on the armor of hatred before the crucifiers,
and opened his mouth to speak with oaths.
A third time, more strongly still, the steadfast one denied,
swearing, "I do not know who the man is."
The chosen one sank into the great sea of falsehood,
and its fullness and the turbulent waves of hatred covered him.
His soul was dyed in wickedness, full in that hour [?],
until it took on the hateful color of wrongdoing.
Our Lord showed great love to the whole world,
for no one loves as he loved mankind.
Even to death he gave himself for love's sake,
for one who loves is not parted even by death.
Our Lord alone was equal to that contest,
and no other was taken in his trial, for none could have been.
When Simon saw him from afar, he denied and swore;
had he drawn near and borne his trial, what would he have done?
At the Son's pain, while he was far off, he looked and was terrified;
had he himself been made to suffer, how much more would he have feared!
The sound of mockery cast trembling on his limbs,
lest he too be mocked, far off as he was, if he were sought out.

He heard a threat and denied the Son, that he did not know him;
had nails and spear reached him, what would he have done?
For these sufferings none but our Lord was fit,
and it was fitting for him to endure them all for the sake of all.
Simon denied and swore many times, "I am not persuaded by him,"
and with oaths he warded off the sufferings, so as not to bear them.
And when he had been filled with falsehood, our Lord looked at him,
and he came to himself, and his heart was struck at his fault.
The cock crowed, and Simon remembered the word of the Son,
and shame seized him at what he had done without noticing.
He looked at himself, and saw that from that height of the apostleship
he had slipped and fallen into the great pit of falsehood.
He scorned himself, that in place of the love of discipleship
he had sunk into the hateful depths [?] of falsehood.
He entered into reflection and sat over it like a judge,
and was scourged by his thoughts as if with rods.
He was ashamed of himself and sought no excuse;
he was condemned by himself and cast himself into guilt.
Our Lord looked at him when his denial was complete,
and without a voice, in silence, he judged him wisely.
Our Lord's gaze was full of understanding and wisdom,

for one who loves is turned aside by no trial.
A true friend shows his love in the time of ordeal;
and you, beloved, head of my friends, why do you deny?
Because pain and mockery have come upon me, you did not know me,
and because of the sufferings surrounding me you have forgotten me.
In peace you followed me, and when war came, see, you abandoned me,
and now you deny that you know anything of him at all.
The times have given you a hand to deny, O steadfast one,
and love that is cut off by changes is lacking.
Because you saw that I am humbled in the house of the crucifiers,
the times have carried you off, so that you too deny me and turn from me."
The Son's silence signaled these things to Simon,
and Cephas, too, despised himself for what had befallen him.
Do not say, then, that Simon was destined to deny,
because our Lord foretold it just as it came to pass.
It was not because our Lord said so that the steadfast one denied;
rather, our Lord had foreseen the denial that would take place.
He knew beforehand what was going to happen, before it happened,
and not on that account was Simon free of blame when he denied.
If his denial had not truly been hateful,
then his repentance would not have been beautiful either.

His denial was hateful, and again his repentance was beautiful;
he sinned in truth and repented in truth, and not in pretense.
And so, when he denied, he was a denier,
and again, when he wept, he was truly a penitent.
It was not in pretense that he denied the Messiah, that he did not know him;
he sank into great falsehood without feeling it.
And so he also wept in truth,
for he saw himself in the great pit of denial.
Denial took him out of the company of the apostleship,
and tears brought him back into the number of discipleship.
While he was swearing he was a denier and not a disciple;
and after he wept, a chosen apostle and not a sinner.
Neither while he denied did he have a share in the apostleship,
nor after he confessed was there in him any scent of denial.
He denied the Son and was estranged from his company,
and so he grew bitter with tears of suffering.
He saw that he had lost the great truth of discipleship,
and began to weep because he was estranged from that greatness.
The sin that had stood before his soul fled from him,
and his road was lit up, and he began to come to repentance.
Denial completed the work of wickedness and departed from him,
and remorse entered after it to sweep it out as with a broom.

He began to judge himself with discernment,
and to accuse himself wisely:
"Woe is me, for I have fallen from that height of the Son's love,
and see, I stand with the crucifiers in denial!
It is a great disgrace—whom have I denied, and hated my own life?
Instead of head of the apostleship I have become a denier.
Why did they not bind me for trial with him, so that I would not have denied him?
For death with him would have been better for me than treasures.
It was right for me, when he was swallowed up, to be swallowed up with him,
and when the house of the crucifiers was striking him, that they strike me too.
Where shall I go to seek my life, which is lost?
And to whom shall I confess, after I have denied the Son?
Why did I not bear the sufferings of death for his sake,
and stand firm on this one thing, that I know him, before the eyes of many?
It was fitting for me not to deny him, even if I died,
for death with him is good life without end.
Instead of a disciple I have become a denier—what shall I do?
Instead of a companion who ate his bread, a companion of the crucifiers.
I was a brother to the apostles, and their first head;
and among the crucifiers he hates his master and curses himself!

Let my ten companions weep over me bitterly,
for great is the grief that has truly come upon me today.
It would have been better for me had I fled as they fled;
because I did not flee, I became a denier instead of a fugitive.
Let Thomas weep over the fault of Simon his brother,
when he hears of me that I denied the Son before many.
Let James lament, and with him Matthew and Bartholomew,
over the report of the disgrace I committed today in the house of the wicked.
Come, John, learner of mysteries, weep for Simon,
for like Caiaphas he has denied the Son, that he did not know him.
All you my brothers, raise a 'woe' for me over what has befallen me:
for I was an apostle, and now I am mixed with deniers.
In the light I denied, and see, I stand in the house of darkness;
I hated the day, and night has surrounded me on every side.
I let go of life and seized death in the house of the left;
what shall I do? Who will bring me across to the right?"
With these words Simon grieved intensely,
weeping in great suffering over his fault.
The great error fled from his mind,
and he sighed over what he had done, because it had happened.
And now he said, "Who will grant me to suffer with him,

and by my sufferings to blot out the bond of denial?
Who will give me a place in the trial, to draw near to him
and bear with him pain and mockery and persecution?
Who will grant me to receive spittle on my face,
and to hold out my cheeks to the blow for his sake?"
Simon was hard pressed on this side and that—what was he to do?
He feared to draw near, and because he had kept away he suffered again.
He could not go in and take on the Son's trial,
and because he had denied him he was ashamed and humbled, and wept and wailed.
He swore and lied, and lost both sides at once,
and was like neither the disciples nor the crucifiers.
He is not an apostle, and with the murderers he was not at peace;
he was cut off from his companions and did not join the crucifiers.
To remain [?] in denial was a great disgrace,
yet to go to the disciples seemed contemptible to him.
By denial he had come down from that rank of perfection,
and to remain in it in sin was a grief to him.
He was accustomed to truth, and when he tasted falsehood,
he wept and sighed at how bitter the taste he found.
He stood in wickedness and hung his soul on righteousness,
and there was nothing at all he knew to do but weep.

And when distress had come in and buried him on every side,
goodness came and spread its wings over his storms:
"Come, Simon, bring the tears of repentance;
weep and do not stop—weeping befits you today.
Your great wound needs many tears,
for this pain is healed by nothing but tears.
Come, let us go to Justice, who is set against you,
and with groans I will win her over to hear us.
Take tears and bring them before her when you go in,
and at once all the fury of her severity will subside.
Pour out weeping, and in place of incense kindle groans,
and all wrath will truly be appeased toward you.
Nothing extinguishes the fire of wickedness but weeping;
pour tears on the coal that is set against you.
Take care not to come near cutting off hope, for that is death;
take confidence and ask for mercy, and you will be received."
Great suffering had chastened Simon like a judge,
and drew him to walk the great road of repentance.
His soul was lit up by the goodness that dawned upon him,
and he began to groan in great suffering over his fault:

A fever of denial has broken out in me and is burning me up;
good Physician, spread your medicine on me, that I may be healed by it.
The Crafty One struck at me and handed me a denial to offer you;
now take from me also the confession that I give you.
Good Shepherd, go out in search of the lamb that has strayed,
and do not leave me in the hands of the Evil One, who seeks my life.
With these stirrings of repentance Simon was moved,
and in shrill laments he struggled.
On the threshold of the Son's mercies he knelt, wailing,
that his boldness might open the door of the Judge's house.
Here is an example for anyone who needs forgiveness:
let him too be bold in his petition, and see, he is pardoned.
Simon's denial became an occasion for repentance,
so that its way might be plain and clear before many.
From that chosen one take your pattern for when you plead,
and wail in sorrow, bitterly, over your offense.
Weep as he wept, and you will be received as he was received;
suffer in truth, and see, you are truly pardoned.
Look at Simon as he wept bitterly,
for, being discerning, he felt the pain of iniquity,
and sought to drive from him the sin that had entered him and was embittering him,

for he did not want it to dwell with him as a neighbor.
He saw Gehenna roaring fiercely to meet him,
and he broke open a flood of tears and put it out, and it was quenched before him.
The Evil One surrounded him with the ranks of the troops of denial,
but he roused up weeping and with laments defeated his legions.
The wise man saw the fire of iniquity clinging to him,
and from the head of his body he opened a channel to quench it.
With the voice of weeping he silenced the thunder of denial,
and with confession he tore up the bond of wrongdoing.
He saw in his soul the filth of iniquity, and it grieved him deeply;
he poured out pure waters and scrubbed it wisely.
Defilement had come out of his mouth and soiled him;
he poured tears from his eyes, washed, and was cleansed.
He went astray like a fool, then turned and set things right like a wise man,
so that you too may learn how to set things right when you go astray.
The tongue sinned, and the eyes of that discerning man paid for it,
for he had authority over his members, to employ them as he would.
He saw sin turning about within him to take hold of a place,
and he choked it with tears, so that it would not come back into his thoughts.
He saw an accursed morsel that had stuck in him as he swallowed it,

and he poured out waters that were salty, so that it might be [?].
He washed his soul in the clear waters of repentance
until it became white, a garment fit for the royal palace.
He had lost his beauty, and wept greatly as he sought it,
and found what was his, and then he ceased from his laments.
Simon has given you great comfort, O penitent,
for he will open the door of mercy to you when you plead.
It was fitting, too, that the Church should learn from Simon
which is the door through which all penitents enter.
For who can build a house without a foundation?
It is right that Simon should be first in everything.
To this Rock, then, it is fitting that everyone should be conformed,
in all the structures that are in the Church on every side.
He is the head both of the chosen and of the upright,
and he too was made first among penitents.
He is perfect among the apostles, and his lot is mingled with sinners,
so that all the orders in the Church may resemble him.
In him there is a mirror both for the righteous and for sinners,
so that each may see in it what is his own as he gazes into him.
He was made an example both for the perfect and for penitents,

so that everyone in the Church may set himself in order by him.
Perfect in truth, and perfect, exceedingly, in denial;
perfect when he sinned, and more perfect still when he repented.
Eloquent in denial, and like thunder in the voice of confession;
rich in tears, and foremost in revelations.
For he was the first to confess the Son, who he is and whose Son,
and he again was the first to deny that he knew him.
He became head and first in repentance as well,
and it is right that the Church be built on him in all its variety.
For the carpenter's Son, who laid its foundations, is wise;
therefore he built it on Simon from the beginning.
The Church glories in repentance more than in anything,
for through it all her congregations are richly enriched.
If the harlot is eager to enter, or the robber too,
who would have opened the door for these without repentance?
And for this reason the Church was built on the denier,
so that all her structures might fit together without disorder.
Who could have built himself on John,
whom sin or folly had never touched?
The breast of fire bore him in splendor and with love,

and who could resemble him and not be afraid?
In Simon the chosen it is plain for you to look and be filled with hope,
for after he denied, he turned back and was truly received.
From him you learn that there is such power in repentance
that it reaches the lofty rank of perfection.
He was first, and after he sinned and repented in truth,
he did not come down a rank to become second or third.
He rose by tears and stood in his place without change,
and bore in his hand the keys, the title, and the authority.
Whatever he had lost through denial he took back by tears,
so that everyone who comes to repentance may find hope.
All the orders in the Church are supported on him,
and he is mingled and made equal with the lofty and the lowly.
For above him in perfection there is no other,
nor among sinners was anyone beneath him, for he was a denier.
When he confessed, his revelation reached as far as the Father,
and when he denied, he swore that he did not even know the Son.
He went down in sin to the very end of denial,
and by repentance reached the rank of perfection.
In one place he heard from our Lord, "You are Cephas";

in another place he changed his word and called him "Satan."
At one time the sea carried him, while he was Cephas,
and a little later the deep swallowed him because he doubted.
In him are ranks both very lofty and very lowly,
so that all the orders in the Church may be arranged upon him.
The perfect who are in the world come to him to be strengthened,
and sinners, again, by repentance stand at his side.
In him there is a place for the harlot and for the robber,
for the righteous and for sinners, for all alike.
For he is a foundation, and all the structures extend upon him,
so that in every way the whole house may be completed on him.
Look at Simon and set yourself in order upon his building,
for whoever you are, there is a place for you in him, if you wish.
If you are righteous, let your faith resemble his;
and if you are a sinner, be bitter with his tears and his repentance.
If the waves of iniquity surround you to drown you,
cry out as he cried, "Lord, help me!" and he will lift you up.
If a great sin wraps around you like a flood,
"Lord, Lord, lift me up!"—call on the Son, and he will save you.
If you are held fast in a wickedness as strong as denial,

weep like Simon, and through your laments you will be pardoned.
If you fall as he fell, rise as he did,
for he is an example for you, and if you look to him you will be adorned.
The Son's door is open in mercy to those who seek him;
blessed is he who has called us to repentance, that we may be pardoned through it.
Here ends the memra of Mar Jacob the teacher
on the denial of Simon Peter, head of the apostles.
From the memra of Mar Jacob on repentance. On admonition.
There was a fever in the soul of Simon, head of the disciples,
for iniquity lay in wait for him and threw him down in denial.
And when he took refuge in repentance and brought tears,
Christ bound up his wounds and gave him back that former beauty of his.
Before he sinned he had been made head of the company of disciples,
and after he denied, he gave him back his place because of his repentance.

He did not bring him down to be fifth or third,
but raised him up to that first rank of his.
Before he denied he was the steward of the house; he denied and went out,
and when he repented he brought him in and again gave him his flock to pasture.
He gave him his keys, which he had lost when he denied,
and added to him besides lambs and sheep and ewes.
As beauty was added to him through repentance,
so he added to him authority over the flock that he had found.
The Son of God loved his flock and died for its sake,
and gave it to Simon, for he trusted him to guard it.
This man is the disciple of repentance,
and it was she who brought him back in when he had gone out—but for her!
He denied his Lord, and swore and vowed that he did not know him,
and in agitation he went out of his house and went away.
And repentance ran after him as he fled,
and turned him back to kneel on his Lord's threshold.
And she taught him to bring tears instead of an offering,
and he took them and brought them, as he had been made wise by repentance.
And at once Christ looked upon him, and he became fair,
and, as though he had never denied at all, he joined him to himself again.

And after this, the whole flock for whose sake he had died
he gave to him as to one who loved him and had never sinned.
And he made him an image and an example for penitents,
so that they might know what the power of repentance is.
And with the beauty that nature has before it sins,
the moment one repents he enters and stands in the house of God.
And over a sinner who repents even the angels rejoice,
because the image of the King, which had been lost, has been found.
So now, O soul, you may be confident, and it is sure for you,
that your beauty is restored to you: repent before God.
As it was restored to Simon, head of the apostleship,
all that beauty of your nature will be restored to you.
From the memra of Mar Jacob
on the five talents that our Lord gave to his servants. (Simon Cephas)
He uprooted and cast down the lofty temples of idolatry,
and planted the Church, and Cephas first built himself into it.

He set himself as a foundation for the bride of light,
and on her walls he built his fellow apostles, beloved structures.
He was the foundation and his companions the footings, and the building stood,
and Christ came at the head of the corner and became its roof.
In her midst he set a lofty lampstand, the Light, our Lord,
so that she has no need of the sun to shine around her.
He opened in her the spiritual womb of baptism,
which conceives the dead, bears the living, and gives them to the Father.
He built in her an altar, a king's table full of life,
and on it he set the banquet of the Body and the Blood.
He broke the bread of life, mixed the cups, called the guests,
and distributed the wealth his Lord had given him, and traded with it.
By Mar Jacob. Homily 22. On the commemoration of the departed and on the offering of bread, and that the departed benefit from the offerings and alms that are made on their behalf.

If there were an ear that would listen with love,
I would long now to speak with discernment.
But if love does not hear me, why should I speak,
since without love my word is stripped of profit?
Love for what is beautiful has grown stale among people,
and teaching is no longer loved when it shines forth.
Little by little the world has let go of good customs
and has put hope and love and faith far from it.
The fear of the Lord, which is the cause of all good things,
has dwindled today, and so discernment has ceased.
Wickedness has taken control and has seized hold of humankind's law,

and it gives goodness no room to serve.
Not only alms have people abandoned today;
they have also withheld the offerings for their departed.
Of all the vows and offerings and tithes as well,
this one remained with humankind, and it too has been forgotten.
This sacrifice was left to the world so that it might be sanctified by it,
and now they have neglected it and do not honor it with discernment.
In the bread and wine, which is the mystery of the body and blood,
all the sacrifices were spiritually brought to completion.
Through it the ancients too drew near to God,
and those who came later also had pardon from the Majesty.
With bread and wine Melchizedek the great priest entered
to minister before God in mystery.
With this sacrifice, without stench and without smoke,
he served as priest, to depict the type of the things to come.
He who became a priest forever in his perfection
chose bread and wine from all sacrifices to offer.
As a spiritual man who judges all things, he knew beforehand
that only by this would the whole world be pardoned.

Since he had before him the vision and the types of Noah and of Abel,
he did not wish to bring the blood of animals before God.
Spiritually he drew a stirring up within his soul, and perceived
that it was fitting to offer bread and wine alone.
These mysteries, by which the Church stands today,
Melchizedek was already using back then.
Moses too, the great prophet who offered sacrifices,
pointed to this pure sacrifice, and how fair it is!
With the bread of the presence, which never left the table,
he adorned all his sacrifices in mystery.
Though it was good for him to offer lambs and bulls,
he honored the bread above them all, continually.
Before the face of the Lord he set it upon the table,
and the great prophet called it the bread of the presence.
This bread adorned all the sacrifices,
for in it shone the great mystery of the Body that grants pardon.
And if the ancients displayed it in their hands,
how much more fitting is it for those who came later to cleave to it!
And if the Old Covenant displayed it, that it might be honored through it,

how much more right is it for the New to be eager for its honor!
And if, when it was only bread, it was more honored than all sacrifices,
now that it is the Body, what sacrifice is as great as it?
For the ancients drew types in their offerings
and gave those who came later a good view of the truths.
But the King's daughter did not take likenesses from the ancients,
and it is not by them that she breaks the bread of the mysteries today.
In the upper room she saw her Lord break His body,
and from Him she learned to do daily as He prescribed for her.
It was not Melchizedek who taught the Church how to do it;
she looked to her Lord, and as the Celebrant did, so she does every day.
It was not from Moses, a mere man, that she took the pattern;
Jesus, who was God, taught her the mystery.
And see, she is careful with it, displays it, and glories in it,
for it is the great sacrifice by which the living and the dead are made perfect.
Why then has this exceedingly great benefit
dwindled today among many, and is not performed?
People have neglected the holy bread and do not bring it,
and what shall I say, and why, and how, or to whom?

Shall I keep silent out of deference to the discerning,
or shall I speak, since I am indebted to those who know?
O you who listen to me with love, to you I say:
receive it in love, for love also moves me to speak.
Let not the Lord's bread be lacking from His table because of you,
and pour out the wine of His holiness spiritually every day.
Bring bread and wine and love to the house of pardon,
so that the priest may enter with your remembrance before the Majesty.
On the stones of the ephod Moses had the names of the tribes written,
so that the priest might bring their memorial into the Holy of Holies.
And you, inscribe your own remembrance and that of your departed on the oblation,
and give it to the priest to offer before God.
Make a banquet and invite your dead; they will come
to the altar, which is the haven and the rest of all spirits.
O friend of the deceased, show your love for him in this way,
not by holding great mourning, which does him no good.
Give his name and his memorial to God with your offering,
and your faith will not be cheated of what is just.
Place his memorial on the table of the house of pardon,
in the bread and wine, which is the mystery of the body and blood.
To the women I will now speak with discernment,

if they will listen to me with love, with the ears of the soul.
Look, they go around the graves to weep for the dead,
and with wailing they show their love for their departed.
They leave the Church, its service and its discernment,
and go weeping among the graves for their beloved.
O faithful woman, seek your beloved in the holy temple,
with God, in whose hands all spirits are placed.
Do not call the dead man at the grave, for he does not hear you;
he is not there; seek him here in the house of pardon.
Here the souls of all the departed are gathered,
for this is the haven of life on which they rely.
Here their memorials and their names are set down
in the great book of the Godhead, in which everything is.
The blood of the Crucified sprinkled resurrection upon souls,
and His great power drew them to come to Him.
And since your departed one, O woman, is truly here,
why do you wander around the graveyard like a foolish woman?
Your discernment has failed, or your faith is not perfect;
custom drags you along after these trifles.

You have gone to the trouble of going to the grave to talk with your departed,
and in your haste you have stumbled all the more, without discernment.
If there were love for God in your soul,
prayer would be born in your mouth instead of lament.
Give up the wretched comfort of the untaught,
and lean your soul upon the discernment of faith.
Let your love for your beloved be like true love,
and keep his remembrance with offerings and prayers.
Your dead one gains nothing from your weeping at the grave,
but your offering is good for you and for your dead, and helps.
These tears that were poured out at the grave,
sprinkle them here in the church, with discernment.
The beautiful things are not done as they should be,
and look, the world busies itself eagerly with empty things.
The departed is robbed of the offering that would help him,
and they choose to call him at the grave, though he does not hear.
The necessary things are not done with discernment,
and things that are not fitting are done, unjustly.
Abel offered the firstlings of his flock and their fat,

and righteous Noah sacrificed clean beasts from those that survived.
Abraham gave three-year-old animals in the sacrifices he offered,
and Jacob tithed all he possessed to the Godhead.
Lot, the discerning man, gave up his daughters for the sake of justice,
and the great Moses commanded that all the firstborn be offered.
For the tabernacle the Hebrews brought gold and silver,
fine linen, spun yarn and good garments, each according to his means.
With sacrifices and vows, with tithes and good gifts,
they showed their upright discernment toward God.
But for you today, it is an oblation that falls to you to offer,
and you have neglected and disdained, for lack of discernment, what would help you.
Love has grown stale, for people's faith has become cheap,
and the soul has been darkened, losing its discernment through great iniquity.
The oblation, which is the soul's sacrifice, has been defrauded,
and no one brings it as is fitting to the house of pardon.
Humankind has let go of the custom of beautiful things,
and people are eager only for clothes to wear.
They are anxious to divide the inheritance of the deceased,

but they do not remember to offer for his remembrance.
Neither from what was his nor from what is theirs do they remember him;
the wicked heirs have taken his possessions and forgotten his love.
Like captors they have divided the fine garments he owned,
