and cast lots over his beautiful belongings.
Captors all divide the spoil they have taken in peace,
but heirs with anger, quarrels and contention.
Heirs, then, are worse than captors,
for in everything they wrong the love of the deceased every day.
If the love of the Lord were in their minds,
when they divided they would make him a brother and an heir too,
and from his possessions they would keep a share for him when it is divided,
so that it might serve for his remembrance and his offering after him.
But they, far from justice and from what is fitting,
divided and took and defrauded and forgot the beautiful things.
Whoever has divine love in his soul
shows his love after the death and does not forget him,
and with memorials, with offerings and with prayers
brings his cause before God into the holy temple.

That the dead benefit from the offerings the living make
seems to me to need no inquiry.
But if anyone is bold enough to ask about things that are plain,
it is right that he hear the truths from teaching.
Judas Maccabeus, that mighty champion of righteousness,
acted wisely and offered sacrifice on behalf of the dead.
The man's great faith played its part,
and his merit testified, through his sacrifices, how much they benefited.
That the dead benefited from the offering of that discerning man,
his battle with the Greeks proclaims openly.
He was wise, a hero of divine strength,
a great believer, full of knowledge and zeal;
and for the dead he made sacrifices and atoned for them,
so that the world might learn his lovely deed and imitate him.
And if, while death was alive and ruling and wore a crown,
sacrifices could pardon the dead in the house of its dominion,
now that it is slain, its place uprooted and its crown taken away,
who will any longer dispute the pardon of the dead?
Judas, offering the blood of animals to the Lord, was able

to win favor for the dead and atone for those who had incurred guilt.
The Church today does not pardon the dead with sacrifices
that have been abolished, but with the blood of the Immortal.
And if that lowly sacrifice of Judas brought pardon,
how much more will the great slaying of the Son of God cleanse all!
On behalf of the souls of the dead the priest enters and stands,
and places the holy bread and wine upon the table,
and there he commemorates the death of Jesus and His resurrection,
and calls upon the sacrifice to pardon all who have departed.
All who set apart and brought an oblation he commemorates in love,
and he signs the mystery for the remembrance of their departed.
On behalf of all the dead who have fallen asleep he offers sacrifices,
and calls upon the Father as he reminds Him of the death of His Son.
And the Spirit stirs and descends and rests upon the offering,
and the mystery is embodied in the bread, and it becomes the Body.
By His hovering He makes the mixed wine blood,
and from then on it is the body and blood, a sacrifice that sanctifies all.
With this sacrifice the priest pardons all the dead,
for in it is the power to vanquish death and lay waste its place.

To the fragrance of life that wells up from the great sacrifice
all souls gather and come to be pardoned.
And from the resurrection that the body of the Son of God makes blossom,
the dead draw life every day and are pardoned by it.
Be eager, then, for the remembrance of your beloved,
and for the offering, which can pardon your departed.
And if someone says of the departed that he is not pardoned
by the offering a living person makes, and does not benefit from it:
'Others made it while he did not perceive it; how could it help him,
when a person benefits from his own works, not from his companions'?
It is the discernment of the living man that grows great through his offering,
for he makes it, and he benefits from it, and not others.
For the offering a living person makes for the departed,
how can the departed benefit from it apart from him?
What concern of the one is the other's righteousness?
He set it apart and brought it, and he is helped, not the departed'—
then I say in reply to whoever says these things:
Is it a custom of the Church to pardon one who does not perceive?
The infant who is baptized without perceiving it in baptism,

does he then receive what is his, or perhaps not, as you say?
The Church pardons those who do not perceive and those who do,
for faith raises the dead without distinction.
She receives from its parents a child only days old,
and baptizes, pardons and sanctifies it, though it does not perceive.
But if holiness does not pardon the dead, as you say,
neither does baptism benefit the infant who does not perceive it.
Then all the mysteries of the Church are empty,
and she labors wearily in vain to pardon the departed.
Why does the priest say, 'Pray for all who have departed,'
and why does he baptize and sanctify the infant who does not perceive?
Believing parents bring the infant to baptism,
and the Lord sees their faith and sanctifies him,
and brings him into the adoption of sons though he does not know it,
and writes his name in the Church of the firstborn while he does not perceive.
So likewise the faithful heirs of a dead man who has departed
bring bread and wine in his name to the holy altar,
and the priest and the people offer prayer for the departed,
and the Lord pardons the dead man whom they commemorate.
But if the dead man is not pardoned by means of the offering,
neither did the infant enter among the sons through baptism.

If the living man's discernment profits only the living,
it was the parents who set apart and baptized the child who benefited.
Where then is the faith that gives life to the dead,
that makes prayer for the departed so as to pardon them,
that brings infants down to baptism to sanctify them,
and has the hope that nothing it asks is withheld?
True is the hope of the King's bride, and it does not lie;
fitting and great is her faith, and it is beyond reproach.
With glorious mysteries she serves her Lord spiritually,
and the Watchers marvel at her service, in holiness.
This is the faith of the Church, O discerning ones:
that she can make bread and wine into body and blood.
She breaks bread and knows it to be nothing but the Body;
she mixes wine, and blood dwells in her chalice.
She calls out the names of all her dead over the offering,
and mingles them with herself in spiritual sacrifices.
She gathers them to the banquet of the body and blood,
and they delight with her, spiritually, in her rites.
O discerning ones who know the mysteries of the faith,
make offerings without distinction for your departed.
Why have the customs the Church taught her children diminished,
grown stale and dwindled among many, and are no longer practiced?

For with contempt, even with disdain and meanness,
the oblation comes to the house of God to be offered.
There are many who have stopped altogether and do not bring it at all,
and there are some who, when they do bring it, do not bring it with discernment.
He sends his sacrifice to the house of God by the hands of his maidservant,
as though it were a disgrace to him to bring his sacrifice to the Lord with his own hands.
The lowly servant boys of his house, who are held of little worth,
these he commands to bring his sacrifice while he stays far away.
Why do you not bring your sacrifice with your own hands, O discerning man,
like Abraham, who carried the calf to the angels?
He and his wife were ready and stood to serve,
and did not perform righteousness by the hands of others.
Today the faith of humankind has dwindled,
and love has grown stale, and discernment and faith have become cheap.
What rich man brings an oblation to the house of God
and carries it in his own hands as he brings it into the house of pardon?
Either he does not bring it, or if he does, he gives orders
to the lowly ones of his house to bring his sacrifice while he is not present.
Blessed is the widow who lays down her sacrifice with her own hands,

and the poor woman who carries it and glories in it.
She does not send her oblation to the Lord as the rich man does;
she offers it herself and cries out with deep feeling that He may accept it from her.
Like a priest, she brings her vow before God,
remembering her dead with deep feeling over her offering.
She knew how to set apart and bring sacrifices to the Lord,
not like the rich man who sends it as though to someone in need.
Lovely is the poor woman's offering when it is offered,
for tears and love and faith are mingled in it.
The oblation in her hands, tears in her eyes, praise in her mouth:
as great as her offering is the discernment of her faith.
For an offering is accepted only with love.
Blessed is He who in His love sacrificed His Only-begotten for many.
Here ends the homily on the oblation for the departed.
By the holy Mar Jacob. Homily 23. The first, on the holy Fast of the Forty Days.

Toward the meeting of your praise my word will run, Son of God,
for all who speak are required by you to give praise.
To you let my tongue lift up its voices in its songs,
and through you I will sing to you, in wonder, with a voice that is because of you.
From you I will take, and to you I will turn to speak,
so that in all our fruits you may be praised by those who hear.
Yours are voices and words, and tongues too,
mouths and minds, and thoughts along with reflections.
Give me from what you have to give to those who ask of you,
and take praise for yourself from your own gift, abundantly.
Your praise is in yourself, and those who praise you bring you no profit;
since you are in need of nothing, accept my words, Son of God.
I have opened my mouth to you; fill it, as you have promised,
so that your great story may be told through it with a loud voice.
An open mouth, a vessel fit to hold — this is mine, and I give it to you;
in your goodness fill it with praise, for the sake of your love.

From your fullness, which is yours, all the needy receive;
let the needy one be filled by you and proclaim your gift.
If you give speech to a she-ass, who is praised:
the one that speaks, or the giver of wonders?
A beast spoke with the diviner, that he might be rebuked;
the amazement is hers, but to you belongs the glory in every respect.
A new word came from a she-ass, to great wonder,
yet all the praise returned to you, and she gained nothing.
Let me not be like her, bare of profit:
I am your image, Lord; increase what is yours by your care.
Let me be neither a she-ass nor a flute for your word,
but earth that yields choice fruits a hundredfold.
Sweet music, which brings the flute no profit —
give me to be sweet along with those who lean on your songs.
The she-ass, too, possessed speech without discernment;
grant me to discern, and fill me with love to speak.
Give me also, our Lord, hearers who hold fast to you,
and who hunger in love for the word of life as for bread.
Bread and water are the portion of the body's life,
and the word of the Lord is the spiritual life of the soul.
From eating bread come heaviness and surfeit,

but the word of life grows wings for the soul to fly.
Let us eat by measure, and hear the word without measure;
let us cut back on delicacies and lengthen divine meditations.
The soul grows dark from foods when they are many,
and the mind grows rich in learning if it is trained.
In these days, when the body goes short of food,
let teaching increase for the soul, that it may be nourished by it.
On the day when the great fast shines in the congregations,
let me lift up my voice rightly for whoever listens to me.
Today, when the mouth of gluttony is muzzled and shut,
let the ear open a door to the voice of teaching.
On this day, when the belly is content and the soul awake,
speak, O mouth, speak, and profit whoever listens to you.
In this month, when authority has been taken from gluttony,
the word has authority to prosper abundantly.
Not at all times can you eat sweet fruits,
for there is a season when the tree is bare even of leaves.
Nor do you find grapes in your vineyard every day;
the time is fixed when you will gather all your produce.
Nor are there stacks and sheaves in the field every day,
for it is the month of the year that brings forth the harvest heap in the field.

And if the produce of the body runs with its seasons,
the produce of the soul will run profitably in its season.
In this season, when the soul's harvest is gathered in,
let everyone be roused to fill his baskets with all good things.
In this season, when the sick soul is healed,
come, you who fast, to the Physician's door, and have your sores bound up.
In these days, behold, a festival is gathered for the Lord;
go out, merchants of the Spirit, and grow rich by trading.
In these days a market is held for righteousness,
and behold, it is sold for nothing to those who seek it.
The Son of God has set out his kingdom at your doors;
give him pieces of bread and buy it, for he accepts them.
Scatter alms on the poor and receive the kingdom,
for he wants to give, and he looks for a pretext to scatter his treasure.
For worn-out rags and tatters that no one wants
he will exchange with you a garment of glory, if you give them to him.
The threads that hang loose from the hems of your rags —
give them to him, and he gives you a robe of glory full of light.
Patched and torn cloths that have fallen from your bed —
give them to him, and take for yourself a bed that pains do not enter.
Throw the crumbs from your supper to the needy,

and go and take your delight with Lazarus beside Abraham.
Mix a cup of water for the thirsty and receive a reward:
a whole treasure full of wealth without limit.
Open the door of your house lovingly to the stranger,
and all the doors of the house of the kingdom will be opened to you.
It is fitting that righteousness should run in the fast;
give the fast what belongs to it; do not be a stranger to its blend.
Give to the hungry what you have cut back from your food,
lest you turn out a miser rather than one who fasts.
What you have saved, give to the one whose belly is hungry,
so that in a single fast two merits may be found in you.
Honor the fast with two mouths, if you are one who fasts:
with your own, which abstains, and with that of him who eats from your food.
Fast for God, give to the needy, and double your profits,
for this is how righteousness wants those who serve it.
Make your soul shine as you fast from foods,
and with alms buy the kingdom of God's house.
All the expense the fast has cut from your table,
let it be given to the one who lacks food.
Do not keep for yourself what the fast has cut back from you,
but put it in the belly of the hungry while you are fasting.

If you have not eaten it but kept it, behold, it is still your own,
and your fast is undone, along with the expenses you kept for yourself.
But if you give the hungry what the fast has spared,
your fast is a fast that wears the crown of righteousness.
At sowing time no one is sparing in scattering his seed,
for he knows that he gathers a harvest in proportion to his seed.
Sow alms and do not hold back, O you who fast,
for you will reap sheaves of glory in the new world.
The needy are good earth: cast your seeds into it,
for it is boundless and never fails in its yield.
There is earth that withholds the seeds sown in it:
some it gives back and some it defrauds, and they do not sprout in it.
There are fields that defraud their farmers of the seed,
but the field of the poor never defrauds the one who sows in it.
All the seeds of every kind that are sown in it
it receives and keeps, and yields fruits with ardor.
Even a cup of water, if one sows it, sprouts too,
and he gathers a sheaf and comes to a storehouse full of good things.
Whatever you sow you will reap abundantly;
the seed is kept safe; do not doubt about the yield.
The produce of all farmers has adversaries every day:
frost and heat and locust and hail and every kind of damage.

Even if it comes in and reaches the storehouse, there is anxiety over it,
for it has pests [?] and evil injuries without number:
all the thieves, all the claimants, all the plunderers,
all the takers by whom the produce is diminished.
But for alms that are sown there is no anxiety,
and their produce has neither harmer nor damage.
The produce of righteousness is laid up above in heaven,
where heat and hail and locust have no power,
in a high place where neither thieves nor claimants
nor plunderers can harm it in any way.
The produce of all who fast is kept in the hand of the Lord,
and in it all alms are kept for those who do them.
In that right hand which weighed the mountains and measured the heights
the produce is kept of everyone who sows righteousness.
That little coin you give to the poor at the door —
go and look for it in the hand of the Lord: behold, it is there.
Sow among the needy, and behold, you reap from God;
scatter here, and there gather all good things.
Take your treasures out of the earth, which is full of anxiety,
and lay them up in heaven, in the place secure from thieves.
Behold, at your door stand laborers who toil with you:

for a small wage they do great work with their hands.
With bread in their mouths hire the poor, and they will prepare for you
a high place in the world of light; lay up your treasure there.
They build a great fortress full of good things,
that you may enter and dwell, and find there all your treasures.
They tread out steps upward from your alms,
and by them you climb without toil to God.
They tread the path of life ahead of your steps,
that you may run to the bridal chamber of light without stumbling.
They become your company on the fearful road,
and at that great crossing they plead to rescue you.
They stand at the crossing that is full of fire
and sprinkle dew, being the image of the fourth one.
They make a ship of water on the sea of fire,
so that as you cross, the flame will not come near you.
They open the Bridegroom's door before you knock,
and receive you and make the wedding feast pleasant for you.
They call Lazarus too, for he is their brother,
and in their company he comes to you, if you call him.
They testify to your alms in the house of the angels,
and because of them you are loved in the house of those on high.

They stand and point you out, as if with a finger:
"This one fed us in our need and did not hold back."
Be a friend to them, that they may receive you into their tents,
for they are the whole beauty of righteousness.
Whatever you have, send it with them to God,
and go and find it at the King's door with its profit.
Put provisions for the road beside them before you depart,
so that when you move from world to world you will lack nothing.
With them it is good, and you will journey through the regions of the hosts,
and if your possessions go with them, they will not be plundered.
Whatever of your possessions you leave behind is lost to you;
pluck some of it for yourself and give it to the poor man: he keeps it for you.
As long as you do not give what is in your hands, it is not yours;
but when you have entrusted it to the poor, it has become yours.
As long as what you have stays with you, you are not its master;
but if a poor man takes it from you, he keeps it for you.
If you are wise, so that all you have may be your own,
send it ahead with the poor to God.
If you long for possessions, to possess them truly,
do not leave them here behind you and become poor.
Give the needy your whole load to carry,

that you may go and find in the place of light all you have acquired.
If you want to be rich, be rich in truth,
not for a season, but rich for all seasons.
Load your wealth on the shoulders of all who are needy,
and behold, in the land of the living you will find your whole treasure.
Give, and be confident that all you give is yours;
send it on and sleep, and be confident that it is not plundered.
Lay it on those who wander begging; let them carry your wealth on the road,
and they will bear it all with you freely to the house of the kingdom.
As long as your money lies in your purse, it is foreign to you;
but if you scatter it, behold, it is kept under God's seal.
As long as you have gold in your house, you live in dread
of thieves and of robbers and of moneylenders,
of oppressors and of plunderers and of judges,
and of chiefs, lest they pick a quarrel with you without cause.
But what you have given, by which all the needy were supported,
has passed beyond dread and gone in freely for you to the house of the kingdom.
No one steals it from you there or harms you,
for the one with whom you deposited it guards it carefully for you.
He adds not only interest to what you gave him:
he has promised to repay you a hundredfold.

Here a hundredfold, and beyond, life without end:
he pays wages to whoever performs good deeds.
O you who fast, call the poor man and give him bread;
he will not come — you go after him and fill his belly.
Lands do not come after their farmers;
the farmers carry the seed and go to the lands.
You, carry seed to the furrowed fields;
go out quickly, and look to the harvest without anxiety.
If a needy man comes to your house to ask of you,
you owe him a fee for his feet, for he has made your journey for you.
The trouble you were spared was your own: you should have gone to him;
and since he came himself, double your gift and let him go.
If a field were to walk and come to the farmer,
how he would rejoice in it and sow it with the seed it needs!
A poor man has come and stands at your door; do not keep him waiting:
give the field its seed and send it away while you rejoice.
A poor man knocks; do not say to him, "Our Lord provides";
it is an empty word, with no reward for the one who says it.
He does not want to learn who feeds him; he wants to receive,
for he knows better than you who feeds him.
Give, give to him, and do not say to him, "The Lord provides";

rather, it is through your gift that the Lord feeds him, if you give to him.
If you truly trust that the Lord provides,
give a gift and then say the word, and it will not ill become you.
But if you say it without giving, you are a liar,
for by your hands the Provider did not feed the one you entrusted to him.
Bread is precious, and a word is cheap to the one who says it;
give him bread, and he has no need to hear a word from you.
The hungry man came to fill his belly from your table;
what does he gain by hearing a word? Let him rather receive.
The poor man did not look to you for a teacher; be quiet, do not teach:
give your gift, which by its silence bears witness to the Provider.
If a farmer says to his field, "You have seed,"
and repeats to it again, "You have, you have ten thousand seeds,"
yet does not sow seed in it, there is no profit,
for neither stack nor harvest comes from words.
So too with the poor man: many times
you may tell him, "The Lord provides, the Lord provides,"
but if you do not give him a gift and fill his belly,
your seed is wind and yields you no harvest.
Be silent as you give, and stretch out your hand to the poor man,
and while you are silent, speak with him through your gift.

Do not explain to him that he is hungry and bent and full of trembling;
support him with bread so that he does not collapse while listening to you.
If you have a gift to give, give it in silence,
and that gift of yours is itself teaching about the Provider.
But if you are poor and needy and short of food,
answer the poor man, "The Lord provides for me and for you."
If you lack a gift, give him a word;
but if you have something, give in silence and let him go on his way.
O you who fast, sow your alms with both your hands,
for you will reap with your right hand and with your left.
The earth receives much from you today;
sow in it and multiply, for all of it sprouts and gladdens you.
The mouths of the hungry, behold, are faint at your doors;
go out, you who fast, support the needy and gain profits.
Weave for the fast a great crown out of alms,
that it may be glorious in the house of the kingdom with all good things.
A garment needs beautiful figures woven into it,
and the fast needs many alms.
Like a skilled painter of the Spirit, Isaiah painted
a portrait of the fast, so that all creation might see its beauty.
Because he saw that there are fasts that are not beautiful,

he painted this one with all its spiritual beauties.
That harp of prophecy made it plain
that there is a faster who angers God even by his fasting.
There is a faster who is puffed up and exalted with vainglory,
and there is one who, while he fasts, is quarrelsome, troubled and full of wrath.
There is one who shuts his mouth to food by fasting,
yet sees the needy and does not relieve him of his distress.
There is one who humbles himself by fasting and bows his head,
yet has no wish to break his bread for the poor.
There is one who spreads sackcloth and ashes for his bed,
yet wrongs the needy by oppression and has no pity on him.
This fast Isaiah rebuked and scorned;
he disgraced it, cast it aside, rejected it and overthrew it before the fasters.
And he painted a portrait of the chosen fast of righteousness,
that it might be known in the congregations of all who fast.
The prophet of wonder showed the world what the fast is,
so that everyone might learn its divine distinctions.
This is the fast: that you loose from yourself the bonds of iniquity
and cut the snares of deceit from your mind.
The bond of iniquity is a bond tied fast in your mind,
and through greed the judge is muzzled and does not loose it.

The snare of deceit, too, is wickedness of heart,
which sets traps and deceives and defrauds all its neighbors.
You have a lawsuit that stands knotted, and the fast has arrived:
settle it with your brother who wrongs you, if you are fasting.
Cut off the deeds of crookedness, iniquity and fraud,
and stretch out on the road of righteousness: this is the fast.
The Lord's love is that you go in and untie the knotted lawsuit,
for this is a beautiful work to walk with in the fast.
Every deed that strife has knotted in greed —
these are the bonds of iniquity: loose them, you who fast.
Every scheme that seeks to strangle its brother in secret,
that is what he calls the snare of deceit: cut it off, you who discern.
From Isaiah a command went out to those who fast:
that one should loose bonds and cut the snares of deceit.
Whatever is bound, whatever is hidden, whatever is deceitful,
cut it off and loose it, and fast to God with a pure heart.
This prophet, the chamberlain of the Godhead,
came forth and showed you the way of fasting and its works.
He teaches you to break your bread for the hungry as you fast,
for this work befits those who fast before God.
From the mind of the Lord he learned what he loves,

and revealed it to mankind, so that everyone might learn his works:
that a traveler who comes from a foreign land should come into your house —
the Lord loves this, and the prophet revealed it to whoever listens to him.
That you should cover the naked with a garment, God desires,
and like one who shares his secrets Isaiah revealed it before many.
He greatly wishes that no one should hide from his own flesh,
and this will of the Godhead Isaiah sang.
Your own flesh is the needy man fallen on your threshold;
know it from your own soul and fill his belly, and your fast is great.
His body is a body, not a stone flung out and stripped bare,
that cold and heat should batter it while you have no pity.
From that lump of clay from which mercy fashioned you, it fashioned him too;
it is one clay, and however great you become, he is your kin.
Why do you fast, if not to have mercy on your neighbor?
For this is the fast the Lord has chosen: that one show mercy.
See that you do not shut the door of mercy before the poor,
lest you become an accursed faster, whose fast is a disgrace.
See that you do not hate your brother in your heart while you fast,
lest a foul stench from your fast reach the King.
See that you do not curse anyone who hates you while you fast,
lest your fast stink with your curses and not be accepted.
As your mouth fasts from foods, let it also fast

from curses and from insults and from mockery,
from vainglory and from scorn and from strife,
and from oaths; and in your yes and your no be truthful.
See that during the fast you do not speak a word that undoes your fast
and defiles you along with the dissolute, even while you are fasting.
A word can defile the one who speaks it;
for this reason, guard your tongue, O you who fast.
Isaiah placed it among the observances of the fast,
and commanded the one who fasts not to speak a word.
Not all the words a person speaks are alike,
nor does the speaker harm his soul by all of them.
Glory, too, and thanksgiving are words,
and the songs of the Spirit, and the stirrings of prophecy.
These words are life to those who speak them,
and no one should neglect to complete them if he is fasting.
And when Isaiah said, "Do not speak a word in the fast,"
it is known which word ought to cease.
Let no word be spoken of iniquity or envy,
or of jealousy, slander and strife.
Let the mouth refrain from insults and from mockery,
and from every word that strays aside into darkness.
A word can shut the door before the one who fasts

and cause him to be rejected from the divine rule.
A word can hurl its master into Gehenna
and cast the one who spoke it into burning forever.
By a word of his mouth Moses, the treasury of prophecy,
provoked the Lord, though he was beautiful in his deeds.
The prophetess Miriam, sister of Aaron the great priest,
put on leprosy because of a word her mouth spoke.
And what shall I say of the thief on the right hand,
who spoke a word and became an heir in the garden of good things?
Since every word the mouth speaks comes to judgment,
who would not be afraid to say too much?
Since by his words a person is justified or condemned,
who would not weigh his word with trembling before he speaks it?
Since by his words a person is defiled even while fasting,
why does he not tremble to speak a word that is not good?
Moses provoked God, Miriam became leprous, and the thief entered in:
faults and beauties that came not from deeds, but from words alone.
From now on, then, tremble at a word, O you who fast,
lest you surrender your mouth to sin while you are fasting.
Do not enslave yourself to speaking empty tales,
nor recount the deeds of people that are not good.

Why do you insist on peeling off a scab that is not yours? / Why do you muse on your neighbour while he is far away? / Fool, why are you so careful to recount your brother's faults? / He has a master: beware of judging a servant who is not yours. / David counted it a great virtue when he said: / “The evil deeds of men never passed over my mouth.” / Well did that harp of prophecy speak: / let no one recount the evil deeds of his fellows. / Let your mouth not be a passage for idle tales; / what do you gain from reviling your companions? / If a man who fasts from bread sins with a word, / what profit is there? He has built, torn down and lost his reward. / He fasted and was justified, then spoke and ruined his righteousness; / his belly goes hungry, his fast is undone, and he does not see it. / His fasting is fair, but his foolish words are hateful; / he has put both incense and dung on his censer, and it is not accepted. / O you who fast, beware of speaking a word, / for it too is murder, and a great evil to the one on whom it falls. / The mouth is free to praise or to sing psalms, / or to glorify, or to choose pure silence for itself: / all that builds up, all that consoles, all that profits, / all the tales from which their hearers benefit.

Give to the needy, visit the poor, support the beggars; / provide for the orphans and cover the bodies of the naked. / Call the widow and fill her lap from your table; / lead the orphan and load his arms with your produce. / Keep silent from any word that [?] the sores of your companions, / and keep your tongue from churning out idle words. / The fast has come to meet you: make your soul ready for good things, / and like a diligent man tear up the bonds written against you. / This is the time when the great door is opened to all who fast; / rise up, penitent, and pay off your debts with your alms. / Let every sinner provision himself with righteousness; / blessed is he who gave us the fast, so that we might [?] our fellows.
Here ends the first memra on fasting.
Again, by the holy Mar Jacob: Memra 24 / (2), on the holy Fast of the Forty Days.

Sweet fruits of fasting I have plucked from teaching:
O Lord of Eden, accept my offering at your table.
Choice kinds of humility have come to knowledge,
and see, it shares them out to its neighbours, that through you they may be set in order.
Fasting, in its love, has captured my mind to speak of it:
to your praise, Jesus, are all my words, as I worship.
The season demands of me that I speak of it rightly;
may my word be a sweet crown in the house of mercy.
For fasting, which is the beauty of righteousness,
the tongue is stirred by you to turn to your glory.
Give me a hearing, you who love your own lives,
for I am bringing before you a matter that is wholly life.
We have been very idle in spiritual gains;
let us run now, so that poverty does not overtake us.
We have long slept, leaving good deeds undone;
let us wake now and open a door to fair works.

O will, who stands between body and soul,
arise, show us that you divide uprightly.
Two partners demand their needs of you;
divide, then, uprightly, if you are just.
All the [?] you gave to the body for its provisions,
and the soul remains with no share in the divisions.
For the body you multiplied every feast, every delight,
every dish, every choice food,
fine and soothing perfumes all the year long,
while the soul is trampled and not even counted as a partner.
O divider, who gave so much to the body, what are you doing?
Give the soul her own share, so that she too may live.
All the year you wronged her and she was idle from gains;
now that the fast is with you, give the soul her provisions.
For now too is the month that is free of harvests;
toil with the soul, whose work does not perish.
In this season of no grape-gatherers and no reapers,
support the weary one with the fast, by which the toiler grows rich.
Today, when the season is hard for bodily labours,
let us set the soul to good works, that she may do them.
Today, when all farmers rest from their labour, arise,
you penitents, and gather the harvests of righteousness.

Come, will, divide, and treat the two brothers equally,
and as you did for the body, give the soul what she needs.
In summer both of them ran diligently to the field;
assign the soul her share, that she may take of the harvests.
Give the soul's share to the needy and to beggars,
and food to the hungry, so that you may be upright in dividing.
It is not fair that the soul laboured with her partner
and should be wronged of the needs she requires.
She wishes you to clothe the naked with a garment along with her;
save from the body's expenses and let her do it.
The soul longs for the body to save from its foods,
so that from its provisions, by its fasting, she may feed all who are in need.
O you, body, bend your shoulder and labour with her,
for the soul seeks to keep life both for you and for herself.
She has set her yoke on your neck; perform every good work.
Her labour is fitting, for all that she runs after does not perish.
It is not for herself alone that she seeks to gather wealth,
for it is shared; [?] let her run, eager in fair deeds.
O you, soul, compel your partner to run with you;
do not grant him rest, lest he sink in lusts.

The teacher compels the child to learn what he needs,
and because he loves him he does not leave him idle, lest he be ruined.
Subdue your disciple, lest he rebel against your teaching,
lest, falling from good order, he overturn you too.
Do not give the body comforts that are not good for him;
crush him, enslave him, for the more he toils, the more beauty he adds.
This is love: that you do not let him loose in lusts;
give him toil, that through disciplines he may find life.
Out of love the teacher chastises the child to learn,
and beats him while he loves him, so that he may become wise.
But if he spares and pampers him and does not teach him,
he treats him as an enemy would, while he loves him.
The child wants to play, to drink and to chatter,
and if the teacher gives him his desire, it becomes a snare.
The body wants to have comforts along with pleasures;
do not grant him his desire to do so, lest he be lost.
Give him fasting and cut off his provisions from him,
for hunger does him more good than bread, and nurtures him.
O you, body, incline your ear to the teacher,
hear good counsels from her and do them.
Go after the soul, who loves fair deeds:

for if you obey her, your beauty will flower in the house of the angels.
Walk with her who loves to fly on high;
rise from the clay, for she wants to dwell in heaven.
Your dust is precious if you give the soul your hand;
she is able to raise you from the dunghill to the kingdom.
Your nature is mire, and if she obeys you and comes with you,
you will perish in the stinking pit, both you and she.
Spare the beauty of the radiant one, lest she be corrupted,
and toil with her in fair deeds, that you may reign with her.
If she gives you fasting to keep, let it not grieve you;
accept it and rejoice, for great is the crown you find in it.
If she strips you of foods, do not be angry,
for by her abstinence she has invited you to the King's table.
If she wears you out with long vigils and prayers,
wake up and toil, that you may become a companion of the heavenly ones.
In all the works of righteousness give her your hand,
that you may find with her all spiritual beauties.
O will, by which soul and body are commanded,
you have authority over good things and over evil things.
Body and soul obey you, each in its own way;
urge them on, that they may do fair deeds.
Arise, will, and command like a king commanding his armies:

body and soul obey you and do not resist you.
If you so wish, the partners triumph in their deeds,
but if you grow slack, the whole frame is left to corruption.
O faster, it is your will that leads you;
love victory, and in every way you can attain it.
While there is time that lends a hand to righteousness,
do good works, that they may be found for you as treasures.
It is of your own accord that you love fasting and abstinence,
and if you wish, you have gained complete health.
You are free to eat, and free to fast, if you wish;
choose humility, faster, and see, it has pleased you.
Nature is free, and lends itself to every change,
and however much you press it, it has the strength to receive.
It can even ascend to heaven, if it strives;
it can even go down to the abyss, unless it is diligent.
As much as you demand of it, it is able to do fair deeds,
but if it is let slack, it sleeps and lies down beside wickedness.
If you awaken it, see, it becomes a companion of the heavenly ones,
but if you let it slack, it sleeps on the clay and its dust [?] grows dull.
O faster, awaken your soul rightly,
for as much as you wish, you can practise righteousness.

Righteousness is very easy for one who loves it,
and he gleans and gathers it from small deeds.
Now he stretches out a little bread to the hungry and fills him;
now he supports a little one in need and helps him.
At times he takes pity on a poor man and takes pains over him,
and again he grieves for a beggar and does not despise him.
There are times too when he visits the sick and needy,
and with nothing [to give] he satisfies his longing by his gift [?].
Little by little he keeps himself from foods,
and though he lacks nothing, he scorns wine and does not drink it.
He keeps himself from oaths, and it is easy for him;
it is a habit that prevails, and without labour it has become firm.
He restrains his mouth from mocking his companions,
and no hateful word is uttered from his lips.
He binds his love to the door of the house of the Godhead,
and daily seeks grace from the Physician to heal him.
He greatly fears spiritual harms,
and is watchful in his hidden things and in his open ones.
A small sin is a lament to him if it meets him,
and he flees from it as from a nest of serpents.

Every small gain he finds he snatches to himself,
and rejoices as if over something great when he acquires it.
Whoever loves righteousness is careful in this way,
guarding even the glance of the eye from harms.
By small things the doer of righteousness gathers,
until it becomes a high mountain rising from the earth.
The bee too, little by little, from roots
gathers and makes a sweet comb full of wonder.
She does not disdain even thorns and tares,
but flies to them and takes what her need requires.
Every day the weary one adds to her gain,
and little by little from drops she lays up her store.
Not from a great treasure does she take and fill her treasury,
but by labour, from the petals of every flower.
Today a little, another day less than a little,
and what she gathered became much through her diligence.
Righteousness, which in its taste is like a honeycomb,
a man gathers little by little from deeds.
If laziness had taken hold of the bee,
so that she despised thorns and would not settle on tares,
and gave it up because there is labour in its making,

and despised honey because it lies scattered over the heights,
and sought rest instead of the toils of distant places,
that sweetness which has been gathered for her would never have been gathered.
In its likeness, righteousness is a honeycomb,
and whoever is careful like the bee gathers it.
But if he despises small things when they are to be done,
and this he scorns, and this he belittles, and this he holds in contempt,
and the needy man begging from door to door who met him he leaves and passes by,
and from the one who is sick he turns away in disgust and does not visit him,
and if some matter presses, he swears without fear,
and since he is not lying, he does not count the oath a sin,
and he breaks his fast on every pretext, being clever,
and for his friends' sake drinks wine, out of love, so he says,
and the observances of fasting he has ruined by his laxity,
for he slept and took his rest, and it is no sin, as he supposes,
and he is careless of a small gain and does not snatch it,
while from the great one his love is cut off and he does not seek it:
little by little all righteousness leaves him,
and whoever is negligent in his deeds does not acquire it.
He was not diligent like the bee, who laid up her store
from small things, and see, she is praised for a great store.

Righteousness a man acquires by perseverance,
and whoever grows weary flees from it and does not attain it.
See, these are the days of righteousness; toil, faster,
that you may gather that sweetness full of life.
Hope dawns, and those who toil rejoice in their rewards,
and boldness awaits the dawning of the great day.
Run in the fast like a diligent man who seeks his life,
that when the resurrection appears your soul may be joyful.
Fast for the Bridegroom, that you may rejoice with Him at His banquet,
for He is coming to make the fasters glorious with their crowns.
On His great day, when boldness will be required,
how will you rejoice, unless you have mourned with the fasters?
At that time which makes bright the faces of all who are sorrowful,
what gain will you find in it, that you are cheerful now?
When all delights are given to all the fasters,
what will you receive, if from today you are a reveller?
When rest comes in its order to whoever has toiled,
unless you have wearied yourself, how will you rest with the fasters?
If the suffering of the Only-Begotten does not pain you,
neither have you a share in His joy, to delight in it.
The great day that is coming to make all fasters forget their toil:

what will it make you forget, if fasting has not wearied you?
When hope pays the reward of observances,
what will it give you, unless you have kept them rightly?
Give to fasting the labours and runnings of righteousness,
that you may go and find at its end a great crown.
The crown of fasting is the resurrection of the Only-Begotten,
and unless you fast, you are a stranger even to the crown.
Fasting and vigil and prayers, together with alms,
like gifts to the Bridegroom, enter in when He rises.
The fast departs, and the resurrection of the Only-Begotten comes;
what will you offer Him, unless you fast rightly?
While the fast is here, gather from it all gifts for yourself,
that when the Bridegroom sees you on His day He may rejoice to meet you.
Like the bee, gather sweetness from your alms,
that you may bring a honeycomb with you to the banquet.
Righteousness is a sweet taste at the great feast;
let it go with you, or else the Bridegroom will not rejoice in you.
When the fasters enter before Him in their ranks,
each one bearing his vigil, his fast and his humility,
when alms shine at His feast like lights,
what will you bring, if you are dark in your deeds?
When the Watchers surround His tomb in their white robes,

and the women disciples with their spices and their perfumes,
in the great morning when the faces of all the fasters shine,
be first in boldness to claim your reward.
Run to the hope swiftly, like John,
and see the resurrection, lacking nothing in uprightness.
For the resurrection put on a garment woven of alms,
that you may be fair as the angels in their white robes.
Toil and make ready for yourself glorious vessels for the great feast:
a pure fast, and righteousness full of beauties.
Who will grant you to rejoice at the feast spiritually,
unless you weary yourself with the fast bodily?
Arise, be diligent in prayers and in alms,
and in the observances that the fast requires of fasters.
Let each in his rank guard himself from harms,
for the fast is common to all; let each toil in fair deeds.
Let the shepherd fast for his flock and for himself,
and with prayers bear the burden of the whole flock.
Let the [?] too close all doors during the fast,
and in their idleness guard the flock from robbers.
Let the chaste order of the covenant run after holiness,
for without it no one can see the Lord.

Let the old man fast who has shrunk, whose measure of years has dwindled,
that with the remnant of life left to him he may please the Lord.
Let the child fast, for victory befits childhood,
and let it see that its soul is very prone to falling.
Let young men fast, for the storm of youth is hard,
and unless fasting subdues it, its abundance goes astray.
Wives, adorn yourselves with fasting,
and in purity please God and your husbands.
Fasting is fair for virgins and for the betrothed,
for it gave Esther the beauty to prevail through fair deeds.
Let the widow too, who has buried her husband, love fasting,
for it brings her near to God, that He may be her husband.
Let the orphan who has lost his father fast, entreating
the Father of orphans to fill his lack.
Let the farmer fast for his field and for his soul,
that crop and soul may be kept from harms.
Fasting helps the merchant too, travelling on the road,
that with his trade he may gather all the gains of the Spirit.
Fasting profits the rich as well, that through alms
they may gain friends who will receive them into their tents.
Fasting befits the poor man too, whose belly is hungry,
that he may offer that very hunger of his to his God as a willing fast.

Let the solitaries, the sons of the kingdom, fast much,
for theirs are the contest and the struggle, and the victory too.
Let the sinner fast, whose debt is greater than his strength,
that perhaps he may pay off a little of his bond.
Let the righteous man fast, to add beauty to his righteousness,
for however high he climbs, there is still a step to the height above.
Let the penitent fast, for it is a season that helps the wounded,
and if he is careful, all his sores are healed by it.
In this fast let virgins and holy ones fast,
for in it the Son of the Virgin fasted for our sake.
Let the married fast, and gain new alms,
and since it is good and pure, let them honour the bed of union.
Even the adulterer, if he fasts, will not be ruined,
for he drives out passion by fasting and quenches it.
Even the harlot would lose nothing if she fasted,
for fasting can wipe away the shamelessness of loose women.
Let all the orders, in their ranks and in their degrees,
each in his place, honour the fast full of gains.
Righteousness that comes from many is greatly beloved,
and it has the strength to obtain all its requests daily.
Drops of rain, one by one, are only drops,
but when they are gathered they become a torrent that cannot be crossed.

From many drops comes a great flood,
and fasting befits the prayers of the whole people.
The Bride of light asks for mercy with all her children,
that prayer may multiply from every mouth, and see, it is heard.
It is as if to say: drops from the cloud,
and it becomes a torrent that cannot be crossed for its greatness.
In a multitude of mouths a single praise is spoken,
and it asks and receives and is not held back by the Judge.
In all fasters and in all measures she keeps the fast,
and with all mouths she calls upon her Lord richly.
From each one's fast she gathers and makes a great fast,
which is like a river gathered from drops.
Come, fasters, gather and mingle your abstinences,
that there may be a great fast in the assembly of the Daughter of lights.
The Bride's beauty is fasting, a brightness from many,
and her adornment is her vigil and her prayers, like necklaces.
The Virgin of light keeps herself from food,
for at the end of the fast she longs to eat the Bridegroom.
All delicacies are despised, loathsome and worthless to her,
and unless she eats Him the Daughter of the day finds no relief.
Therefore she fasts and restrains herself, the daughter of delights,

that when she eats Him she may be kept from greed.
By fasting the Bride longs to partake of the Bridegroom,
and see, peoples and worlds are invited, that she may feed them.
She fasts in her love, and because she longs to eat of Him
she forgets bread in her desire for the Bridegroom she yearns for.
Where have you ever seen a bride who eats the bridegroom,
or a virgin whose betrothed is set upon the table?
She desired, she loved, she fasted, she hungered, she drew near, she ate,
she delighted, she grew rich, she entered, she inherited the Father's treasure.
In fasting she saw Him contending with the Archon;
she fasted with Him, and since He became a sacrifice she broke Him for her children.
She longed for Him in the desert, since He was contending for her sake,
and see, she pleads to eat and be filled with the Fair One.
Sweet is fasting to the Church, the betrothed of the Only-Begotten,
and at its end she sees the Bridegroom in great glory.
See, the fasters look toward your feast, Son of God;
let your peace come from your treasure-house to the four quarters.
Accept our fast and make your peace upon our lands;
praise be to the Mercy that sent you to the earth, that it might be reconciled through you.
Here ends the second memra on fasting.
By the holy Mar Jacob: Memra 25 / (3), on the holy Fast of the Forty Days.

3. On the Holy Forty-Day Fast.
Once more I am about to speak the story of the fast;
make me worthy, my Lord, to speak and to profit those who hear me.
Concerning the days that call for the race of righteousness,
see, the word stirs within me: grant me to speak through you.
My true Teacher, teach me a story full of profit,
that I may tell its story to the Church you acquired by your sacrifice.
See, the teaching longs to speak clearly;
my beloved, lend me a true hearing, that it may delight you.
Come, fasters, let us recline at the King's table,
and let us feast today, spiritually, without bread.
Come, athletes who have entered the contest of righteousness,
let us speak now of the spectacles of the fast, what they are.
Come, you who are clothed in armour forged from almsgiving,
draw up in battle against the Devourer, whose legions are deployed.
Come, valiant ones who shoot the arrows of prayer,
take up [?] the battle, for demons are threatening your fasts.

See, the left stands arrayed in battle against the right;
run toward heaven, which in the contest is prepared for your victories.
The fast is accustomed to bring crowns of righteousness
to the one who loves it, and to enrich him with victories.
It is accustomed to overthrow the Adversary before the fasters,
and in the struggle to bring low the might of the prince of the air.
It is accustomed to bring out the hidden mysteries of God's house
and to reveal to the world things concerning its Creator, to great wonder.
The fast is able to interpret dreams and to loosen knots,
and to bring out all hidden things and spread them on the rooftops.
It is easy for the fast to quench the power of fire,
and from the furnace to sprinkle dew upon the fasters.
There is power in it: the fast tames wild beasts
and puts a muzzle on the mouth of the fierce lions.
Through fasting Moses attained to see the Shekinah of the Most High,
so that He spoke hidden mysteries with him from the thick darkness.
Moses ate the fast on the mountain as though it were bread,
and grew stout and fair, and was radiant with it, without food.
He fasted from bread, and at God's table he reclined;
he ate light and drank splendour, and acquired beauty.
He feasted on wine pressed from the clouds of darkness,

and in a sweet manner took on the colour of a flame.
The fast prepared for him a banquet full of life,
with that food whose flavours never cloy.
The sight of the Lord was the food that filled that faster,
and on His revelations he was nourished spiritually.
The fast brought him into the house of mysteries and stood showing him
the creation of the world as it was being built from nothing.
He had been purified of heavy foods,
and his mind shone to see hidden things openly.
Through heavy food the senses of the soul fall away
from the hidden knowledge of the divine mysteries.
Every disciple who eats much is no learner,
for through his food his mind grows too heavy for learning.
Moses and Adam were two disciples of God:
one fasted and learned, and the other, because he ate, lost his book.
Out of season the disciple ate fruit in Eden,
and for that reason he forgot what he had learned from God.
His great Teacher had strictly commanded him not to eat,
and because he ate he received no more teaching.
Through his eating his mind and heart grew dull,
and he was unable to learn that law which gave him life.

His soul was dulled by the fruit he ate from the tree;
the brightness of his spiritual understanding grew dark.
He ate, and was torn away from that order of spiritual beings,
and could no longer learn, for he had grown heavy.
That food he craved weighed heavily upon him,
and because he took it in lust it killed him, and he could not digest it.
But Moses, son of the Levites, entered to learn as well,
and kept himself from food, so as not to be weighed down by it.
He perceived in Adam that his Lord drove him out because he ate,
and he kept his mouth from foods so as to become luminous.
With his great mind he perceived that the fast is able to teach
the hidden and concealed mysteries of God's house.
In his humility he learned that through the fast are opened
the eyes of the soul, so that it gazes upon hidden things.
He saw that because Adam ate they put him out of Paradise,
and he fasted, so that he might enter and see the Tree of Life in its beauty.
He set the fast in array against the lust for that food,
so that he might be enlightened to receive many things.
He was stripped of heavy foods
so that he might grasp all the depths of the Godhead.
Through fasting he shone like a torch of great light,

until he could touch all the folds of creation.
Forty days he reclined with God at the banquet,
and without bread he feasted on the waves of splendour.
The fast refined him until he was entirely light,
and he went to see what lies beyond the world and what lies within it.
He scorned foods and rejected bodily tastes,
so that what he meditated on would not be hindered in his learning.
He became a stranger to bread and water, for he knew
that through foods the mind is darkened and the soul grows heavy.
Through fasting Moses saw God and learned His mysteries;
had he eaten, he would not have mastered that teaching.
By scarcity of bread and abstinence from foods
he made his mind a spacious bosom, to hold a great deal.
He learned many hidden mysteries of the Godhead,
and in learning he forgot bread, so that he did not eat.
The disciple shone through the scarcity of provisions,
until his whole face was great light.
The teaching grew sweet, and because he was deprived of food
he had great capacity, until he saw all hidden things.
The head of the race became mortal through food,
while Moses the prophet, through fasting, learned the story of creation.
Because Adam was greedy they put him out of Paradise,
and because Moses fasted he entered within God's thick darkness.
The faster went up the Lord's mountain and saw there
creation coming from nothing to become something.
The sight of his soul entered and stood upon hidden things;
he learned them, and brought their revelations to the world.
Through a great fast the Hebrew acquired a great mind,
able to contain beings and worlds and their ordering.
He was radiant, and he dwelt in God's thick darkness,
and there He taught him all the folds of creation.
On two tablets his Lord wrote a book for Moses,
for He knew that he was skilled and could receive many things.
His Teacher saw that he was a faster and longed to learn,
and He filled two tablets with treasures and gave them to him, that he might be enriched.
He gave him two, so that he might read one and keep one
for the New Testament, when it would be revealed in His Son.
On one tablet He wrote the Law and its commandments,
and gave the other tablet to the Gospel, to be interpreted on it.
Each Testament was written on its own tablet,
and because there are two, two tablets were needed:
one for the Law, to speak on it in terms of deeds,
one for the Gospel, to be interpreted on it spiritually.

He gave him two so that, when the New came down in its time,
no one would say, 'Why have two been newly made for us?'
So that the generations and the worlds and the peoples of the earth might know
that both the new and the old come from One.
In the two tablets the great prophet perceived
that God has another time in which He will speak.
'In this time He has given teaching to the world through my hands;
in another time He will teach the whole earth through His Son.
A prophet like me will arise after me from among your brothers,
who will also teach the earth by fasting, and it will be enlightened by Him.'
In the fast of Moses this fast of our Lord was being honoured,
and that number was being matched to that reckoning.
In that very number the Son of God was tempted;
Moses, when he fasted, kept that honour in his fast.
Elijah too, who was a son of the mystery of the Godhead,
ran the road in that same number, by the fast he took up.
Moses began, and our Lord completed, the great fast;
Elijah too ran in between, the stretch that fell to him.
Both Elijah and great Moses were gazing on our Lord,
and because of His fast they took up a fast, to resemble Him.
Through the fast of Moses creation learned about its Lord:

how He made it, and how it came into being from nothing.
Through that of Elijah, he drew up revelation, and He gave him power
to remove kings and to set up kings in their authority.
Through this one of our Lord, demons are overthrown from their ranks,
and rulers are stripped of their authority.
The prince of the air fell like lightning and was scattered,
and mercy upheld fallen Adam, and he rose up and fought.
The spectacle began, and the Son of God came down to the contest,
and in Adam's place He took up his battle and fought in it.
He walked on the road that His Father's prophets had trodden for Him,
so that the world might learn that He is no stranger to the One who begot Him.
Like Moses He fasted forty days while He was tempted,
and like Elijah He ran in the athletic contests of righteousness.
For the Lord's sake the servants fasted, to sketch Him in outline;
but the Lord fasted for Adam's sake, and was tempted.
For Moses fasted, and it was no help at all to Adam;
Elijah fasted, and the common debt was not repaid.
Nor did they fast for Adam's sake, so that he might be helped,
but to show how his Lord would fast in his place.
With their fasts they painted an image of the Son's fast,
so that the earth might perceive the goodness of His road when He dawned upon it.

But when Adam's Lord came and began His fast,
the prophets rejoiced in Him, that He had come to fulfil their revelations.
The first ones and those in between all became His witnesses
that He is the Lord who came down to the contest in His servant's place.
He came down to renew the battle between Adam and the dragon,
and for this reason He took up the fast as He fought.
That food which the serpent brought in, He repaid with a fast,
that hand for hand He might acquit Adam of his debts.
Because the first one ate, his Lord held back from food,
so that that gluttony might be exchanged for abstinence.
The battle in the garden among the trees was lost,
and for this reason the battle was renewed in the wilderness.
Forty days He drew out that victorious battle,
so that through them He might repay the common debt as He fought.
About the forty I shall now tell why it is
that this number is set down in Scripture, in all the books.
Among the people, the law commanded a woman who bears a male child
to bring after forty days a sacrifice that purifies her.
And for a woman who bears a female child it likewise commands
that she remain forty and forty days in her blood, and so be purified.
Moses too, the treasury of books and revelations,

fasted forty days and learned the mysteries of the Godhead.
Elijah too, who displayed the image of the Son of God,
walked forty days, for he too was guided by a mystery.
Without my counting up many, you will understand
that this number stands out greatly in all the books.
Forty days the Son of God fasted and was tempted;
if you listen spiritually, come and consider.
Our Lord came down to win the battle for this nature,
and on behalf of all of it He came down to the contest, though He was innocent.
Now nature has elements of which it consists,
four of them, equal and opposite in their forms.
And when that nature fell in the battle with the Accursed One,
the elements were defeated in that race of righteousness.
Therefore to each element He gave ten days
as a race, and so it is honoured in the athletic contest.
This number ten is the limit,
and beyond it you find no further number.
Therefore He gave ten days to each element,
as if to say: the whole race of righteousness.
And He folded these ten four times over,
for the whole of nature rightly consists in these.

Forty days were given as a contest to the four that had fallen,
so that they might rise in complete victory, triumphant.
For this reason our Lord came down to the battle as a remedy,
that through Him the whole of nature, which had been guilty, might be acquitted.
For this reason, a mystery kept and set down in the Scriptures,
these forty were celebrated in the readings.
But in the Gospel a race of fifty days is extended to us,
and unless it is within fifty, you cannot run the forty.
This mystery shows that the senses and the elements
rise by fasting from the fall into which the serpent cast them.
For the five senses, fifty days of righteousness,
and so the sin that conquered the house of Adam is purged away.
Of the fifty, forty stand as decreed,
for in them the four that were defeated among the trees are victorious.
This is the mystery of this fast, full of victories:
arise, valiant ones, run in the contest of righteousness!
Lift up your mind here a little, O listener,
for this is not the kind of discourse a speaker usually gives.
The mysteries of the fast stir within me spiritually,
and whoever listens in a bodily way does not hear me.
For forty days He fasted and fought with the Ruler,

and gave victory to the whole of nature in the great battle.
And see, the fast is extended to fifty days for the Church today,
while those that are in the contest are forty.
If you read the Law spiritually,
you will find in it the mystery of fifty clearly.
The fiftieth year is the year of jubilee,
a year of return, of release, and of comfort.
In it all the lands that had been sold were returned,
and went back to their former owners, to their joy.
Poverty had forced them to sell them,
and through the release they became heirs of their inheritances.
The fiftieth year returns villages to their owners,
and fields to the former masters who had left them.
Whoever had lost his land by sale, so that it was estranged from him,
in the fiftieth year has it returned to his hands, and he takes possession of it.
Destitute heirs who had sold and abandoned their holdings
return in the fiftieth year and stand within their borders.
Here is the resurrection, and that great day of the Gospel,
which comes at the fiftieth, and was proclaimed in the Law.
On the fiftieth day the heir of the Garden rose from the grave
and took possession of Eden, which the serpent had bought from him by deceit.

On the fiftieth day our Lord comes to His lands,
and that expeller who cheated and bought what is His is undone.
After fifty days He dawns upon the souls
that had been sold like fields, and He returns them.
The Devourer deceived and bought and led astray and acquired,
and after fifty they return to their Lord, that He may possess them.
The year was spiritually signified by a day,
for Ezekiel too then took a day for a year.
In the fiftieth year is return and release,
and joy for the heirs who regained their holdings.
On the fiftieth day is rest and comfort,
and on it souls return to God, that He may possess them.
At the completion of the fast the Son's resurrection is given to us,
and like that fiftieth year it returns what was sold.
All the souls that had been sold for nothing,
He redeems them and returns them for nothing.
In these mysteries Moses spoke with the Hebrews,
that in that year of jubilee there should be release.
Because of this great mystery of righteousness
he wrote 'fifty', and at its completion he named it 'release'.

For fifty days the fast runs, and at its completion
a single release brings resurrection to all debtors.
In these fifty days righteousness runs,
and at their completion release arose to renew them.
In the fifty days: humility, battle, and valour,
and after these a great crown, and victory too.
This fast consists in these hidden mysteries;
O fasters, do not slacken in your labours.
In these days the image of righteousness is painted;
let everyone bring choice colours from his pigments.
Because of these fifty days Moses wrote
that the fiftieth year should be a year of return for the people.
Therefore, so that nature might be made fair and righteous,
for forty days the battle stands with the victors.
In forty they conquer, but only in fifty are they rewarded,
for at the completion of fifty stands the Saviour of the earth.
Desirable are you, O fast; blessed is he who has struggled in you,
for all the mysteries and all the types are found in you.
Forty are yours, and you richly have fifty:
the battle is fierce, and at its completion a great crown.

in all the means that lend a hand to good things,
in all the races in which righteousness is cultivated.
In all that the fast requires, choose from among the fasters;
run, faster, so that you may be able to save your soul.
It is a great contest, and valour is required in it;
toil in the contest and look to the crown that comes from justice.
Do not slacken: sleep little and lie down little,
lest you lose the harvest that gives the soul abundant life.
This fast is the theatre of athletic combat:
whoever falls dies, and whoever does not fall is victorious.
Fear, faster, the dragon who watches the air,
for see, he stands stripped for combat, eager to engage the fasters.
Take Jesus to yourself, for except through Him no one conquers,
and through Him you can subdue all the proud.
The fast is armour, and Jesus gave it to all the victorious;
servants of the King, take up breastplates for the contest of blood.
This fast is that contest in which a man stands
firm unto blood, so that he may bring his life through the struggle.
In this contest the soul kills or is killed;
it conquers and stands, or is defeated and falls greatly.

This fast is decreed for the battle of righteousness,
and no one can slacken from the struggle.
There is the fast, and there are fasts, and there are distinctions;
and this fast is unique for the contenders.
To the Israelites the Law gave ten fasts in a single year,
with many observances.
And these fasts were given for various reasons,
for deliverances and for the feasts of the whole year.
This fast is unique and divine,
and a great thing, for the whole of nature is renewed in it.
The Son of God fasted to justify the whole race of humankind,
and His reason is greater than all reasons.
Forty days He set it, like a furnace of fire,
for the whole of nature, and refined it to make it fair, for it had grown corrupt.
By His great fast He brought low the might of the Adversary,
and raised up the fallen, who had been cast down from of old.
See, the common debt is being repaid by the Son's fast,
and everyone is bound to toil with Him for his own salvation.
And if the innocent One came down to the contest on behalf of the guilty,
how can the guilty be idle in the struggle?

In this fast He fought three battles
with the Strong One, and humbled his pride in all three.
Satan set three snares of three passions,
and the Son of God broke all three of them.
Love of the belly, love of glory, and lust for riches
were arrayed in battle against the faster who chose to hunger.
All these things by which Adam had been made guilty,
all these He brought forward, that the contender might conquer through them.
And when the Strong One stood alert and set his snares,
the Watchful One broke them by His fast and made him a laughingstock.
Love of the belly He trampled by the hunger He endured,
and love of glory was defeated by His humility.
Lust for riches He trampled by love of poverty,
and by a single fast three passions were brought low.
By His fast He set out teaching for the solitaries,
how they may conquer the Devourer in their contests.
He rebuked Adam: had he been willing to fight,
he would not have been defeated in the battle of lust and gluttony.
He made light of the robber [?] who brought Him down to battle, and stood and fought,
and the Strong One was defeated, and the nature that had been guilty was acquitted.
In the person of Adam the Son of God was fighting,

and the victory the Lord won He gave to His servant.
For that in which Eve was guilty, the Virgin's Son paid off her bond.
Blessed is He through whose fast the fasters have conquered in their contests.
End of the third memra on fasting.

By the holy Mar Jacob.
Memra 26.
On love: the Son of God, who came in His love to renew all:

Give me your love, that with it I may speak to the one who hears me.
O Exalted One, who came down from your dwellings to our wretchedness,
grant me to rise to the place of your love and recount its beauties.
O you who in your love endured the sufferings of crucifixion,
let it now well up in me to speak of your goodness.
In the fervor of your love let my word be stirred to tell of your good tidings,
that I may richly tell your story among the earthly.

Come, beloved ones, whom the womb of baptism has borne,
let us acquire love, for it is great wealth to the one who acquires it.
Brothers, who from within the waters became brothers to the Only-Begotten,
come, let us delight with discernment in the story of love.
Dear children of my great Father, in the likeness of his Son,
give me a hearing, that I may speak with feeling the discourse on love.
For in every story, whatever is told, its flavor is within it,
and in every discourse the word about its subject is like that subject.
Since love stirs me today to speak,
it is a sweet theme: come, let us delight in its flavors.
O discerning one, who runs after the virtues,
hunt down love for yourself, for it brings one near to God.
O teacher, advocate of the divine mysteries,
speak with love, for otherwise you cannot do any good.
O disciple, who inclines his ear to what is discovered,
give me love and take for yourself the word full of life.
One who teaches without loving is like a byword:
how he toils in an ordering of words that brings no profit!
And whoever hears without love, let him stop his ears,
for sounds and words are of no use to him when he hears them.
A skilled master who wishes to enrich the one who hears him

should love much and speak little with his disciples.
And you, learner, hear a small speech with great love,
and be enriched by it, for without love no one grows rich.
As soon as love enters the soul, its thoughts grow bright;
the mind goes in and stands in the place of the divine mysteries.
And though the virtues are beautiful to those who practice them,
if they are performed without love, they are not beautiful.
Purifying salt seasons foods,
and the virtues need love to be performed with it.
The virtues are set like members in a body,
and love fills the place of the soul for the whole body.
Fasting is beautiful, but if a man fasts without love,
his mouth stinks and there is no profit in his abstinence.
Prayer is lovely, but if love does not lift it up,
its wing is weak and it does not see the Exalted One in his place.
Very lovely is righteousness to the one who practices it,
but if he does not love while he practices it,
if he does not love while he practices it, his labor is empty.
Glorious is the crown of virginity and holiness,
but if the holy one lacks love, he is like an adulterer.
Great is the reward of one who breaks his bread for the hungry,

but if he breaks it for him without love, it is without profit.
For a martyr to give his body to fire and burning,
he needs love, and then he takes the crown with the martyrs.
Love prevails over prophecy and faith,
for without it there is neither prophesying nor believing.
From its deeds you learn what love is,
and its works bear witness how beautiful it is.
In love the Father delivered up his Son for sinners,
for without love this deed would never have been done.
Love drew the Lord, and he came down from his dwellings;
it mingled him with humankind, that the Lord might become a companion to his servants.
Love brought the Son of God from his Father's house,
made him a man, and he endured the sufferings of crucifixion.
Love shut up in the womb and in the tomb
the mighty Son who upholds creation by his hidden nod.
By the love of the Father, which was in him from eternity,
he lent his likeness, that he might create man in the image of his Son.
In that same love he created the creatures when he was creating,
and by it again he delivered up his Only-Begotten when he was redeeming.
In what king was there the power to do such a thing:

to deliver up his son for an exile, to bring him back to his place?
What rich man would think it right to scatter all his wealth
on beggars out of his love, and make them rich?
Who would give his son as a burnt offering, to be a sacrifice,
for servants who had fled from him, to bring them back?
Who among the good would not fear to cast away his life,
to taste death in place of the wicked and give them life?
And what living man could explore the depths of Sheol,
and bind himself in order to set the prisoners free from darkness?
What exalted one would make a tomb his dwelling,
and raise the dead to the lofty dwelling of the heavenly ones?
This deed love wrought for the Son of God:
that in place of mankind he should taste death and give them life.
Therefore love is higher than all excellences,
and beneath its heel all the virtues are set.
Righteousness and perfection fall short of it,
for no one can become perfect except through it.
However much a righteous man is justified by his works,
he needs love, and then he is made complete in perfection.

It seems to me that the discourse I have taken up is hard,
and very weighty for the hearers is the story I have set forth.
No one hears a discourse on love except with love,
and where shall we seek it, or with whom is it, that we may speak of it?
Among us there are anger and wrath and hardness of heart,
envy and deceit and lying and slander,
all quarrels, all strifes, all tumults,
all contentions, all pretexts for hateful talk.
This one quarrels, that one is angry, another is deceitful:
where is love, that it might tell its story without confusion?
If it were present, it would be good for us to speak of it,
but where it is absent, the story about it is wronged and spoiled.
Love never consents to be angry with anyone,
for it loves those near and those far alike.
Love cannot hate the one who hates it;
it looks to its Lord, who for everyone endured the cross.
Come, you who are angry; come, be reconciled to the one who hates you,
for anger destroys your soul if it lodges in it overnight.
For this reason the Apostle commands the one who hears him:
let not the sun set and find you angry.

Now, discerning one, seek reconciliation while it is still day,
for if anger lodges in you, at night it does its work.
It darkens your soul, confuses it and makes it stink;
it pains the heart and begets all filthy thoughts.
It makes the mind bring forth confused dreams that are not good,
and at night it stirs up every contention in you with evil agitations.
It brings your enemy in a dream and sets him in array against you,
and all night long it humiliates and torments you.
It sorely presses you to drive him away, since you hate him,
yet it took the dream and brought him in and set him in your bedchamber.
You drove him off to be gone, but it brought him at night and mingled him with you,
for once anger lodged in you, dreams of confusion choked you.
From that preoccupation of the day the visions sprang,
and all night long it brought your enemy to keep watch with you.
Woe to you because of him, for see, he lies stretched out with you on your bed,
and while you sleep he quarrels with you and abuses you.
The anger that lodged in you painted the image of the one you hate,
and in the dream set him before you, so that you stumble over him.
If you hate him, be reconciled to him and have rest from him;
put love in yourself before you sleep, and he will not wear you down.

Take enmity out of your soul while you are awake,
and put love in it, that it may give birth to divine dreams.
From evening on, bring peace into your mind,
and then you will find sweet sleep all night long.
Let the sun set, and love dawn upon your mind,
and let the light of love overcome the night, so that it does not grow dark for you.
The darkness of night and the darkness of anger—if you give your soul to both,
who will enlighten you or gladden you?
The day has set: take love for yourself, a great sun,
and go in, and by it light up your soul at night against evils.
Look upon your enemy with love when you lie down to sleep,
and then sleep will be pleasant to you and you will have rest from strife.
All thoughts, good and evil, are seeds;
the soul is the soil, and the will is like the farmer.
If you sow evil thoughts in your soul in the evening,
you will reap filthy dreams all night long.
But if you bury love in your soul when you lie down to sleep,
a sweet fragrance will rise in your sleep from your bed.
Anger troubles your soul with confusion when it enters it;
purge it out and fill your soul with peace when you lie down to sleep.
Paul, the physician of souls, saw fit to bind it up;

this bandage he laid on the soul, that it might be healed by it.
