He commanded the angry man that the sun should not set upon him,
but that he should drive the anger out of himself, lest he sleep with it.
Anger is rust in the soul of the one who acquires it,
and if it lodges in him overnight, it rots and makes him stink.
For this reason reconciliation is granted to the one who is angry,
that anger may not putrefy in him at night if it lodges in him.
While it is light, enlighten your soul, O discerning one,
lest when it grows dark you be seared by the suffering of a wicked heart.
What will you do to your enemy who has offended you?
Love him and acquit him, for if you hate him, he overcomes you.
As long as you hate him, he becomes a thorn in your mind
and pricks you; unless you love him, you will have no rest from him.
In the image of the Son you were formed, O man who hates his brother;
how will you resemble him unless you love the one who hates you?
Jesus your Master changed water into good wine;
do a new deed like his, and resemble him.
Come, in your mind change hatred into love,
so that in small measure you may see all new things in your soul.
You have called the Father on high "Our Father" in the house of atonement;
show that you have some of the likenesses of the Only-Begotten.

He made wine from water, for he is the Son of God;
you, make peace from strife, and resemble him.
Without murmuring he gave his cheek to the one who struck him,
while you, at a single word, are upset and troubled and full of anger.
Spitting on his face and scourges on his back for sinners—
he endured them, to taste death in their place.
While they hated him, the Son of God loved them,
and while they crucified him, he was offering himself for their life.
Come, show me, angry man who hates his brother,
what has he done to you, that it is hard for you to be reconciled to him?
If he has wronged you, look to God, who was also wronged;
if he has cheated you, they cheated him too, and he accepted it.
Your insult, your reproach, your being cheated by your brother—you are still bound to bear them,
for the Son of God endured the cross without hating.
And after all this, unless you love him, you cannot
call "Our Father," if you are the brother of the Only-Begotten.
Forgive the one who offended, and run to him and be reconciled to him,
for this deed gives hope to the one who heeds it.
O disciple, unless you love the one who hates you,
seek yourself a master, for the Crucified Master is not yours.
If Jesus is your teacher, this is what he teaches:

that you should be loving toward your enemy and show him affection.
But if you do not listen to him, the serpent is your teacher, the one who by his deceit
raises all contentions and rifts among disciples.
Two teachers the world has had from of old,
and this one does not teach his disciples as that one does.
In their teachings the serpent and our Lord are the teachers of the earth:
one a killer, the other a life-giver to their disciples.
The serpent teaches hardness of heart and an evil eye,
hatred of brothers, rage, and constant deceit,
great fury, jealousy, wrath, and agitation,
strife and anger, with quarrels and evil rifts,
theft and lying and adultery,
and division, with strife and the shedding of blood.
And Jesus teaches purity of heart and a good eye,
love of mankind, cheerfulness, and fellowship,
great peace, serene harmony, and pure love,
integrity, uprightness, and humility,
serenity too, and simplicity, and faith,
and righteousness, and that a man should love the one who hates him.
Come, disciple, take for yourself one of these teachers,
and do not waver in his teaching, if he is your master.

Choose a teacher for yourself and learn from him as he tells you,
for you cannot listen to both.
If your mind longs to be a disciple of the serpent,
be angry, rage, and hate your brother while he loves you.
Be troubled, perverse, gloomy, and a hater of men;
set ambushes, stir up strife, and rouse anger.
Call for strife and riot and trouble, and draw the sword,
and like a [?] disciple of the serpent, be bitter.
Your friend, your brother—hate him; why are you idle?
And if he hates you, hate him as he hated you, and repay him.
Set a snare for him, dig a pit for him, cast him to destruction;
devise evils and heap up his reproach, because he offended you.
And if he comes to be reconciled with you, do not accept him,
lest your master, the evil serpent, be angry with you.
He teaches you not to be reconciled nor appeased,
and not to let anyone get the better of you, lest you be counted among the weaklings.
Rather, repay with evil injuries the one who offended you,
and do not forgive him, or else he will despise you and laugh at you.
Do him a greater evil than the one he did to you,
so that everyone will fear you and honor you.

These things the serpent teaches his friends and his disciples;
woe to the one who inclines his ear and accepts him.
After these, come, hear Jesus, what he says to you,
and become a disciple of the teaching of God's house:
Love the one who hates you, and turn your cheek to the one who strikes you,
and give up your life for your friend, if it is demanded of you.
Love your enemy truly, if you are my disciple,
and if he offends you, be reconciled to him seventy times seven.
Endure insult, and do not insult the one who hates you,
and be good even toward the wicked who abuse you.
Forgive your brother all the evils he has committed,
for thus Jesus your teacher teaches, if you are his.
Look upon the Crucified, and look upon the crown of thorns he wears,
and at once anger and wrath will fade from your mind.
To reconcile the human race, which had been angry,
he swallowed his pain and suffered, and made peace in the whole world.
The teaching of the Son of God has been forgotten,
and everyone runs in his deeds against it.
The disciples have fled from the teacher of truths,
and despised the commandment that teaches peace to the one who hears it.
Wickedness has grown strong, to the point that the priest is angry,
and the steward of the mysteries hates his brother and scorns him.

Shall I be silent here, or speak, though I am afraid?
Shall I raise my voice, or shut my mouth from teaching?
The priest is the salt and the reconciler of all who are angry,
and if he is angry, who will reconcile him with his neighbor?
No one throws salt into salt to season it,
and if it has lost its savor, what flavor can restore it?
If it has rotted, who will salt what is tasteless?
For if it has lost its savor, the hope of its flavors is gone.
Come, our salt, and bring your flavor to season us;
do not you rot, for we look to you to be purified by you.
Scatter yourself among us, for we have lost our savor and are troubled;
cut away our slackness and give abundant taste to our insipidity.
Everyone looks to your flavor to be purified by you,
and if your flavor is lost, it is cause for weeping over your ruin.
You are salt, O priest: see that you are not angry with your neighbor,
lest it be said by outsiders that the salt has lost its savor.
You are the salt of the earth and the peace of the land,
the light of the world and the stewards of the houses of the Godhead.
Through you the one who is angry with his neighbor is reconciled;
through you the one who is upset with his spouse is appeased.
From you the world learns to love the one who hates it,

and from you it hears the teaching full of life.
You proclaim from the lofty bema of the Godhead:
"Forgive your brother, if he offends you, seventy times seven."
On your lyres the gospel of the Son of God is sung,
the voices of love: that everyone should love the one who hates him.
From you the serene assembly of the church of the nations hears
that no one should ever repay evil for evil.
I have loved my enemy because of the reading you taught me,
and if I see that you hate your brother, what shall I do?
You teach me that I should love the one who hates me,
yet you do not think it fitting to be reconciled with your angry brother.
You made me fear that unless I forgive, I will not be forgiven,
and yet you are unwilling to forgive the anger of the one who offended you.
If you transgress what is right, who will teach you?
It is a dreadful thing for me to stretch out teaching toward you.
From what you read, learn for yourself about reconciliation:
that the angry man is not accepted in the house of atonement.
"Go, be reconciled, and then come and offer"—so it is said
to the angry man: once he is reconciled, he is permitted to come.
Incense of spices without reconciliation is a foul odor,

and if an angry man carries the censer, he insults the sanctuary.
The love of the soul is the incense of the house of atonement,
which the mind gathered from the blessed roots of Eden.
The choice spices that the priest brings into the Holy of Holies
are thoughts that are serene and pure of evils.
The lampstand of the branches, sevenfold of light, mighty in its shining,
is the mercy of the Lord that is set within a serene soul.
The fragrant oil with which the priest is anointed when he is consecrated
is love, which proclaims that its fragrance is sweeter than [?].
The stones of perfection and of light that were on his breast
are a chosen crown and the serene light of faith.
When his hand and his foot and the tip of his ear were anointed,
it was that he might be known as a minister of the Crucifixion.
He was commanded to put salt on all the sacrifices,
and by this it was made known that love serves all sacrifices.
The garment of fine linen that the priest wears within the sanctuary
is love, spread over his mind when he serves as priest.
The robe he wears when he goes out to the people in the assembly
shows that he is open and mingles lovingly with everyone.

With bells of gold and embroidered pomegranates
he is stirred, the priest, to fear, to love, and to take heed.
The crown, the bridal robe, and the plate he wears when he ministers
are hope and love and faith that is not divided.
The crown of the priest proclaims to the people the priest's love,
which becomes for him the strength of all the virtues.
By love the priest can enter before God,
for unless he loves, the layman who loves is better than he.
I do not presume to extend teaching to the priest,
nor would I disgrace myself by meddling with those higher than I.
No one lights a lamp in the sun when he walks,
for the sun lights every path for all who walk.
Be silent, speaker, lest the sun be offended by you;
cover your mouth: the story you have set forth is greater than you.
You are a lowly man; what business is it of yours to speak?
Your mind is dark; what will you say before the luminous?
Pass over this story, for there is no place for the word before them;
it is a lofty step: be silent, sinner, and look at yourself.
Turn the teaching to the congregation; speak, for it is serene and simple;
there you have a place, and love that listens with pleasure.

It is not for you, man, to speak before those who enter the sanctuary;
leave the shepherds of the flocks alone: their deeds are watched.
Speak to the flocks, the little ones and the innocent,
for whose sake the Son of God endured the cross.
Hear, you innocent ones, bought with the blood of the Only-Begotten,
for again the discourse on love is spoken to help you.
If the virtues are not perfected except by it,
let whoever is eager for gain run after it.
Love one another, as members love their fellow members,
for one is the head of the whole body, the Lord Jesus.
Whoever is angry with his neighbor and is not reconciled
is like a member cut off and thrown away from the members.
Love is the soul; whoever love has left
remains a corpse, cold and rotten, and is not among the living.
Who will reconcile a man who is angry with his neighbor,
except love, which is the sum of the new life?
Tell me now, how does the story of anger go?
Among those who are angry, who should be eager for reconciliation?
A quarrel breaks out: one is insulted and another gave the insult;
the one who was insulted ought, as is fitting, to seek love.

The one who offended is anxious to uphold his own side;
he is ashamed to come—so go to him yourself and be reconciled to him.
And if a poor man is angry with a rich man,
that rich man ought to plead for reconciliation.
But the poor man, when he has offended him, is afraid and troubled;
he trembles and holds back, and does not dare to be reconciled.
In every case, whoever is cleared of the blame
is the one for whom it is fitting to seek peace with his neighbor.
Whoever is higher, exalted and glorious, let him humble himself
before the sinner and be reconciled to him in humility.
At the beginning of the world arose the strife that the serpent sowed,
and the Lord and Adam had been at odds from then on.
Who was the lesser, who was poor, who had offended,
and who went to face his fellow to be reconciled with him?
Adam offended; he despised and was arrogant; he erred and rebelled;
he stole and did wrong; he snatched and ate; he was angry and went out.
And after all this the King's Son came down from beside his Father,
and came and appeased the one who had become angry of his own will.
The Honored One humbled himself before the lowly;
the rich one, too, sought reconciliation from the poor.
The Lord of the Garden came down to win over the thief;
he was reconciled to him and gave him the fruit of life to eat.

The good shepherd, in his love, carried the lamb that had strayed;
it had grown angry and gone off, and he came and lifted it on his shoulders.
Tremble, you who are angry, and press every day for reconciliation,
for the Lord in his love was reconciled to us when we had angered him.
Let no one say, “Since so-and-so offended, let him come to me;
I am better than he, and it is a disgrace for me to go and be reconciled to him.
He offended against me; let him come and appease me, and I will accept,
so that by his humbling everyone may learn of his folly.”
The Lord did not choose to deal this way with Adam, who had offended,
that Adam should humble himself and ask him for reconciliation.
Had the Lord stayed in his place until our own day
and not come to him, he would still be estranged from him even now.
But knowing it would help for him to humble himself,
he himself appeased the servant who had fled, so that he might be reconciled to him.
The Exalted One came down in his compassion to those below,
and was reconciled, and led them, and brought them up to his place to make them great.
The Rich One turned his path toward the poor,
and made peace, and enriched them, and brought them up to his Begetter.
The Mighty One made reconciliation with the weak,
and honored and redeemed and brought back those who had been lost.

The Lord of servants and King of kings humbled himself;
God himself came down and was reconciled with the children of men.
O you who are angry, look at your God and become like him,
and make peace with your neighbor with discernment.
Wash away from yourself wrath and grudges and wickedness of heart,
and the Lord’s mercy will dwell in your soul as in a kingdom.
Whoever is angry with his neighbor and does not love him
hates the Lord, for he will not submit to loving his brother.
For human beings are the image of the Godhead,
and whoever honors the king’s image loves the king.
But if his image is despised or wronged by anyone,
the king demands satisfaction for the insult to his image from those who despised it.
No one can love God
and at the same time hate his brother or be estranged from his neighbor.
God is hidden, but your brother is near, and he is God’s image:
show honor to the One far off through the one who is near.
But if your heart hates your brother, who is visible and near,
how will you love the Lord, who is hidden and far from you?
Your brother shows whether your soul passes the test of having love in it,
and so it will be confirmed that you love the Lord, who is exalted above you.

The king is far off and his image is near, and if the image is wronged,
the image is angry with you, and the king demands satisfaction for its injury.
All the debts you have to lay before God
your brother shows, and for his sake the Lord cancels your debts.
Honor the image, cherish it, love it, and be reconciled with it,
and the King, who has no need of your honor, will pay your debts.
Love God and love your brother with all your mind;
blessed is he who in his love reconciled the world with his Begetter.
Here ends the homily on love.
By the holy Mar Jacob: Homily 27, on admonition.

The infant needs the one who nurses it, so that it may live from her,
and creation needs the Creator, so that it may be sustained by him.
If a mother abandons the baby she has borne,
it would have been better for it never to have come to birth from her.

And the Lord of the world, had he abandoned it after creating it,
it would have been better for it never to have existed from the beginning.
But he does not abandon it; for not even a woman abandons her baby,
and even if she should forget, he never forgets creation.
Had he only created it, he would only be the Creator,
and he would have had no other name but this.
But because he carries it after creating it, he also nourishes it,
and so he is called both Mighty One and Nourisher.
And because his judgement is upright, he is just,
and because he shows mercy, he is also called Merciful.
His judgement is just, and mercy cleaves to it;
he is full of zeal, and kindness is found in him.
All his governance flows from goodness,
and all his working stands firm in justice.
He does not stray from justice when he shows mercy,
and when he exacts requital his goodness incurs no reproach.
Both justice and goodness are beautiful in him,
and each always helps the other as they shine.
He has mercies and he has scourges, and therefore
he is loved and feared by everyone who is full of discernment.
Grace is his, zeal is his, love is his,
and he has anger against whoever has turned away from justice.

When he sees iniquity being done, he becomes zealous,
and if humility meets him, he becomes gentle.
For if he did not hate the wicked, he would not be just,
and if he did not have mercy on the humble, he would not be kind.
And because he is just, he is also kind;
upright and exalted above reproach is his governance.
There are times when he sees iniquity and is patient,
as though he had not seen it: the iniquity prospers and he does not overturn it.
And there are times when, the moment wickedness occurs, he stirs up
the heat of his anger against those who did the wickedness that was done.
There is one who runs in iniquity all the days of his life,
and neither chastisement nor correction ever touches him.
But another, if he merely thinks of doing wickedness,
justice overtakes him, and its sword is drawn to strike him to destruction.
At one and the same time some of his servants are swallowed up by the wicked,
and they are not delivered, nor does he take it upon himself [?] to avenge them.
At another time, if one of the just is distressed,
he begins to execute judgement for the unseemly deed.
Look at righteous Hur: the people who cast the calf stoned him,
and his case never even came to inquiry, as to why they stoned him.
Yet because Miriam spoke a word, she was clothed with leprosy:

requital for the word, while for the stoners there was no chastisement.
Isaiah was sawn apart, and the Lord his Master did not avenge him;
yet because righteous Lot was distressed, he burned up the region.
There were times when he showed his power in the furnace
and held back the fire so that the boys could tread it underfoot.
At another time a woman uttered threats against a certain man,
and he did not exact requital from the mouth that was insolent toward the righteous man.
The fire is held back, and Jezebel is allowed to cause distress:
for at times he exacts requital, and at times he delays requitals.
Whoever sets out to inquire into these things is bewildered:
why is his whole course not uniform, in a single manner of conduct?
Why is one swallowed up, as it seems, and another not,
and why does he delay with one and exact strictly from another?
Moulded clay, why are you insolent toward the potter,
saying to him what he should or should not do?
The wisdom of the Exalted One is set over the governance of the world,
and in it all affairs run their course along with their times.
By that knowledge which fashioned the sun and made the moon,
by it the turbulent world is governed by God.
When he exacts and when he delays, it is wisdom;
and because a man is too dull to grasp it, he thinks it is confused.
He is not confused when he gives sustenance to the Watchers,

and to men their food within their bounds.
He did not grow weary in his work as he gave
light to the sun, and stretched out its phases for the moon,
names to the stars, and an ordered course to the hosts;
and they do not go astray as they run along their paths.
Nor does he go astray when he spreads out the rays of the sun
and spreads light by day over the lands.
It is no great thing for him when he gives sustenance to the fish,
in the heart of the seas, to the dwellers in the waters, food in plenty.
The numbers of the hairs do not weary him to count them,
so that apart from him not one falls and reaches the ground.
The grains of sand and the drops of rain and the waves of the sea
lie plainly under number before the Godhead.
The weight of the earth and the great heaviness of the whole world
he carries, and it stands, while he neither tires nor is shaken.
All creation receives life from him every day,
everything in its place, and their provisions are allotted by him.
The governance of the turbulent world, too, is provided for by him,
by that knowledge which created these courses that run every day.
And when he exacts and when he delays requitals,
his one aim is to benefit mankind every day.

Do not, when you see iniquity being done and the Exalted One silent,
think that he is not zealous or does not exact requital.
Nor, when he exacts strictly, should you suppose
that wrath counselled him and he was stirred to punish the iniquity he saw.
He is the same both when he exacts and when he delays,
for God does not change from what he is.
And because he truly has two worlds,
he delays here so as to execute judgement in the great world.
To each of them he has given deeds by which they may be set right:
when he sees iniquity and at once executes judgement,
that deed is meant to let the world perceive that there is judgement;
and when he delays while wickedness is committed, he teaches
that God truly has another world,
since the people's deeds [?] are not avenged here in our place.
Let the world learn that God is to execute judgement:
when a man does iniquity openly and he does not exact it of him,
he shows that his punishment is kept for him in that world, there;
and when he does not swallow him up, let the world learn that judgement is kept for the beyond.
And the deeds bear with great force on both these lessons,
for in both there is profit for the whole world.
If all deeds had remained unavenged,

who would have confirmed that there is a God who executes judgement?
And if every wickedness that happens were avenged here,
it would be thought that there is no other world.
If whoever did evil had his evil come upon his head,
and whoever did good were repaid his good here,
this would have been the judgement, and another judgement to come would not exist;
so it would seem, and so it would appear, to whoever looked at it.
But since some deeds are avenged and some are kept in store,
it stands proven that another world and the Lord of the world exist.
And when justice stands in judgement over a deed,
it shows that there is a Just One who exacts from the unjust.
And when, again, he delays over a deed and does not exact it,
it confirms that that other world holds judgement.
So too with his servants when they are persecuted:
one he rescues, and for another he delays and does not rescue him.
Great and fitting and worthy of praise is his governance,
both when he rescues and when he delays the rescue.
Some of them he delivered from fire and from wild beasts,
but others he let be burned and did not deliver.
He rescued the three and left the seven without rescue;
yet all ten are his. Why, then?
If he had delivered all his servants from blows,

the love of them all would have fallen far short of glory.
It would have been said that no one is ever swallowed up for his sake,
since whoever came to be swallowed up, he would rescue from blows.
And for this reason those who come for his sake would come:
because they know that he rescues them from affliction.
He would let no one at all be swallowed up for his sake,
and if he had let them be afflicted, they would not have come.
The glory of the servants God has would have become tasteless,
if he had delivered them all and rescued them from affliction.
And outsiders would say that he does not even exist,
or, if he does, why has he delayed in helping his beloved?
He would be reproached for seeing his servants laid waste
and never delivering a single one of them from affliction.
Therefore he delivered as he willed, so that the world might perceive
that these servants have a Lord who has power.
And therefore he let them bear afflictions at times,
so that the world might see how true the love of his servants is.
When he let them be burned, their love grew,
and when he chose to rescue them, he triumphed.
And therefore he did not deliver all his servants,
so that he would not be the only one praised when he is praised.

He let them die by the edge of the sword and by wild beasts,
so that they might receive glory for how much they endured for his sake.
And therefore some of them he delivered and some of them he let go,
so that he might be praised, and his servants be praised with him.
When he delivers, he takes all the glory for himself;
and when he does not deliver, he wishes to glorify them with himself.
He has tender care for them, and lets them die for his sake,
so that they might claim their reward from him openly,
and be praised for the fire and the knife as well;
and before the wild beasts they set their love ablaze for his sake,
so that the world might perceive that God has such servants,
who, when death presses on them, draw near to it for his sake,
and that the love of his servants might be victorious in all the earth,
and he be praised by the onlookers because of them.
And it shall be their blessedness that, by reason of their deeds,
he was praised who is worthy of praise and acclaim.
Therefore, when he does not rescue from affliction,
it is as fitting for him, to the discerning, as when he rescues.
Yet he who lacks knowledge at times
hates the governance of the world in his eyes, and even plays the wise man;
and how wise he mistakenly supposes himself to be, in his haste,

thinking that if he had authority over the governance he would set it in order!
When he saw iniquity being done, he would put a stop to it,
and the wicked man, when he grew insolent, he would overthrow.
He would not allow a single one of the just to be swallowed up,
nor would he let the unjust man lift up his head.
There is one who hates, and in his rashness loses his understanding,
and thinks the affairs of the world are not well ordered.
And though it is proclaimed that no one should envy the wicked,
he envies them and is full of rage against the wicked.
He would even wish, if he could, to bring down fire
upon the wicked and upon the unjust and burn them up.
Woe to you, fool! You do not bear with things as God does;
why, turbulent one, would you take his governance away from him?
He is patient with the doers of iniquity so as to win them;
he is not a partner of the wicked because he bears with them.
And when the righteous are tested, if he does not rescue them,
he adds beauty to their beauty through their afflictions.
But you, because you are hasty and turbulent and full of anger,
find fault with a Governor full of wisdom.
And of the affairs carried on in the evil world
you think: let him take away from this one and add to that one.

You make a case about riches and poverty:
that you would take from this one and give to that one, if you could.
You even say: why is this one honoured with his gold,
while this other lacks even his daily bread?
Why is one rich to the point that he forgets even God,
while his fellow is in want to the point that he murmurs against the Creator?
Why is one anxious to count his gold and never finishes it,
while this other dies of hunger in his need?
O you who lack understanding, from whom the governance is hidden,
do not find fault with the Governor who is full of good things.
It was good of him to create riches and poverty,
and in either one a man who endures can live.
Behold, in poverty Lazarus is with Abraham,
and in riches, behold, there is Abraham, in a royal household.
Both of these, one rich and one poor,
behold, dwell together in one place, exalted and lofty.
His riches did not harm the one (and turn him aside?) toward evils,
nor did poverty keep the other from good things.
His riches became a good occasion for that rich man,
for through them he gave relief to rich and poor alike.
And poverty became a good occasion for the other,

for he endured and was patient, and his contest pleased the angels.
Riches and poverty are alike for the one who meets them:
in either he can excel, if he is discerning.
In the body there is both a right hand and a left,
one weak and one strong, and yet it is one body.
In the world there are riches and there is poverty,
and the world is one, like one body that is not divided.
And whoever says, why was poverty created,
let him say, then, why was the left hand created too?
The body needs both the right hand and the left,
and each always helps the other in their tasks.
The strong one does not reproach the weak one,
nor does it think itself in any way better than the other in the body.
And if the left gets tangled while working and finds it hard,
at once the right runs to help it.
And both have a single fine purpose:
that each should serve the other always, lovingly.
The body is the world, in which there are riches and poverty,
and so they are set to help one another.
The rich man is set to have mercy on the poor man,
to care for him and to supply all his needs.

The poor man, for his part, is set to bow down and to be subject,
and to work without murmuring, and to find rest in the house of the rich.
For if poverty did not bend his neck,
he would not give himself to work in the house of the rich.
He would kick back if he had even a little strength,
and would not bow his head to stoop like a poor man.
And much work would lie neglected in the house of the rich,
and their affairs would be left undone and not carried out.
Therefore the wisdom of the Lord created the poor,
so that the rich might have relief in their affairs,
so that their need might bend them toward the rich,
to be subject to them and serve their affairs.
So the poor man is bound to be subject,
and the rich man is bound all the more to show mercy.
And for the poor man it is right to be patient
and to bear sickness and poverty without murmuring.
But for the rich man, mercy is what befits him
toward the poor man, and that he supply all his needs.
Let him not be puffed up, not be arrogant, not be haughty;
let him not think that the poor man is not of his kind.
Let him not be proud, nor exalt himself over the poor,
but let him know they are of one kind, and equal.

Like the right hand and the left they are set in the body
by him who fashioned the body and the world as pleased him.
Look at the body: there is a member set apart for shame,
yet of all the members it is honoured more than its fellows.
O rich man, behold, the poor man is your member,
and the Lord has made caring for him your honour.
He is of your town, of your clay, a son of your race,
of your own body; do not look on him as a stranger.
Who sees his own member naked and does not clothe it,
or exposed, and does not care for it and cover it?
The poor man is weak and stands like the left hand in the body;
O rich man, draw near like the right hand and support him.
Do not suppose that he loved you and gave you much,
and hated that one and so created him poor.
He gave you riches; he did not add a member to your body,
and whatever lies outside you is not yours.
The Creator is upright, and his creation exalted above reproach,
and partiality is far from him in all matters.
He made men equal in members and in forms,
and the whole body of rich and poor is alike.
He made them equal in the womb and in the grave,
in birth and in death, and one is not told apart from the other.

The nature of the rich man and the poor man is one,
and like a skilful painter he painted their images.
The things they need he gave to men equally,
and the things they do not need he gave more to this one and less to that.
He gave light and life equally to the whole body,
and when he gave to the rich man he gave him no advantage.
He gave equally, too, the food that keeps men alive,
and the food of rich and poor is one and the same.
On that same food the king is fed [?] and lives by it,
and on it the beggar is fed too, without difference.
The light of the sun that dawns in the court of kings
dawns, unchanged, in the house of the poor.
Wind and breeze and rain and dew and all the air,
they are the same for the rich and for the poor.
See the distribution of the just Distributor, and fear,
lest you find fault with him who is high and lifted above reproach.
Nature was equal before him, and he made his creation equal when he created it,
and equally he gave it all it needs to live by.
Life and light and food and speech and pleasantness,
the shape of the body and the build of the frame, without difference.
O you who murmur over distributions that are not fair,

learn from them and in them, and see how fair they are.
Look at the painter: when he draws the forms of a man,
he shows no partiality, but distributes them rightly.
And when he was painting the poor man and the rich,
he coloured them with one pigment and one likeness.
Over riches, which are nothing, behold, you murmur,
but at the body, which is something and is equal, you do not look.
At that lofty bed of the rich man
the fool is envious, as though the One who distributes were not upright.
He does not see that he distributed sleep rightly,
and that the bed is nothing to the one who acquires it.
It is not the bed that refreshes the body, but sleep,
and this he gave both to the rich and to the poor.
He even went further and gave more of it to the poor man,
so that he might rest on a bed that is not costly.
Sleep belongs to the body, but the bed does not come from the body,
and in what belongs to the body he did not let one of its kind win out over another [?].
The rich man is worn down by care for gold and possessions,
and his sleep flees, and wakefulness even (wastes?) his body.
And instead of sleep, that bed does not satisfy him,
and behold, nothing is gained from it, costly though it is.

Had he made one man to sleep and another not to sleep,
that one would have prevailed and this one lost out in the distribution.
But since sleep, which refreshes the body, is equal,
in a lofty bed there is neither gain nor loss.
What gain is there in the vessels stored up in the house of the rich,
since nature cannot carry them as it would wish?
And if a man adds another garment to his body, it will not take it,
for it weighs on him, and he throws it off and does not carry it.
And of myriads of garments, if he has them, he needs one;
the body, when it was laid bare, made do with fig leaves.
However many there may be beyond one, they are superfluous,
for the body asks of you no more than one garment.
And because the body cannot carry any more,
behold, greed wraps them up and stores them and hides them in chests.
Behold, the poor are naked in the markets like beasts,
while the moth gets into the chests in the house of the rich.
But God did not create the rich like this,
to be greedy and stingy and neglectful of good works,
but to be compassionate and merciful,
and to supply all the wants of the poor,

and to give clothing to the naked, to whoever is stripped,
and covering from their chests to those who are bare.
Let the rich man who has gold know
that he was made a steward to provide for those of his own nature.
And let him fear, for he too must give an account
of all he acquired, and how he provided for his fellows.
If he does not show mercy, mercy will not meet him there;
the words spoken by Abraham bear witness.
If he alone received his good things,
he will come to need a drop of water, and they will not give it to him.
And therefore blessed are the merciful:
it is written in the Gospel that mercy shall be upon them.
Nature makes a man a debtor to show mercy to his own flesh,
and if he does not show mercy, he is liable to be swallowed up by justice.
'Do not hide yourself from your own flesh,' says the Lord,
reminding you of how you were fashioned, lest you forget that he is your kinsman.
Your body, he says, is not of gold while his is of clay,
but you are both moulded clay, you and he alike.
That poor man, cast out and stripped, is your kinsman;
come, show mercy to your own flesh, and so go on your way [?].
Adam, the father of us all, begot you too,

and you are brothers, O rich man: spare your brother.
See how God gave him a body like yours;
his forms and his members are like yours.
Behold, he resembles you, and it is plain that he is your brother,
and 'Do not hide from your own flesh' is said to you.
He is no stranger, that you should hide from him; he is your neighbour,
and of your neighbour it is written that you should love him as yourself.
And if you feel no pity for your own kind when it is brought low,
honour the image of your Lord, as a discerning man.
And if you have no wish to show mercy to the poor man,
he is the image of God: honour the image of that Majesty.
And if you have forgotten the scripture of Moses, who will teach you?
See that you do not forget the new mother, baptism.
Behold, the poor man has put on Christ, just as you have put him on,
and from within the waters you are brothers of the Only-begotten.
Either because 'Do not hide from your own flesh,' as it is written,
or because he is the image of the Great One, show him honour;
or because he has put on baptism and is your brother,
care for him, so that you are not condemned by justice.
In the body of the world, behold, you are arranged like members,
both rich and poor, and it is one frame.

By Mar Jacob: Homily 28,
on repentance. The face of the world is full of stumbling blocks for whoever looks upon it:

Upon you, my Lord, I will gaze, for you are full of beauties to the one who looks on you.
The world is dark, and its way is tangled with stumbling-blocks:
by your light, our Lord, I will walk with you to the place of your Father.
The world is a dream, and whoever strays in it finds regret:
waken us, my Lord, for you are the morning that wakes all natures.
The way of the world is full throughout of pits and snares:
be a way for us, O shining Son, and we shall walk in you.
At the crossings of the world are falsehood and favoritism;
sin is its wage, and its trade is nothing but losses.
Its rulers take bribes, and its judges steal:

iniquity fills its markets, and favoritism its assemblies.
Its peace deceives, its love strangles, its beauty leads astray;
it is all bitter and full of woes for the one who loves it.
At its watch-posts stand the demons, children of darkness;
they set snares and hide nets for whoever travels in it.
The way of truth the demons have covered over with their traps,
so that no one may see the snare and turn aside so as not to fall into it.
Freedom has grown idle and fallen asleep to good deeds,
while iniquity is awake, and all creation is choked by it.
Each one stretches out his foot into the snare into which he will fall,
for the snare does not run to hunt down the one who falls into it.
The Evil One entices and confuses,
for he cannot overcome freedom by force.
He covers his snares, and whoever wishes to see them
turns aside and passes by and mocks the hidden snare.
For not everyone takes care to look and see the snare;
yet if he wished, he would pass it by and it would not harm him.
Great error the demons spread over the roads,
and that it is error, everyone knows, if he so wishes.
Who does not know that at the end of life is death,
and that the day of the end hangs like a [?] above his head?
Who does not know that the world is a dream, and a shadow too,

that it changes and does not stay with those who love it?
Who does not know that the way of the world is set toward the grave:
a little later, a little sooner, there he is.
Who does not know that if he gains myriads of talents,
they will not let him take anything with him into the grave?
Who does not know that even if he grows as rich as the day is broad,
his wealth stays behind here at the time of his death?
Who does not know that if he gave all his gold,
at the time of his end no bribe would be accepted from him?
Who does not know that a virgin is better than a harlot,
and holiness better than the enticements of adultery?
Who does not hate the drunkard whenever he sees him,
and flee far from talking with him when he babbles at him?
Who loves one who quarrels at random and is unruly,
who scorns the elders and is not ashamed before the honorable?
Who does not hate falsehood and theft,
which are not fair, nor anything at all to those who practice them?
So then, the snares of the Slanderer are plain to see,
and while a man looks on, he stretches out his foot to fall into them.
Gold is loved, though he knows that it does not last;
possessions too, though he sees that they change.
Adultery he hates, yet he does not let it go,

and he craves wine, while he rebukes the one who is drunk.
Nature is upright, and creation very beautiful,
and beautiful things are pleasing to it, that it should do them.
Nature hates evil things when they are done,
yet while hating them, it serves them lovingly.
Who would not weep over freedom, how it has sinned,
loving good and doing every evil every day?
God desires the good and gives a reward for it,
and nature too helps the one who is pure in it;
the good is beautiful and praised by those who see it,
yet no one is willing to do good, though he loves it.
Everyone hates evil and rejects it,
and God too hates it and takes no pleasure in it;
nature also hates it, for it was not created within it,
and though this is so, evil is diligently practiced.
When God created nature, it was beautiful,
and whatever is hateful in it now is not from him.
When he made it, God saw it, and behold, it was very good;
these blemishes the serpent brought in upon freedom.
Since the Creator did not place sin in nature,
it is contemptible and regretted whenever nature sins each day.
Hateful desire came in from outside upon the beautiful,

(troubling it, so that it would lose) its first beauty.
Therefore, when the soul sins and corrupts itself,
it suffers and is ashamed, and the sin it sinned does not please it.
Since the soul is not compelled to sin,
how its own will reproaches it for its evils!
Since it would not sin if it did not wish to, it is bitter to it,
and whom should it blame but itself in all its corruption?
The tyrant Pharaoh took Sarah from Abraham:
a proud king took her from the exile who wandered in the land.
The king's table was not sweet to that free-born woman
as that little bread she had left behind in Abraham's house.
In the king's lofty bed she lay grieving,
and sleep was not sweet to her there because of her husband.
To that exile she had bound her love, and she did not forget him,
though the king's dishes were arrayed on her table.
Pharaoh's wealth was despised in her eyes and grieved her,
and she was distressed that she had been taken from Abraham's side.
Woe to you, O soul, whom the Evil One has led away from God!
Let not his bread be sweet to you, for he is a murderer.
Return to God as Sarah returned to Abram;
he is your portion: do not trust in the deceiver.

Against her will Sarah went to the house of that Pharaoh;
great is your shame, for you of your own will have been enslaved.
Remember, O soul, his great image painted upon you,
and that redemption which he wrought for you through his Only-begotten.
He mingled you with himself (and wrote you in his name), and behold, you are his:
who is this, then, who sat at your ear and carried you off from him?
The world with its enticements has confused you and led you to its desires,
and behold, with its pleasures as with harsh fetters it has bound you.
Like the table of the king of Egypt, arrayed and full,
is the evil world, with the goods of time that do not last.
To Sarah the free woman that table was not sweet;
look at her, O soul, and let not the evil world be sweet to you.
Remember God as Sarah remembered Abram,
and return to him as she returned to her partner.
Behold, the Egyptians guard the doors so that they need not release you
(lest you return to the Righteous One who watches) and waits for you.
The demons are distressed if you return to God:
distress them by your repentance, which is full of beauties.
It is better for you, O soul, to live with God,
and not with the world, which is full of death for whoever looks into it.

The Evil One, Pharaoh, has taken you, wanting you away from God;
see that you do not ruin your partnership, which is full of beauties.
O daughter of Sarah, return like Sarah to the righteous one;
do not be corrupted with the wicked one who seeks your soul.
On the day you come out of Pharaoh's house, the Watchers rejoice,
but the Egyptians sit in mourning over your deliverance.
They led you to the house of Ham and wickedly gave you to the Egyptians,
and you were brought low in the dwelling of slaves, who enticed you and led you away.
Flee from the world, O soul that loves beautiful things;
flee from Pharaoh, free woman whom they led away from her partner.
Do not trust in the Egyptian, who confuses you
with proud garments and choice foods.
Let not the world, which seethes like a flame, lead you astray:
its beauty is a dream; look to God, who does not change.
Cut off your converse with the Egyptians, for they are deceivers;
let not the filthy demons lead you astray with desires.
How sweet to you is Pharaoh's bread, that you eat of it?
Remember God, and come like Sarah to Abraham.
Free soul, full of beauties and without blemish,
bride of the King and great image of the Godhead,
creature higher than creatures in the beauty that is upon it,
daughter of the luminaries, whom the Great One chose and in whom he painted his image:

beloved form of the Great One, higher than all forms,
who has corrupted these beauties that are pure in you?
"Sin struck me and entangled me; it bit me and tore away my features,
and filled me with blemishes, and my lovely beauties have faded.
Pharaoh led me away from God whom I love;
he seduced me and imprisoned me in his tyranny, and behold, he mocks me.
Sin has blown like a blight on the radiance of my face,
and behold, I am hateful and dark, for I have done wickedness.
Satan has hated me, the free-born, as the Egyptian did,
and he separated me and led me away from God to mock me.
And behold, the demons, children of darkness, guard the gates against me,
like the Egyptians, so that I may no longer return to God.
The world has bound me, and imprisoned me with deeds of iniquity:
who will bring me out of the darkness in which I dwell?
I sinned and was broken; I did wickedness, and I stand ashamed:
who will bind me up, and who will tell me that I shall be healed?
The beauty of my creation has been ruined by the iniquity of my hands,
and if I return, hateful as I am, who will open to me?
They will not let me enter the place from which I came out,
and see the Bridegroom who dearly loves beautiful things."
Come, O soul, who served iniquity in the evil world,

return to God, and he will restore to you the wealth you lost.
Abraham too received Sarah when she was defiled,
and she was sanctified by him, and in purity he united her with himself.
Pharaoh sent her away with defilement upon her limbs,
and the moment she came to Abraham's side, he made her pure.
He did not reproach that free-born woman, nor blame her,
but rejoiced in her, and she was with him in a pure union.
The Lord too rejoices in you, for he wants you to return to him,
and he receives you, sanctifies you and purifies you.
Come, then, come out of the defilement into which you were cast down,
for the Holy One does not shrink from purifying you through himself.
As Sarah was sanctified, who had passed through defilement,
so the Lord of Abram sanctifies you through his union.
O penitent soul, come, enter in to God
by repentance, which opens the door and loosens the knots.
Come, then, come out of the palace of that wicked one,
and at once the Lord your Lord opens the door to receive you.
He spreads out his arms, receives you and embraces you,
and rejoices over you as though you had done no wickedness at all.
He does not reproach you for having sinned, nor accuse you,
but rejoices because you have returned, and he loves you.
It is you who hold yourself back from coming out; he does not hold back from receiving,

for he stands ready to come out to meet you when you return.
(Nor, then, does anything hold you back from turning to repentance,
for you may be confident that the door of the One who receives is open.)
Nor has Pharaoh the power to keep you by him,
for as soon as you wish to leave him, he does not hold you.
Why do you think lightly of it, that though you are not held, you stay with him?
If you wish to depart, he does not resist you.
Behold, the Sanctifier of the defiled stands and waits for you,
and carries a hyssop that sprinkles his blood, to purify you with it.
If you return, he brings you back to himself and mingles you with himself,
and once he has mingled you with himself, because of him you are holy in him.
For the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the one who believes;
how much more by the Lord of holiness, if you cleave to him!
By repentance the soul enters in to God,
and cleaves to him, and becomes one with him in one spirit.
And as Sarah was received when she came from Pharaoh's house,
so the soul is received by God, the Lord of Abram.
Only come, for the One who receives is standing there,
full of grace, and his door is open to whoever comes.
Woe to you, O soul, whom the world has taken captive with its desires!
Flee from the world, the house of Pharaoh, full of iniquity.

Let not the talk of the Egyptian women be sweet to you;
let go of those foreign desires.
Let not Pharaoh's house, full of good things, lead you astray—
the world in which are evil pleasures that are not true.
Better to be with God, even if fire and sword strike you,
than to have delights and choice dainties with Satan.
The sick soul says in its pains: "But who will give me
these beauties that I wore before I sinned?
If God, who is merciful, receives me,
who can restore to me my beauties that are lost?
My beautiful nature, which was lovely as the day,
which has darkened and faded—who will make it shine, that it may be beautiful?
If by grace I am pardoned my debts,
who will raise me to that rank from which I fell?
Forgiveness alone, if he forgives me all that I have sinned,
is very great; why then should I hope for more?
But that beauty which my creation had before I sinned,
where shall I see it henceforth, since I have lost it?"
Come, O soul, image of the King, who lost your beauty:
behold, your beauty is in the hands of your Lord, and is kept for you.
As soon as you come, he gives it to you just as you left it;
he has taken care of it, and it is kept for you, to be restored to you.

Not as a physician does the Lord your Lord bind up a wound,
for a physician leaves a scar on the body when he heals it.
Though with bandages, roots and mixtures
he washes the body so that no scar at all may remain in it,
a scar remains, whether small or great,
for the physician cannot make the body as it was before.
Sick soul, if you show your wound to God,
when he binds it up he leaves no scar on your body.
Not like a physician does he cut flesh from the limbs,
so that a scar is left in the place from which the flesh is taken.
He lays his own body upon the wounds,
and makes the wound level with the body when he heals it.
When the wound is deep, so that it has become hollow,
he anointed it with his body; it was restored, and the body stood splendid.
Not roots, nor hot nor cold remedies,
does he mix as medicine for the wounds to bind them up.
He tears his body in his love and lays it on the blows—
a new deed, which no one has done but (he alone).
Where have you seen a physician who lays his own body on wounds,
except our Lord, who cares for and binds up the stricken?

All physicians draw blood from the body,
but this Physician pours his own blood into the wounds.
What physician has his blood ready to be poured out on wounds,
except Christ, whose side was pierced, and who bound us up with his blood?
Others take, but he gives what he had ready,
that he might give his blood, so that all creation might be healed by it.
His body he lays on the wounds, and his blood he pours into the wounds,
and the scar of iniquity is not seen in the soul at all.
He establishes a new creation: the forgiveness that comes from God,
and the soul, pure in its beauties, sees his face.
In the wound he binds up he leaves no scar at all,
so that the place of the wound cannot be seen when he heals it.
All the beauty that nature had is restored to it,
so that the Lord may say, "Behold, it is very good," as he had said.
By repentance he renews his creation through forgiveness,
and leaves in it no scar of iniquity to make it hateful.
As God, not as a physician, he binds up a wound,
for God creates, and it is ready to his hand.
He who gave beauty to nature when he created it,
he acquires it for it again by repentance when he forgives it.
If he left a scar, it would be a reproach to the One who acquires it.

If he left a scar in the soul when he binds it up,
he would be reproached for having healed the wound while its blemish remained,
and it would be said that either he was not able,
or it was malice that he healed the wound and left the blemish.
He is worthy of praise, and stumbling-blocks and murmurings are far removed
from his knowledge, full of mercies, which cannot be blamed.
There was a wound in the soul of Simon, head of the disciples,
for iniquity lay in ambush for him and threw down his tower through denial.
But when he took refuge in repentance and shed tears,
Christ bound him up and gave him back his former beauty.
Before he sinned he had been made head of the discipleship,
and after he denied, through repentance he gave him back his place.
He did not lower him to be fifth or third,
but raised him up and established him in his former rank.
Before he denied he was steward of the house; he denied and went out,
and when he returned, he brought him in and gave him besides his sheep to shepherd.
He gave him his keys, which he had lost when he denied,
and added to him besides the lambs and sheep and ewes,
so that, as beauty was added to him through repentance,
he added to him also authority over the flock he had found.

The Son of God loved his flock and died for it,
and he gave it to Simon, for he trusted him to keep it.
This man is a disciple of repentance,
and it was she who brought him in; he would have gone out, had it not been for her.
He denied his Lord, and swore and cursed that he did not know him,
and trembled and went out of that house, and behold, he was gone.
But repentance ran after him as he fled,
and turned him back to kneel at his Lord's threshold.
She taught him to bring tears instead of offerings,
and he took them and brought them, as repentance had made him wise.
As soon as he came, Christ looked on him and he became beautiful,
and as though he had never denied him, he united him with himself.
And after this, the whole flock for which he died
he gave to him, as to one who loved him and had never sinned at all.
And he made him a pattern and a mirror for penitents,
so that they might know what the power of repentance is.
With that beauty which nature had before it sinned,
as soon as it repents it enters and stands in the house of God.
Over the sinner who repents even the angels rejoice,

because the image of the King, which was lost, has been found.
Henceforth, O soul, you may be confident, and it is certain for you
that your beauty will be restored to you: come to God.
As it was restored to Simon, head of the apostleship,
so all that beauty of your nature will be restored to you.
And as Sarah was sanctified from defilement by her husband,
so the Lord of Abram will also sanctify you from your evils.
Pharaoh had torn apart the partnership of Abraham's house,
and in his tyranny wrenched a limb from the chaste body.
You too the Evil One has taken and torn away from God,
and estranged and separated you from union with that Majesty.
But Sarah returned, and the limb came back to its place,
and the body that the Egyptian had disturbed was made whole.
So you too, if you return to God,
he will make you whole in himself and unite you with his Majesty,
and the rift that the Evil One made between you and God
will be as though it had never been, nor ever will be.
Sarah was not reckoned an adulteress in Abraham's house
because she went and came; she was free, as though she had not gone.
As soon as she came, it was not even reckoned that she had gone,
662
for partnership with the righteous man made her pure.
Simon too, who had denied, as soon as he came
and shed tears, was received as though he had not denied.
You too, O soul, if you return to God,
it will be with you altogether as though you had not sinned.
After Sarah, though pure, had been in the house of the wicked one,
and had been with him in a union far from God,
and had been settled in his name upon defilement, in great disgrace,
and had been separated from Abraham the righteous man,
and Pharaoh's servants had required of her the customs of Egyptian women,
and that Egyptian had directed her as he pleased,
and, as it seemed, she had gone up with him to his bed like an Egyptian woman,
and behold, she was lost to God and to Abraham—
she returned to Abraham, and what had been ruined was restored,
as though those things that happened in the house of the Egyptians had never been.
The righteous man received his wife without murmuring,
and rejoiced that she had come, and the things that had been heard were done away.
God too, after she returned from Pharaoh's house,
gave her Isaac by Abraham the righteous man.
The Lord showed that Sarah was clean of defilement
by the son he gave her, who is an heir and a son of the promise.
I think that Sarah is a type and an image of the soul,

and for this reason she went, and for this reason she came back to Abraham:
to be a parable for the soul that turns back from evils,
that as soon as it returns to God, he receives it,
and pardons it, purifies it and sanctifies it,
and it puts on and stands in all the beauties that are pure in it.
Both the promises and the pledges of God
he has given in their fullness to repentance.
Nor does anything withhold any of the pledges from it,
just as they were not withheld from Sarah because she came out of defilement.
Take heart, O soul, who have fallen away from God,
and rise, come to him who is crucified and stands waiting for you.
All day long his hands are stretched out on the cross,
and behold, he looks for you, that you may go with him to his Father's place.
From the house of sufferings he has cried out from the cross with a loud voice
that you should come out of the house of the unclean Pharaoh who took you captive.
Answer him, O soul—for behold, he bears the burden for your sake—
and say: "Yes, my Lord, with you I will go wherever you go.
I renounce Pharaoh, his dishes and his table,
and his choice foods, which are full of death.

By that mercy with which you called me from the beginning,
by that same mercy forgive my sins and have pity on me.
(Here ends the homily on repentance:

which was composed by the blessed Mar Jacob the teacher.
By the holy Mar Jacob
Homily 29
On repentance and exhortation.

Very easy is the great road of repentance,
and steps of peace are laid along it for those who travel it.
Who would not need to walk it, like the harlot,
who ran and came in to the Forgiver and was not held back?
Who seized, did wrong and robbed like the bandit,
and yet, when he set his face to run, took hold of it skilfully?
Bound on the cross, he set out on his way to the kingdom,
for to repentance all hardships are easy.
He was fastened with nails, yet the road he had taken did not come to a halt,

for repentance is not lamed, not even by fetters.
These are set like a mirror for whoever falls,
so that, seeing them, he may be roused to rise from his fall.
Let him take heart, for if his soul lives in Christ,
(why should the door not open to the sinner if he pleads?
The tax collector drew near. Who is far from God,
except one who in despair has abandoned his way?
The law trod out a road for the just, and a very hard one,
so that they walk on it and are not justified by the law.
But our Lord became a road for the world out of goodness,
so that even sinners are justified in him without the law.
He stretched himself out so that tax collectors might come to repentance,
and harlots might draw near to him and not be held back.
Our gracious Lord clung to those who had become utterly wicked,
for they needed a physician, since they were sick.
Iniquity had gone out like a disease through the whole world,
and our Lord came down like a visiting doctor to heal them.
Since the world could not come to God,
the Son of God carried it so that it might draw near to his Begetter.
He became a road for those who were weary, and he carried them,
and by him those came who were too weak to walk.

This is the road that walks by itself,
and carries the dead to bring them across to the land of life.
It lifted up those without feet to make them run,
who would not have travelled had it not brought them near.
For had he not become a road full of wonder,
would harlots have run along it to the Holy One?
Had our Lord not walked so that the tax collector might come,
he would have been lamed by iniquity and would not have drawn near to righteousness.
Who, then, is not persuaded to travel the road of repentance,
since our Lord himself carries whoever comes to him?
Who will not come to this path full of good things,
which brings you near to complete your journey without tiring?
The world's road had ceased from travel,
and the just could scarcely travel it to God.
Sinners, for their part, did not come by it at all,
for by the law even the righteous one scarcely lives.
But our Lord came and stretched himself out before sinners,
and became a road for them to walk without the law.
And from then on this road is never blocked,
for who can cut off a road that travels along with those who walk it?
Come, then, sinners, walk on this road,

for it was not Moses who trod it, but the Son of God.
If you are in sins, travel with the tax collector who walks it.
Are you crushed by iniquity? Here is the harlot: cling to her.
Does wickedness bind you? Set out on the road with the bandit.
The excuse is taken away: do not stray from the journey.
It is not in company with the good that I urge you to take up the race:
it is the wicked, sir, who walk this road and are not put to shame.
Do not be wholly idle when it comes to good works,
lest you be worse even than the wicked who did them.
Look at the harlot, and weep with her over your faults;
but if you trample on something [?], I do not know how to portray you.
Ask for the kingdom like the bandit, and it will be given you;
and if you hesitate, you are no bandit but a wolf.
Look at the tax collector, and give back a little of your possessions;
and if you do not repent with these, whom do you resemble, in my eyes?
Then you are more foul than the harlot who repented,
or a worse robber than the tax collector who was justified.
You are worse than the bandit in the deeds of your hands;
how far, then, does your measure reach, if you are like this?
If you are worse than the tax collector, the harlot and the bandit,
O man, is there anything to keep denial from serving you [?]

High above you is that measure, if you are a denier:
then you are like Simon, his equal, and you are received.
Simon's denial is a mirror for you, if you wish,
to build yourself on that Rock through repentance.
Lay your building on a foundation, if you are discerning,
for who bears the weight of the house but Simon?
Unless you lay the courses of your roof on that Rock,
you are outside the house, and how will the master of the house seek you?
Simon wept bitterly for this reason too:
that whoever sins might become like him in repentance.
For without repentance the Church does not exist before God;
it is built upon it, and by it it stood from the beginning.
The Church glories in repentance, for it is her hope;
by it she catches people for God.
The Son of God cast a great net into the world,
which gathers the dead in plain sight, and they become alive.
See this wonder in the gospel, through repentance:
that even the harlot fills the place of virgins.
Simon, who was set in it as the foundation, had been a denier,
so that whoever wishes to build himself on him need not fear.
Now you know what the Son of God did:

he first set the denier as mediator between himself and the Church.
He who stooped to denial among sinners
stood as their companion to lead them to the truth.
He went down into denial and stood at the side of those on the left,
and drew everyone to come and cross over to the right.
In denying along with sinners he was mingled in their number,
to show them how one returns to God.
And when the denial was confirmed and he was about to perish,
the wise one wept and confronted the ranks of the left.
He denied, and confirmed that he was on their side;
and as they were leading him, he turned his hand about and led them.
He became the companion of the wicked by denying, and he taught them
that they can become good through repentance.
He dug a baptismal font there among the wicked,
and filled it with tears, so that they might see in it how one is cleansed.
He himself, in his own person, showed the work of repentance:
that whoever sins should be like him in every way.
He wept bitterly over his fault,
and his weeping was enough to establish him in the rank of apostleship.
The fault leapt on him like a lion and was biting him,
but he threw drops of tears on it and drove it off so that it would not maul him.

Sin kindled a flame and set it blazing in him,
but he poured water on the coal, trampled it, and passed on.
An ulcer came upon him, and he bound up his wound before sinners,
so that they would look at him and bind up their own faults.
His heart had swallowed the arrow of wickedness and grew faint with pain,
and while he wailed he drew the barb [?] out of its veins.
He was a warrior who became a model for the wounded,
of what one who is struck amid the battle lines should do.
With weeping he pulled out the arrow of those who struck him as he fought,
and bound up the wound itself with tears, and changed its pain.
He became a mirror in which all sinners might look
and adorn themselves beautifully.
See, build on this wisely,
so that through repentance you may always be fair, if you pray.
God set steps of love one upon another,
so that by them the world might climb up to him and reach him.
He was on high, and our dust lay where it was trampled [?];
and by the means he put together he raised us up to be with him.
By the birth of the Son he trod down the earth as he descended,
so that it would be easy for those who climb by it to the one who sent him.
Between the world and the Father the Son stood as mediator,

and he in turn set Simon as mediator between himself and the Church.
He trod out the ascent so that no one who travels it would stumble,
by the steps he laid down when he descended to humanity.
At the head of the road stands the denier, and see, he calls to you:
"Come, let us travel by repentance to God."
And when you follow him, you find him weeping [?],
and as you draw near you find him a great apostle.
On that same journey he brings you near to see the Son,
who appears to you as a man full of sufferings.
And when you follow him like a companion, to travel with him,
you find that he is also God, like his Begetter.
Little by little you have climbed, O sinner,
from the depths, to be on high with God.
Because Simon denied, he has boldness before sinners
to encourage them about the forgiveness that comes from God.
Of our Lord too it is written that, because he was tempted, he helps
those who are tempted, when they call on him in their afflictions.
The sinner's heart, when it walks with the denier
and learns from him the practice of repentance,
is strengthened further when it sees Christ crucified,
bearing iniquity and enduring sufferings for the wicked.

For weak people the Merciful One laid out easy steps,
so that they would not stumble as they go up to repentance.
He made a persecutor an apostle among sinners,
so that he himself, in his own person, might show the work of repentance.
And the one who denied he set as the foundation of the house,
so that all penitents might build their buildings on him.
Simon denied, Saul persecuted, our Lord was crucified—
(all these so that the wicked might come to repentance.
See the encouragers: one a denier and one a persecutor;
who, with these, is afraid to travel to God?
The Son, the mediator, also bore sufferings for your sake,
and took your great iniquity upon himself so that you might be pardoned.
Wisely he teaches the world the way of life,
and he set in the gospel the ways that suit repentance.
He mingled the denier in the band of the wicked to lead them,
as one of their companions, and then to come and weep before the Majesty.
Simon's weeping is the great chief mourner of the house of penitents,
whose voice of lament roused them to repentance.
And it is as if Simon said these things to sinners,
that there is hope for the wicked man who turns from his hateful deeds:

"Iniquity once bit me too, threw me down and broke me,
and I gave tears as a fee to the Physician (and he came and bound me up.
I became a denier and despised the Son before his crucifiers;
and what fault in the whole world is greater than this?
All of you who are sinners, come, plead for forgiveness;
be like me, for mercy pitied me in my own pain.
Weep as I wept, and you will be pardoned as I was pardoned;
cry out with lament, and quickly mend your faults.
The snare of wickedness caught me too at one time,
and through repentance Grace broke it, and I escaped.
The fault struck me and tore me up from my foundations,
and I shed tears and wept for myself, who had been overthrown.
I too had this same pain that pains you,
and as soon as I wept I found relief from my distress.
I too fell into this sickness of evil sufferings,
and had weeping not tended me, I would not be standing.
Listen to me, my companions, and I will show you what I did:
I wept bitterly, and I was healed little by little.
With weeping the fault that was killing me fled;
I gave tears and received mercy from the Merciful One.

Do the same, and you will be healed as I was healed;
I have tested it in my own person—do not doubt that there is pardon."
This is what Simon's weeping said to sinners,
to stir them up with a challenge to shed tears.
For while the wicked were dazed and taken up with their faults,
Cephas wailed and urged them on to repentance.
In despair they were sunk as if in sleep,
and the voice of weeping fell upon them to wake them.
He raised the lament so that all sinners would answer after him,
for at the end there is a great hope to sing of.
The chief of the disciples wrote a new book with his tears,
and gave it in love to sinners to meditate on.
Read here, then, until you learn righteousness;
evening and morning, with tears, practise repentance.
When sin presses on the soul, draw it out with weeping,
for it does not come out except with bitter tears.
See, the Lord laid a foundation for penitents,
and taught them how to build themselves up.
Simon's weeping did a great work in the Church,
for never from of old has there been another as great.

With these tears that Cephas shed in his repentance
he left the Church a great example to follow.
Who would have known what to do when he sins,
and who would have believed that weeping would bring him help?
Who paints the image of a king without likenesses,
or the greatness of the hidden soul without anything to show it?
Sin harms the soul, and who would have known how it is restored,
had Simon not wept and taught how it is restored?
The man is not so obscure that anyone should despise his teaching;
it is by him, and not by another, that he teaches you what to do.
Once the soul has been scoured in the waters of baptism,
there is no other sacrifice to atone for it but tears.
Only once did the Son of God die for sin,
and he will not die again; so if you sin, offer something in sacrifice.
No other sacrifice is given for your redemption;
give something of your own that can atone for your iniquity.
Be a priest for yourself in your heart, like Abraham,
and sacrifice your voice, like his only son, in the house of pardon.
Roll your soul in blood, most excellently,
in tears, which become a sacrifice without blemish.

As for you, take pity on yourself in your pain, and weep for your soul;
do not again summon your Lord to insult and blows.
Today let us weep bitterly over our evils,
now that goodness presses us with its urgings [?].
Today let us love repentance, for it has a reward,
since we have laboured at iniquity, slow in our delaying.
We keep righteousness for tomorrow, which is not near,
and give the whole of today to iniquity to use as it pleases.
Sin is close by, and righteousness outside the door:
"Here I will sin, and there, afterwards, I will be justified."
See how many tomorrows there have been, and we have not kept our promises;
every day we put off repentance, and still it is far away.
Every promise comes easily to us, but only about good things,
while wickedness is practised mightily every day.
Day by day we set ourselves a delay for repentance,
and the tomorrow by which we might profit never comes.
We drive good things away from us along with the days,
so that the whole span of life comes to an end without repentance.
Where today is that promise that was made yesterday:
"Wait until tomorrow, when I will turn from evil"?
Rise to your work, now that our delays have proved false;

rise against sin, and fight with your slayer.
Do not let all your days be handed over to iniquity;
take time for righteousness while you still have power.
We sinned yesterday; let us weep today over our faults,
lest sin take hold [?] and tear us apart.
We have grown old in iniquity; let us become children in repentance,
for whoever is like a child is the one who enters the kingdom.
Our Lord took a child in his arms to show
how beautiful creation is in its proper order, if it is kept.
Look at the apostles, to whom he showed him, saying:
"Become like this one" (for this is the hope of perfection.
"My Lord, how can an old man become a child,
when he has spent the bulk of his days in emptiness?"
Is anything added to his creation when someone sins,
that he should add something of his own to its restoring?
As long as his nature is kept as it was created, he is always a child;
but if he sins, he grows old in iniquity and is corrupted.
These courses that the soul built when it went astray,
let it turn back and tear them down from its fabric through repentance.
"Endure, and take out the excess that has got into you,

and give me back only the fair nature, as I created you.
Do not justify yourself by anything of your own, not even a little;
keep for me a nature without stain, and very beautiful.
But if something extra has come in on top of the fabric,
I have no need of it; let it be thrown out through repentance.
Turn yourself back, then, and become a child as I created you,
so that you may be an heir in the kingdom, as I called you.
Whatever is yours that is in you, search it out and cast it from you,
and leave what is mine unchanged, and you are a child of my kingdom.
Whatever sin has built in your soul, uproot it from there;
my creation is beautiful—do not muddle it with desires."
Therefore turn yourself back and become a child,
for this is the hope of perfection and righteousness.
See what the penitent can do, if he is diligent:
even if he is an old man, he can make himself a child.
Denial got in and made the chief of the disciples old,
and through repentance he turned himself back to become a child.
He saw that sin weighed on him like old age,
and with wailing he shook it off, for it did not please him.
Skilful is the soul, and its understanding rises above creatures,
and it has the power to do whatever work it is inclined to.

And when it turns to building up good things,
it uproots the courses of iniquity to clear them from its dwellings.
It goes into itself as into a great house,
and sees that it is in confusion and full of the stench of desires.
Iniquity lies in it as a great mass that came in from the Evil One,
and other faults are ranged in it like stumbling blocks.
It is full of evils, and its door is shut by hateful deeds,
and there is no place on any side where good can enter.
Through repentance the soul is given light to see these things,
and sets to the labour of carrying [?] all the evils away.
But when it sees that this work is too hard for it,
it calls on mercy to help it in its tasks.
It begins to drag iniquity out of its house,
and hires Grace with tears to work alongside it.
It sets about sweeping away the debts that came in from its youth,
and washes itself carefully with the water of its eyes.
It gathers its faults like thorns from its summer,
and seethes with weeping to burn them fervently.
Wisely it casts upon them a fire made of water,
to set them alight in a burning that gives no smoke.
Simon weeps: who would not wail, if he is a sinner?

The bandit went in: who would not take heart, if he is a penitent?
The bandit too became a child through that confession,
and so attained to be an heir in that kingdom.
With a single word, all the mountains of iniquity he had built
he removed, for his faith was strong.
Mercy helped him to come to this great work,
and if you wish, it will come to help you too.
Only begin, and at once Grace travels with you;
it has stirred up the occasion, and your helper does not delay.
It is you who hold back from knocking at the door of repentance.
Glory to the Mercies, which are so glad to welcome penitents!
Here ends the homily on repentance.
